research.q: Startups using AI to produce FAA PMA, DER repair or STC substantiation packages (compliance reports, test plans, drawings). Find every company 2022-2026, funding, traction.
research.headline: No startup found from 2022 to 2026 that uses AI to produce FAA PMA, DER (8110-3) repair or STC substantiation packages, or that holds such approvals itself. The funded activity is all next to the approval: aerospace certification copilots (Xcert AI, CHF 1.1M), auditor-side AI for testing, inspection and certification bodies (Calibre, $3.3M), production quality paperwork (GroundControl, F4, Rapta), reverse engineering from photos (Novineer), and big hardware test and traceability platforms (Nominal at $1B, Flow at $750M, Sift, Istari). Nobody sits in the reviewer's seat for aftermarket approvals.

findings.finding: Many targeted queries ('AI' with PMA, Parts Manufacturer Approval, DER, Form 8110-3, STC, DLA source approval, reverse engineering) returned no startup with a product, funding round or traction for AI-made PMA, DER or STC packages. Incumbents (HEICO, Wencor, Jet Parts Engineering, Chromalloy, JDA, TxAero, Metrea) have announced no AI-native approval workflow. This is a negative search result, so stealth teams cannot be ruled out.
findings.source: WebSearch x3, Google News RSS, HN Algolia, YC directory (2026-10-20)

findings.finding: Xcert AI (Geneva, founded 2024, 12 staff) offers an 'AI Co-Pilot for Certification': compliance documentation, requirements, test procedures and traceability matrices. Customers or partners include ESA and ZeroAvia. Its site does not mention FAA, DO-178 or PMA.

Calibre (London, ex-Palantir founders) builds AI agents for testing, inspection and certification bodies. They review documents, write audit reports against standards and match requirements to norms; its first product is AuditorOS. It is the only startup found that targets the reviewer side, and it is not aviation-specific.
findings.number: $3.3M pre-seed (May 2026), led by Vicus Ventures and CIV, with Nikesh Arora as an angel

findings.finding: GroundControl (YC Spring 2025) automates AS9102 first-article inspection reports. This is the production paperwork downstream of a PMA, not design approval.
findings.number: >70 facilities, ~1,000 reports/month, team of 8, funding undisclosed

findings.finding: F4 Industries (YC Summer 2025) checks GD&T on drawings and generates tolerance stack-ups and first-article reports. Its analysis is deterministic and uses no AI.
Rapta does camera-based inspection at each build station and keeps a per-unit evidence archive. It claims 5 of the top 10 defense contractors as users.
findings.source: https://www.rapta.ai ; Defense Post / AI Insider Sep 2026

findings.finding: Novineer (founded 2022, Embry-Riddle professor) turns 1-4 smartphone photos into an editable STEP CAD file in about 2 minutes. It works with Stratasys GrabCAD and the US Army. Its founder says the approvals and data-governance processes are the unsolved part. The accuracy is too coarse for flight-critical PMA.
findings.number: 0.72mm average / 2.3mm max error on a 100mm part

findings.finding: Nominal (hardware test and evaluation software) has 4 of the top 5 defense primes as customers. It is the most likely funded company to move up into certification evidence.
Flow Engineering's AI agents link CAD to requirements, simulations and tests for new designs. Customers include Anduril, Joby, Rivian and Stoke. It does no aftermarket approvals.
Sift (telemetry and test data, ex-SpaceX founders).
findings.number: $7.5M seed 2023, $17.5M Series A 2024, $42M Series B Mar 2026

findings.finding: Istari Digital is the only funded company working on certification-by-model with a regulator (USAF airworthiness, X-56A with Lockheed Skunk Works). It targets new military airframes, not PMA or DER work.
findings.source: PR Newswire Sep 2023; Defence Blog Jul 2025; Business Journals Jul 2026

findings.finding: Demand signal: UPS says alternative parts have been 'a big focus for the last year' and it is exploring AI to find them. Some lessors require PMA parts to be removed when a leased aircraft is returned. The MRO market passed $136B in 2025 (+8%), with material inflation 100-200bp above plan.

Other adjacent companies, none producing approvals: Saphira (AI FMEA and requirements for robotics), SysModeler (AI SysML models), SkySelect ($9M, AI parts procurement), Donecle (EUR 10M, drone inspection), Hexagon portable reverse-engineering scanners, PhysicsX (AI simulation unicorn; its $135M round is from memory).
findings.source: saphira.ai; sysmodeler.ai; AviTrader Mar 2026; EU-Startups Apr 2026

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a machine-readable certification basis: TCDS, the amendment level of each CFR section, ADs, SBs and FAA policy for every part number and next-higher assembly. Today a DER rebuilds this by hand for every package.

Build an AI 'shadow DER / ACO pre-review' that checks a PMA, 8110-3 or STC package against FAA Orders 8110.42 and 8110.37, AC 21-43 and the certification basis, and outputs findings in the ACO's own format. Sell it to applicants first, then offer it as a reviewer tool to the FAA and DLA engineering support activities.

Build a regulator-accepted evidence library (material allowables, coupon data, earlier test-by-analysis and similarity precedents) so packages cite evidence that has already been accepted instead of re-running tests. Physical clocks remain only for fatigue, burn and environmental tests.

Win delegated authority: build a track record of non-ODA approvals, then apply for an ODA whose procedures manual allows AI-augmented internal review. That is the legal route that turns AI verification into permission.
Score DLA Source Approval Requests against the engineering support activity checklists to cut review times. This could be sold to DLA itself through SBIR or OTA contracts.

Automate the conformity chain: per-unit inspection evidence tied to the approved design data, so the PMA fabrication inspection system becomes an auditable digital record. This also addresses forged airworthiness paperwork, as in the 2023 AOG Technics case.

Close the precision gap in AI reverse engineering. Photo-based CAD at 0.72mm average error has to be fused with metrology (CT, CMM) and material identification to reach flight-critical tolerances, with uncertainty quantification a reviewer can accept.
ai_plays: An AI pre-reviewer for FAA ACO, DER and DLA reviews: a verification copilot that reports package deficiencies before submission. It would be the first product in the reviewer seat for aftermarket approvals, where Calibre (general testing and certification) and Istari (USAF new airframes) show the pattern but nobody covers PMA, DER or DLA.
A certification-basis knowledge graph sold as a data product to PMA houses, MROs and airlines (UPS-style demand for alternative parts).
An evidence-reuse exchange: pooled, regulator-accepted test and analysis precedents that let packages substitute analysis or similarity for repeat tests.
An AI-augmented ODA: an approval-holding entity whose KPI is reviewer hours per approval. It is the 'Approval Factory' expressed as a verifier rather than as an authoring shop.
A digital conformity and anti-counterfeit record linking each produced part to its approved design data and inspection evidence (building on Rapta and GroundControl-style data capture).
surprises: The best-funded companies (Nominal $1B, Flow $750M) are all on the new-design V&V side; capital has not reached aftermarket approvals at all.
The only startup aiming AI at the reviewer/auditor seat (Calibre) is general testing-and-certification, not aviation, and raised just $3.3M.
Novineer's founder says publicly that the bottleneck is approvals and technical-data governance, not geometry, which supports the prior review's 'permission not knowledge' thesis.
F4 Industries deliberately markets 'no AI' deterministic analysis to hardware engineers, a hint that verification buyers distrust probabilistic output.
UPS calls alternative parts a year-long priority but has disclosed no vendor, which looks like open demand with no AI-native supplier.

research.q: Startups and contractors using AI for DoD reverse engineering, technical data package (TDP) reconstruction and DLA Source Approval Requests. Include SBIR/AFWERX/NavalX/Army awards on reverse engineering and parts obsolescence (search SBIR.gov).
research.headline: On the application side, about 20-30 small, non-AI engineering shops (Parts Life, Mentis, Brighton Cromwell, DeVal, Global Circuit Innovations) build DLA reverse-engineering packages (SARs and TDPs) a few stock numbers at a time, paid for by roughly $100M of DLA SBIR money from 2018 to 2025. Since 2024 a group of tiny AI SBIR awardees (Elevate, Mobilio, Tetrahive, Novineer, Quidient, XO Armor, Physna) has been automating pieces of the package. The verification side, where military-service engineers review each SAR, is almost untouched: the only reviewer-side AI award found is a $110k Phase I to Elevate Systems in 2024, and the other certification-AI work (RedShred, Inoviant, Istari) targets whole-aircraft airworthiness certification, not individual parts. That leaves the position of the engineering authority's machine reviewer, or of a factory whose packages arrive pre-verified in the reviewer's format, open.

findings.finding: I filtered the full SBIR.gov award file (219,649 awards) down to defence awards on reverse engineering, TDPs or source approval for sustainment and obsolescence: 364 awards, $178.2M, 126 of them Phase II. By branch: DLA 232, Air Force 62, Navy 29, Army 19. DLA alone gave about $99.7M from 2018 to 2025, peaking at $33.9M in 2022. Its recurring topics are DLA171-002 (26 awards), DLA192-001 (25) and DLA222-001 (20).

The leading recipients are small reverse-engineering and SAR service shops, not AI or venture-backed companies: Parts Life Inc (24 awards, $11.8M), Mentis Sciences (16, $7.6M), Global Circuit Innovations (16, $7.2M), Mainstream Engineering (16, $4.5M), Brighton Cromwell (13, $7.9M), DeVal Life Cycle Support (12, $4.2M), Engineering & Software System Solutions (11, $9.6M), Cepeda (11, $6.1M). DLA's target items are stock numbers with more than $10K annual demand value and fewer than two manufacturers. Each award covers about 1 to 35 stock numbers.
findings.source: SBIR.gov award data; CB Insights Parts Life profile

findings.finding: Only 16 of the 364 awards mention AI or ML, and all date from 2023 on. They automate the applicant's package: Elevate Systems' OPTIX turns legacy 2D drawings into digital data (about $1.55M from the Air Force, plus landing-gear additive-manufacturing work of $1.25M and $1.16M). Mobilio's Kipo AI checks reverse-engineered avionics circuit-board schematics ($1.40M direct-to-Phase-II, 2025, building a 100,000-schematic training set). Tetrahive/RJ Matthews does CT and ML circuit-board reverse engineering ($0.75M + $0.38M + $1.40M). Cornerstone Research scores TDPs for 3D-printing suitability (Navy, $0.24M + $1.0M). In 2025 the Army topic A244-P057 funded six AI reverse-engineering Phase Is at about $250k each (XO Armor, Elevate, Merge Plot, Mobilio, Deep Analytics, Red Balloon).

The only award aimed at the reviewer side of source approval is Elevate Systems' AFX23E-TPCSO1 Phase I (FA8649-24-P-0130, $109,997, 2024). It proposes AI/ML and computer vision 'to save thousands of unbudgeted hours that the engineers have to spend ... reviewing and approving requests for supportability analysis resulting in source approvals'. The dataset shows no Phase II.

AI for airworthiness certification exists, but at whole-platform level (the military airworthiness handbook MIL-HDBK-516C), not part-level SAR review. RedShred's AIRMATE uses LLMs to turn certification documents into system models ($106k + $1.79M, 2024). Inoviant's 'AI for Airworthiness Certification' won $149k in 2025 and claims 18-month timelines costing DoD over $5B a year (self-reported). Mile Two's Morphy-AI won a $1.2M direct-to-Phase-II. Istari has 10 awards worth $12.8M, including physics-informed surrogate models for aeroelastic airworthiness analysis.

Other verification-side building blocks: Nlign Analytics' $1.76M Air Force 'TDP Modernization for As-Built Data' (direct-to-Phase-II, 2024-03-14) carries as-built nonconformances and repairs in an open dimensional-data standard (QIF). Senvol has ML-based probabilistic qualification for 3D-printed parts (Navy $2.28M 2018, Army $1.2M 2023, NAVSEA $1.97M 2025). Toyon and UDRI built 'AI for the Depot', which ingests depot engineering assistance requests (ETARs), inspection results and airworthiness data ($1.5M, 2022).

How the DLA pathway works: a vendor requests a sample through the parts purchase-or-borrow programme (RPPOB). DLA returns demand history, the sample price and any data it holds. For many items the military service must agree before a vendor submits a Category IV (reverse-engineered) SAR. The vendor reverse engineers at its own cost and writes the SAR to the DLA guide plus service-specific guides (NAVAIR via NAVSUP WSS, Air Force via 429 SCMS/SASPO at Tinker, Army via AvMC SRD). DLA forwards the SAR to the service, which approves. SAR categories run from I to IV. Excluded: items already competitive (AMSC G or T), source-controlled items (AMSC B), specification-controlled items, items with a complete approved TDP, items under $10K annual demand, and foreign firms.

DLA material puts typical full approval at 12 to 18 months. RPPOB needs at least $10K annual buy value, and DLA Aviation's Parts Catalog sets a $40K annual demand minimum. Export-controlled data certification (JCP) may be required. These figures come from search snippets of DLA decks and flyers; the dla.mil pages themselves returned 403.

Speed and cost datapoints from vendors (self-reported): Empirical Systems Aerospace said it could submit a completed SAR about 10 weeks after starting (2022). Dynovas planned to qualify parts through the standard SAR process within a 6-month, $100k Phase I. ORBIS, a DLA SBIR success story, showed 25% savings by having one firm reverse engineer many stock numbers. The Oklahoma City Air Logistics Complex reported a gearbox housing with a 24-month lead time at $80k, plus $100k-750k of tooling cost per casting part number.
findings.source: SBIR.gov abstracts; DLA ORBIS success story (via search)

findings.finding: Venture-backed manufacturers are entering through Air Force (AFWERX) sustainment topics as production capacity, not as approval holders. Divergent and the University of Oklahoma won a $106k + $1.79M STTR in 2025 to reverse engineer and print obsolete aircraft parts with AFLCMC and the Rapid Sustainment Office. Machina Labs has 6 awards worth $5.1M, plus a multi-year AFRL RoboCraftsman contract announced 2025-09-19 (value not disclosed). Rangeview won $1.4M for digital investment casting in 2025.

Novineer (founded 2022, Embry-Riddle spinout) turns 1-4 phone photos into editable CAD in about 2 minutes, with 0.72 mm mean and 2.3 mm maximum deviation on a 100 mm part. It has a 2025 OSD Phase I ($150k), an Army agreement and a Stratasys partnership. That accuracy is far coarser than aerospace drawing tolerances (about 0.13 mm), so the output is useful for triage, not for a SAR. The source is a sponsored article written by the company.

Even government-sponsored reverse-engineering work needs the engineering authority's agreement: the NCMS DMSMS project (expressions of interest due 2024-09-10) requires testing and validation 'in concurrence with the platform's Engineering Source Activity (ESA)'.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Target selection: find stock numbers with fewer than two approved sources and more than $10K (Aviation catalogue: $40K) annual demand, with an acquisition code that allows a SAR
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Vendor, using PUBLOG/FLIS and DLA lists
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No one maps the whole universe of eligible items, ranked by value and similarity; each SBIR topic hands vendors a short list

pathway_steps.step: 2. RPPOB request: buy, borrow or inspect a sample; get demand history and any data; service agreement needed before a Category IV SAR
pathway_steps.who_does_it: DLA Aviation / Land & Maritime; service agreement
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Service agreement is a hidden gate before any reverse engineering starts; no data on how long it takes

pathway_steps.step: 3. Reverse engineering: geometry, material, process, finish, function
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: AI is entering here (photo/scan to CAD, CT circuit-board reverse engineering, drawing extraction) but at accuracy short of SAR grade; this is the crowded step

pathway_steps.step: 4. Writing the SAR/TDP to the DLA guide plus service guides (Category I-IV)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Packages are written in prose, not in a machine-checkable evidence format; Nlign's QIF-based as-built TDP is the closest standard

pathway_steps.step: 5. Service engineering review (the ESA disposition)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Service engineers: AF 429 SCMS/SASPO, NAVSUP WSS/NAVAIR, Army AvMC SRD
pathway_steps.cost: government engineering hours ('thousands of unbudgeted hours')
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Almost no automation; only one $110k Phase I (Elevate). Each stock number reviewed from scratch, with no carry-over from similar approved parts

pathway_steps.step: 6. First-article and qualification testing
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Surrogate models and statistical qualification exist only for 3D-printed parts (Senvol) or for platform-level analysis (Istari); not accepted as a routine substitute for first-article tests

pathway_steps.step: 7. Approved-source listing and competitive buy
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Under the statute the government need not delay buys while a source qualifies, so approval value depends on the timing of the next buy

what_would_need_to_be_done: Turn the DLA SAR Guide, the service-specific guides, the referenced military standards and specifications, and past approvals and rejections into executable review checklists for each engineering authority. The output is a pre-filled disposition for the service engineer, with every claim linked to evidence (RedShred-style LLM extraction, applied to SARs instead of the airworthiness handbook).

Build a precedent and similarity graph across stock numbers (geometric deep learning plus FLIS/PUBLOG plus material and process data), so that one approved SAR supports a fast-track review of similar items. Today each stock number starts from zero.
Define a machine-verifiable evidence standard for SAR packages (QIF/as-built enhanced TDP, CT volumes, material certificates, test data with chain of custody) so that reviewers check data, not prose.

Agree statistical test-by-exception and surrogate-model substitution for parts of first-article and qualification testing with an engineering authority (extending the Senvol and Istari approaches beyond 3D printing and platform-level analysis). The physics clock shrinks, but tests still run.

Submit portfolio SARs covering whole commodity classes or subsystems on one legacy platform (e.g. all seals, bushings or brackets on the KC-135), building on ORBIS's 25% saving from one firm handling many stock numbers.

Get a service engineering office to sponsor a pilot (AFWERX TACFI/STRATFI, or a DLA SBIR topic co-sponsored by 429 SCMS) where the AI pre-review is formally accepted as the first pass, using the 10 USC 3243 'prompt opportunity' requirement and the 2025 advanced-manufacturing streamlining clause.

Build a target universe of every stock number with more than $10K annual demand and fewer than two sources, using PUBLOG acquisition codes, demand data, FOIA of approved-source lists, and the 'millions' of legacy 2D drawings DoD holds. This needs export-control (JCP) certification.
Publish engineering and reviewer hours per approved SAR as the KPI; no one in the SBIR record reports it.
ai_plays: The engineering authority's machine reviewer: sell AI pre-review of SARs and alternate offers to 429 SCMS/SASPO, NAVSUP WSS, AvMC SRD and DLA engineering. Priced per disposition, with reviewer hours per approval as the metric. Only one $110k Phase I exists today.

An approval factory whose packages arrive pre-verified in the reviewer's own checklist and evidence schema, so applicant and reviewer cost fall together; the asset is the portfolio of approved-source positions.
An approval-credit similarity engine: carry approval from approved stock numbers to similar parts (shape, material, function), turning one-off reviews into batch reviews.
Evidence-capture stack (CT/metrology/material certificates in QIF, with provenance) as the data layer both sides use. Partners or acquisition targets include Nlign, Tetrahive, Lumafield-type CT.

Surrogate-model and statistical qualification service to cut first-article and qualification test counts, starting with low-criticality items and electronics (circuit-board design-rule checking, as Mobilio does)

Roll up or partner with existing SBIR SAR shops (Parts Life, Mentis, Brighton Cromwell, DeVal) as the human and quality-system layer; they hold the sample access, past performance and approved-source track record but have no AI or scale.
surprises: DLA SBIR is effectively a government-subsidised SAR factory (about $100M over 2018-2025, 232 awards), yet its leading recipients are 10-50-person engineering shops with no AI and no venture funding.
The only reviewer-side AI award for source approval is a $110k Phase I to a 10-person 8(a) firm (Elevate, 2024), with no Phase II found.
AI certification efforts (RedShred, Inoviant, Istari, Mile Two) all target platform-level airworthiness certification, not part-level SAR review, even though part-level review is far higher volume.
For many items, service agreement is needed before a Category IV reverse-engineered SAR can be submitted at all, an early permission gate that is rarely discussed.
Photo-to-CAD tools claim about 0.7 mm accuracy, more than five times coarser than typical aerospace tolerances; geometry capture is not the bottleneck and is not solved at SAR grade by phone tools.
SBIR awards on this theme are flat (24-45 a year apart from a 2022 spike to 70), so DoD's interest has not grown despite the attention on readiness.

research.q: Scan-to-CAD and AI reverse engineering tools (Backflip AI, Physna/Thangs, Geomagic, Creaform, Hexagon, Revopoint and others): what they do, who buys, how close to a qualified design package.
research.headline: Scan-to-CAD and AI reverse engineering tools now automate nominal geometry, and Backflip AI turns a mesh into a parametric feature tree in minutes for about $20 a month. That covers roughly 5-15% of the hours in a qualified DLA/FAA package (my estimate). Nobody has a product for the other 85-90%: inferring tolerances, identifying materials and processes, substantiation, assembling evidence and reviewer acceptance. That gap, plus tooling on the reviewer's side, is where the verification play sits.

findings.finding: Backflip AI (founded 2022 by the Markforged creators, CEO Greg Mark) made its second-generation mesh-to-CAD foundation model generally available on 4 Aug 2026, as an Autodesk Fusion add-in and a web app. It outputs a parametric feature tree as STEP and offers Fast and Thinking (agentic self-check) modes. It is self-scoped to moderate-complexity 3-axis milled and turned parts.

Backflip's pricing is 4 free reconstructions, then from $20/month. The company claims it cuts digitizing a part from about $1,500 to about $10 in 1-5 minutes; this is unbenchmarked. In an Engineering.com test, all 5 candidates for a simple knob missed some geometry. The CEO says the first model 'wasn't good'. Its only customer is an unnamed automaker. It has no GD&T, tolerance or material inference, and mentions SOC 2 only (no ITAR/CMMC).
Two aggregators report about $30M in Backflip funding, with no round name, date or investors, and list 1-10 employees.

Creaform (AMETEK) has a Scan-to-CAD module that builds parametric solids (extrude/revolve/cut), exports IGES/STEP/DXF and transfers live to SOLIDWORKS, Inventor, Fusion and Solid Edge. It targets legacy components without CAD. The page mentions no GD&T or deviation reporting. Its footer now credits FARO and Creaform, consistent with AMETEK acquiring FARO.

Geomagic Design X is the industry-standard human-driven RE software (auto-surfacing, Accuracy Analyzer deviation maps, parametric transfer), at roughly $10-25k a seat. 3D Systems sold Geomagic to Hexagon (recalled; the Hexagon page returned 403).

Lumafield raised a $75M Series C on 13 Mar 2025 (IVP lead) and a $50M SVB credit line in Nov 2025. 85% of its customers are first-time CT users, and the named sectors are EV, medical, athletic and packaging, not aerospace sustainment. Its Voyager cloud AI analysis does not mention CAD/TDP export.

Physna/Thangs does geometric deep-learning search and part matching. Its $56M financing was led by Tiger Global (2021, recalled). It is useful for finding existing TDPs or form-fit-function substitutes, but it produces no approvals.

USAF 448th SCMW (FA8109) posted a Sources Sought on 12 May 2025 for a multi-award, 8(a) set-aside reverse engineering vehicle for mainly DLA-managed parts. Deliverables are TDPs plus prototypes to MIL-HDBK-115 with QC and configuration management; NRE takes 6-12 months per effort. The notice cites 'high pricing, slow supply responses, and incomplete data packages'.

Amentum PROS VI is a $4.6B single-award IDIQ (Mar 2023, 5+5 years) for FMS parts and repair. Its scope includes reverse engineering, 3D scanning, additive manufacturing and replacing obsolete parts. The money flows through services primes, not software.

2026 reverse engineering solicitations include legacy reentry vehicle components for the AF Nuclear Weapons Center (Aug 2026, due 5 Oct 2026) and AFSC Warner Robins obsolete-parts RE sourcing (Jul 2026). These come from aggregator pages; verify on SAM.gov.

Gap analysis (opinion): a qualified TDP/SAR/PMA package covers nominal geometry, GD&T and datums, material/temper/heat-treat/finish, process specs and critical characteristics, stress/fatigue substantiation, drawings to Y14.100 and MIL-STD-31000 with data-rights markings, then first article and qualification test. Current tools cover only geometry, plus partial CAD output.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Multi-sample statistical tolerance inference: CT and optical scans of N surplus or fielded parts, separating wear from manufacturing variation and using mating parts to infer the datum scheme and the original GD&T, with confidence bounds.

Fuse material and process identification into the model: an automated small-sample lab pipeline (OES/XRF, microhardness, metallography, EBSD, residual stress, coating thickness) whose results become AMS/MIL spec callouts in the TDP automatically.
Infer critical characteristics, special processes and NDT acceptance criteria from part function, failure history (e.g., SDR/GIDEP data) and similar parts.

Generate substantiation automatically: estimate the unknown original loads from geometry and system context, then produce FEA, fatigue and damage-tolerance analysis and a test plan for an FAA 8110.42 test-and-computation or a DLA SAR equivalency argument.
Write drawings and the TDP automatically to ASME Y14.5/Y14.100 and MIL-STD-31000, with configuration management and DFARS data-rights markings.
Build a traceable evidence chain with metrology uncertainty budgets (ISO 17025-style) from raw scan and lab data to each drawing callout.

Build reviewer-side tools for DLA/AFSC engineering support activities, DERs and ACOs: automated completeness and conformance checking of submitted packages, which cuts reviewer hours, the bottleneck nobody sells into.
Publish a public mesh-to-CAD and scan-to-TDP fidelity benchmark on aerospace parts with a metrology lab; whoever defines the benchmark shapes what regulators accept.
Offer ITAR/CUI-compliant (CMMC L2, on-prem/GovCloud) deployment, since current AI RE tools are commercial cloud, SOC 2 only.

Win a precedent pilot in which DLA/AFSC accept an AI-generated TDP with a human engineer's sign-off (modeled on RSO additive-manufacturing qualification pilots), and later FAA policy on computational substantiation. No law blocks this; acceptance depends on precedent.
ai_plays: 'Package compiler': take geometry from Backflip/Geomagic as a commodity and own steps 2-6 (tolerances, materials, processes, substantiation, drawings, evidence). Sell output per approved package, not per seat.

'Reviewer copilot': sell to DLA engineering support activities, AFSC RE cells, DER firms and FAA ACOs to pre-check packages against MIL-STD-31000/8110.42 and scan-vs-drawing conformance, shrinking review queues. This could also give privileged insight into what passes.
'Statistical twin from fleet samples': a CT and scan service run on many surplus parts that sells inferred tolerance and material specs, a data asset no single-part RE shop can produce.
'Verification-grade metrology lab-in-a-box': a scanner plus CT plus lab plus AI tied into one uncertainty-budgeted evidence chain, positioned as the trusted verification layer regulators reference.
'Benchmark owner': publish the aerospace RE fidelity benchmark and certify tools against it, making the company the de facto acceptance standard.
surprises: The leading AI reverse engineering startup, Backflip, is a $20/month designer tool scoped to moderate-complexity 3-axis parts, and its CEO admits the first model 'wasn't good'. It has no aerospace, defense, tolerancing or materials focus.

Lumafield, the best-funded CT player, sells mostly to first-time CT users in EV, medical and consumer goods, not aerospace sustainment, even though CT is the key sensor for reverse engineering castings and internal passages.

The Air Force blames 'incomplete data packages' for readiness problems, accepts 6-12 month NRE per RE effort, and routes the work through 8(a)-only services vehicles. The buying channel is set-aside services, not software.
The software layer is being folded into metrology hardware companies (Hexagon bought Geomagic; AMETEK bought FARO), so no independent company owns the RE-to-approval workflow.
No public accuracy benchmark exists for AI mesh-to-CAD on aerospace parts.

research.q: Additive manufacturing qualification and in-situ process monitoring companies (Senvol ML, Phase3D, Additive Assurance, Sigma Additive, EOS/Amiquam, Divergent, Velo3D, Freeform): what evidence they produce and whether regulators accept it.
research.headline: No regulator (FAA, EASA, NAVSEA, DLA, NASA, NRC) has been found to accept in-situ monitoring data in place of the usual qualification evidence: a frozen process, coupon-based allowables and full-volume CT/NDE. Monitoring is only a supplemental record, the standalone monitoring business is close to worthless (Sigma sold all its quality-assurance IP for $1.6M), and the money has gone to integrated part makers instead. The open verification gap is the protocol that would let monitoring plus machine learning earn regulator credit: probability-of-detection studies, linking monitoring signals to real defects, machine-to-machine equivalence, and fewer coupons. Nobody independent owns that work.

findings.finding: ASTM E3353-22: there are not yet well-established procedures for using AM process monitoring in a qualification or certification framework outside a company's or institution's internal use

NASA-STD-6030 still requires full surface and volume NDE for every part class except negligible-risk. NASA MSFC's proposed route to monitoring credit: link monitoring signals to critical defect sizes, then show 90/95 probability of detection like any NDE method. NASA calls that link the hardest obstacle and says closed-loop/adaptive control would need a new qualified-process approach
NISTIR 8538 (Sep 2024, written for the NRC) lists gaps in knowledge, technology and standards that must close before monitoring/NDE can support qualification of AM nuclear plant parts
Sigma Additive sold its PrintRite3D quality-assurance IP to Divergent for $1.6M (agreement 6 Oct 2023, closed 16 Jan 2024), then reverse-merged into the travel company NextTrip

Senvol: 2018 DLA grant to show in-situ data predicts mechanical performance and to show equivalent parts on two LPBF machines. US Navy project Jul 2025 to Jul 2027 on wire-DED aims to write in-situ monitoring requirements into NAVSEA policy. This is the clearest attempt to turn monitoring into regulator policy. No acceptance has been granted yet

Additive Assurance (AMiRIS, founded 2019): claims 90% detection at 95% confidence for defects down to 82 µm, trained on millions of hours of build data. These are vendor claims stated in regulators' detection-rate language, with no regulator credit

Freeform raised $67M Series B on 19 Feb 2026 (Founders Fund, NVentures, Threshold, Two Sigma Ventures and others; PitchBook valuation $179M) after a $14M round in Oct 2024. It says it is AI-native with an on-site H200 cluster and ships hundreds of mission-critical parts a week. It makes no certification claims

Velo3D: preliminary Q3 2026 revenue $19.5-20.5M (+43-51% year on year), Forge 1 Livermore campus opened 21 Jul 2026, joined GIDEP Sep 2026, AS9100D/ITAR. It relies on its Assure quality report and a locked print file for repeatability. No regulator credit for the monitoring
Phase3D (Fringe layer-wise height mapping) was selected by NASA MSFC to put in-situ monitoring into production printers and worked with the USAF/UDRI. No regulator acceptance found

How serial AM parts are accepted today (recalled): frozen qualified process per machine, coupon allowables, first article, CT/NDE of every part plus witness coupons. A new machine or new parameters can trigger requalification. The FAA has no AM-specific advisory circular and approves case by case through issue papers
findings.source: recalled; NASA-STD-6030 / SAE AMS7003 / ASTM F3303

research.q: Hardware test data and test automation platforms (Nominal, Sift, Epsilon3, Stell, NI, Dewesoft): do any target certification/qualification evidence?
research.headline: No. Nominal, Sift, Epsilon3, Stell, NI and Dewesoft each cover one layer: test data storage, the as-run procedure record, requirements traceability, or acquisition hardware. Several now say "audit-ready" or "certify" in their marketing, but none decides what evidence a specific approval needs, writes the package a regulator accepts, holds tool qualification that regulators recognize, or serves the alternate-source and sustainment approval market. That evidence-compiler layer, where an AI could replace hours of reviewer work, is unclaimed.

findings.finding: Nominal sells a hardware test data platform (Core) and edge test apps (Connect). Its site never mentions certification or qualification; the closest wording is 'traceability and quality control'. Named customers: Anduril, Regent, Hermeus, Scout AI.
findings.number: $75M Series B 12 Jun 2025 (Sequoia); ~$80M B-2 at ~$1B valuation, Mar 2026

findings.finding: Sift lists 'reporting and certification' as a use case and says it can 'generate audit-ready reports' and lets customers 'Certify with peace of mind, at software speeds'. It names Reliable Robotics as using Sift 'to earn FAA certification for autonomous flight', where it is the data and review backbone for the applicant's evidence. It is not an approved tool, and there is no mention of DO-178C or DO-330.
findings.number: CX2: 94% less time to root cause; K2: 20M+ points/s

findings.finding: Epsilon3 says it 'helps teams manage' AS9100, FAA Parts 21, 23, 450 and 414, NRC Part 20, EASA, DO-178C/DO-254 and ARP4754B/4761A. What it provides is the as-run procedure record. Its AI turns documents into procedures and drafts procedures from prompts; it does not generate compliance evidence.

Stell is an AI-native requirements tool for aerospace and defense. It imports PDF specs, tracks verification and validation evidence against requirements, and advertises an 'audit-ready compliance matrix in one click'. It also claims an IL5 ATO with the Space Force and CMMC L2. It is the closest of the six to deciding what must be shown, but the user still supplies the requirements and the evidence.

NI SystemLink links each test result to the software version, asset, calibration and configuration that produced it, and tracks calibration due dates and history. That is the provenance chain a reviewer needs, but NI does not market it as qualification or certification evidence. Its Nigel AI does trend analysis and natural-language questions.

Dewesoft sells data acquisition for flight, space, iron-bird and engine testing (users include NASA, ESA, Airbus, Embraer). It names no MIL-STD-810, DO-160 or ECSS standards and offers no compliance reports.
The test reports regulators accept today come from physical qualification labs (TUV SUD, Nemko, Emitech and others). DO-160H is expected around September 2026.

Istari Digital (Will Roper) is the only player whose main pitch is digital certification ('validate and certify system integrity in real time'). Its named customer is the Department of the Air Force ('Industry Øne', May 2026). It targets digital engineering of new systems, not legacy parts.

Opinion: every named customer of these platforms is building new hardware. None serves reverse engineering, alternate sourcing, PMA work or DLA Source Approval Requests, and none sells to the reviewer side (DLA engineering support activities, FAA ACO/MIDO, DERs).

research.q: Requirements, compliance-matrix and certification-workflow software with AI (Flow Engineering, Valispace, Jama, Trace.Space, Collimator, Dassault, Siemens Polarion, IBM DOORS; startups automating DO-178/ARP4754/CS-25 compliance).
research.headline: AI requirements and compliance tools (Flow at $750M, Trace.Space, Jama, Polarion, DOORS, Codebeamer, Visure) serve people designing new systems, and none of them argues that a replacement part matches the original or works for the regulator who reviews it. No funded startup automating DO-178, ARP4754, CS-25, PMA or SAR compliance turned up in 3 searches; the open plays are an equivalence-case compiler, a workbench for reviewers and designees, signed test evidence, and an AI-native house that holds the approval authority itself.

findings.finding: Flow Engineering: AI agents for impact analysis, test coverage and a 'safety and regulatory compliance' agent; customers include Joby, Anduril, Rivian and VW; GovCloud and ITAR support. The compliance agent is generic and sold to designers.

Trace.Space: requirements graph with the 'Trinity' AI layer and agents. AI suggests and deterministic rule checks verify; it has an MCP server. Its FAQ claims DO-178C support through templates and audit export; ARP4754 is not mentioned.
Valispace was acquired by Altium (around Dec 2023) and relaunched as the Requirements & Systems Portal; standalone AI requirements tools have exited small
collimator.ai is now a Namecheap parking page, so the AI-native model-based design startup has likely shut down or pivoted
A search aimed squarely at funded AI startups for DO-178C/ARP4754 compliance evidence returned none, only incumbents (Visure), academic LLM papers for DO-331 and opinion pieces

Industry stance: AI should be an assistant, not an autonomous creator of certified code or documents; all AI output must be independently validated and explainable. In practice that means pairing an AI generator with a deterministic checker.

Nominal captures test-stand context ('every run captures complete context') and automates test reports for Anduril (review time cut from 5+ hours to near real-time for 300+ engineers), but has no certification or qualification feature: test evidence is captured but never turned into compliance findings

The DO-178C verification layer (LDRA, Rapita, VectorCAST, AdaCore, Parasoft, Verocel, SCADE, MathWorks DO Qualification Kit) is deterministic and qualifiable under DO-330. No LLM-based tool is qualified.
Jama is owned by Francisco Partners (2024, reported ~$1.2B); it sells DO-178C/ARP4754 frameworks and the NLP requirement scorer Jama Connect Advisor
Nobody builds AI tooling for the reviewer side: DLA engineering support activities, FAA ACO/MIDO, DERs and ODAs. SAR reviews often take 6-24+ months.

Build a precedent database of approvals (FAA PMA database, 8110-3 patterns, FOIA'd SAR decisions) linked to part class, material and means of compliance, to predict reviewer acceptance
Build an equivalence-case compiler: scan, material and FEA deltas against the OEM baseline become a GSN/SACM assurance case with quantified margins and signed links to evidence
Build a test-minimization planner (value of information, parallel test articles, accelerated or digital-twin tests where precedent allows) to shorten the physics clock
Create an attested evidence chain: instruments sign data at capture so remote conformity can be accepted, piloted through an ODA or a DLA/AF SBIR
Create a DO-330 path: qualify a deterministic checker and treat the AI as an unqualified generator whose output is fully checked
Build a reviewer workbench for DLA ESAs, FAA ACOs and DER/ODA firms that pre-screens packages, cites precedent and drafts the review record while the human keeps the finding
Set up a liability structure: contractual caps or insurance, and eventually an AI-native ODA that holds delegated authority itself

surprises: No funded startup surfaced for AI-automated DO-178, ARP4754, CS-25, PMA or SAR compliance; all the AI money is in general systems-engineering tools for new designs

Collimator's domain is parked, so the AI model-based design startup is likely defunct
Valispace exited at only about $16-20M, a warning that standalone requirements tools end up as tuck-ins
Nobody builds for the reviewer, even though reviewer hours are the binding constraint

research.q: Materials informatics and AI material allowables (Citrine Informatics, Mat3ra, Polymerize, Uncountable, NASA/CMH-17/MMPDS digitization): could they produce regulator-grade allowables from fewer coupons?
research.headline: No. None of the named materials-informatics firms (Citrine, Polymerize, Uncountable, Mat3ra) touch allowables or certification, and no ML or virtual method has an FAA-accepted A- or B-basis today. The only accepted way to use fewer coupons is shared databases plus reduced equivalency testing (NCAMP, MMPDS). The open AI play on the verification side is an equivalency and model-informed-allowables engine, plus a pooled data trust and a written acceptance standard under 14 CFR 25.613(f), which allows other design values with FAA approval.

findings.finding: Composite qualification baseline: about 1,200 coupons in the NCAMP standard matrix, about 5,000-7,000 in the CMH-17-1G recommended matrices, and 1,500-3,000 coupons per material form (Lockheed). That is about $500k of coupon testing and about 18 months (at least 9) per material, including about 2 months of wet conditioning.

Vendor claim from e-Xstream/Digimat: a full program of 31,104 coupons and about $5.7M could drop to about $476.5k with virtual allowables. Peer consensus at the 2016 American Society for Composites conference was that virtual allowables have 'no use in certification'.

Getting one metal AM alloy-machine pair (Ti-6Al-4V on the EOS M290) into MMPDS under FAA JAMS/NIAR JMADD took about 1,029 tension, 501 compression, 508 shear, 397 bearing, 395 fracture-toughness and 412 fatigue specimens across 5 machines and 10 heats. Partners included Boeing and OSD ManTech, with 33 government steering members. MMPDS requires 100 x 3 orientations of tension data across at least 10 heats.

14 CFR 25.613 requires design values set on a statistical basis: 99%/95% (A-basis) for single-load-path structure and 90%/95% (B-basis) for redundant structure. Paragraph (e) allows higher values if each item is tested before use. Paragraph (f) allows 'other design values' with Administrator approval, which is the legal opening for model-informed allowables.

The FAA accepts NCAMP specs and design values (Memo AIR100-2010-120-003), and EASA accepts them (CM-S-004). Users adopt a pre-qualified system with a reduced equivalency test. The AGATE heritage claims about 4x faster and about 10x cheaper certification, and roughly 22 systems are listed. This is the only accepted fewer-coupons mechanism.

Senvol ML (America Makes/USAF, Nylon 11 FR on polymer PBF, 2022) produced properties 'analogous to' allowables with reduced data. It published no numbers and has no regulatory acceptance. A follow-on NCMS/AMMP OTA project compared against MMPDS, and the company calls ML allowables 'a work in progress'.

Citrine, Polymerize, Uncountable and Mat3ra all sell R&D formulation, data or simulation platforms. None of their sites mention allowables, qualification or certification; the only certifications listed are ISO 27001 and SOC 2. Citrine has raised about $76M in total (CB Insights, unverified), including a $16M Series C in Jan 2023.

Bayesian updating of analytical predictions with test data cut the probability of an unconservative failure-stress estimate from 12.5% to 1% (UF/NASA Langley). SAMPE papers claim a 60%+ coupon reduction from progressive failure analysis plus Bayesian methods. None has been adopted into CMH-17 or MMPDS as an acceptance method.

Northrop Grumman is funding UT Arlington (Dr. Xin Liu) on AI for aerospace materials certification and B-basis allowables (July 2026). Primes are paying for exactly this question now. Only the search snippet confirmed it; the page returned 503.

pathway_steps.step: Material and process specification (approved spec, process control document)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Specs are written by hand. Nothing links spec limits to in-process data automatically.

pathway_steps.step: Coupon matrix: fabricate, condition, test (multiple batches/heats, environments)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Physics clock (wet conditioning ~2 months, fatigue). Coupons are chosen by a fixed matrix, not active learning.
pathway_steps.cost: ~$0.5M composites; thousands of specimens for one AM alloy-machine pair

pathway_steps.step: Statistical reduction to A/B-basis (STAT-17, MMPDS methods)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Only frequentist pooling is accepted. There is no accepted Bayesian or model-informed method, and no validation corpus.

pathway_steps.step: Regulator acceptance (handbook publication, FAA memo, or per-program approval)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: MMPDS/CMH-17 committees, FAA ACO/DER, DoD airworthiness
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: 25.613(f) exists, but there is no guidance on how to use it with models

pathway_steps.step: Equivalency or conformity of a new source to the qualified population (the PMA/DLA case)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Done with ad hoc comparison testing. No predictive or ML equivalency engine, and no pooled cross-shop data.
pathway_steps.cost: a major share of the ~$100k per-package cost (opinion)

pathway_steps.step: Per-part acceptance (25.613(e) premium selection)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Not productized. Could replace population allowables with in-situ sensing plus witness coupons.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a public validation corpus. Re-derive every public NCAMP, MMPDS and JMADD allowable using Bayesian or ML methods on 20-30% of the coupons, scored leave-batches-out, and show the results are never unconservative beyond the stated confidence.

Write the acceptance standard (a CMH-17 chapter or MMPDS guideline on model-informed basis values) and obtain an FAA policy memo like AIR100-2010-120-003. In parallel, set a precedent through a 25.613(f) issue paper on one program, or with a DoD airworthiness authority that has more discretion.

Create a consortium data trust that pools coupon data across primes, shops and NCAMP (today siloed per customer inside Citrine or Uncountable instances), exchanged for reduced-test equivalency rights.

Build an ML equivalency engine. Use chemistry, microstructure, NDI and process signatures to show a reverse-engineered part's material sits within the OEM/MMPDS population with minimal confirmatory tests, and output DLA SAR/FAA PMA-ready reports.
Stand up robotic, parallel coupon labs with active-learning specimen selection and accelerated conditioning, to attack the physics clock and N together.
Productize 25.613(e) per-part certification: in-process monitoring plus a digital twin plus witness coupons, giving a statistical acceptance for each serialized AM spare.
Handle liability with calibrated conservative tolerance bounds that revert to classical methods when the model is uncertain, plus E&O cover and acting as the test house of record.
ai_plays: Equivalency engine for repair and PMA material conformity: shrink comparison testing to a few confirmations. This feeds the Approval Factory directly and is the highest-leverage play for legacy metal parts.
Model-informed allowables as a service with an owned robotic test lab, aimed at AM spares, composite repair materials and obsolete-alloy substitutes: sell finished allowables and specs, not software.
An 'NCAMP for AM and repair materials': a pooled data trust where shops qualify onto shared databases with tens of coupons instead of 1,000+.
Per-part statistical certification under 25.613(e) for serialized AM replacement parts on legacy fleets.
Standards-authoring moat: own the validation corpus and draft the CMH-17/MMPDS model-informed-basis method, then sell compliance tooling around it.
surprises: None of the named materials-informatics companies (Citrine, Polymerize, Uncountable, Mat3ra) mention allowables or certification at all. The space is empty, not crowded.

For legacy metal parts (C-130, KC-135) the allowables usually already exist in MMPDS. What drives coupon count is equivalency and conformity, not new allowables, so AI allowables help the Approval Factory mainly on AM, composite and substitute-material parts.
One AM alloy-machine pair took thousands of specimens and years to reach MMPDS. Every new machine or powder change repeats much of it, which makes this a recurring tax.
The law already permits other design values (25.613(f)) and per-item test-before-use values (25.613(e)). The block is missing guidance and validation evidence, not a missing statute.
Northrop Grumman began funding university AI B-basis allowables research in mid-2026, which signals prime demand.

research.q: Counterfeit and authenticity detection for electronic and mechanical parts (Cybord, Battelle Barricade, IDEA/SMT labs, ERAI, Sentry, Chipscan, XRF/CT AI vendors): what is automated and what is not.
research.headline: In counterfeit detection the measuring is automated (XRF, X-ray, ATE, and Cybord's visual AI on SMT lines), but four things are still done by hand. First, a known-good reference to compare against. Second, proof the paperwork is genuine: AOG Technics and EASA's forged-8130-3 case were caught only by phoning the issuer. Third, the accredited suspect-counterfeit call itself. Fourth, finding every installed part once a lot is flagged. The verification-side play is an AI-native, accredited AS6171 lab ('Authentication Factory') that shares its metrology and AI stack with the Approval Factory, since spotting a fake and reverse-engineering a part are the same job: measuring an unknown part against a reference.

findings.finding: Cybord: visual AI inspects every component as it is placed on SMT lines. It flags counterfeit, tampered and off-AVL parts, country of origin and lot genealogy. Customers include Cisco, NVIDIA, Intel and SpaceX. Raised $8.7M Series A (Sep 2024) and a $7M extension (Apr 2026, Capri Ventures). Claims a database of over 4bn component images, more than 60 lines, and 99.3-99.9% accuracy (vendor claims). It works after the parts are bought and never mentions replacing AS6171 lab testing.

DMEA/CALCE/IAI DATUM (2020): ML compares design data with radiography, acoustic tomography and spectroscopy images of the device under test. Humans still generate the images and define the defects. Research stage; I found no sign it was fielded. EU ChipCheck (automated X-ray in original packaging) is also research only, completed with no visible product.

GAO-12-375: all 16 parts GAO bought were bogus (re-marked, sub-spec metal, altered date codes). Four were delivered against part numbers that do not exist. 334 of 396 responding vendors were in China, and delivery took about two weeks.

Forged FAA 8130-3 on a Cessna landing-gear part (EASA OC-EASA-2022000331) was caught by a human emailing the named US repair station. Concord International used a deceased DAR's signature. No authoritative registry of issued 8130-3s or Form 1s exists.

ERAI runs the largest database of counterfeit components and high-risk suppliers (25-30 years old) but offers no AI product. Chip Scan is a DMEA Accredited Trusted Supplier doing design and trojan assurance, plus Deep Lift reverse engineering of legacy FPGAs/ASICs, not authentication of open-market parts.

(recalled) The governing stack is NDAA FY12 Sec. 818, DFARS 252.246-7007/7008, and SAE AS5553/AS6081/AS6171 (risk-based test levels, accredited labs) plus IDEA-STD-1010. A typical lot test costs about $1-5k and takes 1-3 weeks, with destructive decap and 48-168 h burn-in. AOG Technics (2023) forged EASA Form 1s on thousands of CFM56 parts and was exposed by TAP checking with the issuer.

Patents USPTO 12656277 (AI anomaly detection on X-ray CT) and 12105857 (counterfeit and cyber component detection) show activity in the field. 12656277 itself says reliable discrimination often requires destructive inspection.

Verification by probability: lot-level risk scores that replace fixed test levels, with regulator acceptance as the wedge
surprises: Neither of the two biggest recent paperwork frauds (AOG Technics; EASA's forged-8130-3 case) was caught by technology. Both were caught by someone contacting the supposed issuer
Cybord, the best-funded AI player, inspects only at placement on the SMT line, after the parts are bought. It is not a substitute for receiving inspection or AS6171
ERAI, the largest counterfeit database, offers no AI product
Chip Scan's Deep Lift already reverse-engineers legacy FPGAs/ASICs, putting a counterfeit-adjacent firm on the Approval Factory's legacy-electronics turf

research.q: Aviation records, back-to-birth trace and parts provenance AI (ProvenAir, FLYdocs, Bluetail, Aerotrax, GoDirect Trade, Moog VeriPart, AMOS): funding, traction, what they verify.
research.headline: The aviation records and provenance companies are small and lightly funded: ProvenAir has raised about $3M, Bluetail about $4.3M and Aerotrax $0.5M, while incumbents such as Lufthansa (FLYdocs, AMOS), Hearst (CAMP) and Honeywell (GoDirect Trade) own the systems of record. Every one of them checks paper against paper; none checks that the issuer is real, that the physical part matches its documents, or that the part conforms to its type design, and that gap is the verification-side opening for an Approval Factory.

findings.finding: ProvenAir: AI/OCR back-to-birth timelines and exception reports for engine, landing gear and APU life-limited parts. It claims 10,000+ human errors found, 5,000+ major assets analyzed and 28x faster than leading document systems. Logos include AAR, United, BA, BBAM, WLFC and GA Telesis.
findings.number: $3M total raised (CB Insights); Michigan Capital Network invested Aug 2024

findings.finding: AAR signed a marketing partnership with ProvenAir on 5 May 2022 and already used it for its own parts supply and landing gear.

Bluetail: AI logbooks for business aviation and helicopters. Features are Ask Bluetail Q&A with citations, Auto Research for AD/SB proof of compliance, and auto-built timelines. Site claims 30M records and $10B in asset value; the 2023 release said 600M+ records and triple-digit growth in 2022. It finds the evidence; the DOM/A&P/IA still signs.
Aerotrax: R3 Corda blockchain digital twin per part, a permissioned marketplace, and a Triumph Group MOU pilot. The aerotrax.io domain no longer resolves (likely dormant; inference).

FLYdocs (Lufthansa Technik group, majority stake around 2018, recalled): digital records, lease-transition back-to-birth and gap management, and AI component inspection with AMOS. 75+ customers including easyJet, Qantas, Cathay, Qatar and Virgin Atlantic.
AMOS (Swiss AviationSoftware, part of Lufthansa Group) is the maintenance ERP system of record, used by hundreds of organisations. Its site makes no AI or back-to-birth claims.

GoDirect Trade (Honeywell, around 2018) is a used-parts marketplace with trace documents visible before purchase and a blockchain history; Moog VeriPart (around 2019, Azure blockchain) tracks provenance of 3D-printed parts and print-at-point-of-need, with ST Engineering and US Army trials. Both recalled; their sites failed to fetch, and VeriPart looks stalled.

Across the category, what gets verified is document-to-document consistency, compliance lookup, immutability after entry, and presence of trace in a sale. Nobody verifies that the issuer is authentic, that the physical part is the one described, or that it conforms to type design. AOG Technics (2023) forged EASA Form 1s on CFM56 parts that got past records systems.
findings.source: Synthesis of product pages above; AOG figures (recalled)

research.q: AI in NDT and inspection acceptance (Gecko Robotics, Waygate/Baker Hughes ADR, Voliro, Eddyfi, Scientific Ultrasonics, Avonic, Boeing/Airbus AI borescope, Rolls-Royce IntelligentEngine): who signs, what regulators accept.
research.headline: Regulators approve a procedure and a qualified person or organisation, never an AI model, so no aviation AI inspection tool carries the signature or a qualified probability-of-detection (POD) curve. The first FAA-accepted case (Delta/Mainblades drone visual inspection, Sep 2025) still has humans deciding, and only nuclear steam-generator automated data analysis has legitimised machine accept/reject, via performance demonstration. The open AI play on the verification side is the qualification layer: physics-simulated POD, the missing ML-qualification standard, a reusable third-party method acceptance, and automated part-equivalence evidence packages.

findings.finding: First FAA-accepted drone-assisted autonomous general visual inspection (GVI): Delta + Mainblades, at ATL/MSP/DTW, 17 models, about 990 aircraft. Inspectors still review the images and disposition defects. The acceptance mechanism was not disclosed (likely an alternative method inside Delta's maintenance program).

GE Aerospace + Waygate AI-assisted defect recognition (ADR) for the Mentor Visual iQ+ borescope (GEnx and LEAP high-pressure compressor) makes no regulatory claim. It is positioned as an assist to the inspector.
Gecko Robotics is a well-funded robotics-as-a-service inspection company with a Navy contract. No ASME, API or NAVSEA acceptance of its data as a sign-off is documented.
findings.number: $1.25B valuation, $125M Series D Jun 2025, ~$347M raised, $71M 5-yr Navy contract

findings.finding: Voliro sells contact-NDT drones through NDT service firms (Acuren, Osprey Integrity). The service firm's certified technicians sign the reports.
MIL-HDBK-1823A POD studies need roughly 30-100 realistic flaw specimens per method, part and procedure. This is the physics-clock bottleneck. Model-assisted POD is still mostly at the research stage.

An academic review names the lack of accepted code provisions for AI-based accept/reject as a key barrier, and notes that ML accuracy/F1 is not qualified POD (read from a search snippet only; the page returned 403).

NRC uses EPRI PDI (ASME Section XI Appendix VIII) performance-demonstration results to estimate inspector POD. Nuclear qualifies demonstrated performance, which is the template for qualifying a machine.

(recalled) EPRI steam-generator eddy-current automated data analysis, qualified per the SG Examination Guidelines Appendix H/I, can replace one of the two independent analysts. It is the only mainstream regime where software holds an accept/reject role.
findings.source: recalled - EPRI PWR SG Examination Guidelines

findings.finding: Vendor opinion: AI crack detection must produce a POD curve feeding the AC 25.571 damage-tolerance evaluation. The relevant guidance would be FAA Order 8110.105A and RTCA SC-216. No FAA decision is cited.

Who signs: in aviation, a Part 145/121 certificated person with NAS 410 Level 2/3 qualification (employer-based) and RII inspectors. In nuclear, Appendix VIII qualified personnel witnessed by an insurer-employed ANII. For PMA, a DER signs the 8110-3. For DLA source approval requests (SARs), the engineering support activity reviews the evidence. In every case the AI counts as equipment inside the procedure.
Avonic (avonic.ai is a parked domain) and 'Scientific Ultrasonics' could not be verified as operating companies.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Build a flaw/specimen set (realistic cracks and corrosion in representative material)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No shared, statistically designed flaw library per platform. Every study rebuilds one. Physics clock.

pathway_steps.step: 2. Run a POD study (MIL-HDBK-1823A hit/miss or a-hat)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: OEM/operator NDT Level 3, FAA Tech Center, AFRL, EPRI
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Not done for AI-assisted methods. Model-assisted POD is not routinely accepted. ML metrics are not POD.

pathway_steps.step: 3. Write the procedure and get Level 3 approval
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No standard language for a frozen ML model as equipment (versioning, drift, re-qualification triggers).

pathway_steps.step: 4. Qualify personnel or organisation
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Employer written practice (NAS 410/EN 4179), PDI for nuclear
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Qualification is employer-based, so an organisation owning both the model and the Level 3 could hold the qualification. Nobody does this.

pathway_steps.step: 5. Regulator/OEM acceptance
pathway_steps.who_does_it: OEM manual revision, operator's FAA principal maintenance inspector (PMI), EPRI PDI/NRC, DLA engineering support activity, DER
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No reusable third-party route (an STC-like path) for qualifying an inspection method once for many operators.

pathway_steps.step: 6. In-service assurance
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No continuous field POD, drift monitoring or miss feedback loop.

pathway_steps.step: 7. Part-equivalence evidence for reverse-engineered parts (CT/CMM, materials, FAI, qualification tests)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: PMA houses (HEICO), DLA SAR applicants, test labs
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Hand-assembled per package. No automated equivalence evidence package formatted for engineering support activity or DER review.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Qualified POD for AI methods as a service: physics simulation plus generative flaws, calibrated on a small physical set, delivering MIL-HDBK-1823A a90/95 curves in weeks. Get model-assisted POD acceptance via a joint program with the FAA Tech Center, AFRL and EPRI that publishes empirical-vs-model agreement.

Draft the missing standard (ASTM E07 / SAE AMS-NDT / ASME Section V) for qualifying ML data analysis: hashed frozen model, qualified data sets, POD at stated confidence, drift monitors, re-qualification triggers. Model it on EPRI steam-generator ADA Appendix H.

Create a reusable third-party method-acceptance route (STC-like): qualify sensor + model + procedure once, operators adopt by reference. Near term, replicate the Delta/Mainblades alternative-method acceptance operator by operator.
Build a shared flaw-specimen bank and virtual-twin library for legacy military platforms (C-130, KC-135, T56) to serve both POD and training.
Continuous fleet-level POD and false-call tracking from every AI flag and human disposition, so regulator evidence accumulates instead of being rebuilt.
Automated part-equivalence evidence packages (CT-to-CAD deviation, material fingerprint, statistical comparison to OEM parts) formatted for DLA SAR categories and 8110-3, to cut reviewer hours.
An insurer-backed verification organisation, modelled on nuclear's insurer-employed ANII, that underwrites its AI dispositions and so carries the signature.
ai_plays: Qualification house for AI inspection: sells regulator-acceptable POD, procedures and Level 3 sign-off for any vendor's AI+sensor method. It sits upstream of Gecko, Waygate and the others and owns the step none of them do.

Inside the Approval Factory: an AI verification engine that turns CT, metrology, materials and test data into DLA SAR/DER-ready equivalence and inspection-criteria packages, attacking the reviewer-hours KPI directly.
Standard-setter play: write the ASTM/SAE/ASME ML-qualification standard and be the first organisation qualified under it.
Continuous-assurance SaaS: fleet POD and drift monitoring that makes the AI method's evidence base grow with use (a data moat regulators come to rely on).
Simulation-first flaw and POD library for legacy defense platforms, sold to depots (Warner Robins, Tinker, Oklahoma City Air Logistics Complex) as a shared evidence asset.
surprises: The only FAA-accepted autonomous-inspection precedent (Sep 2025) is a drone that replaces access, not judgment. Humans still disposition everything.
Nuclear, the most conservative regime, already lets qualified software act as one of two steam-generator eddy-current analysts. Aviation has nothing equivalent.
Law is not the binding constraint. 14 CFR does not bar qualified automated analysis inside an accepted procedure. The constraint is the absence of a standard and of POD evidence.
Gecko reached a $1.25B valuation without any documented regulator acceptance of AI as the signer. Its value is data capture and analytics, not sign-off.
Avonic and 'Scientific Ultrasonics' from the prompt could not be verified as real operating companies.

research.q: Obsolescence and DMSMS intelligence and continuation (Rochester Electronics, SiliconExpert, Z2Data, Lytica, Sourceability, QP Semiconductor, GaN/IC re-creation like Revasum? and FPGA-based legacy chip emulation firms such as Sarcos? find real ones).
research.headline: Yes, someone already does this for chips. DLA's GEM/AME program, run by SRI since 1988, has supplied 175,000+ re-created parts across 30,000 device types for 560+ weapon systems, and got a new $73.7M contract in Oct 2025 that runs to 2031. Rochester Electronics, Lansdale and Innovasic/ADI do licensed or clean-room continuation, but one re-creation still takes 48 weeks (GEM) to 18 months (Rochester). The open AI play is on the verification side. It means autonomous characterization of the old chip, a formal equivalence proof, and an "approve once, use on every platform" evidence package. A cross-service where-used graph would serve as the data wedge. Obsolescence intelligence (SiliconExpert, Z2Data) is crowded and only tracks parts, not platforms.

findings.finding: DLA awarded SRI International a $73.7M Advanced Microcircuit Emulation Improvement contract (Oct 17, 2025, through Jan 2031). It covers logic, ASICs, FPGAs, microprocessors, memory, op-amps, additive manufacturing of ceramic and metal packages, and radiation-tolerant analog parts. Results feed the GEM production program.

GEM has supported 560+ weapon systems and supplied 175,000+ parts across about 30,000 device types. One emulation can take up to 48 weeks, in batches of 1-50 units. A redesign without GEM costs about $1M per circuit card. One part (GEM34301QPA) fixed obsolescence on about 30 systems. DoD's share of the microcircuit market fell from 60% to under 2%.

GEM NRE is about 20% of a single board redesign. An AN/UYK-44 part took 8 weeks and saved $1.2M (15:1). Equivalence is shown only by form-fit-function testing on ATE, with no vector-coverage figures reported. Screening follows MIL-STD-883. An estimated 40-60% of fielded military microcircuits face DMS problems.

Rochester Electronics has made 20,000+ device types, says it can make 70,000+, and holds 12B+ die. It runs QML and Class Q/V flows to MIL-PRF-38535 using data transferred from the original manufacturer, and claims 70+ authorizing OCMs. Revenue is an unverified third-party estimate of about $275M.
A Rochester recreation takes about 18 months, with prototypes at about 12. It works best for digital parts and is hard for RF and embedded-flash parts.

Z2Data counted 528,546 end-of-life notices in 2021, 756,087 in 2022 and 473,910 in 2023. About 30% came with no change notice and 78% were driven by low demand. Its database covers 1B+ parts. Z2Data is self-funded and bought AMSYS in July 2025 (secondary source).
Lansdale makes 3,000+ classic ICs (AMD, Fairchild, Intel, Motorola designs) in their original packages.
Two names in the question are not in this market. Revasum makes CMP and grinding equipment for SiC wafers, and Sarcos (now Palladyne AI) makes robotics. Neither does chip emulation. (recalled)

pathway_steps.step: 1. EOL detection (PDN, GIDEP, forecasts)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Solved and commoditized; ~30% of EOLs arrive with no notice

pathway_steps.step: 2. Where-used impact (chip to board to LRU to NSN to platform to demand)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Each program office or OEM separately
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Broken: no cross-service graph exists, lower-level BOMs are often not owned by DoD, and one chip may sit in 30 systems

pathway_steps.step: 3. Resolution choice (SD-22 options)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No quantified fleet-level cost and risk optimization

pathway_steps.step: 4. Golden-sample characterization and spec reconstruction (probing, delayering, imaging)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual and the weakest step: undocumented behaviour and scarce samples

pathway_steps.step: 5. Replacement design (gate array, ASIC, FPGA, die re-use)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: A knowledge problem that AI can make cheap

pathway_steps.step: 6. Equivalence verification (ATE, temperature, timing, board and system test)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No formal equivalence proof and no reported coverage; system retest is repeated for each platform

pathway_steps.step: 7. Qualification and screening (MIL-PRF-38535 QML, MIL-STD-883 burn-in and life test)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Manufacturer under the DLA Land & Maritime qualifying activity
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Qualification by similarity and physics-of-failure arguments are underused

pathway_steps.step: 8. SMD/QML listing and part number
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Queue-bound

pathway_steps.step: 9. Platform engineering acceptance (ECP Class I/II, airworthiness; DO-254 if an FPGA replaces an ASIC)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The most expensive permission step: repeated for every platform, and FPGA emulation triggers complex-hardware certification

pathway_steps.step: 10. Cataloging, source approval (NSN, DLA SAR) and lifetime buy
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Ties into the Approval Factory's DLA SAR wedge

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a fleet-wide where-used graph by ingesting IPBs, tech orders, GEIA-STD-0007 provisioning data, FLIS, GIDEP, SMDs and demand. Map every microcircuit to every board, LRU, NSN and platform, and rank targets by the redesign cost avoided (~$1M per card)

Build an autonomous characterization cell: robotic ATE with adaptive AI test generation on golden samples, plus SEM delayering and ML netlist extraction, cutting spec reconstruction from months to days

Issue formal equivalence certificates: prove the replacement netlist/RTL equivalent to the extracted original, add differential ATE testing of old and new parts with coverage metrics, and win DLA L&M and program-office acceptance of this in place of repeated system testing
Build a qualification-by-similarity / physics-of-failure engine to cut the number of qualification lots. Burn-in and life tests still must run, and qualifying-activity policy has to change
Create an 'approve once, use everywhere' instrument, such as an SMD-level drop-in equivalence designation that automatically clears Class II changes on every platform using the part
Generate DO-254 / AC 20-152A evidence automatically so FPGA or new-ASIC replacements in airborne LRUs become economic
Pool the 1-50 unit demand across services so one NRE covers many buyers
ai_plays: Equivalence-as-a-service for obsolete electronics: characterize the golden part, extract its netlist, prove equivalence formally, run differential tests, and auto-fill the dossier for SMD, ECP, DLA SAR and DO-254. The KPI is weeks and reviewer-hours per approved replacement, against 48 weeks (GEM) and 18 months (Rochester)
Fleet obsolescence where-used graph as the data wedge, sold to program offices and DLA; it also picks the highest-ROI emulation targets
Become an AI-throughput second source or partner to SRI under AME/GEM, or a sub on DMEA ATSP; the $73.7M budget line already exists through 2031
Offer OCMs and continuation houses an AI pipeline to port legacy designs to modern fabs, aimed at the RF and embedded-flash parts Rochester says are hard
surprises: DoD has run an 'approval factory for chips' (GEM) since 1987. The economics are validated, but it still takes up to 48 weeks per part through one contractor, so the bottleneck is throughput, not feasibility
One GEM part solved obsolescence on about 30 systems, so the value lies in making one approval count across many platforms
Replacing an ASIC with an FPGA in airborne hardware turns a part swap into DO-254 complex-hardware certification, which is why FPGA emulation is uncommon in flight hardware
Revasum and Sarcos, both named in the question, are not in this market; the real players are SRI, Rochester, Lansdale, Innovasic/ADI, QP Semi, Micross, Teledyne e2v and DMEA
The obsolescence intelligence layer is crowded and commoditized but stops at the part, not the platform

research.q: Nuclear: AI for licensing, commercial-grade dedication and obsolescence (Atomic Canyon, Nuclearn, Blue Energy?, EPRI tools, Curtiss-Wright, Paragon Energy Solutions, Ultra Energy): who automates CGD packages?
research.headline: Nobody sells AI that turns out a complete, signable commercial-grade dedication (CGD) package. The funded nuclear-AI startups do licensing search and plant paperwork (Atomic Canyon: search and licensing review; Nuclearn: corrective-action (CAP) screening and an undescribed "Parts AI"; Everstar's Gordian: claims qualification "at scale" but publishes no detail), while CGD and reverse engineering are still manual services firms (Paragon, now Mirion; Curtiss-Wright; Westinghouse; Park Nuclear; utility in-house staff). The verification-side opening is to become the NQA-1/NUPIC-audited dedicating entity that takes Part 21 liability and uses AI to cut hours per package, starting with a fleet-wide generic dedication library, evidence traceability and model-based test reduction.

findings.finding: The CGD pathway follows 10 CFR 21, NQA-1 and EPRI 3002002982. It has two halves. The technical evaluation covers safety function, performance requirements, FMEA and critical characteristics. Acceptance uses Method 1 (tests and inspections), Method 2 (supplier survey), Method 3 (source verification) or Method 4 (performance record). Equipment qualification (seismic, EMI, aging, radiation) and software dedication are added on top.
findings.source: Paragon CEO D. VanTassell, NRC CGD workshop, June 14, 2018, https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML1815/ML18150A373.pdf

findings.finding: Paragon named the main CGD bottlenecks: no access to design information (the utility lacks the safety function and host requirements, and OEMs are proprietary or gone), more engineering and testing hours, and more documentation required by the new EPRI revision. Its proposed fix was to move from PO-specific to product-line generic dedication (for example GDP-210 for molded case breakers), so the technical evaluation is reused rather than rewritten.
Paragon reports more than 12M nuclear parts, more than 22,000 components supplied with dedication plans or qualification reports, and 175 facilities served. Its site mentions no AI.
Mirion completed its acquisition of Paragon Energy Solutions on Dec 1, 2025. The price of about $585M is recalled, not verified.

The only public demo of agentic AI on reverse engineering and CGD steps is MIRAE-EN's REDiX pilot (Korea). It covers LLM extraction from datasheets into tech-spec templates, Bayesian-network PFD reclassification of the quality class of reverse-engineered parts, and screening for counterfeit, fraudulent and suspect items (CFSI). It is a pilot, not a product.
findings.source: Korean Nuclear Society Spring Meeting, May 7-8, 2026, https://www.kns.org/files/pre_paper/55/26S-563-손권우.pdf

findings.finding: Atomic Canyon's FERMI models were trained on more than 53M pages of the NRC's ADAMS archive using ORNL's Frontier supercomputer. They power the Neutron search platform. An ORNL MOU (July 22, 2025) covers AI-assisted license review, and INL is building a RAG benchmark with the company. It raised a $7M seed led by Energy Impact Partners, and Axios reported Nvidia backing in Aug 2026. No CGD or parts product was found.

Nuclearn raised a $10.5M Series A in Sep 2025 (Blue Bear lead) and is deployed at more than 70 facilities. Its product list includes Parts AI, Equipment AI, Engineering AI and CAP AI. The model is that AI drafts and a human signs, with uncertain items routed to people. Parts AI is not described, and there is no evidence it produces dedication packages.

Everstar's Gordian claims its qualification work will 'clear materials, parts and suppliers at scale' and offer 'verifiable weld quality'. The site lists no customers, funding or CGD detail. It is the most direct stated competitor intent.
NUPIC (all US utilities are members) is the shared supplier-verification layer: a supplier needs 5 sponsoring members to be audited, and audits run on a standard 33-month schedule.
Westinghouse and GE Hitachi are adding AI to their existing service contracts, which squeezes standalone point tools.
