pathway_steps.step: 1. Obsolescence identification and design-basis recovery (safety function, host requirements, original spec)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Data is scattered across utility records, ADAMS and dead or proprietary OEMs, and POs carry dated specs. Search AI (Atomic Canyon, Nuclearn) helps but does not produce a structured design basis

pathway_steps.step: 2. Technical evaluation: FMEA and critical characteristics per EPRI 3002002982
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Rewritten per PO; generic dedications are rare and kept in private PDFs; no shared fleet library

pathway_steps.step: 3. Reverse engineering of obsolete part (if no commercial equivalent)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Separate from CGD, and the technical data package and CGD evaluation are not generated together

pathway_steps.step: 4. Acceptance Method 1 testing and inspection, plus seismic, EMI and aging EQ
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Physics clock and lab capacity; sampling plans are conservative and not model-optimized

pathway_steps.step: 5. Supplier verification (Method 2/3) and approved supplier list via NUPIC audits
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: 33-month cycle with manual audit of paper evidence

pathway_steps.step: 6. Digital item and software dedication (firmware, tools)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: A major I&C obsolescence bottleneck; review is manual

pathway_steps.step: 7. Part 21 acceptance and sign-off under an Appendix B/NQA-1 program
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Permission and liability gate: only an audited dedicating entity can sign

what_would_need_to_be_done: A fleet-shared, machine-readable generic CGD library keyed by part number (safety function, critical characteristics, acceptance methods, evidence), so dedications are cloned rather than rewritten. Paragon's 2018 'generic dedication' idea, done at scale by AI.
An evidence-to-claim traceability graph linking each critical characteristic to its test record, instrument calibration and signer, exportable for NUPIC audits and NRC vendor inspections.
Model-based, Bayesian test and sampling reduction for Method 1, with an acceptance path through EPRI guideline revision and RG 1.164.
A single pipeline that produces the reverse-engineering technical data package and the CGD evaluation together, from CT scanning, metallurgy and electrical characterization of the physical part.
Automated counterfeit/fraudulent/suspect item (CFSI) screening from imaging and electrical signatures, fed into acceptance.
AI static analysis, formal verification and test generation for digital commercial-grade item firmware dedication.
Become a NUPIC-audited NQA-1 dedicating entity (5 sponsoring utilities, then the 33-month cycle) that carries Part 21 liability, measured on engineering hours per dedicated item.
ai_plays: A reviewer-side CGD co-pilot for utility procurement engineers that checks vendor packages against EPRI 3002002982 and flags missing basis (lowest-liability entry).
AI-native dedicating entity: the nuclear version of the Approval Factory, competing with Paragon/Mirion and Curtiss-Wright on hours per package and turnaround.
A verification-evidence platform plus audit-ready exports for NUPIC and the NRC.
Physics-informed test-minimization service for Method 1 and EQ.
Firmware and digital I&C dedication engine.
One shared engine across DLA SAR, FAA PMA and nuclear CGD: all map design basis to critical characteristics to acceptance evidence to a liable signer.
surprises: The biggest independent CGD house (Paragon) was bought by Mirion on Dec 1, 2025, and its site still mentions no AI.
The only public agentic-AI CGD and reverse-engineering demo is a small Korean firm's conference pilot (REDiX, May 2026).
Paragon publicly described the generic-dedication reuse idea to the NRC in 2018, but it stayed manual.
Everstar explicitly claims parts and supplier qualification 'at scale' but shows no evidence. It is the startup to watch as a direct competitor.

research.q: Medical device regulatory AI (510(k) drafting startups, Formation? Gradient? find real ones) as an analog: traction, FDA attitude, does it compress review time?
research.headline: AI for writing medical-device submissions is a crowded, cheap category: Complizen sells 510(k) builds "from $11,000", and Cruxi and Sentium Bio offer agent drafting. A former FDA reviewer calls the output a "C-minus 510(k)", and there is no published evidence that it shortens FDA review (2025 AI-device median is still about 142 days). What has actually moved the regulator's clock is procedure: structured submissions (eSTAR), delegated third-party review (3P510k) and pre-approved change protocols (PCCP). That is where an Approval Factory's AI belongs: on the verification and sign-off side, owning the delegated reviewers, not only the drafting.

findings.finding: Complizen sells AI-plus-expert 510(k) builds at a fixed fee 'from $11,000'. Its Submission Builder goes from device profile to eSTAR 'in days, not months'. It shows no investors and no clearance-rate data.
Cruxi (agent-chain 510(k) drafting, launched 2025) has close to zero traction: 3 followers, 7 upvotes, solo maker.

Former FDA reviewer Michael Nilo says a 'one-click' AI submission platform 'can spit out a C-minus 510(k)': useful, not finished, and 'that gap is closing pretty quickly' (Market Pathways, 16 Jun 2026).

The real cost is evidence and process, not paperwork. For AI devices, median time from first funding to first 510(k) is 25.7 months (n=37), with median funding of $11.0M-$16.0M. Each follow-on clearance costs about $11.6M. The FY26 510(k) user fee is only $26,067.

In 2025, 295 AI/ML devices were cleared, with a median of about 142 days from submission to clearance. 24% took under 90 days and 22% over 200 days. This is close to historical norms, so there is no visible step change from AI.

FDA launched Elsa, its internal LLM, on 2 June 2025 for reviewers: summarising adverse events, comparing labels, and choosing inspection targets. It does not train on industry data. FDA published no metrics. Makary's claim of '3 days to minutes' is anecdotal.
FDA does not regulate the drafting tools sponsors use and requires no disclosure of AI use in a 510(k). The sponsor stays 100% accountable. FDA encourages structured, clean submissions.

Morgan Lewis advises sponsors to expect AI-generated reviewer flags, contest them with traceable data, and submit files with tight structure because AI catches inconsistencies. It says whether review times actually shrink 'remains to be seen'.

The companies with real traction sell systems of record and data rather than drafting. Ketryx (traceability and design history files from Jira and GitHub) claims 4 of the top 5 device makers and also targets aerospace, defense and nuclear. Basil Systems (700M+ regulatory records) and RegDesk show large-medtech logos.

Drug-side analog: Peer AI raised $12.1M (Oct 2025) for FDA drug documentation. Formation Bio is an AI-native drug developer, not a drafting tool. Its $372M round is recalled. I found no device-regulatory company named 'Gradient'.

(recalled) The levers that actually shortened FDA time were structural: eSTAR, mandatory from Oct 2023, replaced the refuse-to-accept screen. Under the 3P510k program, accredited private reviewers do the review and FDA decides within about 30 days. Under PCCP (final guidance Dec 2024), FDA pre-authorises future device changes, so they need no new 510(k).

pathway_steps.step: Classification and choice of pathway / predicate (or for aviation and defense: identifying the part and its certification basis)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Regulatory affairs consultants plus precedent databases
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Largely solved by AI search (Basil, Cruxi). Commodity.

pathway_steps.step: Pre-submission agreement on the test plan (Q-Sub)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Slow and manual, but the most leveraged step for avoiding deficiency loops. No AI product predicts reviewer objections from historical deficiency letters.

pathway_steps.step: Evidence generation: bench, verification, clinical and standalone performance, biocompatibility, IEC 60601, cybersecurity
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Bound by physics clocks. Drafting AI does not touch it. Simulation and digital evidence are accepted only partially, case by case.

pathway_steps.step: Package drafting (eSTAR)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: RA staff, consultants, AI drafting startups
pathway_steps.time: weeks to months, falling to days
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Being commoditised. Output quality is roughly a 'C-minus' that needs expert finishing.

pathway_steps.step: Regulator review and additional-information loop
pathway_steps.who_does_it: FDA reviewers (now with Elsa) or 3P510k accredited reviewers
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No one sells verification tooling to reviewers or delegated reviewers. No machine-checkable evidence standard exists. The delegated route (3P510k) is underused.

pathway_steps.step: Change control after clearance (PCCP or new 510(k))
pathway_steps.time: each change can restart the cycle
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: PCCP allows verifying a process once and then executing changes under it. Few sponsors use it well. This is the template for a 'factory' approval.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a machine-checkable evidence format: requirements linked to test data, raw data and analysis code, so a reviewer or delegated reviewer can re-run and verify automatically rather than read prose. eSTAR structures the form, not the evidence.

Build a reviewer-side verification copilot for delegated reviewers (FDA 3P510k orgs; for aviation, DERs and ODA units; for DLA, engineering support activities). It would check packages against the certification basis, precedent deficiency letters and cross-document consistency, and pre-clear them before they reach the regulator.

Train a deficiency-prediction model on historical additional-information requests and deficiency letters (FOIA plus sponsor archives). It would flag likely reviewer objections before submission and so remove review cycles.

Pursue a PCCP-style 'process approval' for the Approval Factory. Get the regulator to approve the AI-driven reverse-engineering and verification process once (like an FAA ODA or a DLA qualified-source process), so each part becomes an execution under an approved protocol rather than a new review.

Own the signers. Since liability and sign-off cannot move to AI, the company should hold its own delegated authority (DER and ODA holder, or an accredited 3P review org) so that AI-driven hour reductions turn into calendar-time reductions.

Turn physical tests into accepted computational evidence where physics allows: validated simulation and digital-twin credibility (FDA has an ASME V&V40-style framework, recalled). Pre-agree the simulation's credibility with the regulator.
Publish measured review-time data with a cohort comparison (AI-verified packages versus control) to persuade regulators to give a faster lane. Today no one has causal data that AI shortens reviews.
ai_plays: A delegated-reviewer verification house: an AI-native accredited third-party review organisation (FDA 3P510k analog; FAA ODA/DER group; DLA engineering support contractor) that verifies other people's packages in hours and sells calendar time, not documents.

Verification compiler: a product that turns test data, CAD/metrology and requirements into a re-runnable, machine-checkable evidence bundle. It would be sold first to the Approval Factory itself, then to regulators and reviewers as the verification standard.

Deficiency oracle: predict regulator or engineering-support objections from historical deficiency, additional-information and SAR disapproval data. It would be used internally to drive rework cycles toward zero.

Process-level approval: win approval for the AI reverse-engineering and verification pipeline itself (PCCP/ODA-style), so each new part flows through without a new full review. This is the real moat, which drafting startups lack.
Avoid the pure drafting play. The medtech analog shows it commoditises fast (fixed fees around $11k, many clones, 'C-minus' output, no review-time evidence).
surprises: The medtech drafting startups are tiny and undifferentiated. The companies with traction (Ketryx, Basil) sell traceability and data infrastructure, and Ketryx explicitly targets aerospace, defense and nuclear, so it is a possible adjacent entrant for an Approval Factory.

FDA itself is the most aggressive adopter of verification-side AI (Elsa, agency-wide since Jun 2025). The regulator builds its own tools, so selling to the regulator is hard. Selling to delegated reviewers is open ground.
Despite the AI rhetoric, the 2025 median clearance time (~142 days) shows no visible compression, and FDA has published no metrics.
Paperwork is a small slice of the cost. Evidence plus the review loop dominates a 25.7-month, $11-16M path, which mirrors the ~$100k and 300-1,000 hours per SAR/PMA package.

research.q: Simulation credibility and certification-by-analysis vendors (Ansys, Synopsys, Hexagon MSC, Altair, NASA CbA roadmap, ASME V&V 10/20/40, Vanderplaats): what the state of "simulation as evidence" is in aerospace and medical.
research.headline: Simulation is already accepted as evidence in both aerospace and medical, but always as a negotiated data package (model plus anchoring tests, a validated domain and margins), never as an approved tool. The work that is missing and not productized is the credibility argument itself, plus the regulator's review of it; solver vendors (Synopsys/Ansys, Siemens/Altair, Cadence/Hexagon MSC, Dassault) do not touch that layer, which makes it an open AI play for an Approval Factory.

findings.finding: The FAA certifies parts, not tools: parts are certified by test or by analysis supported by test. There is no preapproved FEA/CFD software list; regulators certify data, process and method.
findings.source: Safarian (FAA), Digital Engineering 247, 7 Mar 2018; Wong, DE247, 29 Jan 2026 https://www.digitalengineering247.com/article/a-peek-into-the-certification-process

findings.finding: CbA is routine for derivatives and minor changes; for new designs physical testing cannot yet be eliminated (Segaud, Synopsys). Siemens calls certification 'a continuous negotiation, involving simulation and tests'.
The FAA accepted RANS CFD in place of flight tests for internet antenna/radome installations (2018). Boeing estimates CbA could cut up to 50% of flight-test points; TC flight test takes 12-18 months.

EASA decides case by case and says it lacks the resources to vet tools, so it pushes vendors toward QA standards. It proposed a CM 'Modelling & Simulation - CS-25 Structural' (2020); final status unverified.
findings.source: Aerospace America 2022; Polimi RoCS paper ref 14

findings.finding: NASA/CR-20210015404, 'A Guide for Aircraft Certification by Analysis' (May 2021, Boeing/P&W/Stanford/Wyoming), gives the CbA vision and computational roadmap. Alonso: UQ is 'the holy grail'; target four to five nines; RANS vs LES CLmax differ by 10-15%.

EU Clean Sky 2 RoCS project: rotorcraft CbS guidelines (Jan 2023) built on an Influence x Predictability matrix with confidence ratios. It states the UQ methods exist in the public domain and that 'what is now required is for Industry to take the process forward'; the method is not productized.

FDA final guidance on CM&S credibility in device submissions (16 Nov 2023): a nine-step risk-informed framework built on ASME V&V 40-2018 (context of use, model risk). It covers physics-based models only and explicitly excludes ML/AI models.
findings.source: Exponent, HPN, Mondaq summaries (FDA site returned 401)

findings.finding: No regulator has rules for ROMs or ML surrogates. Vendors say ROMs are acceptable only within their training range and correlated with test data. The 2026 Ansys/Synopsys CbA webinar with FAA (Safarian) and EASA (Doeland) refers only to 'emerging guidance'.

Vendor consolidation, all figures recalled: Synopsys-Ansys (~$35B, closed 2025), Siemens-Altair (~$10.6B, closed 2025), Cadence-Hexagon D&E incl. MSC Nastran (~EUR 2.7B, announced Sept 2025). Dassault's CbA page names only an Airbus wing demonstrator and gives no numbers.

Medical precedents, all recalled: FDA VICTRE in silico imaging trial (2018); MRI implant RF heating shown by simulation under ISO/TS 10974; MDDT qualification of a few computational tools. Simulation rarely replaces a pivotal clinical trial.

Uncertainty-driven autonomous test lab that runs only the tests the model needs

Standards leadership on ML-surrogate credibility to shape the rules early

EASA openly says it lacks the resources to vet simulation tools
FDA's 2023 credibility guidance explicitly excludes ML/AI models, so there is a regulatory vacuum for AI surrogates
The three biggest CAE vendors were all absorbed into chip-design (EDA) or Siemens in 2025; none sells the credibility argument

research.q: New defence manufacturing startups that touch qualification (Hadrian, Divergent, Machina Labs, Firestorm, Rangeview, Freeform, Isembard, Cuby, Re:Build): do any own approvals or sell qualified parts for sustainment?
research.headline: None of the nine new defence manufacturing startups was found to hold sustainment approvals in its own name (approved-source status from a DLA SAR, a government-accepted technical data package, FAA PMA, or engineering authority). They sell capacity, and the government engineers or OEMs keep the approvals. The closest are Machina Labs (robotic cells at Robins AFB, with part qualification by the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office and UDRI still in progress) and Rangeview (Navy contract, Aug 2026, to run foundry capacity for MRO replacement parts). That leaves the layer that produces approvals unclaimed, and these firms look more like manufacturing partners for an Approval Factory than competitors.

findings.finding: Machina Labs' Deployable System is in use at Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex (Robins AFB) to make repair and sustainment parts for aging aircraft; the depot's own expert says it is 'up to six months faster'. The announcement gives no contract value, platform, or qualification status.

A second RoboCraftsman goes to the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office (RSO) at the University of Dayton Research Institute (UDRI), which will 'train, identify and qualify replacement parts for multiple aircraft'. Qualification is still under way, not finished, and no part numbers are named. Machina reports $14M in total defense awards.
Machina's defense page (vendor claims): depot lead times up to 56 weeks cut to days, more than $1M saved per design by needing no tooling, AS9100D. It names no approved parts and no platforms.

Rangeview won a contract to 'operate foundry capacity producing MRO replacement parts for U.S. Navy programs'. No value, Navy command or qualification is disclosed. Separately, Kratos picked Rangeview for turbine engine castings.

Hadrian sells build-to-spec parts, manufacturing-as-a-service, factories-as-a-service, and Opus, AI software that 'interprets legacy designs'. Its site does not mention sustainment, DLA or qualification. Funding of $260M Series C (Jul 2025) is recalled, not verified.

Firestorm Labs holds a $100M, 5-year Air Force IDIQ for 3D-printed drones and raised an $82M Series B ($153M in total). It says the money pays for DoD qualification of its OWN 3D-printed airframes. Its xCell containers make spare parts, but it has no approvals for legacy parts.

Isembard is a capacity network: over $50M raised, 17 factories (11 live) across the UK, US, DE and FR, 71,290 parts made, AS9100/JOSCAR. Customers include Anduril UK. It offers no sustainment or qualification service.
Re:Build Manufacturing has 400+ engineers, 14+ US sites and 1M sq ft of floor space, and offers end-to-end A&D engineering. It does not list reverse engineering, spares or qualified-part products.

DLA still buys replenishment parts through competition, approved manufactured part numbers or qualified products lists, and non-approved sources must file a SAR. 2026 solicitations from DLA Aviation and DLA Land & Maritime still openly ask for SAR packages.

Divergent, Freeform and Cuby: their sites could not be reached (503/403). From memory, Divergent and Freeform sell to the design authority on new programs and hold no legacy approvals. Cuby makes mobile factories for housing and has no defense qualification relevance; the founder may mean a different company.

research.q: Defence sustainment software and spare-parts AI (Vannevar? Govini, Rune Technologies, Craitor, Systecon, PTC Servigistics, Palantir in sustainment, Shift5): who targets sole-source parts and price spikes?
research.headline: None of the named sustainment-software companies is building approved second sources for sole-source parts. They forecast demand and set stock levels (Rune, Servigistics, Systecon), flag sole-source risk without fixing it (Govini, Palantir, Exiger), or collect platform data (Shift5); Craitor prints parts and Vannevar does intelligence work. The open AI play on the verification side is the evidence-and-review layer: auto-compiled Source Approval Request (SAR) or substantiation packages, plus a reviewer copilot sold to DLA's Engineering Support Activities (ESAs) and FAA reviewers. That layer goes after the real bottleneck, scarce reviewer capacity, which today leaves similar DLA obsolete-part work with a median of one bidder.

findings.finding: Rune raised a $24M Series A (July 2025) and won a 5-year Army contract vehicle worth up to $99M (IDIQ, 23 June 2026). TyrOS covers inventory, personnel, equipment and distribution, and its 'Saga' agent forecasts consumption. It has no sole-source, pricing or approval features.

Craitor (San Diego, founded 2019) makes rugged field 3D printers. Caplight lists $3.42M raised, mostly grants, and tags it Non-AI; CB Insights says $130K, so the sources conflict. It makes parts but does not get them approved.

Systecon Opus Suite+ optimises spares, maintenance and life-cycle cost for the US Navy (F-35), USAF, BAAINBw, Thales UK, BAE and Saab, and has an AI copilot. It has no obsolescence or sole-source feature.

Shift5 turns onboard serial-bus data into cyber, predictive-maintenance and fleet-compliance products. It does nothing with spare parts or approvals, though its data could serve as in-service evidence.

Price-spike evidence: a 2021 DoD Inspector General audit found TransDigm made about $20.8M excess profit on 105 parts across 150 contracts. An earlier audit led to a $16M refund and flagged a 9,400% markup on a half-inch pin.

Live 2026 sole-source demand at DLA: a Moog long-term spares contract (SPE4AX26R0010, closed 15 Jul 2026) and 123 Patriot spares sole-sourced to Raytheon (SPRRA226R0077). A DLA Aviation Oklahoma City notice for obsolete-part reverse engineering notes that similar work draws a median of 1 bidder, with 52% of awards single-bid.

Microcircuit emulation (Sarnoff GEM, DMEA) has been DLA's long-running obsolescence workaround, with QML certification from DSCC. Buying from trailing-edge suppliers costs 1.5x to 5-8x the original part price.

Parts Life Inc (Moorestown, NJ) won a DLA SBIR in 2019 to reverse-engineer obsolete seals for the Air Launched Cruise Missile. Small human-labour reverse-engineering shops like this are the direct incumbents.
findings.source: DLA small business PDF (search snippet; fetch blocked)

findings.finding: Lumafield sells industrial CT scanning with AI analysis and lists First Article Inspection and Reverse Engineering as applications. Nominal's hardware test-data platform cut Anduril's test review from 5+ hours to near real time for 300+ engineers. Both are verification tooling, but neither is aimed at approvals.

Recalled, not verified: Govini Ark maps sole-source and foreign dependencies in supply chains (large DoD production contract around 2025). Palantir's ShipOS (~$448M, Dec 2025) and Army Vantage show industrial-base bottlenecks. Vannevar Labs does foreign-intelligence OSINT, not sustainment.

research.q: Incumbent approval holders using AI: HEICO, TransDigm/JPE/Victor Sierra, Chromalloy, Wencor, StandardAero, AAR, Lufthansa Technik, GE/Safran repair development. Any public evidence they use AI to speed PMA/DER/repair engineering?
research.headline: I found no public evidence that any incumbent (HEICO/Wencor, TransDigm/JPE/Victor Sierra, Chromalloy, StandardAero, AAR, Lufthansa Technik, GE/Safran) uses AI to cut the engineering or approval hours for PMA, DER repairs or SARs; their AI sits in shop-floor inspection, fleet analytics and procurement, and in filings AI appears mostly as a risk factor. HEICO, the only one that names a bottleneck, names FAA review throughput, so the verification and reviewer side of the pathway is open ground with no incumbent claiming it.

findings.finding: HEICO adds about 400-550 PMAs per year (about 20,000 total). FSG R&D was $43.7M in FY25, up from $26.4M in FY23, so roughly $80-110k of R&D per new PMA (derived, assuming DER repairs share the budget). The only AI mention is a cyber risk factor. The 10-K says approvals are limited by 'the resources available to the FAA' and by the agency's confidence in the applicant.

HEICO Q4 FY25 call (2025-12-19): PMA and DER repairs credited for FSG margin (24.1%); military PMA called 'medium-term', depending on government execution; a call summary flags concern about the pace of FAA approvals for new PMAs. No AI discussion found.

AAR is the incumbent with the most AI: Airvoyant, 'an artificial intelligence platform that automates the procurement workflow ... using data science and agentic AI', plus Trax, Aerostrat and Airinmar software. It also acquired ART, whose FAA ODA lets AAR issue STCs and PMAs 'without reliance on third parties', and it designs proprietary DER repairs. The AI is applied to procurement, not approval engineering.

StandardAero holds an FAA DER designation to 'simplify the approvals of our component repairs' and has a Reliability Centered Maintenance patent. All 16 of its AI mentions are cyber, EU AI Act, regulatory or ESG boilerplate.

TransDigm: about 90% of net sales from proprietary products and about 55% from aftermarket. AI is not mentioned in operations. Its JPE/Victor Sierra PMA-DER acquisition (about $2.2B, 2025) is recalled, not verified.

Chromalloy and Lufthansa Technik developed six V2500 PMA turbine blade types. The FAA-certified blades are installed in a double-digit number of engines (about 1,800 FH and 1,100 FC). The challenges cited are manufacturing yield and underused engineering resources. No AI is mentioned on Chromalloy's innovation pages.

GE Aerospace plans more than $130M of European MRO investment by 2026, including 'AI-enabled inspection techniques' to shorten turnaround and widen component repair capability (including XEOS, its JV with LHT). Separately, GE uses AI in shop visits, on-wing inspection and repair workflows, with no metrics given. AI-enabled borescope and blade inspection and the Wingmate generative AI assistant are recalled. None of this covers repair development or approvals.

Lufthansa Technik's AVIATAR offers analytics, failure forecasting and condition monitoring. A newsroom search through Oct 2026 found no AI article about repair engineering. Its HEICO PMA JV and AI borescope work are recalled.
Safran bought Preligens (about €220M, 2024) to form Safran.AI (recalled). It focuses on defense imagery and industrial uses; nothing disclosed on repair development.

research.q: Government organic capacity using AI for reverse engineering and qualification: Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office, Tinker/Hill/Robins reverse-engineering cells, NAVAIR, Army DEVCOM, DLA R&D, Navy Maritime Industrial Base program. Budgets and tools.
research.headline: Every depot has a reverse-engineering (RE) cell: Tinker REACT, the REARM teams at Robins, Tinker and Hill, the Navy FRCs and RESTORE lab, and Rock Island. They scan, model, print and test tens to hundreds of part numbers. Not one public source mentions AI in RE or qualification. Government money goes to equipment, prize challenges, about $100k-per-part SBIR subsidies and AM capacity, never to approval throughput. So these cells are customers and validators for an AI Approval Factory, not competitors. The open slot is software that turns physical evidence into a reviewer-ready technical data package (TDP) and Source Approval Request (SAR), plus a copilot for the engineering-authority (ESA) reviewer. Avionics/electronics RE is the starkest unserved case: a $46.7M sole-source F-16 computer buy where an industry RFI drew zero responses.

findings.finding: RSO was founded in 2018 for obsolete parts. In 2021 it sought an automated 3D scanning system for RE. Its Advanced Manufacturing Olympics had 64 teams and up to $100k in prizes, with events in RE and in certifying flight-ready F-16 parts. No AI in the RE workflow; RSO's AI spend is predictive maintenance (CBM+), e.g. C3 AI PANDA (recalled).
USAF had printed nearly 10,000 parts by 2020. On the C-5M, over 6,000 phenolic wedges were printed: 88% faster, 35% lighter, about $1M cheaper. Roper: sustainment is about 70% of the USAF budget.
OC-ALC Tinker's REACT lab (76th CMXG) does 3D scanning, printing, low-volume tooling and dimensional verification. Its B-1 work grew from 8 to 76 reverse-engineered interior panels.
A Mar 31, 2026 Department of the Air Force SAM notice asked industry for white papers on RE and repair development at Tinker. The organic depot is outsourcing RE.

REARM teams sit at Robins, Tinker and Hill. Robins redesigned obsolete circuit cards (about 75% reliability gain). 3D CAD still has to be flattened into 2D drawings for legacy storage and emailed around.
DLA's RE bailment program (RPPOB) has almost 200 items. DoD owns data for about half; the rest must be reverse engineered at the vendor's expense.

DLA SBIR topic DLA231-001 pays up to $100k / 12 months in Phase I, with the TDP and SAR due in the first 6 months. Phase II is up to $1M / 24 months. Covers four RE/SAR paths; needs a CAGE code and JCP certification. This is effectively DLA's per-part RE subsidy, and it matches the roughly $100k-per-package estimate.

Sep 27, 2026: Raytheon got a sole-source DLA award of up to $46.7M for F-16 Mission Modular Computer LRUs. Raytheon declined to sell data rights in Apr 2025, and a Dec 2025 RFI drew zero industry responses.

An OSD Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment (IBAS) grant of about $1.8M over two years went to the Great Plains Innovation Network / K-State. It builds TDPs for at least 3 obsolete assemblies from the DLA catalog where data no longer exists. No AI.

Navy Maritime Industrial Base (MIB) / BlueForge: a US$1.84M AML3D order for 5 non-safety-critical obsolete submarine parts, gated by Navy hydrostatic testing on an already-qualified NAB alloy. The Navy AM Center of Excellence has delivered more than 300 components; the RESTORE lab does RE. The Navy's 2022 position was to qualify materials and processes, not individual parts.

Submarine Industrial Base / MIB funding is several $B per year, mostly workforce and supplier/AM capacity, not RE software (recalled). Army: Rock Island AM Center of Excellence, DEVCOM AvMC airworthiness, Organic Industrial Base 15-year plan of about $16B (recalled). No AI-for-qualification program found for the Army or NAVAIR.

research.q: Testing, inspection and certification (TIC) majors and their AI moves: UL Solutions, SGS, Bureau Veritas, Intertek, TUV SUD/Rheinland, DNV, Element, NTS. Are any building AI-driven qualification or certification?
research.headline: No major testing, inspection and certification (TIC) firm is building AI-driven qualification of physical parts. Their AI moves are certifying AI products (UL 3115, SGS CertX, TUV labs, DNV recommended practices), using AI to cut their own operating costs, and testing AI data-center hardware. The verification-side AI play is still open: an applicant-owned layer that writes the evidence package, cuts the test plan to the minimum and earns credit for simulation, while accredited labs like Element/NTS stay as suppliers. Lab billing per hour of testing and impartiality rules keep the majors from building it themselves.

findings.finding: UL Solutions launched AI safety certification under UL 3115 (Outline of Investigation for Safety of AI-Based Products, published 31 Oct 2025). The first certifications came in March 2026, for the Qcells EMS and Omniconn Platform 4.0. This certifies AI products; it does not use AI to qualify parts.

Bureau Veritas set a target of EUR1B revenue from 'AI-driven markets and services' by 2030 and has 'one governing framework to deploy AI across operations'. The release gives no example of AI being used to qualify or certify parts. 24 acquisitions since LEAP|28 launched.
SGS bought Granite River Labs (high-speed data validation for AI and hyperscale) in Mar 2026 and is scaling AI and autonomous-system certification under the CertX brand in its Digital Trust unit.

Element (which owns NTS) reorganized on 29 Jul 2026 into Element Aero, Space & Defense (qualification, mission-critical assurance, nuclear equipment qualification) and Consumer & Industrials. It has run Element Digital Engineering since 2021 (simulation and modelling, FEA, CFD, digital twins, ML) as a side service. It is selling Life Sciences to Eurofins.

DNV has published recommended practices on assurance of AI-enabled systems (RP-0671), data-driven algorithms (RP-0510) and simulation models (RP-0513). This is the most reusable framework for earning regulator credit for simulation, but it is applied to maritime and energy work, not to aviation PMA or DLA source approval.

TIC firms are not the approval authority on this pathway. The FAA certification office plus a DER approves PMAs, and the service Engineering Support Activity approves DLA source approval requests. Labs supply test reports to the applicant. ISO 17025/17065 impartiality rules stop them designing the parts they test.
TIC revenue is billed per test and per lab-hour, so AI that removes physical tests cuts their own sales. Their AI spending goes to margin and to new AI-certification markets instead.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build an applicant-owned AI verification layer. For each part it produces a requirements-to-evidence graph (regulation or MIL-spec clause to test to result), a minimal physical test matrix and a simulation credibility case (ASME V&V 40 / DNV-RP-0513 style), and it sends the physical tests to accredited labs to keep impartiality.

Win regulator credit for simulation and analysis in place of physical tests on spare parts that are not safety-critical: a pilot with an Air Logistics Center engineering office (Ogden or Tinker) for C-130/KC-135 source approval requests, then an FAA issue paper or DER-led precedent for PMAs.
Replace PDF test reports with a machine-readable evidence format, plus a reviewer-side tool, so DLA engineering offices, the FAA and DERs spend fewer hours per package.
Shrink the queue part of the physics clock with autonomous robotic test cells (fatigue, vibration, thermal, environmental, flammability) running around the clock with AI-run setup and reporting.

Put Bayesian/statistical test-reduction methods into practice: choose the fewest coupons and tests that still close the equivalence argument at stated confidence, and pre-agree the method with regulators.
Set up a pool or marketplace for scarce aerospace qualification test slots, since lab lead times often set real cycle time.
ai_plays: Qualification copilot sold to labs and DERs (Element/NTS and independent labs as customers): takes in a technical data package or reverse-engineered model and outputs the minimal compliant test matrix and a draft compliance report.

Simulation-credibility assurance for replacement parts, adapting DNV-RP-0513 and ASME V&V 40 to PMA and DLA source approval packages so regulators accept fewer physical tests (possible DNV partnership).
Structured-evidence standard plus reviewer tool targeting regulator and engineering-office review hours, the second half of the hours-per-approval measure.
Autonomous qualification test lab selling capacity to the Approval Factory and the wider market.
Approval Factory as the applicant/design house that buys test capacity from TIC firms rather than competing with them; impartiality rules keep TIC firms out of the design-house role.
surprises: Every major's AI-certification product certifies AI systems; none uses AI to cut the evidence burden for qualifying physical parts.
DNV has already published rules for trusting simulation models and digital twins as assurance evidence; they are a ready but unused template for aviation/defense spare-part approvals.

Element, the most aerospace-heavy major, has had a digital engineering unit since 2021 but still runs it as a side line next to physical testing; its July 2026 reorganization around Aero/Space/Defense makes it a natural partner or acquirer.
Bureau Veritas's EUR1B AI revenue target is undefined: mostly AI markets and operations, not AI-driven certification.
Several company sites returned 403 to automated fetches; figures marked (recalled) are from memory and not re-verified.

research.q: Classification societies and rail approval bodies digitizing approval (DNV, ABS, Lloyd's Register, Bureau Veritas Marine; AAR M-1003, FRA; EN 15085, ECM): AI use and remote/digital approvals.
research.headline: Classification societies and rail approvers have digitized how approval paperwork moves (DNV eApproval, ABS remote surveys, FRA's ATI waiver), and their AI so far only searches rules (DNV RuleAgent Mar 2026, ClassNK Survey Compass Aug 2026) or helps applicants draft documents (LR plus Microsoft nuclear permitting, Mar 2025). No public evidence turned up of AI doing the reviewer-side engineering check. That check is the open slot: executable rules plus an AI plan-review and evidence engine, sold to private approvers who keep the stamp and the liability. It is a better first buyer than FAA/DLA because class societies compete and are commercial.

findings.finding: DNV eApproval on Veracity is a portal for uploading drawings, tracking status and downloading approved drawings. It gives no turnaround figures and has no AI. The 3D Approval Platform is linked but not described.

DNV RuleAgent: LLM retrieval over more than 30,000 pages of class rules, aimed at crews and managers. It returns traceable paragraphs and filters by ship type and notation. The article does not mention plan approval.
ClassNK Survey Compass is a retrieval-based survey assistant in beta. The user keeps responsibility for the technical assessment. Flag-state rules and vessel-specific data are planned.

Lloyd's Register and Microsoft (Azure OpenAI) built a generative tool that drafts nuclear-maritime permitting documents from historic licensing data. It works on the applicant side and no savings are quantified.

FRA granted a 5-year waiver on automated track inspection with 12 conditions: automated inspection at least monthly, visual inspection cut from twice to once weekly, monthly and annual reporting, and derailments reported within 24 h. Automation entered by waiver plus data conditions, not by rule change.
Senate Democrats led by Cantwell opposed the ATI waiver, showing that political and labor resistance is the binding constraint on replacing human inspection.

ABS allows remote surveys for continuous machinery, tailshaft extension, minor damage and ROV underwater exams, and for alternate annual surveys except the 5th. ABS decides on a request within about a day.

Opinion piece (no numbers): AI-assisted structural analysis is said to shorten design review, and class is embedding rules in yard workflows. ABS: 'Modeling and simulation have become foundational to class approval.' KR and Singapore DSTA are working on AI V&V frameworks for USVs.

Recalled: AAR M-1003 (MSRP Section J) QA certification is required for shops that build or repair freight cars and components used in interchange. New component designs need AAR committee conditional approval plus service trials, often taking years. Railinc's Component Registry tracks serialized critical parts.

Recalled: EN 15085 welding certification (CL1 to CL4, mostly through DVS ZERT) and ECM certification under Regulation (EU) 2019/779 are paper-and-audit regimes run by certification bodies, with no AI review.

Build a reviewer-side AI plan-review copilot that extracts scantlings and systems from PDF, DWG or 3D models, checks them against rule code, and drafts comment sheets. The class society keeps the stamp and liability, so no law needs to change.
Create an IACS 'approved digital review supplier' category, analogous to UR Z17 for thickness firms, so a third-party pre-review report is accepted and fast-tracked.

Build model-based equivalence and accelerated-fatigue evidence that shortens AAR conditional-approval service trials for reverse-engineered rail components, building acceptance by running parallel trials.
ai_plays: Sell AI plan review and executable rules to class societies as their reviewer engine. They are private, commercial and compete with each other, so they are a faster buyer than FAA or DLA, and liability stays with them.
Run applicant-side pre-review as a service (a 'first-time-right submission') that measurably cuts class comment cycles and reviewer hours per drawing.
Cross-society equivalence engine for type approvals: one test campaign, many certificates.
Provenance and evidence layer for robotic inspection data, so drone or crawler output becomes approval-grade evidence and not just pictures.

Rail aftermarket Approval Factory: reverse-engineer sole-source freight-car components and win AAR approval and M-1003 certification. This is a near-copy of the DLA sole-source problem with private approvers.
surprises: Even in 2026, class society AI is only rule search (RuleAgent, Survey Compass) or applicant drafting (LR nuclear). Nobody publicly automates the reviewer's engineering check.
FRA admitted automation by waiver with data-reporting conditions rather than by rulemaking, which is a reusable regulatory template. It still drew strong Senate opposition.
LR is already certifying AI artefacts (AiP for Navantia's AI digital twin). Class sees itself as the certifier of AI, which could make it a partner or a competitor.

research.q: European and Asian AI-for-certification startups (EASA AI work with Daedalean, Airbus UpNext, Fraunhofer, German/French/Japanese/Korean startups doing AI certification or reverse engineering).
research.headline: No European or Asian company reverse-engineers orphaned parts and also carries them to a regulator approval. The field splits into AI-in-avionics certification (Daedalean, sold to Destinus for about CHF 180M in Jan 2026; the EASA AI concept papers), small compliance-workflow software (Xcert AI, CHF 1.1M), geometry and part-triage tools (Hexagon, 3YOURMIND, Spare Parts 3D, CADDi), and deterministic verification tools (Rapita, AbsInt, TrustInSoft). The open verification-side opportunity is to use AI as a tool that generates compliance evidence while a qualified deterministic tool checks every claim, and neither EASA nor FAA has written guidance on that.

findings.finding: Destinus (Netherlands) agreed in Aug 2025 to buy Daedalean (Zurich) for about CHF 180M in cash and stock, and the deal closed on 5 Jan 2026. Daedalean is being repositioned as a defense AI and autonomy hub. As of Aug 2025 its ML avionics were still not certified, though it had a certification method agreed with EASA and FAA.

EASA's AI Roadmap 2.0 dates from May 2023, Concept Paper Issue 2 from Mar 2024, and a new issue went out for public comment on 3 Jun 2026. All of it covers ML inside the product. None of it covers AI as a tool that generates compliance evidence.

Xcert AI (Geneva, founded 2024, 12 staff) raised CHF 1.1M, led by Spicehaus, for an AI platform that automates aerospace certification and compliance workflows. It is the only pure-play AI-certification startup found in Europe. It sells software and holds no approvals.

Hexagon released a scan-to-parametric-CAD workflow for cabin MRO parts that have no CAD data, claiming it is 3-8x faster and takes hours. The release says nothing about a certification path, so geometry recovery is becoming a commodity sold by incumbents.

Donecle (Toulouse) says its drone and image-analysis inspection is the first drone solution approved by authorities and listed in the Boeing and Airbus maintenance manuals (AMM). It shows that an automated verification method can be accepted through the type-certificate holder's maintenance data.

3YOURMIND (Berlin) and Spare Parts 3D (Paris/Singapore; details recalled) use AI to pick candidate parts for on-demand manufacturing. CADDi (Tokyo) applies AI to legacy drawings and procurement, with claims such as 100k hours saved at an automotive OEM. None of the three mentions aerospace approvals.

Rapita's verification suite has DO-178C qualification kits and the MACH178 multicore tools, but no AI features. Incumbent verification tools (AbsInt, TrustInSoft, AdaCore, LDRA, Validas; recalled) are deterministic and already qualified, which makes them natural checkers behind an AI that generates evidence.

Neural Concept raised a $100M Series C (Dec 2025). PhysicsX (recalled ~$135M) and Monolith (recalled) also build AI simulation and test-reduction tools. All three speed up design, and none produces evidence that a regulator accepts.

EASA has no equivalent of FAA PMA. Under the EU-US bilateral (BASA TIP), FAA PMA parts for non-critical uses on US-designed products are accepted. In Europe, approval rights belong to organisations holding a Part 21J design organisation approval (DOA). (recalled)

Fraunhofer IKS works on ML safety lifecycles and on generative AI for safety engineering with reviewable outputs, but lists no aviation work. Spleenlab (now part of Quantum Systems) builds safety-focused drone perception but makes no DO-178C or EASA claims.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Triage ranks parts by printability and cost, not by how approvable they are (approval path, criticality, test burden)

pathway_steps.who_does_it: Test labs; Rapita and others for software; Donecle for inspection

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Reviewer time is the bottleneck; there is no machine-readable submission standard and no AI pre-check

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: First-article inspection and conformity checks are manual; no automated CT or CMM check against a digital technical data package

what_would_need_to_be_done: Get EASA or FAA to accept, through a DOA procedure or an EASA Innovation Partnership Contract, a method in which generative AI writes compliance evidence and a qualified deterministic checker validates every claim, so the generator itself never needs qualifying
Draft a machine-readable compliance-package standard that maps CS/Part 25 paragraphs to evidence objects and checks, and push it through EUROCAE or SAE
Build an open approvability dataset joining FAA PMA, STC and AD records, EASA approvals and DLA Source Approval Request outcomes, to predict approval path and test burden per part
Automate material and process identification (spectroscopy, microstructure ML) well enough to produce an accepted alloy, temper and coating spec from a physical sample
Build a credit-by-similarity library that pools test data across families of parts, with a surrogate-model validation envelope the regulator accepts
Close the conformity loop with automated CT or CMM checks against the digital technical data package, accepted by Part 21G and FAA Part 21 Subpart K holders
Acquire a small EASA Part 21J design organisation and run it AI-native; the EU-US bilateral (BASA) then carries FAA PMA output into Europe for US-designed platforms
ai_plays: Pre-review engine for DOA certification engineers (CVEs) and later regulators: checks a substantiation package for traceability, gaps and inconsistencies before a human signs, sold by reviewer-hours saved
Evidence pipeline where AI generates and a deterministic tool checks: the LLM writes analyses and reports, qualified tools recompute every claim, and only the checker needs DO-330-style qualification
Approvability scoring that turns the Hexagon, 3YOURMIND and CADDi triage tools into a ranked pipeline of approvals
Credit-by-similarity surrogate models anchored by a few physical tests, accepted through the OEM's maintenance manual or a DOA procedure, as Donecle did
AI-native Part 21J design organisation as the permission holder, using AI to raise approvals per reviewer-hour
surprises: Daedalean exited through defense repositioning after years of regulator work, with ML avionics still apparently uncertified by mid-2025: making AI itself certifiable is a slow, low-revenue path
The only EU pure-play for AI-assisted certification (Xcert AI) has raised just CHF 1.1M, so the space is nearly empty
Hexagon is commoditising scan-to-CAD reverse engineering for cabin parts, and its July 2026 launch mentions no certification at all
EASA's AI guidance covers only AI inside the product; AI as a tool for producing compliance evidence is regulatory white space, not a prohibition
EASA has no PMA equivalent, and the EU-US bilateral accepts non-critical FAA PMA parts, so a US PMA factory reaches Europe largely for free on US-designed platforms (recalled)

research.q: YC, a16z, Founders Fund, Lux, 8VC, Shield Capital and other investors: list every 2023-2026 startup funded for "AI for regulated hardware", certification, compliance, qualification, reverse engineering or parts approval.
research.headline: No funded startup was found, verified or recalled, that runs the full Approval Factory loop: AI reverse engineering, then the technical data package, then winning a DLA SAR or FAA PMA, then holding the approval and selling the part. Investors (Founders Fund, Lux, a16z, YC) have funded the tools around verification (Nominal test data, Lumafield CT inspection, Ketryx and Saphira compliance traceability, Xcert certification workflow) and the factories that build to print (Hadrian), but nobody owns the approval itself or sells tools to the reviewer.

findings.finding: Nominal (hardware test data platform plus Nominal Analyst AI agent; acquired Fid Labs) raised $80M at a $1B valuation, led by Founders Fund, on 5 Mar 2026. Verticals: aviation, space, defense, energy.

Xcert AI (Geneva) builds an AI platform that automates aerospace certification and compliance workflows. Its customers are in pilots and it names no standards. It is the only funded 'AI for aero certification' startup that search surfaced.

Saphira AI (YC S24) keeps requirements, tests and standards in one place and automates compliance reporting and traceability for ISO 10218/12100/26262, MIL-STD-810, UL/CE/TÜV and FCC. It is a documentation tool; it does not obtain approvals.

Ketryx sells AI traceability and documentation for regulated product development. Its standards include DO-178C, DO-254, ARP4754A, MIL-STD-882E and the nuclear standards IEC 61513/60880. It claims up to 90% less documentation work. The a16z-led Series A of about $14M (2024) and Series B of about $39M (2025) are recalled, not verified.

Lumafield (industrial CT scanners plus Voyager AI; offers first-article inspection and serves aerospace/defense) raised a $35M Series B (Spark, Lux, Kleiner, DCVC) and a $75M Series C (IVP, G2VP, Wellington). It is the best tool for capturing a part's internal geometry when reverse engineering.

Novineer's NoviVision turns 1-4 smartphone photos into editable STEP CAD in about 2 minutes, against about 5 hours by hand. The company has a US Army CRADA. Its partner AM Craft holds EASA Part 21G. No funding is disclosed, and Novineer itself makes no certification claims. It captures geometry only.

Everstar says it compresses nuclear engineering and licensing 'from years to days' with its Gordian AI backbone. It runs the same AI-for-regulator-submissions thesis, applied to the NRC. Atomic Canyon and Nuclearn are similar; their funding figures are recalled.

Incumbents keep approvals as a stockpile. AST Korea received a Korean PMA covering 6,395 items in July 2026. HEICO adds roughly 400-550 PMAs a year. AV8 Group offers reverse engineering plus PMA as a service and is not venture-backed.

DLA's reverse-engineering SAR route: companies build packages at no cost to the government and keep the data rights. Navy and Army ESAs require at least 180 days to evaluate a new source. The reviewer queue, not engineering, is the binding clock.
Founders Fund and Lux co-led Hadrian's Series C of about $260M (Jul 2025). Hadrian automates precision machining that builds to print, so it depends on approved data packages it does not create.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Own approvals as assets: an AI-native firm that holds SARs and PMAs and sells parts. No venture-funded startup does this today; the holders are HEICO, Wencor (Boeing) and consultancies.

Automate materials and process equivalence evidence. Current tools stop at geometry. What is missing: deriving the material, heat treatment and process of the original, generating the test plan, comparing results statistically, and writing a report a DER or ESA will accept.
Reviewer-side tooling for DLA ESAs, FAA ACOs and DERs to triage and pre-check SAR and PMA packages. The ESA's 180-day-plus queue is the binding clock, and nothing sells to the reviewer.
Build a replay corpus of past approvals and rejections (SARs, 8110-3 forms, PMA supplements) so a model can predict which packages reviewers accept and pre-fix them.
Get DER/ODA delegation inside an AI-native firm so findings of compliance happen at machine speed under existing law.
Combine CT and photogrammetry capture (Lumafield or Novineer class) with metallurgy and test robotics into one closed loop, from the physical part to the TDP.
Link test-data platforms (Nominal, Sift) to a regulatory evidence schema so every test produces audit-ready compliance artifacts automatically.
ai_plays: Reviewer copilot sold to DLA ESAs, NAVAIR, AFLCMC and FAA ACOs: pre-screens SAR and PMA packages, flags gaps, and cuts the 180-day queue. A government buyer, funded through SBIR/OTA.
Equivalence engine: AI that infers material and process from CT, spectroscopy and hardness data, designs the minimum test matrix, and writes the 8110-3- or SAR-ready substantiation.

An approval prediction model trained on decades of approved and rejected source-approval packages; it scores a candidate part's likelihood of approval and its cost in engineering hours before any work starts.
A neutral evidence ledger: tamper-evident records running from capture to test to report, accepted by regulators as standing conformity evidence that is reused across packages.
Automated first-article and conformity inspection (CT plus AI) that issues AS9102 FAI reports and submits them directly as approval evidence.
Approval Factory as a vertically integrated house: build on Lumafield, Nominal and Hadrian-class partners and own the SAR/PMA portfolio. That portfolio is the moat none of these funded companies has.
surprises: Founders Fund put $80M into Nominal at a $1B valuation in March 2026, and it and Lux back Hadrian, yet neither has a company that owns approvals. The investors bet on the tools, not on owning the approval.
The only funded aero certification AI startup that search surfaced, Xcert AI, raised just CHF 1.1M. The category is nearly empty.
AST Korea received a single Korean PMA covering 6,395 items in July 2026. Approvals can come in very large batches, which supports the factory thesis.
Nuclear has more AI-for-regulator startups (Everstar, Atomic Canyon, Nuclearn) than aerospace parts approval does.
The strongest AI reverse engineering tool found (Novineer, photo-to-CAD in 2 minutes) is an unfunded Embry-Riddle spinout.

research.q: Electronic and PCB reverse engineering firms (TechInsights, ChipRebel?, Grayscale?, Nanoscope, Sandia/NSWC Crane RE, board-level FFF redesign houses): capability and AI use.
research.headline: Nobody does AI-native form-fit-function (FFF) replacement of legacy electronics with approval evidence. The big reverse-engineering (RE) houses (TechInsights, ChipRebel) produce patent and competitive-intelligence evidence about current chips. Government labs (DMEA, NSWC Crane, Sandia, the Air Logistics Complexes) have the capability but little capacity, and board RE tooling (Seica flying probe) still has the parts list typed in by hand. The open gap on the verification side is proving the new board behaves exactly like the original, and generating its depot test program and approval package automatically. Today a few hand-written tests and bespoke test programs stand in for that, and those test programs are themselves sole-source assets.

findings.finding: TechInsights (founded 1989, merged with Chipworks 2016, majority owned by Oakley Capital) claims 100K+ chip teardowns, 650+ customers and 35+ years. Its government offering covers current-chip teardowns, supply-chain and geopolitical intelligence and export controls. It says nothing about obsolescence, sustainment or FFF.

DMEA's only visible AI multimodal PCB RE award is an STTR Phase I to Terraverum LLC (Austin TX) with the University of Florida, Feb-Apr 2024. Scope: optical vision to produce a BOM, plus CT netlist extraction after layer dewarping. Phase II/III would auto-generate netlists and Gerbers.

Air Force Materiel Command SBIR FA857120C0023 produced a patent on nondestructive CT RE of PCB inner layers. The motivation: destructive methods consume the last surviving legacy boards, and probing alone yields only connectivity, which is not enough for FFF reproduction.

State-of-the-art board RE tooling (Seica flying-probe RE) learns the netlist through impedance signatures, but GND points and the parts list are entered by hand. It cannot tell resistors under about 5 ohms, low-value inductors or normally-closed relays from shorts.

Academic CT-to-KiCad PCB reconstruction (Univ. of Florida, ISQED 2025) was validated on only 3 layers of one sample board, with no accuracy metrics. UT Dallas/Texas A&M MTBoM extracted BOMs from metal layers across 10 PCBs. SPIE 2024 work does multimodal X-ray plus optical netlisting. All of this is research grade.
Rochester Electronics' IC-continuation moat is permission: authorization from 70+ OEMs, 15B+ devices and 12B+ die in stock, and 20,000+ device types made under licence.

Cybord sells AI inspection of every placed component on the production line: approved-vendor and BOM enforcement, counterfeit detection, genealogy from date and lot codes. Logos include Cisco, NVIDIA, Intel and SpaceX; defense is listed as a market. Funding: a $7M extended Series A.

Lumafield sells industrial CT plus AI analysis (Voyager, Quality Agent), inline at up to 5 parts/s, with a USMC logo among customers. It has a CT front end that could feed RE but no RE or design-file product.

(recalled) DMEA runs ATSP4, a multi-billion IDIQ that re-creates obsolete microcircuits through emulation and redesign, plus Trusted Supplier accreditation. Innovasic and Lansdale re-create obsolete ICs through behavioural capture and FPGA/ASIC re-implementation. The Air Logistics Complexes (Warner Robins, Oklahoma City, Ogden REACT) run organic circuit-card RE cells.

(recalled) DO-254 hardware design assurance, plus DO-178C if firmware is involved, is why civil FAA parts approvals (PMA) for electronics are rare. Test program sets for depot ATE often cost $100k to $1M+ per card and are sole-source.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Obtain golden units
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Destructive RE consumes the 1-3 surviving exemplars

pathway_steps.step: 2. Physical capture (optical, CT, delayering)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Air Logistics Complex RE cells, small shops, labs
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: CT segmentation and dewarping still manual; research-grade only

pathway_steps.step: 3. Netlist + BOM extraction
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: BOM typed by hand; low-impedance ambiguities

pathway_steps.step: 4. Component ID + obsolescence + alternates
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Not automated from image to lifecycle to alternate

pathway_steps.step: 5. Behaviour capture (firmware, PLD fuse maps, analog tolerances, timing)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Hardest and least done step; read-protected parts; DMCA/data-rights grey zone

pathway_steps.step: 6. FFF redesign (FPGA emulation, new layout)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Design houses, OEMs, Air Logistics Complexes
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Bespoke each time; no reusable library of emulated legacy blocks

pathway_steps.step: 7. Equivalence verification old vs new
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: A few hand-written tests; nobody measures coverage or proves equivalence

pathway_steps.step: 8. Depot test program set (TPS) for ATE
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: TPS is itself sole-source; rehosting is costly

pathway_steps.step: 9. Environmental/EMI qualification (MIL-STD-810/461, DO-160)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Cannot be skipped; similarity arguments are underused

pathway_steps.step: 10. Design assurance (DO-254/DO-178C for civil airborne)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Main reason civil electronic PMAs are rare

pathway_steps.step: 11. Technical data package (TDP) / DLA Source Approval Request (SAR) + First Article Test
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Reviewer hours are the bottleneck; inconsistent packages

pathway_steps.step: 12. Production + counterfeit control (AS5553/AS6081, DFARS 7007/7008)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Paper evidence; AI provenance (Cybord) only just emerging

what_would_need_to_be_done: A behavioural-equivalence engine: instrument golden boards in a bench harness or in-system, learn digital automata and analog transfer models across temperature and voltage, auto-generate coverage-maximizing vectors, run old and new boards side by side under differential testing, and issue a signed equivalence report with coverage metrics.

A consensus standard or DLA/Air Force engineering-authority policy that accepts exhaustive differential-equivalence evidence plus a mechanical and thermal similarity argument in place of part of the qualification test matrix (an MMPDS-like data path for electronics).

Fully automated non-destructive capture: CT + optical scans turned into a netlist, a BOM with AI part-marking reads and lifecycle lookups, then KiCad/Gerber files, validated on a public benchmark set of real multilayer legacy boards (none exists today).
Firmware and PLD fuse-map recovery, followed by formal equivalence checking of the FPGA re-implementation against the recovered logic.
Auto-generation and rehosting of test program sets from the learned behavioural model, for depot ATE platforms such as CASS, VDATS and eTPS.

An evidence compiler that emits DLA Source Approval Request / technical data package and DO-254-style trace artifacts (requirements to tests to results) directly from RE and verification runs, priced on reviewer hours saved.

A legal and permission layer: a government RE authorization per national stock number (NSN), clear purpose or government-purpose data rights, and a DMCA 1201 position for government-owned sustainment hardware, obtained through CRADAs with an Air Logistics Complex or NSWC Crane for golden units and failure data.
Insurance-backed equivalence certificates so that a non-OEM can carry the liability for signing off.
ai_plays: Behavioural equivalence-as-a-service for legacy circuit cards: the core verification product, with the KPI being reviewer and engineering hours per approved card
Auto test program set generation and rehosting for depot ATE: monetizes sole-source test programs even when the replacement part is not made
Image to netlist to BOM to obsolescence pipeline, built on CT plus vision (compete with or acquire Terraverum/UF; partner with Lumafield for CT)
Formal verification of FPGA re-implementations of obsolete ICs and PLDs against recovered logic
An approval evidence-package compiler for DLA source approval and technical data packages and for DO-254, sold to contractors and to reviewers
Per-unit AI provenance and counterfeit evidence (Cybord-style) bundled with the replacement part to satisfy DFARS 7007/7008
surprises: TechInsights, the largest RE firm, does no sustainment, obsolescence or FFF work; its government offering is about current chips and geopolitics
State-of-the-art board RE tooling still has the BOM typed in by hand and cannot tell low-ohm parts from shorts
The only visible AI multimodal PCB RE award (DMEA to Terraverum, 2024) was about $98.6K Phase I
Academic CT-to-KiCad reconstruction was validated on 3 layers of a single board, with no accuracy metrics
Rochester Electronics' moat is 70+ OEM authorizations (permission), which matches the thesis that monopolies are held by permission rather than knowledge
Equivalence verification and test program sets, not capture, are the least automated and most sole-source-locked steps

research.q: Gas turbine and industrial reverse engineering / non-OEM parts approval: PSM, EthosEnergy, Sulzer, MD&A, Allied Power Group, TurbineTech, Liburdi; any AI use; how they qualify parts with insurers and owners.
research.headline: Industrial gas turbine non-OEM parts have no regulator: owners' fleet engineers, insurers, LTSA terms and users-group reputation approve a part, and the real gate is lead-unit fleet hours (2-4 years to a first hot-gas-path inspection). No neutral body certifies these parts, no shared evidence pool ties a part's origin to its inspection results, and no insurer prices the risk; that verification layer is the open AI play, while incumbents (PSM/Hanwha Power, Sulzer, EthosEnergy, APG, TSL, Doosan DTS) use AI only for operations.

findings.finding: PSM (now Hanwha Power): founded 1999, Calpine 2000, Alstom 2007, Hanwha 2021. Redesigned capital parts for GE 6B/7E/7F/9E/9F and Siemens/Westinghouse 501F; 350+ upgrades, FlameSheet 33+ installs, LEC III 100+; 105,000 sq ft Jupiter FL plant. Its site does not mention reverse engineering.

PSM's AI work is for operations: an Advanced Data Analytics & AI team, AutoTune combustion tuning, and planned digital twins of its monitored 7F fleet. None of it is used for reverse engineering or qualification.

Sulzer makes new hot- and cold-section GT parts (blades, vanes, liners, casings) for Siemens V84.2/V94.2/V64.3A, Ansaldo AE64.3A, GE 6FA/7FA/9E, F-class compressor vanes R14-R16 and Alstom GT13E2. It says it incorporates design improvements; its page discloses no qualification, warranty or insurer details.

Turbine Services Ltd has made 600+ non-OEM GE heavy-duty components since 1972 (50+ blade styles, 30 vane/diaphragm types) for 600+ customers. It qualifies through on-site supplier audits, first-article qualification and ISO 9001; no formal industry standard is involved.

Allied Power Group (Houston, founded 2005): AEA SBF bought it June 2019, then Warren Equity Partners (Baird deal card dated May 2024). It acquired Combustion Parts Inc (2020), Eta Technologies (Siemens V-series parts) and EthosEnergy's Generator division (Farmington NM, 46k sq ft; announced 2026-04-07). The sector is consolidating under PE.

Doosan entered the GT aftermarket by buying ACT Independent Turbo Services (2017-07-26, now DTS La Porte TX, 100k+ sq ft). It has repaired 40 GE rotors (Frame 3 to 7FA), makes 7EA/7FA rotor discs, and cites a 'Tier-1 F-class rating from major power producers'. Qualification here means an owner's vendor rating, not a certificate.
Liburdi automates repair execution (laser powder/wire, plasma, GTAW, additive, 'Adaptive 4.0' welding machines, FEA and failure analysis). Its site states no qualification approach.
A utility tender (EGAT) asks GT parts vendors to show reverse-engineering and redesign capability: utilities qualify the vendor, not the part.

In aviation, FAA AC 33-12 notes wide variation in how applicants substantiate the dimensions of reverse-engineered turbine replacement parts, and says testing confirms reverse-engineering assumptions. The industrial world has no equivalent framework.

(recalled) Insurers (FM Global, HSB/Munich Re, AEGIS, Zurich) do not formally prohibit non-OEM parts, but they examine provenance after losses and ask about LTSA status at renewal. OEM LTSAs penalise third-party parts. No published insurer approved-parts scheme was found.

research.q: Automotive and heavy equipment aftermarket parts validation (CAPA certification, NSF automotive, OE-equivalence testing, Dorman, LKQ engineering): how equivalence is proven and any AI.
research.headline: In US automotive and heavy-equipment aftermarket parts, no regulator approves equivalence. Proof is private: CAPA/Intertek comparative testing for collision parts only (NSF quit in 2019), federal self-certification for safety items, and in-house validation backed by warranties (Dorman ships about 1,600 new-to-aftermarket designs a year with about 490 engineering and product-development staff). So the barrier is OEM IP, tooling and electronic pairing rather than verification cost. No one was found doing AI-generated equivalence evidence, a shared OE reference twin, or automated lot conformity, but the market will pay less for this than aerospace does.

findings.finding: CAPA certifies by comparative testing against the OEM service part: full benchmark measurement, material ID, mechanical tests, Vehicle Test Fit (>10,000 VTFs since 1999), plant audits, random material retests over the part's life, and marketplace monitoring. Intertek runs CAPA.

The CAPA 501 bumper standard (3 Nov 2010) requires full-part dynamic or quasi-static testing for every part number. IIHS crash-tested two 2008 Ram 1500s, one OEM and one CAPA-501: both rated Good at 40 mph offset, with repair cost $1,120 OEM vs $1,053 aftermarket at 5 mph.

NSF International exited automotive parts certification, distributor/recycler certification and mirror/camera registration effective 30 Sep 2019, citing strategic focus. CAPA is now the only US third-party certifier left.

Dorman FY2025: about 144,000 SKUs; 5,560 parts introduced, 1,608 of them new to the aftermarket (1,659 in 2024, 1,791 in 2023); 256 quality/engineering and 233 product-development staff. That is roughly 3+ new designs per engineering head-year, against HEICO's ~400-550 FAA PMAs a year.

Dorman's 10-K risk factors name OEM IP claims and OEM restrictions on 'testing equipment, software, telematics, and repair data', and say failing to adopt AI in product development could hurt competitiveness. No AI product is disclosed.

CAPA's Tier 1 Verification program (Hella first, June 2022) requires the supplier to be contractually allowed to sell its own-brand version. Stellantis/FCA and DENSO have said OEM tooling and IP cannot be used, so OEM data access is the gate.

CAPA certified parts must follow OEM material changes. In 2011 an uncertified aftermarket energy absorber for the Ford Fusion was labeled with Ford's material but was a different plastic, and it broke apart on impact. Material substitution is the core failure mode, and lot sampling catches it only sporadically.

(recalled) LKQ v. GM (Fed. Cir. en banc, May 2024) overturned the Rosen-Durling test for design-patent obviousness. For collision parts, design patents and repair-clause legislation are the real gate, not testing.

(recalled) Safety-regulated items (FMVSS 108 lighting, 111 mirrors, 106 brake hose, 205 glazing) are self-certified by the manufacturer, and NHTSA enforces only after the fact. In the EU, ECE R90 requires type approval of replacement brake parts with comparative testing against OE.

Lot-level conformity checks at distribution centers (spectroscopy plus vision on every inbound lot) to catch material substitution, the failure mode CAPA can only sample

Opinion: automotive is a cheaper, faster place to tune the verification engine and benchmark throughput (Dorman ~3 designs per engineer-year), but its margins are thin. Regulator-gated aerospace and defense is where verification hours carry value
surprises: NSF quit auto-part certification in 2019 despite insurer demand, a sign that standalone equivalence certification is low-margin
Dorman produces about 3x HEICO's annual PMA count (1,608 vs ~400-550) with no regulator in the loop, which shows how much of aerospace cost is reviewer and permission time
CAPA's own Tier 1 program depends on OEM contractual permission, confirming that permission, not knowledge, is the gate even in an unregulated market
The real gates in automotive are legal (design patents, ADAS position statements, electronic pairing), not testing

research.q: Digital inventory and on-demand spares with qualification (Replique, 3YOURMIND, Craitor, Ivaldi, Spare Parts 3D, Siemens Mobility AM, Wabtec, Deutsche Bahn Mobility Goes Additive): who owns the qualification step?
research.headline: No digital-inventory platform owns part-level qualification; Replique, Ivaldi, 3YOURMIND and Craitor send it back to the customer. It sits with whoever holds the permission: the rail ECM/keeper, the OEM, the class society, the Navy technical authority or the FAA. Outside certification exists only at facility level (ISO/ASTM 52920 via TÜV NORD), so safety-relevant AM spares still face a "time-consuming individual acceptance process" with "no binding calculation basis" — an open lane for an AI equivalence/approval engine on the verification side, starting in rail where DigiZug3D (Oct 2023 – late 2026) is trying to create that basis.

findings.finding: DB has 200k+ printed parts in use, has saved EUR 20M+, runs 12 processes and holds 1,000+ virtual templates. Its target is 10% of maintenance spares digitized by 2030. The article says nothing on who approves parts.

TÜV NORD certified DB's Neumünster AM facility to DIN EN ISO/ASTM 52920:2023, one of the first such certificates. At that point DB had about 100k parts fitted, mostly seat trims, lamp holders and HVAC parts. TÜV NORD says AM use is limited to non-safety-critical parts, that safety-relevant metal parts need individual acceptance, and that there is 'no binding calculation basis for component design and... proof of component strength'.
DigiZug3D (EU + BMWK funded) works on approval conditions and a calculation basis for safety-relevant AM rail parts. Partners are DB, Hamburger Hochbahn, ÖBB, Siemens and TÜV NORD.
DB itself certified Essentium's HSE printer and materials (9085 FR, HTN-CF25) to ISO/ASTM 52920. Here the asset owner acts as the machine/material qualifier.
Mobility goes Additive is a network and standardisation association with 140-150+ members, founded 2016. It does not certify.

Siemens Mobility's RRX Rail Service Center prints spares on Stratasys Fortus 450mc. Manufacturing time for selected parts fell by up to 95% against ~6-week casting, and the depot sees ~100 trains/month. Siemens qualifies the parts as OEM-maintainer.

Replique (BASF Chemovator spin-off, June 2023, seed led by STS Ventures, amount undisclosed) works with 80-100 print partners. Customers include Miele, Alstom, Danfoss and MAN. It makes parts to customer specification through 'certified partners'; part qualification belongs to the customer.

Ivaldi (18 staff, ~$9M VC, sap.io) sends files instead of parts. It self-attests 'physical and algorithmic verification' and keeps each part's documentation in an 'envelope'. No outside certifier is named.
3YOURMIND sells AI part identification and distributed-manufacturing ordering software. Its site says nothing about qualification.

Craitor's FieldFab is a ruggedized polymer printer qualified to MIL-STD-810H, in service with all four US services. It has a CRADA with USMC, NIWC Pacific and Army DEVCOM and is on GSA. It qualifies the printer, not the parts it prints.
Senvol (ML for AM parameters and materials) got US Navy funding for an AM sensor-fusion project in January 2026. It is adjacent to qualification but does not own part approval.

(recalled) In EU rail, the Entity in Charge of Maintenance owns maintenance and substitute parts under Reg 2019/779, with CSM-RA (Reg 402/2013) and an Assessment Body for significant changes. EN 45545-2 is the fire gate for polymer parts. In maritime, DNV-CG-0197 governs AM and the class society owns qualification. In the US Navy, NAVSEA/NAVAIR technical warrant holders approve parts.
