what_would_need_to_be_done: Part-level equivalence engine: infer loads from the original part and its service context, then run AM-specific FE with allowables and knockdowns. It would output a minimal test matrix and an auto-written approval dossier in each authority's format (CSM-RA hazard log, EN 45545 evidence, NAVSEA package, DNV-CG-0197 file, FAA PMA test/computation report).

Shared probabilistic AM allowables pooled across printer networks (Replique, Ivaldi, DB, OEMs), with a B-basis-style statistical method that regulators accept, so each machine-material pair does not need its own campaign.
Per-build acceptance from in-situ sensor data, validated against CT, so distributed printers can ship safety-relevant parts without destructive or CT inspection of every build.

A portable 'qualified digital part' record (geometry, recipe, allowables, inspection plan, approval pedigree, field history) that crosses organisations; this is the digital product passport TÜV says is being standardised.

A non-OEM permission holder: become an Assessment Body, a 52920 certifier, an ECM maintenance function, a NAVSEA/DLA-recognised AM qualification shop or a DNV-approved manufacturer, so the house signs instead of routing.
Turn DigiZug3D results (due ~late 2026) into a standard, and be the first tool that implements it at fleet scale.
Fleet-scale criticality triage: sort 100k+ SKUs into self-approvable, equivalence-approvable and OEM-only, with the argument written out, to open the parts the platforms now skip.
ai_plays: Equivalence-as-a-service for rail ECMs and defence depots: scan to substitute design to minimal tests to an approval dossier, priced per approved part, with the KPI being reviewer hours per approval. Start with safety-relevant rail metal parts (DB, ÖBB, Hochbahn, Siemens), the market DigiZug3D is trying to open.

Verification layer for digital-inventory platforms: shared AM allowables plus in-situ per-build acceptance certificates, so Replique, Ivaldi and DB can move from seat trims to critical parts. Senvol, Phase3D and 1000 Kelvin are adjacent, but none owns approval.

AI-native signer: an Assessment Body, 52920 certifier or NAVSEA/DLA-recognised qualification house whose throughput comes from AI-generated evidence. This is the direct rail/maritime/defence AM version of the Approval Factory.
Criticality triage plus a dossier generator sold to asset owners' engineering departments, to enlarge the substitutable SKU set.
surprises: DB grew from ~100k printed parts (2024) to >200k (Dec 2025) without touching safety-critical parts, so the non-critical market scales on its own without new qualification.
The asset owner (DB) acts as qualifier of the machines and materials themselves (Essentium HSE), not just as a buyer.
TÜV NORD says outright that there is no binding calculation basis for strength proof of AM safety parts; the gap is acknowledged and funded, not hidden.
None of the venture-backed platforms claims to own part approval; all route it back to the customer. Craitor qualifies the printer (MIL-STD-810H), not the parts it prints.

research.q: Legal/IP side: AI tools for freedom-to-operate, clean-room reverse engineering audit trails, trade-secret risk in RE (patent search AI like PatSnap, IP firms). Is anyone combining clean-room RE with AI?
research.headline: AI freedom-to-operate (FTO) and patent tools are a crowded, well-funded market (PatSnap, Solve Intelligence, Patlytics, IPRally), but all of them work on patent text. I found nobody combining hardware clean-room reverse engineering with AI and an evidence-grade audit trail; the only "AI clean room" offers are in software and legally contested (MALUS, the chardet rewrite). The opening on the verification side is an independent-derivation provenance ledger, plus FTO that checks a part's scanned geometry and materials against patent claims, so each reverse-engineered technical data package can be defended in court and insured.

findings.finding: US law treats reverse engineering of a lawfully obtained product as a proper means. Lawyers now argue AI makes OEM secrets 'readily ascertainable', and the 11th Circuit held that bot-scraping of public data was 'improper means'. So AI-assisted reverse engineering is safe only if the inputs are measurements, not scraped OEM data.

United States v. Lange: a former employee of RAPCO, an aftermarket aircraft parts maker, offered RAPCO's reverse-engineered drawings and certification data for $100k. RAPCO's development took 1-2 years, and identicality let it skip some tests. He argued reverse-engineered data can't be a trade secret and was convicted; affirmation recalled. So reverse-engineered packages are themselves a protectable moat.

In replacement-parts trade-secret cases (Rockwell v. DEV; Colt v. Springfield Armory), the aftermarket defendant loses when it cannot prove where each drawing came from, or when the OEM argues reverse-engineering every part was too large a task, so the drawings must have been copied.

Solve Intelligence's Charts product: FTO templates for US, European (EPC Art. 69), UK and German law; claim-element charts; search across 170M+ publications in 107 jurisdictions; clearance memo drafts for attorney sign-off. It reports 700+ IP teams and claims 60-90% efficiency gains (vendor figure).

PatSnap Eureka FTO: semantic search across USPTO, EPO and WIPO, mapping of product features to claims, and risk scoring. It reports 18,000+ customers and 2B+ data points, and claims '75% faster' with no stated method. It says traditional FTO takes weeks and costs tens of thousands of dollars.

MALUS sells AI 'Clean Room as a Service': one team reads docs only, a separate team re-implements, and the output carries the vendor's own license. It claims audit logs and indemnity, routed through an offshore subsidiary; none of this is verified and the site shows 'temporarily unavailable'. It is the only 'AI clean room' product found, and it is software-only.

chardet 7.0.0 shipped as a 'ground-up, MIT-licensed rewrite' of a formerly LGPL library. The public dispute over whether an AI-assisted rewrite counts as a clean room (recalled) shows the law on AI clean rooms is unsettled.
Reverse-engineering parts approval (PMA) firms such as Av8 PMA (500+ FAA/EASA-approved parts) publish nothing on AI or IP-provenance tooling. No aerospace clean-room-plus-AI player was found.

(recalled) The FAA and DLA do not rule on IP: the applicant carries infringement and trade-secret risk. Data developed at private expense keeps the contractor's rights under DFARS 252.227-7013/7015. LKQ v. GM (Fed. Cir. en banc, 2024) loosened the obviousness test for design patents, which matters for spare-part FTO. Reverse-engineering a defense part creates technical data controlled under ITAR.
findings.source: recalled; 14 CFR Part 21 Subpart K, FAA Order 8110.42, DFARS 252.227

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Done on text only, never on the scanned geometry, material or process; no portfolio-wide FTO across thousands of part numbers (NSNs)

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Data not cryptographically tied to the specific physical specimens and their chain of custody

research.q: Space and launch qualification startups and tools (radiation testing, NASA-STD-6016, qualification-by-similarity, Apex, K2, Stoke supply chains): AI in qualification by similarity.
research.headline: No company sells AI-generated qualification-by-similarity dossiers that space buyers accept today. The only data-driven attempts are agency research: NASA's JPL SEL predictor from 2018 never got past a prototype, and ESA's CORHA-2 (2024-2027) covers just 22 parts. A 'Similarity Engine' would combine die-identity proof, a pooled radiation corpus, calibrated prediction and active-learning tests that cut beam hours. It could start in space, where acceptance is set by contract rather than by a regulator, and the same method carries over to DLA Source Approval Requests and FAA PMA identicality arguments.

findings.finding: In 2018 NASA NEPP/JPL built a 'COTS Metadata' database, a datasheet scraper and an entropy decision-tree plus linear model that predicts SEL LET threshold for untested parts. Its own future-work list says flavor consolidation 'just tak[es] first flavor and assum[es] it is very similar, which is not always the case'. It stayed a research prototype behind JPL login.

ESA CORHA-2 (Seibersdorf Labor plus University of Padova, 2024-2027) is building an open COTS RHA database and investigating AI-supported failure prediction. Of 133 parts submitted, 46 met the requirements and 22 were selected. Tests: TID to 50 krad Co-60 (ESCC 22900) and SEE at UCL Louvain plus pulsed laser (ESCC 25100). Sample size is 5+5+1, with destructive SEE on 2 samples at 2 LETs.

NASA GSFC's reasoning on Google Edge TPU radiation rested on an unconfirmed process node ('thought to be 16 or 12 nm ... would be expected to [have] similar radiation response as the Intel VPUs'). They still tested 14 devices each at GSFC, NSRL, LBNL and MGH. So similarity claims today are informal expert judgment, and die identity is the weak link.

Europe had no space-tailored high-energy heavy-ion facility, and HEARTS (EU grant 101082402, ends 2026) is building one at CERN and GSI. The second CERN industrial pilot drew 16 users and over 200 irradiation hours, but only 6 paid.

NASA-STD-6016C with Change 1 (dated 2021-09-30, changed 2023-11-15, next review 2026-09-30) covers all flight hardware, including off-the-shelf and vendor-furnished items. Deviations go through per-program MUAs (MUA process recalled).

Apex Factory One: peak capacity over 200 buses per year, a 66,000 lbf vibe table, and the 'Octopus' OS linking inventory, scheduling and work instructions. K2 says '80% of each satellite is built in-house' and describes radiation-tolerant architectures. High-rate, COTS-heavy builders are the natural buyers of fast similarity qualification. Funding (recalled): Apex about $200M Series C in 2025, K2 about $250M at about $3B in Dec 2025, Stoke about $510M Series D in 2025.

Istari Digital (Will Roper) markets real-time validation and certification of system integrity, and the Air Force and Istari unveiled 'Industry Øne' on 2026-05-20. This is the closest commercial 'digital approval' narrative, but it is horizontal data plumbing, not part-level evidence.

Nominal's test-data platform cut Anduril's test review from 5+ hours to near real time across 300+ engineers, and Regent and Hermeus are customers. It owns the layer where evidence is created but does not build acceptance arguments.

Heavy-ion beam time costs roughly $1-2k+/hr, US queues run months, and the National Academies' 2018 report flagged an SEE test infrastructure shortfall (all recalled). This is the binding physics and capacity clock.
findings.source: recalled; National Academies 'Testing at the Speed of Light' (2018)

research.q: Robotics/drone inspection-to-signoff players (ANYbotics, Square Robot, Flyability, Skydio, Percepto, Energy Robotics): do any hold signing authority or accredited inspection status?
research.headline: None of the six robotics companies signs inspections in its own name or holds ISO/IEC 17020 inspection-body accreditation. What they hold is product certifications (ANYmal's ATEX/IECEx Zone 1 rating), drone flight permissions (Percepto, Skydio) and acceptance of their data by the body that does sign (ABS certified Elios 3 UT data for class surveys). The signature still belongs to a person with the right credential: an API 653 inspector, an ASME/NBIC Authorized Inspector, or a class surveyor. That leaves room for an AI-native accredited inspection body that sells signed findings rather than robots.

findings.finding: Square Robot says its API 653 reports are 'all analyzed by certified NDT Level IIIs and API 653 inspectors'. It claims 400+ tanks inspected and $150M of downtime avoided. Its page still shows an unfilled placeholder where the regulatory-allowance date should be, and it claims no ISO 17020 accreditation. The signing authority belongs to the individual inspectors, not to the company.
Square Robot, working with TVA and EPRI, inspected 3 in-service fuel-oil tanks in 3 days with its SR-1 submersible robot.

ABS 'certified' data from the Flyability Elios 3 UT payload 'for use in class surveys' (5 June 2024). This is acceptance of the data, not signing authority: the ABS surveyor still credits the survey, and service firms such as Diaplous fly the drone.

ANYbotics holds product certifications only: ATEX/IECEx Zone 1 for ANYmal X and ISO/IEC 27001. It announced a partnership with Energy Robotics in June 2024. Neither company claims accreditation as an inspection body.

Percepto lists aviation permissions only: a nationwide US waiver plus approvals from EASA (BVLOS), CASA, Transport Canada, Israel and others. It cites no acceptance of its inspection data by NRC, PHMSA or under EPA OOOOb.

Adjacent player Gecko Robotics has a US Navy deal of $71M (Mar 2026), with the IDIQ expanded to $300M (Oct 2026), and claims savings of up to $8M per ship. Its homepage cites no formal NAVSEA approval. It shows that the value lies in data feeding maintenance decisions, but sign-off still stays with the Navy.

(Recalled) The only company-level 'accredited' slots that exist are class-society Service Supplier approval (IACS UR Z17; IACS Recommendation 42 and ABS Remote Inspection Technologies guidance), ISO/IEC 17020 inspection-body accreditation, and National Board Authorized Inspection Agency status. These are held by testing, inspection and certification firms (BV, TUV, SGS, Mistras, HSB), not by robot makers.
findings.source: recalled: IACS UR Z17, ABS Guidance Notes on Using Remote Inspection Technologies, NBIC

research.q: AI-native engineering services firms (e.g., Hadrian-style for engineering, CoLab, Diffuse Bio?, "engineering copilots" like Leo AI, Kittyhawk? Quilter for PCBs, Zoo CAD, Autodesk AI): could they produce substantiation?
research.headline: No. AI engineering copilots (Leo AI, CoLab, Quilter, PhysicsX, Luminary, Zoo, Autodesk) do design, analysis and internal design review. None of them produces regulator-format substantiation (a CFR compliance matrix, a test plan, 8110-3/SAR packages), uses accepted allowables or methods, or takes on signer liability. The few certification-focused players (Xcert AI with CHF 1.1M; Istari Digital) target new-type development and model-based digital certification, not equivalence for reverse-engineered parts. So the reviewer-side and equivalence-side of the pathway is open, and copilots are suppliers to an Approval Factory rather than competitors.

findings.finding: Leo AI is a mechanical copilot that 'identifies the right formulas, runs the calculations and cites trusted sources'. It claims about 1/3 fewer design mistakes. It makes no certification or substantiation claims. Seed led by Flint Capital (~Sep 2025). Customers include Scania, HP and Siemens.

CoLab's AutoReview is an 'AI Peer Checker trained on your design standards'. It auto-annotates drawings and CAD and flags non-conformances against the customer's internal standards, not against regulatory rules. It has a multimillion-dollar AI contract with Bombardier. This is the closest analog to cutting reviewer hours.
Quilter automates PCB placement and routing and 'shows you every physics check it ran'. It is marketed to A&D for 'validation and TRR', but makes no DO-254 or qualification claim.

PhysicsX and Luminary Cloud sell AI physics surrogates. These speed up search, but regulators accept 'tests and computations' only with validated methods and accepted allowables (MMPDS/CMH-17). An ML surrogate is not an accepted means of compliance.
findings.number: PhysicsX $135M B (Jun 2025) + reported $300M C at $2.4B; Luminary $72M B (Sep 2025)

findings.finding: Xcert AI (Geneva, founded 2024, 12 people) automates aerospace certification and compliance workflows: documentation, verification planning, test procedures. It has unnamed pilots. The Air Current reports about 50% of outputs are usable, and its CEO says it will 'augment, not replace'. It is aimed at new development, not PMA or reverse-engineering.

Istari Digital (Will Roper, recalled) is a digital-engineering platform claiming to 'validate and certify system integrity in real time' and to cut 'validation cycles from months to minutes'. Its site headlines Department of the Air Force 'Industry Øne'. It makes no explicit airworthiness-acceptance claim. It is the strategically closest player on government acceptance of model-based certification.
Smaller CAD and simulation agent startups (Navier AI $5.6M Dec 2025, unverified; MecAgent $3M seed May 2025; Hestus $7.4M seed) all target design productivity. None targets approval packages.

Substantiation needs things copilots structurally lack: proprietary legacy specs, accepted allowables, physical test and conformity (a physics clock), a Part 21 quality system, and a DER, ODA or ESA signer (law and liability). Copilots touch only the analysis and documentation layers.
findings.source: 14 CFR 21.303, FAA Order 8110.37 (DER), DLA SAR process (opinion and recall)

research.q: Software compliance automation (Vanta, Drata, Secureframe, Hyperproof) and regulated-industry compliance AI (Norm Ai, Hebbia for compliance, Greenlite? for building permits, PermitFlow, Pulley?): the analog business model and whether anyone ports it to hardware certification.
research.headline: Vanta's model (about $300M ARR, $4.15B valuation) works because it automates the applicant's evidence and pulls the verifier onto its platform: 100+ audit firms and 26k audits run through it. Nobody I found has ported that model to FAA PMA/DER, DLA Source Approval or other legacy-part certification. The closest cases (Ketryx in medtech software, Flow Engineering and Nominal for new hardware programs, Xcert AI with CHF 1.1M in aerospace) all work on the applicant side for new designs and leave the reviewer bottleneck and signed physical evidence untouched.

findings.finding: Vanta passed $300M ARR (tripled in two years) with 16,000+ customers, ~60% YoY customer growth, NRR above 100%, $500M+ raised and ~1,000 staff
Vanta valued at $4.15B in its July 2025 $150M Series D led by Wellington

Vanta's auditor network: 100+ partner audit firms (A-LIGN, Schellman, Coalfire), 26,000+ audits completed through the platform, an Auditor API, and audits about 50% faster. The moat is co-opting the verifier, not replacing it
Drata at about $98M ARR as of Jan 2025, last valued at $2B (Dec 2022)

Norm Ai encodes regulations as agents and runs Norm Law, an AI-native law firm, so it owns the sign-off. Funding: $48M Jan 2025, +$50M Blackstone Nov 2025, then a $120M Series C at $1.2B led by Khosla in June 2026

PermitFlow runs applicant-side permit agents across 7K+ jurisdictions. It raised $54M (Series B), claims $20B+ construction value permitted, and its moat is a corpus of 12M+ data points on reviewer comments and approval decisions

CivCheck/ComplyAI (now a Clariti company) does verifier-side AI plan review. It is free to cities and applicants pay a prescreen fee; reviews take 20-30 minutes versus 1-1.5 hours. This is the template for a verification-side play
Greenlite is AML/KYC AI for fintechs, not building permits. greenlite.ai now 301-redirects to Bretton AI (YC S23), which sells financial back-office agents, so a rebrand seems likely (not confirmed)

Ketryx does AI validation and traceability for medtech software, producing FDA/EU MDR-ready docs. It closed a $39M Series B in Sept 2025 ($55M+ total), counts 3 of the top 5 medtechs as customers, and claims 90% less documentation time. It is the closest Vanta-for-hardware-regulator analog but covers software lifecycle only

No company was found doing Vanta-style evidence packaging or a reviewer portal for DLA SARs, FAA PMA or DER 8110-3 packages. This is a negative result from a limited search budget

research.q: Building permits and code compliance AI (PermitFlow, Greenlite, CodeComply, UpCodes, Archistar, Singapore CORENET X): did AI plan review get regulator acceptance? Speed-ups achieved?
research.headline: No regulator I could verify accepts AI as the legal approver of building plans. Everywhere it is deployed, AI is either an advisory pre-check (Archistar in Austin and LA, Singapore's CORENET X model checker, CodeComply) or sits inside a licensed human's stamp under private-provider statutes (GreenLite). The real speed-ups (6+ months down to about 10 days, 90-120 days down to 21-45) came from the legal lever that lets a private licensed reviewer replace a backlogged agency queue, and the money went to whoever holds that permission, which is the same pattern as the Approval Factory thesis.

findings.finding: Austin adopted Archistar eCheck in Oct 2024 after a 3-month pilot, as a pre-check for single-family zoning only; it 'does not review every element'. A second pilot with the ICC covers the IBC. No time-savings metrics were published.

LA City and County use eCheck as an 'AI Pre-Plan Check' for the wildfire rebuild (Executive Directive 10, EO1 like-for-like zoning, EO8 iteration Sept 2025), funded by philanthropy (RiseLA). Applicants attach the report link to their application, humans still review, and the county is 'checking for accuracy'. Archistar's vendor claim is review cycles cut from 3+ to 1 and some unnamed cities allowing 0 (full automated approval), with permit time from 12 months to instant or under 1-2 months.

ICC became a reseller of Archistar eCheck on 24 Jul 2025 and integrated its Code Connect API (machine-readable I-Codes). An 11-city pilot reported 'significant improvements' with no figures. ICC does not certify the AI.

GreenLite raised a $49.5M Series B (Insight Partners, Sept 2025) on the thesis of 'privatization of permitting' through private plan review, and claims 75% faster timelines. Its site claims 90-120+ days down to 21-45 days, first comments in 7 days, and 0.5 resubmission cycles. Certified in-house experts stamp the plans.

In East Hampton NY, GreenLite is one of 4 outside firms clearing a backlog of more than 6 months. A licensed GreenLite architect QA's each AI review, and the town gives final approval; the town itself uses no AI. One builder got his review back in 10 days. Complaints: AI flags items 'not relevant or actually wrong', goes beyond the town's 100-point checklist, and misreads plans.

CodeComply.Ai partnered with CivicPlus on 19 Mar 2026 and claims to cut reviews 'from months to minutes'. Its own disclaimer says automated checks 'do not replace professional review' and that final determinations stay with qualified reviewers. No jurisdictions or metrics are named.

PermitFlow ($54M Series B) is an applicant-side expediter with AI agents for intake, research, submission, coordination and issuance. It covers 7,000+ AHJs and $20B+ in construction value, and claims 2.5x faster approvals. It does not do code review and has no regulator acceptance as a reviewer.

Singapore CORENET X: Qualified Persons submit one coordinated BIM model and 11 agencies return one consolidated response. It became mandatory for new projects on 1 Apr 2025. The Automated Model Checker (7 agencies' rules, as a pre-submission check) 'will be implemented progressively in later phases', with no date. No approval-time reduction is claimed. Its predecessor, e-PlanCheck (early 2000s), was 'not quite working yet' in 2005.

The legal lever is private-provider statutes. Under Florida 553.791 a licensed engineer, architect or code administrator can do the official review, with deemed approval if the city misses its deadline. Texas and others added third-party review when deadlines lapse. GreenLite says nearly 25% of states advanced such laws in 3 years. (Florida and Texas details are recalled; flsenate.gov returned 429.)
findings.source: recalled; GreenLite release for the 25% figure

research.q: Battery, EV and grid equipment certification (UL 9540A, UL 1741, IEEE 1547, NRTL field evaluation): any AI acceleration players; queue times at NRTLs.
research.headline: I found AI startups only on the paperwork layer of battery, inverter and EV-charger certification: Fuchsia (YC Spring 2026) and Hardware Compliance draft technical files and test plans and match products to labs. Nobody AI-native sits where the permission is held: the testing lab (an OSHA-recognised lab, NRTL, or a field-evaluation body), reuse or simulation of fire-test data in place of physical burns, or local fire-marshal review. The NRTL timeline is mostly queue and manual work rather than physics. An inverter grid-compliance test (UL 1741 SB / IEEE 1547.1) took 9-12 weeks of lab time in 2022, plus about 18 weeks for certificate, listing and logistics, while an automated test bench now claims about 32 hours of actual test time.

findings.finding: IREC (a clean-energy standards nonprofit) estimated 9-12 weeks of NRTL test time per inverter family for UL 1741 SB / IEEE 1547.1. At 9 weeks, the labs could clear 85% of inverter families in about 54 weeks. The estimate is based on a survey of 11 manufacturers, 95 inverter families and 3 major NRTLs.
findings.number: 9-12 weeks per family; 54-72 weeks to clear 85% of families

findings.finding: IREC's guidance was to add about 18 weeks to test time for certificate, listing and logistics. The certificate itself takes about 1-2 weeks, the CEC's qualified-equipment list about 1 month, and shipping logistics 2-6 months (3 typical).

An automated test bench from Pacific Power Source, QualityLogic and Tektronix EA, launched April 30, 2026, claims about 32 hours of actual test time against IREC's 8-12 weeks of manual NRTL testing. This is a vendor claim. It suggests most of the calendar time is scheduling and manual work, not physics.

SunSpec projected about 50 companies and about 1,000 products needing 10-12 weeks of testing each, a surge on NRTL capacity. UL noted the 1547.1-2020 standard is 263 pages, versus 54 for the first edition.

UL 9540A is the battery fire-propagation test, run at cell, module, unit and installation levels; it produces data rather than a pass/fail. The 6th edition drops unit-level testing for most systems and adds a large-scale fire test that assumes a post-explosion condition. UL publishes no cost or lead time. From memory, not verified: large burns cost hundreds of thousands to over $1M, each destroys the hardware, and only a handful of sites worldwide can run them.

Fuchsia (YC Spring 2026, San Francisco, founder Tony Gao, team of 3) pitches itself as 'Vanta for hardware'. AI agents draft technical files and test plans and coordinate partner labs, for robots, medical devices and IoT. It does not mention grid or battery storage.

Hardware Compliance (launched around March 2026) is an AI platform that reads standards, drafts technical files, test plans and hazard analyses, and matches products to labs, with expert review. It lists UL 3100, UL 3300, IEC 62368, FCC, CE, 510(k), FAA and MIL-STD. It does not name UL 9540A or UL 1741.

UL Solutions launched AI-safety certification under UL 3115 in November 2025; the first certificates went to Qcells' data-center energy management system and Omniconn. The incumbent is positioning to certify AI products, not to use AI to shorten its own queue.

Hardware startups hire in-house certification engineers with a track record at UL, CSA or Intertek specifically for UL 9540A and UL 1741 (example: an Exowatt job posting). The work is done by people today.

research.q: Pharmaceutical/biotech AI that shortens regulatory proof (in-silico trials, Certara, Unlearn.AI digital twins, FDA model-informed drug development) as an analog for parts qualification.
research.headline: Pharma has already industrialised "model evidence instead of physical evidence". It uses a risk-tiered context-of-use credibility framework (ASME V&V 40, FDA 2023/2025, ICH M15), models that replace ancillary studies (Simcyp: 120 FDA-approved drugs supported in lieu of clinical studies), and AI methods qualified once and reused, whose statistical validity does not depend on the AI being right (Unlearn PROCOVA, EMA-qualified Sep 2022). Parts qualification has none of this formal machinery even though its physics is far easier to model than biology, so the verification-side play is to import it: a credibility standard for reverse-engineered parts, covariate-adjusted specimen reduction, a qualified inverse-characterisation method, and a reviewer-side tool, all run inside the Approval Factory rather than sold as a Certara-style tool (Certara is only about $419M revenue and a $1.5B market cap).

findings.finding: Simcyp PBPK has supported 120 FDA-approved novel drugs in lieu of clinical studies; 80 recent PBPK-using approvals used Simcyp; 11 regulatory agencies themselves use or license it; it was built via a 25-year, 37-company consortium with 29 population libraries
What models replace in pharma is mostly ancillary studies (DDI, organ impairment, paediatric dosing), not the pivotal efficacy trial
Certara revenue $335.6M (2022), $354.3M (2023), $385.2M (2024), $418.8M (2025); market cap about $1.49B. A near-monopoly verification-tool vendor captures modest value

EMA CHMP final qualification of Unlearn PROCOVA (Phase II/III, continuous outcomes) on 28 Sep 2022; control arms cut by up to 35%; application April 2021, so about 17 months to qualification and about 5 years from founding

Unlearn's acceptance came from designing the method so that model quality affects only efficiency, never validity (type-I error and bias guaranteed). It abandoned synthetic external controls because regulators saw them as biased
Unlearn has raised about $130-135M ($12M A 2020, $50M B 2022, $50M C led by Altimeter Feb 2024)

FDA MIDD Paired Meeting Program runs FY2023-2027 (CDER/CBER), with packages due 47/60 days before the meetings; these are not milestone meetings; ICH M15 MIDD general-principles guidance announced June 2026
findings.source: FDA MIDD page via search snippet (fetch returned 401): https://www.fda.gov/drugs/development-resources/model-informed-drug-development-paired-meeting-program

findings.finding: Credibility frameworks (recalled): ASME V&V 40-2018 (model risk = influence x consequence for a stated context of use); FDA CDRH final guidance on computational modelling credibility, Nov 2023; FDA draft AI guidance for drugs with a 7-step credibility framework, Jan 2025; FDA Modernization Act 2.0, Dec 2022; FDA animal-testing phase-out roadmap, Apr 2025

Parts side has building-block 'certification by analysis' (CMH-17, AC 20-107B, 14 CFR 25.307 'analysis supported by test') but no ML/COU credibility guidance for reverse-engineered-part equivalence (none found)
findings.source: https://cw.mydigitalpublication.com/may-2025/page-10 ; NIAR Olivares slides; absence is opinion

findings.finding: Senvol ML is the closest parts analog to PROCOVA: ML to qualify AM processes and allowables with less data, under a US Army Research Laboratory (ARL) contract via NCMS/AMMP with Lockheed MFC and EWI

Build 'PROCOVA for specimens': covariate-adjusted allowables and equivalency testing using twin predictions, with a type-I error guarantee independent of model quality, and get one-time method acceptance from NCAMP/CMH-17, MMPDS or AFLCMC/NAVAIR

research.q: Defense electronics FFF replacement and legacy chip emulation (e.g., Rochester, GEOTEK? Ultra Librarian? Teledyne e2v continuation, Sarnoff? Find real companies; DMEA Trusted Foundry; SRI) and whether AI is used for netlist/firmware reconstruction.
research.headline: Rebuilding legacy chips is an old, crowded business. Rochester (licensed continuation plus the SRP re-creation process), Tekmos, KaiSemi, DMEA's ATSP foundry, Innovasic and Lansdale all do it, mostly with deterministic SEM-to-netlist tools and engineers fixing errors by hand; AI for netlist extraction exists only in academic work (CNNs, GNNs, fine-tuned SAM2), and this run found no company or DoD award for it. The open gap is on the verification side: working out what an old part actually does, measuring and proving that a replacement matches it, and packaging that proof so DLA and program-office reviewers accept it. That points to an AI 'behavioural equivalence engine' that feeds the Approval Factory, not a competitor to the re-creation houses.

findings.finding: Rochester's Semiconductor Replication Process re-creates exact replicas (delayer, SEM image, redesign on a matched mature process): 83 replication projects in 18 months and 30+ in progress (2010); has agreements with most major semiconductor manufacturers; in one case two earlier emulation attempts failed before SRP worked
Rochester holds about 15B devices in stock and reverse-engineers legacy ASICs, including for A320 life extension (2025 interview)

Tekmos flow: SEM each layer, then GDS, SPICE netlist and gate-level Verilog; opens and shorts fixed by hand against the images; FPGA emulators run in customer systems to catch rare cases; no AI mentioned
KaiSemi automatically converts EOL FPGA/ASIC netlists into drop-in ASICs with zero NRE, delivery in up to 20 weeks, and claims 500+ conversions (vendor claim, 2011)
Navy SBIR N05-031 'ASIC Forensic Redesign' (Crossfield Technology, 2005): extract transistors, build a gate netlist, map to a standard-cell library on an older process
IARPA RAVEN (2016): image all layers of 1 cm2 of a 10/14nm IC in 25 days; performers Varioscale and MIT; T&E by national labs and NIST
SoK of 187 hardware-reverse-engineering papers: key results reproducible for only 7 (about 4%); no benchmarks; legal barriers to sharing data; widening gap to modern process nodes

Academic AI for IC image and netlist analysis: GANs, CNNs and GNNs (NTU's Gwee, 2024); SAM2 with a topology loss for metal-line segmentation (2026); destructive imaging produces hundreds of GB of images
A 2021 survey says netlist extraction is well understood but specification discovery (what the circuit does) remains open
(recalled) DLA's GEM and later AME microcircuit emulation programs were run by Sarnoff (now SRI); DMEA runs the ATSP flexible foundry for obsolete parts and accredits Trusted suppliers

research.q: FAA PMA by identicality and by test & computation (14 CFR 21.303/Part 21 Subpart K): every step, who does it, elapsed time, cost, where the queue is (ACO/MIDO staffing), what is manual, what nobody does well.
research.headline: FAA PMA by test and computation takes about 9-18 months for complex parts (each FAA comment cycle adds 4-8 weeks). Most of that time goes to reviewer queues and rework, not to physical tests. Identicality without an OEM licence is effectively a data-rights route, since reverse engineering is not accepted as proof of identicality (recalled). The verification-side AI play is to own or arm the reviewer seat (DER/ODA delegated compliance finding, pre-submission gap prediction, process forensics, digital conformity) rather than only generating packages. My three web searches found no AI-native PMA house; the nearest is Xcert AI, a 12-person general aerospace-certification startup.

findings.finding: 21.303(b): the design needs drawings and specs for dimensions, materials and processes. Test reports and computations are required unless the applicant shows the design is identical to a TC design. A licensed design needs evidence of the licence. A T&C applicant must certify compliance.

Identicality or simple parts take 'a matter of months'. Complex or engine-critical T&C packages take 9-18 months, and each comment cycle adds about 4-8 weeks. Top causes of delay: filing incomplete packages, not mapping requirements at project start, engaging the DER late, and overlooking the quality system review.

Under the older process, each replacement design needed ACO approval regardless of risk, so low-risk proposals compete for limited ACO resources. Order 8110.119 created a streamlined path for non-safety-significant articles using a uniform data package.
Reverse engineering is not accepted as evidence of identicality. Identicality without a licence needs lawful possession of the type design data, so it is a data-rights route.

Production approval needs an organization document, an accountable manager (21.305), and a quality system per 21.137 (21.307), evaluated by MIDO. A PMA is non-transferable (21.314), facility moves need approval (21.309), and major changes need prior approval (21.319).

Large PMA houses (HEICO units, Wencor, Chromalloy) hold PMA ODAs that let them find compliance internally. That delegation is a structural throughput advantage and helps explain HEICO's roughly 400-550 new PMAs a year.

Xcert AI (Geneva, founded 2024) raised CHF 1.1M led by Spicehaus in Dec 2025. Its AI platform for aerospace certification and compliance workflows is general rather than PMA-specific, and it has 12 staff.
Fleetcraft raised a $3.2M seed in Jan 2025 for an AI aircraft-inspection co-pilot, adjacent to verification rather than PMA.
PMA parts can cost 30-50% less than OEM parts. PMA Products (acquired by McFarlane) has 35,000+ FAA-approved parts.

Typical cost ranges: simple parts roughly $20-100k; safety-significant T&C roughly $100-500k; engine LLP or hot-section parts $1M+ and 2-4 years. DER rates roughly $150-300/hr. The FAA charges no application fee.

The FAA charges no PMA fee and publishes no queue metrics, so the cost of approval is entirely applicant engineering plus waiting time

research.q: FAA DER-approved repairs and major repair data (8110-3, Form 337), plus EASA Part 21 Subpart M repairs and DOA privileges: full pathway, time, cost, bottlenecks.
research.headline: Outside the OEMs, getting a structural repair approved (FAA 8110-3 or 8100-9, EASA RDAS or a DOA under Subpart M) is limited mainly by permission: who holds OEM loads and fatigue data, a small and aging pool of people allowed to sign, and lessors refusing non-OEM repairs. Physics tests rarely set the pace. No company turned up in this session's searches that uses AI to produce approved repair data at scale, so the opening on the verification side is an AI house that rebuilds OEM-equivalent structural models, automates static and fatigue substantiation, and has its own repair approval bodies (FAA ODA, EASA DOA) to sign.

findings.finding: The FAA has no repair-design-approval subpart: 14 CFR Part 21 Subpart M is marked [Reserved]. Repair data approval is spread across Part 43 Appendix A, designee orders (8110.4, 8110.37, 8100.15, 8300.16) and FSDO field approvals. EASA Part 21 Subpart M (21.A.431-445) instead requires an approved design for every repair.
findings.source: eCFR fetch (Part 21 Subpart M reserved); SASSOFIA 2020 https://sassofia.com/blog/aircraft-leasing-structural-repair-technical-records-considerations/

findings.finding: Boeing approves repairs outside the SRM on FAA Form 8100-9 under its ODA. A DER signs 8110-3 and can sign 8100-9 only as an ODA unit member. Airbus uses the RDAS/RAS under its DOA for ATA 52-57 and the ATA 27 interface, and a Technical Adaptation for systems.

Practitioner advice: an 8110-3 usually covers one aircraft, and reusing the data means rewriting it as a part-number procedure approved by a DER with procedure authority. Approvals are bespoke and do not build up across a fleet.

Typical out-of-SRM transport repair: 20-200 h for a simple repair, 300-1,000+ h for a complex one. All-in cost about $3k-150k. Consultant DERs bill $150-300/h. Grounded-aircraft (AOG) cost is $10-150k/day. Figures are recalled, not verified.

For principal structural elements, damage tolerance is approved in three stages (static strength to return to service; a fatigue inspection program within about 12 months; special requirements) under 14 CFR 26.43/121.1109 and AC 120-93. Fatigue/crack-growth specialists are the scarcest skill. Recalled.
findings.source: recalled AC 120-93 / Aging Airplane Safety Rule

findings.finding: A non-TCH EASA DOA must show access to type-certificate data or produce its own (21.A.433), so data access is the legal gate. FAA DERs likewise need OEM loads and allowables or have to substantiate from scratch, which pushes them to heavy, conservative repairs.
Roughly 2,500-3,000 active FAA DERs and about 350-400 EASA DOAs; the DER population is aging. Recalled.

Forerunner (YC F24) now calls itself an AI-native factory making precision bent tubes for aerospace and defense, not a repair-engineering company. Aiir Innovations (NL, EUR 0.5M) does AI engine borescope inspection. Neither produces approved repair data.

Industry view (ePlane AI, Mar 2026): AI in MRO is limited to support roles, and the FAA's 2024 AI roadmap starts with low-risk uses away from safety-critical systems. AI as the signer is off the table for now; AI as the producer of data a human signs is not.

Lessors and insurers often refuse DER/independent repairs at lease return, especially without fatigue data, and lease clauses demand OEM approval. Market acceptance is a separate barrier from regulator acceptance.

Give regulators an independent re-analysis tool so FAA ACOs and EASA staff can audit designee packages quickly.

Hold the right to sign: hire consultant DERs, then get an FAA repair ODA (about 1-3 years) and an EASA DOA with 21.A.263(c) repair privileges, so the company appoints its own signers instead of waiting on per-person FAA appointments.
Create a lessor-grade repair dossier (digital twin, fatigue data, records) backed by insurance or a residual-value warranty, to break 'OEM-only' lease clauses.

surprises: 14 CFR Part 21 Subpart M is reserved. The FAA has no repair-design-approval subpart, so US repair approval is a patchwork of designee forms.
An 8110-3 is often tied to one aircraft, so independent repair data rarely builds up into a reusable asset the way OEM SRM data does.
The YC 'AI for MRO' company (Forerunner) pivoted to an AI-native bent-tube factory, so nobody in YC appears to sit on the repair-approval path.
Repairs are mostly analysis, not physical testing, so physics barely limits them. The binding gates are data access, signer appointment and lessor acceptance.

research.q: DLA Source Approval Request (SAR) and AMSC codes, Engineering Support Activity reviews, Category I/II SARs, Critical Safety Items: full pathway, time (data), approval rates, bottlenecks, what is undone.
research.headline: On a DLA Source Approval Request, the slow and scarce step is the Engineering Support Activity (ESA) review, not building the package or running the tests. The published path is about 5-6 months (ESA response target 90 days), most packages that reach a decision are approved (about 91% in DLA's own data), and the value sits in a large backlog. One real case took about 2.5 years, of which roughly 14 weeks was physical testing. The open verification-side AI play is the reviewer's side: tools for the ESA, and the government reference data whose absence causes rejections. Only one $110k USAF STTR award (ELEVAN/UTSA, 2024) has tried it, and I found no Phase II.

findings.finding: Published DLA Land and Maritime SAR clock: CAO logs and forwards to Value Engineering in 5 days; Value Engineering reviews in 15 days with 7 analysts; 30 days for missing data; ESA review has a 90-day response time; VE concurs in 15 days; up to 30 more days for data; notification letter in 5 days. That is about 5-6 months if nothing loops.

DLA Land and Maritime FY16: 211 packages received, 55 approved ($2.35M annual savings), 184 pending ($28.5M annual savings). Value Engineering accepts 90% of packages as complete. The pending backlog holds about 12x the savings of approved items.

RPPOB (government lends or sells stock to firms for reverse engineering), 2014-16: 742 bailment requests from 99 CAGEs and 190 agreements led to only 55 SARs (7%). Of those, 40 were approved, 4 rejected and 11 pending, so about 91% of decided cases were approved. Only 17 NSNs reached a procurement. DLA says full approval typically takes 12-18 months; minimum annual buy is $10K; not available for AMSC B, G or T.
findings.number: 7% request-to-SAR; ~91% approval of decided cases; 12-18 months

findings.finding: Stated rejection reasons include 'Can't validate part (no government data to compare)', 'weapons criticality', business case, incomplete package, and application discontinued. Another response type is 'Need to complete qualification testing: good on paper, but need to prove will work'.

DAG 17.7501-6 (June 2014): a newly approved source gets a multi-source award clause for at least 1 year, and 40% of the award if its price is fair and reasonable even when not lowest. The NSN is pulled from auto-solicitation and long-term contracts. This is a built-in demand guarantee for approvals.

AMSC codes gate SAR eligibility: B (source-control drawing), C (engineering source approval by the design control activity), D (no data or specs) are SAR-able. G and T are competitive and DLA does not evaluate SARs on them. Q means a reverse-engineering candidate; P, R and U mean data rights unavailable or breakout uneconomic. Full screening is 65 steps with a default 25% savings factor; suspense dates are 12 months for limited screening and 3 to 5 years for full screening; status on a code-review request is due in 60 days.

For aviation and ship Critical Safety Items, the head of the design control activity (the service systems command that owns airworthiness), not the contracting officer, decides qualification, and must do so before award. The law also requires written standards, a 'prompt opportunity' to qualify, revalidation every 7 years, and the government may pay small businesses' qualification test costs when fewer than 2 sources exist. Agencies need not delay a buy for a qualification.

JMS Southeast case (DLA SBIR DLA254-P01, $27,205): SAR first submitted October 2023, revised with government engineers through 2024, final first-article testing at Tinker AFB from 24 Sep 2025 to 23 Mar 2026. Tests were dimensions (4 weeks), material (4 weeks) and form/fit/function (6 weeks). About 2.5 years for one NSN, of which physical testing was about 14 weeks.

sbir.gov lists 284 awards matching 'source approval', almost all DLA per-NSN awards to small shops. Examples: Parts Life, Micro-Precision, AMG Engineering (11 bearing NSNs), Form Fit and Function, Bascom Hunter, Dynovas, A&B Foundry. It is a cottage industry, one NSN at a time.

The only reviewer-side AI award found: ELEVAN LLC with UTSA, USAF STTR Phase I AFX23E-TPCSO1, FA8649-24-P-0130, $109,997, Feb-May 2024. It proposed AI/ML plus computer vision to speed review and approval of supportability analysis requests and 'save engineers thousands of unbudgeted hours'. No Phase II was found.

Navy: Ohio-class submarine part lead times reach 1,261 days, and engineers 'manually scour hundreds of sources' for alternates. The paper (NPS Acquisition Research Symposium 2024) proposes an LLM that ranks alternate parts, which shows government-side engineering decisions are still manual.
Novineer's AI reverse-engineering tool (CAD from phone photos, 0.72 mm mean deviation) makes no SAR or airworthiness approval claims. Applicant-side AI produces knowledge, not permission.

(recalled) SAR categories: I is the identical item previously made for the OEM, prime or government; IA, IB and IC are variants such as a changed process or approval by another agency; II is a similar item; III (in several guides) is reverse-engineered with no prior supply and needs a full technical data package plus qualification. Critical Safety Item and Category III SARs reportedly take 1-3 years.

pathway_steps.step: 0. AMC/AMSC breakout coding (65-step screening; default 25% savings factor)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Service and DLA breakout or competition offices
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Codes U, R, P, Q and L are economic judgements from stale cost models. Nobody re-screens the whole file now that AI makes packages cheap, and DLA turns down low-demand items.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Candidate selection (DIBBS, Haystack, SERVA, DLA candidate lists)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Nobody ranks NSNs systematically by approvable value times demand times category.

pathway_steps.step: 2. RPPOB bailment or purchase of a sample part
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Only 7% of bailment requests became SARs, because package cost exceeds expected value.

pathway_steps.step: 3. Package build (Category I/II prior-supply or similarity argument, or Category III reverse-engineered technical data package plus test plan)
pathway_steps.time: ~10 weeks when done well; often much longer
pathway_steps.cost: $27k-$100k+ per NSN in SBIR terms; up to ~$100k and 300-1,000 hours for complex parts
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Hand-built PDFs, no standard structure, every NSN starts from scratch, no batching across NSNs.

pathway_steps.step: 4. Competition Advocate Office intake and logging
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Submission via DoD SAFE file transfer; no structured data.

pathway_steps.step: 5. Value Engineering completeness and business-case review
pathway_steps.who_does_it: DLA VE (7 analysts at Land and Maritime)
pathway_steps.time: 15 days, plus 30 days for missing data
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual checklist; 90% pass. Easy to automate.

pathway_steps.step: 6. ESA / design-control-activity engineering review (Critical Safety Items always go here)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Service engineers at the air logistics centers (Robins, Tinker, Hill), NAVAIR, Army aviation command
pathway_steps.time: 90-day target; in practice 1-3 years with repeated loops (one case about 2.5 years)
pathway_steps.cost: Government engineer hours ('thousands of unbudgeted hours')
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The binding bottleneck: no tooling, no record of past decisions, no government reference data ('can't validate part'), liability pushes toward 'need more data'.

pathway_steps.step: 7. Qualification and first-article testing (AFMC Form 260: dimensions, material, form/fit/function)
pathway_steps.time: ~14 weeks for a simple part; months to years for engine or flight Critical Safety Items
pathway_steps.cost: Applicant pays; government may pay for small businesses
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Physics clock is real but a minor share of elapsed time. No credit for modelling, no remote witnessing, no shared test specimens across NSNs.

pathway_steps.step: 8. VE concurrence, cataloguing the new source, notification letter
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual.

pathway_steps.step: 9. Next procurement (40% share for the new source under DAG 17.7501-6)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Approval does not mean revenue until the next buy cycle.

what_would_need_to_be_done: A machine-readable SAR evidence standard (each requirement linked to a claim and its evidence, with a model-based technical data package) adopted by one ESA and DLA Value Engineering, using 10 USC 3243's written-standards and prompt-opportunity duties as leverage.

An ESA reviewer workbench inside government networks: auto-completeness against the SAR guide, comparison of scan and material data to any government reference, auto-drafted decisions with every claim cited, and a list of physical tests still required. Path is SBIR/OTA with Tinker or Robins, plus authorization to run on IL4/5 networks with controlled technical and ITAR data.

Build the government's missing comparison baseline: CT, scanning and material fingerprints of serviceable stock and fleet parts (RPPOB bailment already allows access), so that 'can't validate part' rejections disappear.

Precedent and similarity qualification: a graph across stock numbers so that one approved reverse-engineered (Category III) SAR turns sibling NSNs into lighter Category II cases. This needs ESA policy accepting qualification by part family.

Re-screen the AMSC file with new cost economics: mine the federal catalog, DIBBS buy history and AMSC codes for P, R, Q, U and L items whose breakout is now economic, and file code-review requests (government must give status within 60 days).
Portfolio SARs covering whole platform subsystems (for example C-130 or KC-135 parts that are not Critical Safety Items) under one shared test plan, replacing per-NSN SBIR awards.

Testing credited by models for non-Critical-Safety-Item parts first, then Critical Safety Items with a probabilistic risk argument, accepted in writing by one ESA. Run the remaining physical tests in parallel in an owned lab.
Signed, tamper-evident instrument data so the design control activity can accept remote conformity and remote first-article witnessing.
A risk-accounting framework (possibly NDAA language) that credits the readiness risk of staying sole-source (lead times up to 1,261 days) against the risk of approving a new source.
ai_plays: 'ESA in a box': a reviewer copilot sold or given to air logistics center ESAs and DLA Value Engineering/Competition Advocate offices; KPI is reviewer hours per decision; the moat is the corpus of past decisions. Only ELEVAN's lapsed $110k Phase I precedes it.
A government digital-baseline service (CT, metrology and material fingerprinting of existing stock) sold to DLA as the missing comparison data; it doubles as counterfeit screening.
An AMSC re-screening and portfolio-selection engine that feeds an Approval Factory with NSNs that are now economic to approve.
A similarity and part-family qualification engine that turns one approval into many.
An applicant-side pre-submission scorer that predicts the ESA's decision, for the 284+ SBIR SAR shops (weaker on its own; useful as a feeder).
Integrated: an Approval Factory whose packages are pre-formatted for the reviewer tool it supplies to the ESA, so it cuts its own queue time.
surprises: Most SARs that reach a decision are approved (about 91% in RPPOB data, 40 of 44). The losses happen before submission (7% of bailment requests became SARs) and in the queue (184 pending against 55 approved), not at the decision itself.
In the one dated case (JMS Southeast), physical testing was about 14 weeks of a roughly 2.5-year journey.
DLA already guarantees demand to newly approved sources: 40% of the award for at least 1 year under DAG 17.7501-6.
Pending SARs at DLA Land and Maritime held about 12x the savings of approved ones.
A top rejection reason is that the government has no data of its own to compare against. That is an information gap, not a quality failure.
There are 284 'source approval' SBIR awards, all per-NSN to small shops; nobody operates at factory scale.
Every primary DLA, DoD IG, DTIC and GAO host returned 403 to this sandbox, so DLA Aviation volume and backlog figures remain unverified (recalled).

research.q: Military airworthiness and Critical Safety Item qualification (MIL-HDBK-516, Joint Aeronautical Commanders Group CSI guidance, Navy/Army/AF technical authority): full pathway and bottlenecks for a non-OEM part.
research.headline: By law (FY2004 NDAA Sec. 802 / DFARS 209.270), only a short-staffed government design control activity (the service engineering authority) can approve a source for an aviation critical safety item, so the main bottleneck is reviewer queue time and the request-for-information loop, not engineering. In GAO B-409950 a request sat about 12 weeks before review began, was reviewed for 3.5 months, then went on hold with information requests in 6 areas while the incumbent won a 5-year contract. Within my limited search (3 web searches, most .mil sites blocked) I found no one building AI for the government reviewers, a machine-readable approval package, or qualification by part family. The strongest verification-side play is an equivalence-evidence engine (CT scanning, metallurgy, inferring how a part was made) combined with a copilot for government reviewers.

findings.finding: For many items, a Category IV (reverse-engineered) Source Approval Request needs the Military Service's concurrence before the applicant can buy or borrow a sample. The sample program (RPPOB) excludes procurement codes G/T and B, specification-controlled items, and items with under $10k annual demand. Reverse engineering is done at the supplier's own expense. Each service (NAVAIR, Air Force, Army) also has its own SAR guidance on top of DLA's.

Rotair's request to become an approved source for overhauling Black Hawk drag braces (a critical safety item): DLA received it Feb 3 2014. Review began Apr 28 (about 12 weeks in queue). On Aug 15 it was put on hold with information requests in 6 areas and a 60-day response deadline. GAO ruled the delay 'not unreasonable' and said agencies need not hold off an award while a request is pending.
findings.number: 12 wk queue + 15 wk review + 60-day response deadline

findings.finding: Because the drag brace is a critical safety item, the competition was limited to 2 approved sources, Sikorsky and Overhaul Support Services. The 5-year IDIQ covered 1,224 drag braces against a backlog of 579, and Overhaul won it.

Engineering-activity backlogs are an old problem: older GAO protests cite a 'long waiting list' (Kitco, 1991) and 6 months of agency inaction after 3 weeks of actual processing. GAO also found 4 months for an alternate-item evaluation 'not unusual'.

Approval requests come in four categories: I same part, II similar part, III new part/manufacturer, IV reverse-engineered part. DLA can only route requests; for critical safety items the service engineering authority must approve.

(Recalled) The statute (FY2004 NDAA Sec. 802, now in Title 10) and DFARS 209.270 put approval of critical-safety-item sources with the design control activity. The airworthiness authorities are NAVAIR AIR-4.0P, the Army's DEVCOM Aviation & Missile Center under AR 70-62, and the Air Force airworthiness authority under AFI 62-601. MIL-HDBK-516C accepts compliance by analysis, test, inspection, demonstration or similarity. DoD has no designee path like the FAA's DER/ODA.
DLA sources-sought notices from May-June 2026 ask companies to submit approval requests under the JACG handbook, i.e. DLA is actively soliciting new sources.

The verification-side companies found are adjacent, not approval players: Lumafield (industrial CT + AI; lists reverse engineering and first-article inspection), Nominal (hardware test data platform; Anduril and Hermeus), Senvol (machine learning for 3D-printing data; Navy-funded project announced Jan 2026).

pathway_steps.step: 0 Pick target parts: stock number, procurement codes, critical-safety flag, demand
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Entrant using the PUB-LOG/FLIS and DIBBS databases
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Nobody ranks parts by sole-source status, contract-justification expiry date, backlog or reviewer queue. Approval timing doesn't line up with solicitations.

pathway_steps.step: 1 Get the technical data or a sample (RPPOB); obtain Service concurrence for a Cat IV request
pathway_steps.who_does_it: DLA Aviation plus the Military Service
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: A permission gate comes before any engineering. Rotair waited about 30 days just for the specs. Locked-in source-controlled items are excluded.

pathway_steps.step: 2 Reverse-engineer: dimensions, materials, and how the part was made (process inference)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No shared library of manufacturing-process fingerprints. Samples are worn or from mixed configurations.

pathway_steps.step: 3 Build the approval package: technical data package, comparison, Nadcap/AS9100 certifications, test plan
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Three service-specific formats in PDF, no machine-readable schema. Packages get rejected for form.

pathway_steps.step: 4 DLA screens and forwards to the service engineering authority
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: DLA can only route; it cannot approve critical safety items.

pathway_steps.step: 5 Wait in the engineering authority's queue
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The main bottleneck. Headcount-limited, with no enforceable deadline.

pathway_steps.step: 6 Engineering review plus information-request loops
pathway_steps.time: 3.5 months then a hold (Rotair); repeated loops
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Serial, document-based review. Each information request adds months, with a 60-day deadline to respond or be dropped.

pathway_steps.step: 7 First-article and qualification testing (fatigue, proof load, non-destructive testing, metallurgy, sometimes engine or rig tests), often government-witnessed
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Entrant pays; government or approved lab
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Physics clock, scarce test rigs, bespoke test plans for every part, little reuse of evidence across similar parts.

pathway_steps.step: 8 Approval, plus airworthiness-authority sign-off if the design changes (MIL-HDBK-516)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Approval covers one part number, one manufacturer and usually one site; it doesn't transfer.

pathway_steps.step: 9 Compete in the next limited-source buy
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Awards don't wait for pending approvals, and a contract justification can lock out new sources for 5 years (Rotair).

pathway_steps.step: 10 Ongoing upkeep: first-article tests on production lots, quality-deficiency reports, quality-escape reporting, re-approval after changes
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: One quality escape can get a source disapproved. Liability makes reviewers conservative.

what_would_need_to_be_done: A copilot for government engineering reviewers: check approval packages against the JACG handbook, service guides and depot maintenance orders, draft information requests, and compare against the OEM technical data the government already holds. Sell it to AFSC, NAVSUP/NAVAIR and the Army aviation center via SBIR, then an OTA contract.

A machine-readable approval package ('approval-as-code', STEP AP242 + model-based definition + linked evidence) that replaces three service-specific PDF formats; needs DLA/JACG to adopt it as a standard.

A quantified equivalence certificate: CT + metallurgy + residual stress + process inference with stated uncertainty, validated on a corpus of matched OEM and reverse-engineered parts, so a Cat IV request can be argued like a Cat I.

Qualification by similarity family: one test campaign plus analysis covers a family of parts with similar geometry, material and process (MIL-HDBK-516 already allows analysis and similarity); needs airworthiness-authority acceptance.
A parallel, robotic 24/7 fatigue and proof-test lab with pre-approved test-plan templates per part class, to cut calendar time where the physics clock can't be shortened.
Acceptance criteria anchored in fleet data, drawn from the services' maintenance systems (REMIS, NALCOMIS, GCSS-Army) and quality-deficiency reports; needs data access.
Target intelligence: rank critical-safety-item parts by sole-source status, contract-justification expiry, backlog and sample-program eligibility, so an approval lands just before the next buy.
Lobby for an FAA-DER-style delegated approval authority in the NDAA, the single biggest multiplier on throughput.
A per-unit digital evidence trail (CT scan of every unit plus process records) that leaves reviewers carrying less liability risk than they do with the incumbent.
ai_plays: Copilot for government reviewers (B2G SaaS / services) at the AF, Navy and Army engineering authorities: attacks the 12-week queue and 15-week review directly, and gives the company a seat inside the permission holder.
Equivalence-evidence engine (CT + metallurgy + process-inference ML) sold to reverse-engineering shops, or used in-house by the Approval Factory.
Approval-package compiler: auto-generates packages in each service's format from scan data plus the parts database; takes package work from 300-1,000 engineering hours down to tens.
Qualification-by-similarity platform plus a robotic test lab, which turns one test campaign into approvals for a whole family of parts.
Target-intelligence model that ranks critical-safety-item parts for approval value and timing, built on DLA/FLIS/DIBBS and contract-justification data.
surprises: Statute puts critical-safety-item source approval only with the government design control activity; DoD has no designee path like the FAA's DER/ODA, so throughput is capped by government headcount.
GAO treats about 12 weeks of queue plus 3.5 months of review ending in a hold as reasonable, and agencies may award a 5-year IDIQ while a request is still pending.
Many Cat IV requests need Service concurrence before the applicant can even buy a sample part.
The sample program excludes source-controlled (procurement code B) items and items under $10k annual demand, often the most locked-in parts.
Most .mil handbooks were unreachable from this sandbox (403), so the primary sources for timelines, the JACG handbook and AFMCI 23-113, still need to be checked by hand.

research.q: NRC commercial-grade dedication (10 CFR 21, EPRI 3002002982, critical characteristics, Method 1-4): full pathway, cost and time per item, bottlenecks.
research.headline: In nuclear commercial-grade dedication (CGD), the permission sits with the program, not the item. The NRC does not approve or witness CGD plans; the gate is the dedicator's 10 CFR 50 Appendix B / NQA-1 quality program, its NUPIC audit standing and its Part 21 defect liability. The per-item work (deciding the item's critical characteristics, the engineering judgment that utilities name as their hardest step, then mostly short Method 1 tests) is exactly what AI and robotics can compress. Incumbents (Westinghouse at ~50k parts/yr, Paragon, UCI, Framatome) hold siloed plan libraries, and Nuclearn is coming in at the paperwork layer. The open opening on the verification side is a vertically integrated AI-native dedicator plus a shared cross-utility evidence graph, with digital/firmware items and advanced-reactor build-out as the growth wedges.

findings.finding: The NRC does not approve CGD plans, does not witness CGD activities and rarely takes part. Paragon had NRC vendor inspections only in 2014 and 2024. The permission is the dedicator's QA program plus Part 21 liability.
Licensees surveyed say identifying and verifying critical characteristics is the most challenging part of CGD and keep dedicated staff for it.

About 40% of reactors worldwide use CGD regularly and another ~40% have piloted it. For more than 20 reactors, 25-50% of safety-related procurement involves CGD. 31% of licensees say use is increasing.

Westinghouse library: 1,000+ CGD plans and 4,000+ instructions covering ~50,000 unique part numbers. About 50,000 CGD parts per year from a 100k sq ft facility with 50+ engineers and ~75 technicians. Claims all of the US market and 75% of global utilities.

Paragon Energy Solutions runs ~1,300 CGD jobs per year and writes 70-100 new CGD plans per month. Digital items are under 5% of jobs but rising. It warns that OEM data sheets are not guaranteed specifications.
UCI has 2,800+ digitized CGD plans covering 270 part classes and uses Method 1 about 90% of the time. Licensees usually do not tell UCI the safety function of the item.

Duke Energy's central dedication facility at Harris handles 25-50% of fleet safety-related procurement and does 95% of Method 1 tests in-house. Leadership tracks a CGD backlog, and Duke says it would do more CGD with more staff. KHNP does ~185 dedications in-house plus 515 outsourced per year.

Part 21 reports: 24 in 2023 (10 CGD-related) and 28 in 2022 (16 CGD-related). 22 of the 26 CGD-related reports were electrical or electromechanical, mainly breakers, contactors, relays and power supplies.

Finland's KELPO process (Fortum, TVO, Fennovoima, with the regulator STUK observing): ~80% of approval comes from joint generic technical characteristics on a shared digital platform the regulator can access. More than 100 components bought over 3 years with no major deviations; being extended to a Nordic version.

Licensees say quality and lead time drive the choice to use CGD and cost matters least. CGD versus nuclear-grade procurement: up to 80% cost and 50% lead-time savings (indicative, research-reactor paper).

Nuclearn raised a $10.5M Series A (Sep 2025, led by Blue Bear Capital) and is deployed at more than 65 reactors. It is launching 'Parts AI' for procurement in early 2026, targeting at least 30% shorter procurement cycles.

Per-item economics (recalled, not verified): a new technical evaluation takes about 8-80 engineer-hours; dedicated price is about 2-10x commercial list for small parts; turnaround is 2-8 weeks when a plan exists and months for new, digital or seismic items.

EPRI (2016) notes NRC precedent that non-process design/analysis software can be a commercial-grade item, with verification and validation treated as a critical characteristic. So an AI evaluation tool might itself need to be dedicated.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Safety classification and CGI determination against the plant licensing basis
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Design-basis and safety-function data stays with the licensee and often never reaches third-party dedicators

pathway_steps.step: 2. Technical evaluation: safety function, failure modes (FMEA), critical characteristics, acceptance criteria
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Procurement or design engineer plus independent reviewer
pathway_steps.time: 8-80 engineer-hours new; much less from a template (recalled)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Hardest step per EPRI's survey. Each company re-derives the same part number in its own library; dedicators over-test to cover unknown functions.

pathway_steps.step: 3. Pick acceptance method (M1 tests/inspections, M2 supplier survey, M3 source verification, M4 performance history)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: M1 dominates (~90% at UCI). M4 is rarely usable because no shared field-performance database exists.

pathway_steps.step: 4. Sourcing from an authorized distributor or OEM
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Minimum order quantities, OEMs wary of selling to nuclear, obsolescence, data sheets not guaranteed

pathway_steps.step: 5. Verification: M1 lab tests (dimensional, XRF/FTIR, electrical, functional, burn-in) or an M2 NUPIC joint audit
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Lab technicians and QC; NUPIC audit teams
pathway_steps.time: minutes to days per lot; an M2 audit is ~1 week and valid ~3 years (recalled)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Throughput is limited by headcount (Duke backlog). Little automation. Digital dependability characteristics are weakly verified.

pathway_steps.step: 6. Seismic / environmental qualification where required (separate from CGD)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: A real physics clock. Shake-table and aging capacity is scarce, and similarity analysis is done by hand.

pathway_steps.step: 7. Counterfeit/CFSI screening, records, Certificate of Conformance
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Paper-heavy; no shared golden-sample fingerprint library

pathway_steps.step: 8. Install, test after installation, Part 21 screening of later failures
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Field failures (breakers, relays) are not fed back systematically into critical characteristics or sampling plans
