what_would_need_to_be_done: Stand up an AI-native dedicating entity with its own Appendix B/NQA-1 program, a passed NUPIC audit and Part 21 liability. LLM agents generate safety-function analysis, FMEA, critical characteristics and sampling plans; qualified engineers sign off.
Robotic Method 1 test cells (CMM/vision, XRF/FTIR, electrical, functional, burn-in) that write QA records automatically, cutting technician-hours per lot by an order of magnitude.
A cross-utility, regulator-readable evidence graph that dedupes part number x critical characteristic x acceptance evidence (US KELPO-style), so each item is verified once and reused.
A field-failure database linking Part 21 reports and corrective-action data back to critical characteristics, which would make Method 4 usable and allow data-driven sampling plans.
Dedicate the AI evaluation tool itself (V&V as a critical characteristic per EPRI non-process software guidance) so licensees can use it inside their own QA programs.
Automated dependability verification for digital items under RG 1.250: firmware extraction, SBOMs, static analysis and fuzzing.
Validated similarity analysis and digital twins accepted under IEEE 344/323 to shrink the months-long seismic and environmental qualification clocks.
Push the NRC's rule-revision window (post-2025 executive orders, ADVANCE Act; recalled) toward performance-based, graded CGD and accredited-lab alternatives.
ai_plays: Dedication Factory: an AI-written technical evaluation plus automated M1 lab plus an owned QA program, sold as dedicated parts to utilities and advanced-reactor builders. KPI: engineer-hours per new plan and turnaround days.
Shared dedication evidence graph / data network across licensees and dedicators, with regulator read access
Digital-item and firmware dedication (security-tech overlap): automated dependability characteristics for commercial digital I&C
Counterfeit and lot-anomaly fingerprinting (spectral, X-ray, electrical) that works across nuclear, DLA and FAA parts
Advanced-reactor supply-chain dedication service (Kairos, X-energy, TerraPower, Oklo) as nuclear-QA suppliers shrink
A V&V'd, dedicated AI technical-evaluation tool licensed to in-house utility programs (a generative successor to EPRI SPEED)
surprises: The NRC approves no CGD plans at all. Unlike FAA PMA or DLA SAR, the moat is a program-level credential, so per-item marginal cost is almost entirely engineering and testing, which AI can compress.
Licensees say cost is the least important reason for CGD; lead time and quality drive it.
Westinghouse alone dedicates ~50k parts per year, so the market is large and already industrialized, but libraries are siloed by company.
Third-party dedicators usually are not told the item's safety function, so they over-test to cover every possible function.
Finland's KELPO already shows a regulator-accessible shared approval platform where ~80% of approval is generic and reused.
Nuclearn is already going after procurement (Parts AI, 2026) at the document layer, but no one integrates the lab, the liability and the AI.

research.q: ASME BPVC / NBIC repair and alteration and R-stamp, plus API 510/570/653 owner-user repairs: pathway, time, cost, what is undone.
research.headline: In ASME/NBIC and API 510/570/653 repairs, the permission itself is cheap: an R certificate costs $1,150 for three years, and more than 5,200 repair organizations use the NBIC. What is scarce is verification throughput (fitness-for-service engineering at Level 3, signatures from the Authorized Inspector, welding procedure qualifications, and speed during refinery turnarounds) and the original design data for orphaned vessels. One search turned up no AI-native company producing the documentation regulators accept, so the opening is an AI-native design-only R holder and FFS house that could later become an Authorized Inspection Agency.

findings.finding: Requirements for an R Certificate of Authorization: a contract with an Authorized Inspection Agency (AIA), a written quality system meeting NBIC and NB-415, the current NBIC and construction code, form NB-12, and an onsite review (joint with ASME or standalone).
findings.number: $1,150 per 3-year certificate; $150 stamp loan; $575 withdrawal fee; $50 revision fee

findings.finding: The NBIC is used by more than 5,200 repair organizations in over 60 countries and underpins four accreditation programs: R, VR, NR and T/O.

NBIC committees took up guidance for R holders with a design-only scope and how they fill in the R-2 form (proposed new 5.2.2 d/e, 2023). This is the legal vehicle for an engineering house that does no welding itself.
findings.source: nationalboard.org Subgroup R&A agenda material, July 2023 (search snippet)

findings.finding: NBIC Part 3 3.3.2 e) lists a closed set of routine repairs where jurisdictions may waive Inspector involvement or R stamping. Committees say the repair-versus-alteration examples are not a complete list, so classification is left to the Inspector's judgment.
Interpretation 07-16: an R holder must prepare a detailed repair or alteration plan before starting work on a Section VIII Div 2/3 vessel.

Gecko Robotics raised a $125M Series D at a $1.25B valuation (Jun 2025, led by Cox; ~$347M raised in total). Its robots capture inspection data, with NDT Level II/III humans in the loop to meet regulatory standards. It sits in the data-capture step, not the approval package.

A targeted search for AI or software startups automating NBIC repair, the R stamp or API 579 FFS returned only forums and training listings. This is weak evidence of absence from one search, not proof.

Typical costs and durations, all recalled: FFS Level 1/2 at $3-20k and 1-5 days; Level 3 at $30-150k+ and 2-8 weeks; a new procedure qualification record (PQR) at $3-15k and 1-4 weeks; Inspector time at $150-250/hr; each day of refinery turnaround overrun at about $0.5-5M.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Damage found at an in-service inspection (by the jurisdiction or AIA inspector, or by the owner-user's API-certified inspector)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Jurisdiction or AIA commissioned inspector; owner-user API 510/570/653 inspector
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Findings are kept as paper or PDF. No pooled dataset links damage mechanism, material and service.

pathway_steps.step: 2. Classify the work as routine repair, repair or alteration
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Rests on judgment because the NBIC examples are not a complete list, so outcomes vary between inspectors and states.

pathway_steps.step: 3. Retrieve the original design basis (Manufacturer's Data Report U-1/U-1A, National Board registration, drawings)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Orphaned data: many old vessels have no data report and the OEM is gone. No accepted standard exists for reconstructing the design basis from measurements.

pathway_steps.step: 4. Engineering: code calculations to the original code (e.g. ASME VIII-1) or an FFS assessment under API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 at Level 1, 2 or 3
pathway_steps.who_does_it: R holder with design scope, a professional engineer (PE), or an FFS specialist firm (E2G, Quest Integrity, Stress Engineering Services, Becht)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual spreadsheet and FEA work. Level 3 is limited by a small pool of senior engineers, and outputs are not checkable clause by clause.

pathway_steps.step: 5. Repair or alteration plan accepted by the Inspector before work starts; some jurisdictions must approve alterations in advance
pathway_steps.who_does_it: AIA Inspector, jurisdiction; on the API side, the owner-user inspector and engineer
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Inspector capacity is the bottleneck, and acceptance is unstructured, with no machine-readable record.

pathway_steps.step: 6. Welding procedure: WPS/PQR qualified under ASME IX (or AWS standard procedures where allowed); welder qualification
pathway_steps.time: existing PQR: none; new PQR: 1-4 weeks (physical test)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Each organization qualifies its own PQRs and little is shared. Coverage of essential variables is not optimized.

pathway_steps.step: 7. Execute the work: weld, PWHT or an alternative such as temper bead, and NDE (RT/UT/PAUT/MT/PT)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: R holder, NDE contractor (ASNT Level II/III)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Defect calls must be made by qualified humans. The code has no route for accepting AI interpretation.

pathway_steps.step: 8. Pressure test (hydro), or NDE in lieu where permitted; API 653 hydrotest waiver by engineering evaluation
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Waivers depend on the Inspector's comfort. No quantified probabilistic standard exists.

pathway_steps.step: 9. Paperwork: R-1/R-2/R-3/R-4 reports, nameplate stamping, registration with the National Board and filing with the jurisdiction; API-side records go into the owner's inspection data management system (IDMS)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Mostly PDF and paper, with no digital thread from calculation to stamp.

pathway_steps.step: 0. Accreditation layer: R certificate, AIA contract, quality control manual, 3-year renewal review; AIAs are accredited by NB-369 and ASME QAI-1 (recalled)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: National Board, ASME, AIAs (mostly insurers: HSB, FM Global, Zurich, Chubb, etc., recalled)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The certificate is cheap. The scarce permission is the Inspector's signature and AIA status, which insurers hold.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Orphan-vessel reconstitution: build a 'reconstructed Manufacturer's Data Report' from nameplate, laser scan, a UT thickness grid, PMI and the code edition of the vessel's era, with explicit conservatism. Then get an NBIC Part 3 paragraph or interpretation defining the minimum evidence for reconstructed design data.

An approval-grade calculation and FFS engine run by an AI-native design-only R holder with in-house PEs: Level 1/2 in minutes and Level 3 FEA, crack growth and creep in hours, auto-verified against benchmarks, delivering a clause-by-clause compliance matrix the Inspector can check.

Machine-checkable, digitally signed R-1/R-2 packages linking calculations, WPS/PQR, NDE and test records, with automated pre-checks against NBIC/ASME/API so the Inspector reviews only the exceptions. This needs NB and jurisdiction acceptance of electronic reports.

A shared PQR library and a high-volume coupon lab in which AI picks essential-variable combinations to maximize coverage per test. This needs broader AWS standard-procedure coverage or an ASME IX code case allowing shared procedure responsibility.
A code case qualifying AI NDE interpretation by performance demonstration, on the model of the nuclear PDI program in Section XI Appendix VIII: build flawed specimens and run blind trials.
A quantified, probabilistic hydrotest-waiver standard combining NDE probability of detection with FFS margin, submitted to the NBIC 2027 edition cycle and to API.
Remote, AI-verified witnessing of hold points (identity, location, preheat, PWHT charts, weld parameters) accepted by jurisdictions, to cut Inspector travel.

An AI-native Authorized Inspection Agency (NB-369/QAI-1) whose commissioned Inspectors each cover 5-10x today's volume. This attacks the one scarce permission and needs insurance capital or a carrier partner.

A pooled, anonymized national repair and damage dataset (R-1/R-2 reports plus owner IDMS data, coded by API 571 damage mechanism) to calibrate FFS and RBI. This needs a National Board or insurer partnership for data access.
A 24/7 turnaround 'discovery desk' that delivers FFS, repair design, WPS selection and the plan within hours of a finding, priced against the $0.5-5M per day cost of outage overrun.
ai_plays: An AI-native design-only R holder and FFS engineering house that sells turnaround speed to refiners and chemical plants. The KPI is engineer hours and Inspector hours per accepted R-2 or FFS, and AI would turn a services-margin pool (E2G, Quest, SES, Becht) into software-like margins.
An Inspector copilot sold to AIAs and jurisdictions: it pre-checks R-1/R-2 packages, matches WPS/PQR records, and audits NDE and test records against code clauses.
An AI-native AIA as the endgame permission play, holding the scarce signature.
A PQR-as-a-service lab plus licensed procedure library.
Code-case factory: draft and push NBIC/ASME/API proposals for AI NDE acceptance, reconstructed design data and probabilistic test waivers, then be the first company qualified under them.
The same 'evidence-package engine' (code compliance plus FEA automation plus compliance matrix) as a shared core with the defense/FAA Approval Factory.
surprises: The R stamp is nearly free ($1,150 per 3 years) and held by thousands of organizations, so unlike DLA source approval or FAA PMA, permission here is not scarce. Value sits in verification throughput and the Inspector's signature.
The National Board was already formalizing 'design-only' R holders in 2023, a ready-made legal wrapper for an AI engineering house with no welders.

The best-funded adjacent startup, Gecko Robotics ($1.25B), sits on the data-capture side and still relies on human NDT Level II/III staff for regulatory acceptance. Nobody seen owns the step from data to accepted repair package.

AIAs are largely insurers, so the gatekeeper of acceptance is a liability-bearing balance sheet rather than a regulator. An AI play that reduces their loss ratio could win them as a customer or partner.

research.q: Rail: AAR M-1003 quality approval, FRA, EN 15085, European ECM and TSI conformity for spare parts; pathway and bottlenecks for a non-OEM spare.
research.headline: For rail spare parts, no single agency approves the part. In North America the AAR's committee approvals and service trials are the gate; in the EU it is the maintenance entity's (ECM's) risk appetite, under rules that already let a like-for-like part go in without re-authorising the vehicle. Non-OEM aftermarket parts are routine in US freight, and no venture-scale company sells AI-built proof that a substitute part is equivalent. The best opening is an AI-backed outsourced engineering service that signs off substitutions (EU ECM maintenance development, or engineer-stamped review for US transit agencies), plus a shared, portable register of approved non-OEM parts that rail lacks.

findings.finding: AAR M-1003 is the quality assurance specification required of rail industry suppliers, and several non-OEM or reconditioned suppliers hold it (Strato's Peoria coupler/yoke shop, Progress Rail side frames M-1003/M214, PowerRail, Longwood Elastomers WABCO AB kits, Alco Spring). Non-OEM aftermarket parts in freight interchange are already normal.
AAR Technical Services processes facility and component approvals, inspections, component approval tests and S-060 certifications. aar.com approval pages now redirect to MxV Rail (former TTCI).

AAR-approved components (couplers, castings, wheels, bearings, brake valves) usually go through conditional approval with a service trial before unconditional approval. That trial is the main physics clock.

FRA does not type-certify spare parts. It regulates through 49 CFR 215/229/231/232/238 (fire safety 238.103) and incorporates AAR standards by reference. The exception is FRA glazing certification under 49 CFR 223.

In the EU the ECM (Reg. 2019/779) owns component substitution through its maintenance-development and change-management function. Replacement in the framework of maintenance (Dir. 2016/797, Reg. 2018/545) needs no new vehicle authorisation. The constraint is the ECM's risk appetite and missing evidence, not the law.

Deutsche Bahn keeps a digital spare-parts warehouse of about 1,000 models and targets 10,000 components by 2030. It has printed more than 7,000 parts since 2015. Conventional lead times for specialist components are often about 24 months. TÜV SÜD tests and certifies.

The Mobility goes Additive Approval working group (Siemens-led, with DB, Knorr-Bremse and TÜV SÜD) won first-time approval of an additively manufactured brake suspension link, in service at Hamburger Hochbahn since August 2019.
SNCF uses 3YOURMIND to manage AM spare-part data. Rail AI startup funding goes to autonomy and monitoring (Futurail €7.5M seed Sep 2025; Railspire $12.5M), not parts approval.

EU manufacturing gates stack up: EN 15085-2 welding certification (CL1-CL4), ISO/TS 22163, EN 45545-2 fire tests, a Notified Body EC declaration for interoperability constituents, and operator qualification such as DB HPQ. Each operator re-audits.
Rail has no equivalent of the FAA PMA list. No portable register of approved non-OEM equivalents exists, so every ECM and transit agency re-approves the same part.

pathway_steps.step: AAR facility M-1003 QMS certification
pathway_steps.who_does_it: AAR QA auditors / AAR Technical Services (MxV Rail)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual audits. Many shops already hold it, so it is not the moat.

pathway_steps.step: AAR component approval: lab tests, committee review, conditional approval with service trial, then unconditional
pathway_steps.who_does_it: AAR committees (staffed by incumbent OEMs and railroads), MxV Rail labs
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Service-trial clock. Committees are incumbent-dominated. No statistical or digital-twin path to earlier acceptance.

pathway_steps.step: Foundry approval (castings: M-201, radiography, traceability marking)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Rules tightened after import casting failures, so new foundries face hostility.

pathway_steps.step: US passenger/transit agency acceptance: drawing equivalence, first article inspection, trial install, FRA 238/223 where relevant, Buy America
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Reviewer capacity is the bottleneck. No portable approval, so each agency redoes it.

pathway_steps.step: EU change classification: like-for-like replacement vs CSM-RA change vs re-authorisation
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: ECMs default to the OEM because of liability. Evidence is assembled by hand.

pathway_steps.step: EC declaration for interoperability constituents (TSI)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Limited NoBo capacity. The dossier is not reusable across regimes.

pathway_steps.step: Manufacturer certs: EN 15085-2, ISO/TS 22163, EN 45545-2 fire tests
pathway_steps.who_does_it: DVS ZERT, TÜV, accredited fire labs
pathway_steps.time: weeks per fire test; months per cert
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Physical fire tests are iterated rather than predicted. Weld documentation is manual.

pathway_steps.step: Operator supplier/product qualification (DB HPQ, SNCF, RISQS)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Each operator audits separately, with no mutual recognition.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a portable equivalence-evidence graph per part that renders AAR, NoBo, ECM change-management (2019/779), CSM-RA, US agency FAI and RDSO dossiers from one source.
Create the missing rail register of approved non-OEM equivalents (a PMA-list analogue) that ECMs and agencies can rely on, ending repeat approvals.

Shorten AAR service trials by instrumenting the trial fleet and using wayside/Railinc data plus fatigue digital twins. Pilot with one Class I or lessor and MxV Rail, then seek a committee rule allowing statistical acceptance.
Predict EN 45545 / NFPA 130 fire and smoke results from material formulation, so physical tests become confirmations.
Automate EN 15085 weld qualification and NDT interpretation, and make M-1003/ISO 22163 compliance continuous, so new micro-factories certify in weeks.
Offer the ECM maintenance-development function (EU) or PE-stamped configuration-control engineering (US transit) as a service, with the company taking liability backed by insurance.
Pair AI reverse engineering with Buy America-compliant US manufacturing for legacy Amtrak/transit fleets (Amfleet I, NYCT R46/R62).
ai_plays: Outsourced ECM maintenance development (EU) or engineer-stamped configuration control (US transit), with AI generating each substitution's equivalence case. This sells permission, not drawings.
A multi-regime dossier compiler: scan or legacy part plus fleet data in; AAR / NoBo / ECM / CSM-RA / RDSO-ready evidence out. SaaS to ECMs, NoBos and agencies.
A statistical service-trial acceptance engine with MxV Rail and a big lessor (GATX/Trinity) that turns multi-year conditional approvals into months plus monitored deployment.
A cross-recognition registry of approved non-OEM equivalents with network effects across operators.
Audit automation for EN 15085 / M-1003 / ISO 22163 (QMS-as-code) to certify factories quickly.
surprises: Non-OEM aftermarket parts with M-1003 are already routine in US freight. The limits are committee-held component approvals and AAR billing price tables, which cap margins.
EU law already allows like-for-like replacement without re-authorisation. The binding constraint is the ECM's risk appetite and missing evidence tooling, which is an AI opening.
Deutsche Bahn is both the biggest EU customer and the most advanced in-house competitor (target of 10,000 digital parts by 2030).
Rail has no FAA-PMA-style portable approval list, so creating one is greenfield.
3 searches found no venture-backed company doing AI reverse engineering plus approvals for rail; rail AI money goes to autonomy and monitoring. With so few searches, this absence is weak evidence.

research.q: Naval: NAVSEA Level I / SUBSAFE material certification, Navy parts qualification, shipyard material approval: pathway and bottlenecks.
research.headline: Navy SUBSAFE/Level I material approval is a human-limited permission pipeline. Navy AM work has a stated rate of "tens of Technical Data Packages per quarter vs a goal of hundreds", one qualified printer procedure took NUWC Keyport 7 years, and castings and forgings (3% of NSNs) are 20% of DLA's 100 oldest backorders. Billions are going to the making side (Hadrian about $900M Navy, Anduril $2.9B Navy, AML3D) but almost nothing to the proving side: AI-native adjudication of objective quality evidence (OQE), TDPs and SARs, OQE forensics, and in-situ/CT evidence accepted as qualification. That is an open verification play that would sell to every new maker and to NAVSEA.

findings.finding: Castings and forgings are only 3% of NSNs but 20% of the 100 oldest DLA backorders; the government often lacks the casting/forging tooling
One spec clarification (Lockheed FPS-1001 foundry qualification class) potentially opened 334 more NSNs to sources, showing spec over-restriction is a lever
NAVSEA SUBSAFE Engineering Support (NSLC) needed outside expert review over multiple conference calls just to check a forging sketch for technical completeness

NUWC Keyport became the first Warfare Center with a NAVSEA-approved metal LPBF procedure (17-4PH, EOS M290) after a 7-year effort. Once qualified, further prints skip machine/baseline requalification. A multi-year in-situ QA monitoring effort is next.

Navy AM part qualification runs via TDP 'recipes' (alloy plus process); throughput is tens of TDPs per quarter with a goal of hundreds; the casting/forging base 'cannot support the one plus two cadence'

AML3D got an initial production order of about AU$0.5M for 3 CuNi submarine fluid components after several years of qualification. It cites a Navy forecast of up to 100 AM systems and 1,600 AM components by 2030.
NAVSEA says AM collaboration cut testing requirements by over 60% and issued MIL-PRF-32802/32803/32804; the activated supplier pool cannot meet demand
findings.source: WebSearch summary of NAVSEA/AMUG pages (NAVSEA page 403 on fetch)

findings.finding: Level I/SUBSAFE suppliers must submit their quality system procedures to the PCO before award, and government source inspection applies; Level I means maximum assurance of chemistry and mechanical properties (SUBSAFE Manual NAVSEA 0924-062-0010)
findings.source: DLA Maritime/NAVSUP solicitation clauses via WebSearch (sam.gov)

findings.finding: Anduril Arsenal-2: $3.7B own money plus a $2.9B Navy contract for Virginia-class torpedo tubes and hull components, starting around 2030. Virginia deliveries are stuck at 1.1-1.2/yr vs a goal of 2.
Hadrian Factory 4 (Cherokee AL): over $2.4B total including about $900M Navy, for submarine components
GAO: $5.8B spent on the shipbuilding industrial base FY14-23 and $12.6B more planned through FY28. The Navy lacks performance metrics for these investments.
Bradken/Kaiser foundry metallurgist falsified test results on about 240 submarine steel castings over about 30 years; Bradken paid about $10.8M. OQE fraud went undetected by the system for decades.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Designation of item as Level I / SUBSAFE in drawings/APL (NAVSEA 0924-062-0010, 0948-045-7010)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Design yard (Electric Boat) and NAVSEA 05 Technical Warrant Holders
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No machine-readable boundary; over-designation and conservative flow-down widen what needs Level I paperwork

pathway_steps.step: 2. Tech data and tooling availability
pathway_steps.who_does_it: NAVSEA/design yard; DLA tooling databases (DECAF, ICON, NFTD)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Missing drawings and lost casting/forging tooling; databases fragmented; nobody reconstructs tooling digitally at scale

pathway_steps.step: 3. Source approval / TDP approval (SAR for spares; shipbuilder supplier approval; NAVSEA TWH approval of AM machine-process-part TDPs)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: NAVSEA ESAs (NSLC SUBSAFE Eng Support, NSWC), TWHs, Austal AT TDP group
pathway_steps.time: 1-3 yrs typical (recalled); Keyport procedure took 7 yrs
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Main bottleneck: tens of TDPs/quarter vs hundreds needed; manual expert review; no AI pre-adjudication

pathway_steps.step: 4. Supplier quality system and special-process qualification (welding S9074-AQ-GIB-010/248, MIL-STD-1689, personnel quals)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Supplier; shipbuilder audits; SUPSHIP/NAVSEA; BlueForge helps
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: 'Activated supplier pool cannot meet need'; paper-heavy; no copilot for WPS/PQR/QMS generation

pathway_steps.step: 5. Material procurement with heat/lot traceability and MTRs; approved lab testing
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Certs are trusted documents; no statistical forensics (Bradken fraud ran ~30 yrs)

pathway_steps.step: 6. Manufacture (cast/forge/machine/AM)
pathway_steps.time: physics clock; casting/forging lead times 1-3 yrs (recalled)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Capacity shortfall vs 1+2 cadence; heavy capital inflow here

pathway_steps.step: 7. NDT (RT/UT/MT/PT per T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, acceptance MIL-STD-2035) plus destructive tests
pathway_steps.time: days-weeks per lot; destructive tests are a physics clock
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Human interpretation bottleneck; no NAVSEA-accepted AI-assisted reading; in-situ sensing not yet accepted as evidence

pathway_steps.step: 8. Government source inspection
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Scarce QAR hours; sampling-based

pathway_steps.step: 9. OQE package, MIC marking, shipping
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: PDF/paper; not structured data; no automated completeness or consistency checking

pathway_steps.step: 10. Receipt inspection at shipyard (OQE review, PMI)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual OQE review; re-tests; rejections cause rework loops

pathway_steps.step: 11. Installation under re-entry control; SUBSAFE certification audit and boat certification
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Audit of OQE completeness is manual; a missing OQE item can hold certification

Spec over-restriction mining across NSNs (like the FPS-1001 class clarification that opened 334 NSNs) and auto-drafted group deviations or waivers
Supplier activation copilot: auto-generate QMS, WPS/PQR, special-process quals and audit-readiness evidence for new SIB suppliers via BlueForge

Avoid naval nuclear propulsion (NAVSEA 08/NNPI) at first; start with non-nuclear Level I fluid-system parts (CuNi, 17-4PH, 316L); use OTA, SBIR Phase III or a CRADA with NSLC/NSWC; get CMMC/ITAR/CUI compliance in place

research.q: Space and defence electronics: qualification by similarity, MIL-PRF-38535/883 screening, DMSMS form-fit-function replacement approval: pathway and bottlenecks.
research.headline: Many companies already find replacement chips: SiliconExpert, Z2Data, Accuris, Kipo AI, Cofactr, and primes like BAE building their own AI tools. I found no company that turns a replacement into a signed approval: the similarity case, the minimal delta test plan and the NSPAR/SMD/ECP package, accepted by a Parts Control Board or DLA. The verification-side AI play is a certified qualifier (a QML/AS6171 house) that runs on a machine-readable evidence graph. MIL-PRF-38535 already lets a certified manufacturer delete tests when it has the data, so that house would use AI to make the data case and cut tests, beam hours and reviewer hours per approval.

findings.finding: QML requires a manufacturer whose quality management (QM) program is certified by the government Qualifying Activity (DLA Land and Maritime), which must approve all changes. With enough quality and reliability data, a manufacturer may modify, substitute or delete tests through its QM program and review board. That is the existing legal hook for AI-driven test reduction.

DLA's 2024 Defense Standardization Program (DSP) award briefing covers adding new radiation-hardened plastic-package (PEM) Classes N and P to MIL-PRF-38535 and cites cost avoidance. The rules are moving toward plastic COTS parts and analysis-heavy qualification. The PDF itself returned 403; this is from the search result.
findings.source: https://www.dsp.dla.mil/Portals/26/Documents/Conference/2024 Briefings/Day 1 - August 6/Success with Standards/Chambers - 2024 DSP Award New RH PEM Class N_P MIL-PRF-38535.pdf

findings.finding: Kipo AI (Mobilio Co.) sells AI agents for parts discovery and procurement, with LLM-standardised data and form-fit-function matching. Its Letterkenny Army Depot (Patriot) case claims 60% faster procurement, with no baseline given. It makes no qualification or approval claims.

Z2Data, founded 2016 with about 50 staff, forecasts end-of-life up to 36 months ahead and offers 'compliant alternates in hours' with 7 AI agents. Customers include Qualcomm, Teradyne, Dell and Airbus. It offers no qualification or approval output.

Rochester Electronics holds more than 15B devices across more than 200k part numbers and more than 12B die, is authorised by more than 70 OEMs, and has built more than 20,000 device types as a licensed manufacturer. In legacy chips, the permission is OEM licences plus die stock.
BAE Systems job postings describe a cloud-based DMSMS service using automation and AI for finding replacements, BOM risk and counterfeit avoidance. Primes are building the detection layer in house.

The physics clocks that cannot be skipped today are burn-in (160 h at 125C for Class Q, 240 h for Class V), a 1000 h Group C life test, HAST/THB for plastic parts, and heavy-ion beam time at about 5 US facilities (TAMU, LBNL, MSU FRIB, BNL NSRL, MGH). Booking is by request through each facility; capacity and price are not published.

The DoD SD-22 DMSMS resolution ladder runs: existing stock, reclamation, alternate, substitute, aftermarket, emulation (DLA GEM program, DMEA ARMS foundry), then redesign. Recalled costs per resolution: an alternate about $5k-20k, a substitute $20k-100k, emulation $50k-500k, and a redesign $250k to several $M plus requalification.

Qualification by similarity is allowed through MIL-PRF-38535 and JEDEC JESD47/AEC-Q100 family rules, DO-160 and MIL-STD-810 box-level similarity, and space-program PCB delta qualification. It breaks on radiation lot variability, hidden die or fab changes, and package changes. The similarity argument is an unstructured engineering memo judged by a human board.

pathway_steps.step: A. Detect obsolescence (PDN/EOL notices, GIDEP, BOM monitoring tools)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: SiliconExpert, Z2Data, Accuris, Supplyframe, AVCOM, prime in-house teams
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Commoditised and crowding with AI layers. Not a moat.

pathway_steps.step: B. Select a resolution (alternate, substitute, aftermarket, emulation, redesign)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Matching is datasheet-parametric only. It does not check behavioural equivalence in the specific application. Resolutions are not shared across programs.

pathway_steps.step: C. Component screening and qualification (MIL-STD-883 screens, Groups A-E, SMD/SCD/VID issue)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: QML manufacturers, upscreen houses (Spirit, Micross), test labs; DLA Land and Maritime issues SMDs
pathway_steps.time: burn-in 160-240 h; 1000 h life test; SMD issue takes months
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Full flows run by default. The test-deletion allowance in MIL-PRF-38535 is rarely used because nobody industrialises the statistical case.

pathway_steps.step: C2. Radiation hardness assurance (TID lot acceptance per TM1019, SEE beam tests)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: RTS, VPT Rad, TRAD, Alter, NASA GSFC; TAMU, LBNL, FRIB beamlines
pathway_steps.cost: beam time plus lab fees (recalled roughly $1k+/h)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No credible pre-beam prediction from process and layout. Pulsed-laser pre-screening is under-used. Facilities are scarce.

pathway_steps.step: D. Qualification by similarity / delta qualification argument
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Prime parts engineering, judged by the program Parts Control Board or Material Review Board
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No standard schema, no quantified similarity metric, no reusable evidence base. It rests on engineering judgement in PDFs.

pathway_steps.step: E. Program approval (MIL-STD-3018 parts plan, NSPAR, ECP Class I/II, design-authority sign-off)
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Prime design authority or government engineering support activity; government change board for Class I
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Packages are hand-drafted. For orphaned legacy systems, a depot engineering activity must sign. Class I versus Class II depends on proving FFF, and no tool proves it.

pathway_steps.step: F. Counterfeit avoidance (AS6171/AS5553, DFARS 252.246-7007/7008)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Ad hoc. There is no productised 'same die' certificate.

pathway_steps.step: G. Logistics approval (NSN cataloguing, DLA Source Approval Request for a new source)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The target of the prior Approval Factory review. The electronics-level evidence feeds it.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a machine-readable cross-program evidence graph covering test reports, DPA images, radiation data (GSFC Radhome, ESCIES, NEPP), datasheets and failure analyses. Each claim should be linked to the conditions and application it covers.

Define a quantified similarity metric for package, die revision, fab or lot changes, validated against historical pass and fail outcomes. Then publish it as a standard through an SAE G-19/G-12 or JEDEC committee.
Auto-generate minimal delta test plans and the full NSPAR/SCD/SMD-draft/ECP package, and measure parts-board and reviewer hours per approval.
Industrialise the MIL-PRF-38535 QM-plan test-deletion case inside a certified QML (Class T/N/P) entity, using statistical evidence to shorten or delete burn-in and screens.
Predict single-event effects and total dose from TCAD and ML on process and layout data, plus pulsed-laser pre-screening, to cut heavy-ion beam hours. Own or contract beam capacity.

Prove behavioural FFF equivalence with a digital twin of the original part in the real board, using formal and differential testing of the replacement or emulation. Aim for Class II ECP treatment instead of Class I.
Offer productised 'same die' certificates using X-ray CT, die imaging and electrical fingerprint libraries, for counterfeit avoidance and similarity claims.
Run a DLA/DSP pilot that reviews AI-generated similarity packages side by side with traditional ones, to build regulator acceptance. Start with Class B/military ground parts before space.
Form a data consortium in which primes contribute test data in exchange for cheaper approvals, handling ITAR and CUI in an accredited enclave.
ai_plays: Similarity Engine and evidence graph: score how much existing qualification evidence transfers to a replacement part, then output the minimal delta test plan and a drafted approval package. KPI: hours per approved substitution.

Certified AI-native qualifier: become a QML / AS6171 / AS6081 upscreen and qualification house that uses AI to argue test deletions under MIL-PRF-38535 QM-plan rights. This owns the permission rather than selling software to whoever holds it.
Radiation prediction plus owned beam or laser capacity, to sell single-event and total-dose assurance with fewer heavy-ion hours.
Behavioural FFF verification and emulation certification: a digital twin of the obsolete part plus equivalence proofs, turning Class I changes into Class II.
Die-sameness and counterfeit certificates from automated imaging and electrical fingerprints.
Accelerated-life inference: Bayesian or physics-of-failure models that stop life and burn-in tests early with statistical justification.
surprises: MIL-PRF-38535 already lets a certified manufacturer modify or delete tests when it has the data. The permission exists, but nobody industrialises the evidence argument.
For legacy chips, much of the 'permission' is Rochester's OEM licences and its 12B+ die stock rather than regulator approval.
Primes such as BAE are building AI DMSMS tools in house. Finding parts and alternates is not where the moat is.
DLA is still adding classes (radiation-hardened plastic Class N/P), so the rules are moving toward COTS and analysis-based qualification. That opens a window for evidence-driven approval.
Every AI player I found (Kipo, Z2Data, SiliconExpert) stops at candidate selection. None claims an output a parts control board would accept.

research.q: Power generation: how gas turbine owners, insurers (HSB, FM Global) and lenders accept non-OEM parts and repairs (no regulator); what evidence is demanded; who decides.
research.headline: In gas turbine power generation no regulator approves non-OEM parts. Approval is private and spread out: the owner qualifies the vendor, the OEM uses LTSA and warranty cancellation as leverage, and insurers like FM Global and HSB/Munich Re act through 'material change in risk', fleet-hours tests, design exclusions and loss adjusting. The insurers' own trade body (IMIA, 2009) says 'there is no independent organisation to assist the Owner' and 'no comprehensive turbine loss register'. That missing independent verification layer, sold first to insurers, is the AI play.

findings.finding: Owners verify non-OEM suppliers and parts themselves. The insurers' trade body says no independent organisation exists to help them.
findings.source: IMIA WGP 64 (09), authors from HSB, Munich Re, Swiss Re: https://www.imia.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/IMIA-WGP-64-Combustion-Turbines-FINALa-4.pdf

findings.finding: There is no comprehensive turbine loss register. Insurers and reinsurers said one should be set up.
OEMs can cancel warranties and service agreements when non-OEM parts are used. As a result, the non-OEM share is much higher for turbines older than 5 years and for smaller units.

Insurers grade turbines as prototype, unproven, proven or problematical. The first 2,000 operating hours are treated as critical. A lead unit running 8,000 failure-free hours has traditionally counted as proven, and FM Global now calls that rule inadequate for cyclic duty.
findings.source: IMIA WGP 64; FM Global (T. Lee), ESD News 7 Feb 2020: https://esdnews.com.au/a-new-approach-to-managing-evolving-risks-in-gas-turbine-technology/

findings.finding: FM Global insures about 7% of global power generation assets. Its clients had about 20 gas turbine failures a year, and blades caused well over three quarters of losses.

Underwriters' tools: claims-free fleet hours, 'material change in risk', high deductibles, insuring only known components, LEG1/LEG2 design exclusions, and Munich Re's Endorsement 011 serial-loss scale.
Insurers should not accept a root-cause analysis team made up only of the OEM's people. LTSAs can block access to failed hardware, put parts in the OEM's ownership, and impose waivers of subrogation.

Owners vet suppliers through references, site visits, consultants and review of quality documents, which takes months. Non-OEM parts save 30% or more. Warranties are based on equivalent operating hours. The service market is about $16-20B a year, and the F-class aftermarket splits 68% parts, 18% repairs, 14% field service.
GE inspects every part for non-GE hardware, including dimensions, material identification and patent review. Gas turbine components are mostly patented.
findings.source: GE Vernova TransAlta case study; IMIA WGP 67

findings.finding: OEMs quote 24-36 months for upgrades, against 7 months from EthosEnergy. EthosEnergy moved to One Equity Partners in December 2024.
PSM (Hanwha) has done 350+ gas turbine upgrades in 30+ countries. It publishes quality-system certificates (ISO 9001, AS9100) but no product-validation evidence.

SPS's ORAP is a reliability database built up over decades. Its Parts-Trac module tracks the expended life of each serialized part. It is the closest thing to an experience register, but it is not an insurer acceptance standard.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Design or reverse-engineer the part or repair
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Every ISP repeats the work. There is no shared definition of equivalence, and OEM patents block copying.

pathway_steps.step: 2. Owner qualifies the vendor
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Owner fleet engineering or a consultant
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No independent body exists; small owners depend on the OEM.

pathway_steps.step: 3. LTSA and warranty
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: OEM threatens to cancel the warranty or LTSA. Parts and data belong to the OEM.

pathway_steps.step: 4. Insurance placement or renewal
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Underwriter engineers (FM Global, HSB, Munich Re, AXA XL, Allianz)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No parts-level loss data. Proven status rests on blunt fleet-hours rules (2,000/8,000 h). Non-OEM parts are tolerated, never certified.

pathway_steps.step: 5. Financing or refinancing
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: OEM LTSA treated as the bankable default (opinion/recalled).

pathway_steps.step: 6. In-service inspection and life tracking
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Data is fragmented and largely held by the OEM.

pathway_steps.step: 7. Loss and root-cause analysis
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: RCA is often led by the OEM, and hardware is inaccessible under LTSAs.

what_would_need_to_be_done: An independent, insurer-recognised standard for qualifying non-OEM parts and repairs (a private 'PMA for power'): a per-part dossier covering scanned OEM population geometry, metallurgy, coatings, cyclic-duty FEA/CFD life, mode testing and a field-trial plan, with insurers giving premium or deductible credit so a qualified part is no longer a 'material change in risk'.

A gas turbine parts loss and experience register (the one IMIA asked for in 2009), built from serialized part histories in owner CMMS, ORAP, borescope video and adjuster claim files, to replace the 8,000-hour fleet-leader rule with Bayesian per-design reliability.
Independent AI forensic root-cause analysis and repair-scope optimisation for adjusters, since insurers should not accept OEM-only analysis and OEMs over-scope replacement.
An MGA warranty and breakdown wrap that insures qualified non-OEM parts, so the OEM's warranty-voiding lever stops working.
Condition-based per-part life acceptance from AI borescope and operating data, to justify longer intervals to insurers.
Shared independent hot-gas and cyclic rig test capacity (FM Global notes 'few OEM test facilities') so test hours can run outside the OEM.
Design-around and freedom-to-operate analysis per part, because gas turbine parts are mostly patented.
ai_plays: 'UL for the turbine aftermarket': AI-generated equivalency and life dossiers per part or repair, recognised by insurers, paid for by ISPs and owners
A turbine loss and experience register plus actuarial pricing model sold to engineering insurers and reinsurers (HSB/Munich Re, FM Global, Swiss Re, AXA XL)
Independent AI forensic RCA plus repair-vs-replace scoping for loss adjusters
An MGA insuring non-OEM parts and repairs, with the dossier as its underwriting engine (Hartford Steam Boiler's 1866 inspect-then-insure model)
A bankability score for lenders' independent engineers on ISP O&M plans in merchant gas refinancings, during the 2025-26 turbine shortage
surprises: The insurers' own trade body said in 2009 that no independent verifier and no loss register exist, and I found no sign that anyone has filled this gap since.
FM Global publicly says the 8,000-hour fleet-leader proof is inadequate, which leaves room for a better evidence standard.
OEMs act as non-OEM providers on rivals' fleets, so their safety objections to third-party parts are partly commercial.
PSM publishes only quality-system certificates and no product-validation evidence, so the market runs on reputation and references.
Because there is no regulator, a startup can become the approver's tool faster than in aviation or defence, but that approval is weaker because owners and OEMs can ignore it.

research.q: Medical device service parts: ISO replacement parts, FDA 2018 servicing report, 510(k) for remanufacturing guidance (2024): pathway for a non-OEM replacement part.
research.headline: US medtech has no approval tier like the FAA's PMA for non-OEM replacement parts. A part either counts as unreviewed "servicing" (it matches the OEM spec, the servicer self-documents and nobody checks) or as "remanufacturing," which means full manufacturer obligations and possibly a 510(k). The verification gap FDA left in its May 2024 guidance is an opening for an AI-native equivalence verification and certification business: no neutral checker, no OEM spec access for third parties, and no field data. It fits better as a second market after aerospace than as a moat by itself.

findings.finding: Under FDARA 2017, FDA delivered its servicing report in May 2018. It found the evidence 'not sufficient to conclude whether or not there is a widespread public health concern', declined to add burdensome requirements, and committed to clarify servicing vs remanufacturing.
The 2018 report found that many adverse events attributed to 'inadequate servicing' were really remanufacturing, so current MDR attribution is unreliable.

FDA finalized the guidance 'Remanufacturing of Medical Devices' on May 10, 2024 (FR 2024-10230; draft June 2021). It sets six principles: intended-use change, significant change to safety or performance specs (individually and cumulatively), whether a new submission is needed, component dimensional and performance specs, a risk-based approach, and documentation an investigator or third party can follow.

Under the guidance, an identical OEM part is 'almost always servicing'. Any non-identical part, even one called 'equivalent' or 'better', needs analysis of dimensions, materials (biocompatibility, aging) and performance. Examples: a CRT swapped for an LCD from another supplier and non-OEM imaging-chain components are likely remanufacturing. Installing non-OEM software or firmware is generally remanufacturing.

Remanufacturers are treated as manufacturers: registration and listing, premarket authorization, QMSR, MDR, Part 806 and UDI. Independent servicers that only service are generally not subject to FDA requirements and self-assess with no registration.
QMSR, which incorporates ISO 13485:2016, took effect February 2, 2026 and applies fully to remanufacturers.

AMDSO (the ISO trade group) says the guidance cannot be implemented unless OEMs provide specs, parts and materials, and OEMs have no obligation to. MITA says unregistered ISOs escape oversight. MDMA opposes compelled trade-secret disclosure. FDA only 'encourages' OEMs to provide service information.

The federal Critical Medical Infrastructure Right-to-Repair Act (Wyden, 2020) appears stalled. State laws mostly cover wheelchairs: CO HB22-1031 and CA SB 1384 (2024). Vermont H.160 was still in progress in 2026.

Innovatus Imaging claims 200k+ ultrasound probe repairs and 50k MRI coil repairs at 'OEM-grade quality at 40-60% lower cost'. It is ISO 13485 certified and makes parts in house through molding and machining, without OEM documentation. OEMs give no IP access for probes and coils.

(recalled) The 2018 report estimated about 16,500-20,800 US firms doing servicing. A 2024 DMCA 1201 exemption covers medical device repair. A 510(k) has a 90-FDA-day review clock with a MDUFA standard fee of about $24-26k (small business about $6k). CMS requires OEM-recommended maintenance for imaging and lasers.

pathway_steps.step: Pick a target part (CT or x-ray tube, detector, MRI coil, ultrasound probe, board, battery, display, endoscope optics)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No public demand or failure data. MAUDE attribution is unreliable.

pathway_steps.step: Obtain the OEM specification
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Nobody; OEMs have no duty to provide it
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: This is the core gap. 'Equivalent to OEM spec' is the legal test, but third parties cannot see the spec.

pathway_steps.step: Reverse-engineer dimensions, materials, electrical behavior and firmware
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Firmware or pairing locks turn the job into a software change, and software changes count as remanufacturing.

pathway_steps.step: Classify the work as servicing or remanufacturing (6 principles plus flowchart)
pathway_steps.cost: 513(g) request about $5-6k (recalled) if you want an FDA opinion
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No neutral checker. The 'significant change' test is subjective. There is no fast FDA determination route.

pathway_steps.step: Servicing branch: document the rationale
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Nobody reviews the file, so hospitals have no proof and OEMs attack it as unregulated.

pathway_steps.step: Remanufacturing branch: registration and listing, QMSR, and a 510(k) decision under the 2017 change guidance
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The predicate is the OEM device, but you have no design file. No platform-batched submissions exist.

pathway_steps.step: Bench testing: IEC 60601-1 and 60601-1-2, ISO 10993, IEC 62304, 524B cyber, 21 CFR 1020 for x-ray
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Labs test against the standard, not against OEM equivalence. No equivalence test protocol exists.

research.q: EASA vs FAA vs Transport Canada vs CAAC differences for non-OEM parts approval (EPA parts, bilateral acceptance): where a global approval house hits friction.
research.headline: An FAA PMA (the FAA's approval for a non-OEM part) is the only one that travels. EASA accepts non-critical FAA PMAs directly (TIP Rev 7 §3.3.4), but the FAA does not recognize EASA EPA or other partners' non-OEM part approvals (TIP §2.2.4.3(b) is 'Reserved'). Critical parts need a separate EASA STC under Non-Basic review, Canada accepts no identicality, and China accepts test-and-computation PMAs for Airbus or Rolls-Royce parts only at minor or no-safety-effect failure conditions, which are not published. A global approval house therefore has to anchor at the FAA, and the open verification play is a machine-readable bilateral/criticality engine plus one test campaign that serves several authorities. Nobody appears to sell that today.

findings.finding: EASA 'shall directly accept all FAA PMA approvals, without further showing' when: (1) the part is non-critical and approved by identicality without licence or by test and computation; (2) it was made under a licence and EASA has validated the TC/STC; (3) it is critical AND EASA has validated the FAA STC or issued an equivalent EASA STC.
The FAA's recognition of EASA parts covers only replacement or modification parts made by the original PAH. The slot for non-OEM parts (EASA EPA) is 'Reserved'. The reverse direction is asymmetric.

EASA validation applications for critical-component PMA parts not made under licence 'shall be classified as Non-Basic', which means EASA technical involvement. Applicants must also describe how part users are told of changes and in-service issues.
A critical component is one identified by the DAH or the SoD authority, typically with ALS/CMR replacement times or inspections. The applicant often lacks those OEM manuals.

An EU MRO must reject an 8130-3 that lacks one of three Block 12 statements ('This PMA part is not a critical component', licence, or EASA STC number), whatever the part's technical merit. EASA says it 'has no authority over US manufacturers exporting to the EU', so enforcement runs MRO to NAA to FAA.

The FAA-CAAC IPA (in force Oct 2017, replacing the 1995 SIP) accepts: PMAs for US-SoD products; STC-based (STC validated in China) or licensed-identicality PMAs for non-US-SoD products; and test-and-computation PMAs for Airbus or Rolls-Royce products only where the failure condition is 'no safety effect' or 'minor'. Failure conditions are not public, and older PMAs often have none documented.

The FAA-CAAC IPA has three paths: Acceptance, Streamlined Validation (35 working days, TC/STC only, when none of the 15 Safety Elements applies), and Limited or Full Technical Validation. A TSOA validation requires a matching CTSO.

A Canadian PDA allows test and computation only. 'Identicality … not an acceptable means'. A licence from the TC holder does not count as design control. The part must be a negligible change and must not add function, major components are excluded, and foreign applicants do not receive PDAs directly.
FAA STCs on grandfathered US Part 23/27 TCs are automatically accepted in Canada (IPA 3.3.3), but parts installed under them still need an FAA 8130-3 or Statement of Conformity under CAR 571.

EASA has no standalone PMA. Non-OEM parts go through a minor change or STC by a DOA holder and are marked EPA. Canada's equivalent is the PDA and Brazil's is the ANAC CPAA. A PDA is reportedly recognized on US aircraft only for non-critical parts.

The EU-US bilateral is actively maintained: TIP Rev 7 and 7.1 are combined, BOB Decision 014 was signed Jan 2026, and TIP-S rev 1 was added Jun 2026. The Bilateral Oversight Board is the mechanism for changing the rules.

research.q: Step: picking which parts to approve (demand and price-spike data: DIBBS, FedMall, FLIS, ILS, airline usage). How targets are chosen today and what data-driven targeting would look like.
research.headline: Today, targets are picked by hand and opportunistically. DLA's screen is only "bought for more than $10k in each of the last 2 years, plus ESA sign-off", contractors work from a small-hardware candidate list or their own digging, and fewer than 10% of 1,650 DLA reverse-engineering projects (FY15-18) finished, some because demand vanished before approval. Nobody fuses the public data (PUB LOG, FOIA price-paid logs, DIBBS awards, the FAA PMA list, platform retirement schedules) with approval probability and part clustering into a ranked list of approval portfolios, so targeting is a cheap, pure-compute first wedge for the Approval Factory and could also be sold to DLA and ESAs to rank their reviewer queues.

findings.finding: DLA started 1,650 reverse-engineering projects in FY2015-18 (600 contractor-funded, 1,033 DLA-funded). Only 141 were completed, 909 were still in process and 600 were canceled.

DLA's entry criteria are a business case, procurement above $10k in each of the past 2 years, and ESA approval before work starts and again for the TDP/SAR. Parts become candidates mainly because the government lacks data rights.

Reasons projects failed include slow ESA responses, contractors underestimating labor, staff pulled to other priorities, and 'the need no longer exists for some parts' (a targeting failure: demand decayed before approval).

Reported savings were at least $22M over FY15-18, gross of reverse-engineering cost. More than half came from the contractor-funded RPPOB program. Two-thirds of projects were low-value categories such as hardware, cables, filters and door handles.

RPPOB contractors choose from a DLA website candidate list of mostly small hardware and electrical items. Critical and classified parts are excluded, and AMSC B/G/T items are barred per a DLA deck cited in prior notes.

Supplier market-research tools: SRVA gives 24-month projected demand by NSN (needs a DIBBS account); WebFLIS gives NSN-to-P/N-to-approved-CAGE mapping (needs a CAC/PIV); PUB LOG is a free monthly FLIS download; the DLA FOIA Purchase Transaction Logs are public and include price paid.
Only about 15% of actively purchased NSNs are 1G (fully open competition), which implies a large restricted-source universe.
DLA bought more than $52B in FY24, $20B of it from small businesses. It manages about 5M items.

Commercial DIBBS intel tools (HigherGov at $500 to $2,500/yr, SAMSearch, Apify scrapers) give price and award history for distributors. They have no sole-source/AMSC scoring and no reverse-engineering candidate ranking.
A PMA maker (ADPma) picks parts on reliability gain, lead time, SDRs, ADs and removal rates, with an airline partner approving. It prices near OEM rather than competing on discount.
OEM part and ICA prices are rising faster than aftermarket inflation, and some ICA licenses require OEM-only parts.

(recalled) DoD IG found TransDigm excess profit on 46 of 47 parts (2019, about $16M) and on about 105 of 107 (2021-22, about $20.8M). The work is a manual, few-dozen-part audit, which shows price spikes are detectable from purchase history plus should-cost.

research.q: Step: data rights and IP clearance (DFARS 252.227, government purpose rights, trade secrets, design patents). How it is checked today, time, cost, failure modes.
research.headline: Clearing data rights and IP for a reverse-engineered part is checked today by hand, one legend at a time. DLA refuses to release limited-rights drawings and looks for patent markings on the part, and nobody rebuilds funding history, sweeps for expired government-purpose-rights periods, or searches design patents systematically. The AI play on the verification side is a per-part 'rights provenance graph' plus a clean-room evidence ledger that produces ready-to-file DFARS 252.227-7037 challenge packages and freedom-to-operate files. The binding constraint is access to the data (JEDMICS/cFolders and contract files), not intelligence.

findings.finding: Government purpose rights on data developed with mixed funding last 5 years (or a negotiated period) from contract execution and then convert to unlimited rights. Data delivered unmarked is presumed delivered with unlimited rights. Contractors get 6 months to fix inadvertent omissions, and 60 days to fix nonconforming markings before the government may correct them at the contractor's expense.

A contracting officer may challenge a restrictive marking within 6 years of final payment or delivery, or at any time if the data is public, was furnished without restriction, or the restriction was fraudulently asserted. The sequence is a written inquiry, a challenge notice, a 60-day contractor response, and a final decision roughly 60 days later, appealable to the boards or the Court of Federal Claims. In practice this means months to years per challenge, so it is rarely used.

Even for data developed at private expense, the government keeps release rights to form, fit and function data, to data needed for operation, maintenance, installation or training (excluding detailed manufacturing data), and to data that is public or already released. That is often the whole specification envelope a reverse engineering effort needs.

From FY2015 to FY2018, DLA started more than 1,600 reverse engineering projects (about 1,000 funded by DLA, about 600 by contractors) using 124 contractors, 83% of them small businesses. The IP safeguards consist only of not releasing limited-rights drawings and checking parts for patent markings (Troop Support skips the patent check). No IP complaints were reported.

In US v. Lange (7th Cir. 2002), an ex-employee of the PMA maker RAPCO was convicted for selling its reverse-engineered drawings. Reverse-engineered output can itself be a trade secret, and reverse engineering is lawful 'proper means' only if no contract prohibits it and no tainted inputs are used.

Trade-secret exposure in aerospace is large. Aerosonic won $116.9M against Joby (2026) over air data probes, arising from an NDA and supplier relationship. Alcoa lost its $265M claim against Universal Alloy (2023) when the jury found no trade secrets in well-known technology.

LKQ v. GM (Fed. Cir. en banc, May 21, 2024) dropped the rigid Rosen-Durling test for design patent obviousness, making OEM design patents on replacement-part shapes easier to invalidate. Design patents last 15 years, so most on legacy platforms have expired.

Under FAA PMA by test and computation, the FAA approves the design data but does not adjudicate IP; the applicant must own its data, and identicality by license needs a licensing agreement (recalled; the FAA Order 8110.42 page returned 403). On the commercial side, OEMs block PMA parts mostly through warranty and lease-return terms, not lawsuits (recalled).
findings.source: (recalled) FAA Order 8110.42; Pratt & Whitney vs HEICO history

findings.finding: Rough cost and time of the IP step (recalled): a freedom-to-operate opinion runs $10-50k per product family, and attorney review inside a source approval request about $5-20k. A marking challenge adds 6-24 months, and trade-secret litigation costs $2-10M through trial. The step is cheap in the median case but carries fat-tailed, program-killing risk.
findings.source: (recalled) AIPLA economic survey ranges; practitioner norms

Create IP-infringement insurance for reverse-engineered parts, underwritten on the clean-room log and FTO output, turning liability into a priced premium.

Policy work: get DLA and the services to accept machine-generated challenge packages, automate the conversion of lapsed GPR to unlimited rights in DLA systems, and push DoD right-to-repair and data-rights provisions (outcome of the FY2026 NDAA right-to-repair push recalled and uncertain; verify).
ai_plays: RightsGraph: per-part rights determinations plus ready-to-file 7037 challenge packages, sold to DLA, AFLCMC, NAVSUP and the Army (SBIR/STRATFI entry), and used internally first by the Approval Factory.
A one-time sweep for lapsed GPR on legacy fleets (C-130, KC-135, B-52), showing program offices which data they already hold with unlimited rights.
Clean-room provenance ledger as the standard evidence format for the 100+ small reverse engineering contractors and PMA houses, and as the basis for underwriting IP insurance.
Automated 3D-scan-to-patent FTO in minutes instead of weeks, including design patent invalidity analysis after LKQ.
An ITAR-compliant AI enclave service that lets small reverse engineering shops process technical data packages with AI legally.
surprises: Data delivered unmarked is legally presumed unlimited, and GPR on mixed-funding data turns into unlimited rights after 5 years. On 1950s-era platforms much 'restricted' data is probably no longer restricted, but nobody sweeps for it.

The statutory form-fit-function and maintenance-data exceptions mean the government can release the spec envelope even for privately funded parts, so reverse engineering only has to recover the internal details.
Under US v. Lange, a reverse engineer's own output can be a protectable trade secret, so a clean-room log is both a shield and an asset.
DLA Troop Support does no patent check at all; GAO found no IP complaints, but the sample was only 19 projects.
LKQ v. GM (2024) weakened the design patent weapon that OEMs use against aftermarket replacement parts.

research.q: Step: geometry capture and drawing reconstruction (CT, structured light, CMM, GD&T inference). State of the art, accuracy, time, what AI could automate fully.
research.headline: Geometry capture is solved hardware: CT, structured light and CMM reach microns. Converting a scan into CAD is being automated (Backflip AI, $30M; incumbent AI features). The approvable part of the step is still manual, and no one sells a pipeline from scan to approvable technical data package: inferring design-intent nominals and GD&T/tolerances, recovering them statistically from several samples, attaching per-feature uncertainty, and producing a MIL-STD-31000 package with an evidence trail. The verification-side AI play is a reconstruction-to-evidence engine that is qualified once as a method against government-owned ground-truth drawings, so reviewers check exceptions rather than every dimension.

findings.finding: Air Force RSO solicited an automated 3D scanner capturing hidden geometry, colour and reflectivity for parts about 1.5 ft x 3 ft and about 110 lb, with little human interaction. Roper said parts must match to 0.0001 in. RFP planned Feb 4, contract targeted Mar 31, 2021. No award found.
In Q1 2017 the Air Force had 10,000 parts requests that received no bidder.
findings.source: Air & Space Forces Magazine via search summary

findings.finding: Backflip AI (CEO Greg Mark) offers generative scan-to-parametric-CAD with a feature tree, launched as an Onshape add-on in Jul 2025, then a Fusion 360 plugin. Funding about $30M. Claims minutes instead of hours. No accuracy benchmarks, no aerospace customers, no GD&T or drawing output.

Lumafield (industrial CT plus AI software: Voyager, Quality Agent) raised a $75M Series C in Mar 2025 led by IVP and a $50M SVB debt facility in Nov 2025; CB Insights reports $192.5M total. Its site lists Reverse Engineering as an application with no features described and shows a Marine Corps logo. Triton production CT takes as little as 10 seconds per part.

Sigmetrix GD&T Advisor (Creo only) recommends controls and validates annotations, but the designer authors each one. It does not auto-generate tolerance schemes. No commercial tool infers a full functional GD&T scheme from a scan.

Industry practitioners (Artec, T3DMC, OR3D, Backflip) say in Feb 2026 that AI fuses, segments and fits features, but engineers still refine. Design intent versus the as-scanned shape is the core ambiguity, and output is only as reliable as its input. No quantified accuracy benchmarks exist.
Engineers re-apply tolerances based on function because a scan cannot show which surfaces are critical.

Government reverse engineering today is depot labour: the OC-ALC branch re-blueprinting dozens of B-1 parts, the WR-ALC REARM team (avionics), Mission Support Inc. (B-52 ducts), and a B-2 heat-exchanger re-core reverse engineering of NSN 1660-01-350-8209FW from 2 government-furnished units.

Typical accuracies (recalled): tactile CMM MPE about 1-2 um + L/300; blue-light structured light about 5-20 um; metrology CT about 4-10 um MPE per VDI/VDE 2630-1.3 on small parts, degrading on dense superalloys and large parts. Scan times run minutes to hours.

Estimated labour (recalled/opinion): mesh to CAD takes 4-20 h for prismatic parts and 20-100+ h for freeform; GD&T and drawing take 20-80 h per part number; materials and process ID takes 1-4 weeks elapsed. Geometry plus drawing is about 15-30% of the 300-1,000 h package.

research.q: Step: material and process identification of an existing part (alloy, heat treat, coatings, grain structure, residual stress; XRF, OES, LIBS, EBSD, hardness, metallography). What can be determined non-destructively, what needs destruction, and AI potential.
research.headline: About 70-80% of what a reviewer needs (alloy grade, aluminium temper, coating type and thickness, hardness, surface residual stress) can already be found without destroying the part, using XRF, LIBS, eddy current conductivity, hardness, Barkhausen and portable XRD. The rest (grain flow, melt practice, gas content, through-thickness properties, invisible steps such as the hydrogen bake) still needs destruction, and sole-source parts often exist only as 1-3 samples. Search found no company that combines the readings from many test methods into a calibrated identification of spec, temper and process, or that plans which test to run so the fewest samples are destroyed. That engine, built on a paired dataset of NDE scans and destructive results, plus a standard regulators accept, is the open verification-side AI play.

findings.finding: Handheld XRF gives surface chemistry but cannot detect C, B, Li or Be, and struggles to tell close Al grades apart (7075/7050/7475, 2024/2124). LIBS adds carbon in steel and light elements but leaves a micro-crater.
findings.source: https://www.sciaps.com/ (LIBS-only carbon claim; Z-903 'H to U'); grade-separation limits recalled

findings.finding: Aluminium temper can be checked without destruction using eddy current conductivity (%IACS, ASTM E1004) plus hardness. AMS 2658 is an accepted heat-treat verification method on this basis, which is regulatory precedent for accepting NDE-inferred material state.
ML on ultrasonic plus eddy current data estimated yield strength, UTS and elongation of Al alloys across compositions and heat treats within about 8% of tensile tests
Eddy current conductivity curves plus a neural network predicted final extrusion grain structure in Al-Mg-Si
AFRL down-selected one eddy current technique and one ultrasonic technique for NDE verification of engineered residual stress (cold-expanded holes) in Al, extended to Ti and steel
findings.source: ASM Residual Stress Conference 2026 abstract, asm.confex.com Paper66607 (via search summary; page now 404)

findings.finding: Portable XRD residual stress samples only about 5-30 um deep. Through-thickness stress needs neutron or synchrotron beam time (months of queue) or the destructive contour method.
findings.source: recalled (ASTM E915/E2860; ORNL HFIR, NIST, APS)

findings.finding: Several properties need destruction: VAR vs air-melt cleanliness (e.g. AMS 6414 vs 6415, ASTM E45), O/N/H by inert gas fusion, forging grain flow (macroetch ASTM E381), coating cross-sections, and fatigue/toughness allowables. Hydrogen-bake, peen intensity and stress relief leave essentially no measurable signature.
Commercial characterization cost and time
findings.number: $300-1.5k basic chemistry and hardness; $10-40k and 2-6 weeks for a full package
findings.source: recalled lab pricing (Element, Applus, NTS, IMR, Lambda)

findings.finding: DISCUS Software was one of 3 picks from about 150 teams in the AFWERX reverse engineering / additive manufacturing challenge (Oct 2020) for AI-driven reverse engineering, TDP generation and first article inspection. Its scope is extracting requirements from drawings by OCR, not material identification.
AI geometry reverse engineering is commoditizing: Novineer NoviVision makes CAD from 1-4 phone photos in about 2 minutes (AIX 2026). Material and process identity becomes the remaining bottleneck.

pathway_steps.step: Non-destructive survey: CT/radiography, XRF, eddy current conductivity, portable hardness, coating thickness, Barkhausen, portable XRD

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Each instrument gives a separate readout. Nobody fuses them into a calibrated spec/temper/process probability. A metallurgist does it by hand.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No rule for when a micro-mark is allowed on a flight part. Indentation-derived properties are not accepted as allowables.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Uses up scarce samples (1-3 often exist). No optimal plan for which cut gives the most information. Samples are not pooled across the fleet.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Access and physics clock. No validated ML that infers the full stress field from surface data plus a process model.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No machine-readable genealogy of spec revisions. Invisible process steps are handled ad hoc, not by systematic bounding-envelope arguments.

Optimal experimental design that picks the next test and the exact cut plan to get the most information per destroyed gram when only 1-3 samples exist

Create the missing paired ground-truth dataset: about 3,000 retired parts of known spec from AMARG (Davis-Monthan), DLA Disposition/DEMIL scrap and airline teardowns, each scanned with every NDE mode then fully destroyed (about $10-60M; data-access agreements are the constraint)
Machine-readable spec genealogy graph (QQ-, MIL-, OEM process specs such as BAC, superseded AMS revisions mapped to chemistry windows, heat-treat cycles, property minimums and modern equivalents)

Validated ML inference of the through-thickness residual stress field from surface XRD plus a process model, checked against contour-method data; or compact lab high-energy XRD/neutron to remove the beam-time queue

Robotic autonomous characterization cell (CT to XRF/LIBS to eddy current/hardness to XRD to auto-section/polish to EBSD to gas fusion) scheduled by the engine: 24-72 h turnaround and about 5-10 reviewer hours, against 2-6 weeks and 40-100 hours today

Sell the engine to DLA, OC-ALC, NAVAIR and FAA DERs via SBIR (AFWERX/RSO reverse engineering topics), as a wedge before owning approvals
Own the paired NDE-to-destructive dataset plus the consensus standard: permission-like, not knowledge-like, a moat that fits the thesis
Spin-out market: suspect-unapproved and counterfeit part detection for DLA and MRO receiving inspection using the same engine
Through-thickness residual stress and process inference service (ML plus surface measurements) replacing beam time
surprises: AMS 2658 (conductivity plus hardness) already makes NDE-inferred temper an accepted verification. Precedent for regulator acceptance exists and could be extended.
Geometry reverse engineering is now a 2-minute phone-photo task, while material identity still takes weeks. The bottleneck has moved firmly to material and process.
The scarce input is samples, not lab capacity. Designing tests to minimise destruction matters more than faster instruments.
Some process steps (hydrogen bake, peen intensity) leave essentially no measurable signature. The answer is conservative-envelope engineering, not better forensics.
Limited search found no company doing multimodal NDE fusion for reverse engineering or approvals (moderate confidence).

research.q: Step: design substantiation by analysis (FEA, fatigue, damage tolerance) for replacement parts. What regulators accept, how long it takes, how AI/compute could replace engineering hours.
research.headline: The FAA already accepts analysis supported by test for structural parts: 14 CFR 21.303 allows "computations", AC 25.571-1D accepts "analysis supported by test evidence", and the FAA accepted an analysis under its CAST policy in place of a repair. So the obstacle is not the law; it is the hours spent gathering inputs and writing reports, plus the clocks for validation tests and reviewer queues. No one found sells an AI-native equivalence-substantiation engine or a reviewer copilot for replacement parts. The verification-side play is to automate comparative analysis on top of verified solvers, send it as a traceable argument graph, and own the test data and the signature (via an ODA, or by selling the tool to the reviewers).

findings.finding: 14 CFR 21.303(a)(4) explicitly allows 'test reports and computations' to show compliance for PMA; analysis is legally an accepted means.

FAA's Chief Scientist for Fatigue & Damage Tolerance (Gorelik) says that for Part 25 DT, 'analysis supported by test evidence' is accepted. For Part 33 LLPs, analysis is accepted but 'should be validated against relevant test data'. AC 20-146 seats is 'one of the few examples of certification by analysis'. Test articles 'should be full-scale (component or sub-component)'.

The CM4QC roadmap (NASA/TM-20260001729, DOT/FAA/TC-26/10) expects computational methods to augment testing in years 1-5 and to expand capability dramatically only after 10+ years. Listed gaps: trust, public validation data, material property data, UQ, and resources for side-by-side campaigns. The steering group has no startups among its roughly 25 members.
Precedent: the FAA accepted a damage-tolerance analysis (fuselage skin and doubler cracking) under the CAST policy, and the aircraft kept its certification without repair.
findings.source: Abdi et al., Aeronautical Journal 118(1200), Feb 2014, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/aeronautical-journal/article/an-analysis-approach-toward-faa-certification-for-damage-tolerance-of-aircraft-components/96F965A0B37C25FA2128BD96ED8A3C04

findings.finding: Effort by part class (recalled): a non-critical comparative static analysis takes 20-80 engineering hours. Fatigue-critical parts take 100-400. PSE/DT parts take 300-1,000+. Engine LLP PMAs take thousands of hours and cost $1M+ per part. Roughly 30-40% of hours go to gathering inputs (geometry, material ID, allowables) and 30-40% to reports and reviewer rounds; little of it is compute.

Physics clock: an S-N coupon at 10^7 cycles and 20 Hz runs about 6 days, and a full curve takes weeks. Component spectrum fatigue takes 1-6 months. DLA/ESA SAR reviewer queues run 6-24+ months (recalled) and are often longer than the engineering itself.
PhysicsX raised $32M (Nov 2023), $135M Series B (Jun 2025) and $300M Series C (Jun 2026). It targets new-design physics AI; its newsroom mentions nothing on fatigue or certification.

Neural Concept raised a $100M Series C; its named customers are automotive, with nothing on fatigue or certification. Xcert AI (Geneva) raised CHF 1.1M in Dec 2025 for certification-workflow and document automation, with no stress analysis.

Verification-grade tools already exist: the FAA-funded SMART|DT probabilistic DT code (UTSA), ESRD StressCheck hp-FEM with error estimation and DaDT simulation apps, and NASGRO/AFGROW crack growth. An AI layer can sit on top of these as the code of record.
