research.q: Step: qualification test planning and execution (coupons, component tests, fatigue, environmental). Cost and time structure; what is truly physics-clock bound vs scheduling/queue bound.
research.headline: Physics clocks are a small part of qualification time. Even for a fatigue-critical metallic part the unavoidable load, cycle and conditioning time is about 4 to 8 weeks when fully run in parallel (1 to 2 weeks for most non-critical parts), yet real programs take 6 to 18+ months. By my estimate 75 to 95% of that time is queue: plan approval, material lead times, specimen machining, lab slots, witness scheduling, re-test loops, and report and regulator review. No one I found sells outcome-priced, end-to-end qualification evidence. Labs sell frame-hours, software firms sell test-data plumbing (Nominal) or simulation (PhysicsX, Monolith), and DERs sell signatures, so the verification-side AI play is a vertically integrated "evidence factory" that compiles the minimum test plan, deletes tests by showing equivalence to existing data, and runs the rest in an owned lights-out lab.

findings.finding: High-cycle fatigue to 10^7 cycles at 20 to 50 Hz takes 2.3 to 5.8 days per coupon. An S-N curve needs 15 to 30 coupons: about 80 days on one frame, 4 to 6 days across 20 frames. So it is physics-bound only per specimen; in aggregate it is a parallelism problem.

The truly irreducible clocks are set by standards or by diffusion and biology: composite moisture conditioning (30 to 120+ days), creep and stress rupture (100 to 10,000+ h), SCC alternate immersion (10 to 90 days), fungus (28 days), humidity (48 to 240 h), and component spectrum fatigue (weeks to months).
findings.number: 28 d fungus; 240 h humidity Cat B; 1,000 h = 42 days
findings.source: DO-160 Sec 6/13, MIL-STD-810 M507/508, ASTM D5229/G44/G47 (recalled)

findings.finding: Shared allowables databases deleted most of the testing for composites. NCAMP says the AGATE shared-database approach cut certification time by about 4x and cost by about 10x.
Lab capacity is constrained and expanding. LTI spent $3M+ on 16 new fatigue frames, reaching 52 total, for aerospace and AM demand. That implies about $190k per frame.
Element, the largest independent lab, has 200+ environmental chambers, 120 dynamics systems and 32 Nadcap labs, but publishes no lead times or prices. Capacity is opaque and quote-driven.

Nominal (hardware test-data software) raised an $80M Series B-2 at a $1B valuation in March 2026, led by Founders Fund, after a $75M Series B in June 2025. It reports 7x revenue growth and a reported $53M AFTC IDIQ. It organizes test data and does not produce regulator-accepted qualification evidence.
Precedent for analysis replacing tests exists but is narrow. FAA AC 20-146A (seats by computer modeling validated by dynamic tests) was issued 2024-11-29. EASA accepts virtual testing case by case.

Fatigue allowables are driven by the tails of the property distribution, so datasets are large and costly. This is the statistical reason specimen counts are high, and it is where Bayesian priors could cut N.

Rough split of a ~$100k package: engineering 40 to 60%, test execution 20 to 40%, DER/DAR and conformity 10 to 20%, material 5 to 15% of cost but the dominant time driver (forging lead times 40 to 80 weeks in 2023 to 2025).

pathway_steps.step: Test plan authoring and regulator/DER/ESA agreement
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Precedent lives in DER heads and is not searchable. N is set by handbook, not by the evidence needed. Agreement takes months.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Machining is outsourced. The conformity visit is an in-person FAA/DAR slot.

pathway_steps.step: Coupon tests (static, HCF, LCF, crack growth, creep, SCC)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Frames run serially at independent labs with weeks-to-months slot lead times. Little automation of loading. Accelerated methods (ultrasonic HCF) are accepted only case by case.
pathway_steps.who_does_it: Element, NTS, LTI, Westmoreland, NIAR, SwRI
pathway_steps.time: physics: hours to 42+ days per specimen; elapsed: 1-4 months

pathway_steps.step: Component/sub-assembly fatigue and functional tests
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Unique fixtures. One failure restarts material, specimen and queue (the biggest variance driver). No cheap pre-screen.

pathway_steps.step: Environmental qualification (DO-160 / MIL-STD-810)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Run serially on one article, the timeline is driven by 10-day humidity and 28-day fungus tests. Fungus is often waivable by analysis, but that waiver is argued fresh each time.

pathway_steps.step: Witnessing
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: In-person scheduling. Remote or asynchronous witnessing is not standard despite COVID-era precedent.

pathway_steps.step: Data reduction, report, 8110-3 / SAR package
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Reports are compiled by hand into PDFs. Traceability from raw data to conclusions is manual.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Thin ACO and ESA staffing. DLA SAR evaluations have historically taken 6-12+ months (recalled).

Auto-generated, regulator-formatted evidence packages (8110-3, SAR) with full raw-data traceability, cutting DER and reviewer hours.
Failure pre-screen with simulation plus cheap surrogate tests so expensive component articles do not fail and trigger restart loops.
Pre-characterized material bank of common legacy alloy heats (7075, 4340, 17-4PH, Ti-6Al-4V, IN718) with certs and allowables on shelf, removing the 40-80 week material clock.
Standard argued-once waivers (for example fungus by material inertness, identical-environment similarity) packaged as reusable rationale libraries.
ai_plays: Evidence Factory: vertically integrated qualification-as-a-service for PMA/SAR (AI plan compiler, owned robotic lab, auto report), priced per approval and measured on calendar days and reviewer hours per approval.
Reviewer copilot for DLA ESAs and FAA ACOs: the same plan and report checker sold or given to the regulator to clear SAR/PMA backlogs, which builds acceptance and gives a data moat.
Test-deletion engine: equivalence-to-existing-allowables plus Bayesian N reduction, sold to PMA houses and MRO DERs.
Allowables commons for legacy alloys and AM (an NCAMP-like shared database for metals reverse engineering), where the company becomes the data clearinghouse.

Witness-grade test data infrastructure (cryptographically signed sensor streams plus chain of custody) layered on frames; adjacent to Nominal but aimed at regulator acceptance rather than engineer dashboards.
surprises: Physics time is only about 5-25% of elapsed qualification time; material lead time and regulator and plan queues dominate.
The precedent for test deletion is shared databases, not better simulation. NCAMP claims 4x faster and 10x cheaper for composites; no equivalent exists for reverse-engineered legacy metallic parts.
Test-data software has reached unicorn scale (Nominal at $1B), yet nobody owns the step from test data to regulator-accepted evidence.
Most test counts come from soft law (ACs, handbooks, ESA practice), not statute, so they can be changed through ARC/issue paper/ESA discretion.

research.q: Step: production approval and quality system (PMA production approval, AS9100, first article inspection AS9102). Cost and time to stand up; could it be shared across a supplier network?
research.headline: Standing up a quality system is cheap in dollars: about $10-50k for AS9100 and perhaps $50-200k (recalled) for an FAA-acceptable 14 CFR 21.137 system. The real costs are the 6-18 month (recalled) MIDO queue on a holder's first production approval and the per-part, per-supplier, per-change FAI and FAT labor that follows (about 8 h per AS9102 report; DLA FAT takes months). The approval can be shared across a supplier network only through one legal holder that controls fabless suppliers under 21.137(c), not through co-holding. Nobody yet sells a verification-evidence format that the regulator accepts in place of re-inspection, and that is the opening for an AI verification play.

findings.finding: PMA application must name the manufacturing facilities and include inspections and tests showing material, design and process conformity; the quality system must meet 14 CFR 21.137's 15 elements

21.137(c) supplier control only requires procedures that make sure supplier items meet the holder's requirements, plus a feedback path. Fabless PMA holders using controlled suppliers are legally allowed. The quality system is approved once per holder, so its cost is spread over every later PMA
AS9100D for a small shop: $10-50k (one estimate $10-20k under 50 employees), 3-12 months; ISO 9001 covers about 75% of AS9100D. NIST MEP example: 12-person R&M Machine Shop certified in 2021

AS9102 FAI reports take about 8 engineer-hours each; one facility did about 15/day. GroundControl (YC) automates ballooning and report generation for 70+ US facilities at about 1,000 reports/month (company claims)
Customers require AS9102 FAI even where AS9100 does not, and shops often fail to price it into bids

DLA: Critical Safety Items need ESA source approval (note H04, DFARS 252.209-7010). DLAD 9.3 requires the buyer to justify FAT over cheaper methods. FAT is waivable if the same or a similar item was delivered within 5 years (3 for CSI). FAT cost goes into the production price unless it has a separate CLIN. CoC is not allowed for CSI without ESA approval
Example March 2026 DLA Navy pin solicitation: government FAT plus production lot testing, with only two approved sources (Sikorsky, Apex Manufacturing)
Net-Inspect gives suppliers a free limited licence to a customer's FAI module and links sub-assembly FAIRs into assembly FAIRs. This is the closest existing shared-verification network
AS9003 is being replaced by IA9150 from Feb 2026
First MIDO production approval for a new PMA holder takes about 6-18 months, driven by the regulator queue (recalled; faa.gov returned 403)

research.q: Step: regulator/reviewer review (FAA ACO, DLA ESA, NRC inspectors). Staffing, queue data, rework cycles, what share of elapsed time is review, and how reviewer-side tools could change it.
research.headline: At DLA, the service engineering office (the ESA) is the long pole even on paper: it is 90 of about 190 nominal days. In FY17 DLA Land and Maritime approved only 111 of 225 decided packages, with 144 still pending and just 7 analysts in its value-engineering screening step. No tool built for the reviewer (submission linting, evidence-linked packages, precedent search, published queue data) exists at DLA, the FAA or the NRC. The verification-side AI play is to be the firm whose packages pass review on the first try and are cheap to check, and to hold a delegated sign-off (FAA ODA) where the law allows one.

findings.finding: DLA's nominal SAR clock is CAO 5 days, VE screening 15 days, missing-data loop 30 days, ESA engineering evaluation 90 days, VE concurrence 15 days, extra-data loop 30 days, notice 5 days. That is about 190 days nominal, and the ESA is about half of it. DLA does not control the ESA step.
findings.source: DLA SAR briefing, E. Wilde, NDIA June 2018, https://ndia.dtic.mil/wp-content/uploads/2018/dla/SARBriefing_SC.pdf

findings.finding: In FY17 DLA Land and Maritime received 282 SARs: 111 approved ($35.5M potential annual savings), 114 rejected, 144 pending ($30.9M). Approval is about 49% of decided packages, and the backlog is about half a year's intake.

DLA's value-engineering screening step had 7 analysts. Its stated rejection reasons include 'Can't validate part (no government data to compare)' and 'Good on paper, but need to prove will work in application'.

DAG 17.7501-6 (17 June 2014): a newly approved source gets a multi-source clause for at least one year and up to 40% of the award if its price is fair and reasonable. This is a built-in demand guarantee after approval.

Historically DLA had no authority over ESA timing. In a 1981 case DLA asked for 21 days, the evaluation took about 4 months ('typical'), and DLA awarded to the incumbent while it waited. GAO has also sustained a protest over unreasonable source-approval delay (1988).
findings.source: GAO decision https://www.gao.gov/products/458026 ; GAO B-232702 https://www.gao.gov/products/B-232702

findings.finding: FAA Aircraft Certification has tracked project wait-listing (sequencing) in a database since at least 2010, and Flight Standards was made to do the same from Oct 2011. The data exists internally but is not published.

More than 90% of FAA certification work is delegated to industry (ODA, DERs). Even so, GAMA testified that FAA engineers often keep work they could delegate, and that ODA use is inconsistent from region to region. That adds delay: FAA review time is small in hours but sits on the critical path.
findings.source: AVweb Feb 2017 citing GAO; GAMA (Bunce) Senate Commerce testimony 21 Apr 2015

findings.finding: FAA certification units are chronically understaffed, and the 2025 workforce cuts and shutdown made it worse.

NRC NEIMA generic schedules, measured from acceptance to the final safety evaluation: license amendments 11-12 months, topical reports 18, exemptions 12. For replacement parts the NRC is mostly not a pre-approver: licensees self-dedicate under Part 21 / Appendix B, and the NRC inspects after the fact.

NRC internal AI: SimplifAI (deployed) for licensing and oversight text retrieval, plus M365 Copilot. ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini and USAi are pre-deployment. No time-saved metrics are published, and the NRC says AI 'is not used as a substitute for professional judgment'. Its AI Strategic Plan was published 29 Sept 2025.

My estimate (opinion) is that review plus rework is about 40-70% of elapsed time for a DLA SAR and about 30-50% for a non-delegated FAA test-and-computation PMA, falling below about 20% when the applicant holds an ODA or DER. Rejection and resubmission cost more time than the review itself.
findings.source: estimate from the DLA clock and FY17 data above plus recalled industry norms

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a 'reviewer-twin' linter that runs each package against the DLA SAR guide checklist, the ESA's known data-sufficiency asks, the FAA Order 8110.42 PMA data requirements and accepted compliance-plan templates before submission. This removes the 30-day loops and the roughly 50% rejection rate that resets the queue.

Define an evidence-linked package standard, an eCTD equivalent for parts. Every drawing feature, material and process requirement links to the evidence behind it (CMM or CT scan, certs, test data, FEA), so the reviewer checks links instead of rebuilding the argument. Offer it free to DLA and the ESAs as the preferred format.

Provide a baseline-reconstruction service that gives the ESA a validated digital baseline of the OEM part, built from multiple teardowns, scans and service history. This directly attacks the stated rejection reason 'no government data to compare'.

Build a precedent and similarity engine over past approvals (by part family, NSN and evidence set). Reviewers could then approve by analogy, and the FAA could accept 'similar to previously approved' arguments.

Assemble queue-transparency data. FOIA and self-collect turnaround times by ESA, ACO office and part family (the FAA already has CSOP wait-list data; DLA has its SAR tracker), then route work to the fastest pathway and lobby with numbers.

Win reviewer delegation. Obtain an FAA ODA for PMA and major repairs, with AI drafting findings and human unit members signing. Push DoD for a third-party, ESA-equivalent engineering authority pilot (MIL-HDBK-516 style reliance), which does not exist today. This is a policy constraint, not a physics one.
Build a model-credibility framework for parts (an ASME V&V 40 analogue) that regulators accept, so validated simulation can replace some qualification tests. This shortens the physics clock.
Offer AI reviewer tools to the government, either as a contracted ESA-support engineering service or as a tool that pre-digests packages for ESA engineers. This turns the bottleneck into a customer.
ai_plays: An Approval Factory with a built-in reviewer twin: the KPI shifts from engineering hours per package to first-pass approval rate and reviewer hours consumed per approval. The firm whose packages are cheapest to review gets reviewed first.

Contracted ESA-support engineering: sell AI-assisted SAR evaluation capacity to the service ESAs or DLA VE (7 analysts, a 144-package backlog, about $31M of savings stuck in the pending queue in FY17 alone). Risk: a conflict of interest if the same firm also submits SARs, so this needs a separate entity or firewall.
Hold an FAA ODA (PMA and repair) and run AI-drafted findings signed by human unit members. This captures the delegation moat HEICO already uses, at a lower cost per approval.
A FOIA-built cross-agency approval intelligence layer (queue times, precedents, rejection reasons), as a data product or as the factory's internal routing advantage.
An evidence-graph format and validated-baseline service licensed to other PMA and SAR houses: the 'TurboTax plus the IRS e-file standard' for parts approvals.
surprises: The only public end-to-end SAR numbers found are from a 2018 NDIA briefing. DLA publishes no turnaround data, and neither does the FAA, even though GAO made the FAA build a wait-list tracker in 2011.
DLA's own rejection list includes 'Can't validate part (no government data to compare)'. The reviewer is blocked by having no baseline, not by the quality of the package.
DLA already guarantees new sources up to 40% of awards for a year (DAG 17.7501-6, 2014), so an approval converts directly into revenue.

At the NRC the bottleneck for parts is not the NRC: dedication is self-certified by licensees and dedicators under Part 21 / Appendix B, so the 'reviewer' to win over is the utility's engineering and NUPIC audits.
The FAA delegates more than 90% of certification work, yet industry says FAA engineers often keep work they could delegate. The constraint is reviewer behaviour and trust, not legal authority.

research.q: Step: first article inspection and conformity inspection (AS9102, CMM, CT). Automation state and AI potential.
research.headline: Turning the drawing into an AS9102 first-article report is mostly automated already. Ideagen claims about 1 hour per report instead of hours to a full day, and DISCUS sells AI auto-ballooning (marking every dimension on the drawing). CT scanning is growing fast: Lumafield raised a $75M Series C in March 2025 plus a $50M SVB debt facility in November 2025. What nobody automates is the step that matters for reverse-engineered parts: measuring many OEM samples to show our part is equivalent to theirs, with quantified measurement uncertainty, packaged as structured evidence regulators can review quickly.

findings.finding: Software that fills in AS9102 Forms 1-3 and auto-balloons drawings is a mature market. Ideagen InspectionXpert claims a first-article report drops from hours or a full day to about 1 hour (vendor claim).
DISCUS IDA uses AI/ML to balloon PDF/TIFF drawings and 3D CAD models automatically, and says data extraction will become 'almost completely automated'. It publishes no metrics.

High QA and Net-Inspect sell first-article, statistical process control and supplier-portal software with CMM connectors. High QA's page does not mention AI. Net-Inspect links part-level reports up into assembly-level reports.

Lumafield raised a $75M Series C in March 2025, led by IVP with Kleiner, Lux, DCVC, Spark, G2VP and Wellington. It added a $50M SVB growth facility in November 2025 to deploy more scanners. Its CT first-article page claims it 'supports AS9102' but names no aerospace customer and gives no accuracy figures.

DLA may require first-article test samples before adding an alternate source to its approved list. Current solicitations include waiver worksheets for first-article and production-lot testing, used when the supplier recently produced the item. GAO decisions let DLA take the time it needs to evaluate alternates and reject unverified ones, so evaluation time is part of the permission bottleneck.
A DoD Inspector General review found that 79 of 103 contracts it examined had no first-article test requirement (reported secondhand).

Writing CMM measurement programs is still largely manual, taking hours to days for each new part. Auto-programming needs CAD models that carry machine-readable dimension data, which legacy C-130 and KC-135 parts lack. The QIF digital-thread standard (ISO 23952) is barely adopted. (recalled)

Formal uncertainty standards for CT dimensional measurement are recent (VDI/VDE 2630; ISO 10360-11). Primes and regulators still often want contact CMM on critical features, so a first-article report based only on CT is not yet broadly accepted. (recalled)

Today this is argued in prose and reviewed by hand.

Measurement-uncertainty budgets and ISO 14253-1 decision rules calculated automatically for each characteristic across CMM, CT and optical measurement, attached to the first-article report, so regulators can accept CT data.

A structured submission package (first-article report + QIF + CT volume + certs) and a free reviewer copilot for DLA engineering reviewers, FAA certification engineers and FAA designees, cutting reviewer hours, which is the KPI that limits approvals.

Precedent-setting acceptance of CT-only first-article evidence: validate CT against CMM on a set of parts, start with non-critical DLA items, then push for an FAA policy memo or advisory circular update on virtual conformity using CT volumes with tamper-evident chain of custody.
AI analysis of micrographs, fractures and chemistry with calibrated uncertainty, to show legacy alloys and heat treatments match the OEM part.
Automatic delta first-article reports when a process, material or machine changes, instead of a human judging which characteristics to re-inspect.
Bring the signature in-house: hire or own FAA designees, eventually organizational delegation, so conformity sign-off becomes an internal step that AI drafts and a human signs.
ai_plays: Equivalence engine (CT of OEM samples to derived technical data package to equivalence report): the core verification wedge of the Approval Factory and a direct fit.
Metrology agent: drawing or scan in; inspection plan, CMM/CT program and AS9102 + QIF report with uncertainty out. Usable internally and sellable as SaaS to AS9100 shops.
Reviewer copilot and structured-submission standard given free to DLA engineering reviewers and FAA designees, which creates regulator lock-in; possible SBIR/AFWERX entry.
An ISO 17025-accredited CT and CMM inspection lab network with FAA designees on staff, run as a service for other PMA and source-approval applicants; brings revenue and a data flywheel.

surprises: Lumafield's first-article page names no aerospace customer and gives no accuracy figures even though it has about $150M in funding. CT first-article inspection in aerospace is still early.
The paperwork layer that people usually call AI first-article inspection is a commodity. The money is in proving equivalence and getting reviewers to accept the evidence, not in ballooning.
A DoD IG review found that 79 of 103 contracts it examined had no first-article test requirement at all, so the formal test burden on DLA spares is uneven. Engineering review is the real gate.

research.q: Step: return-to-service sign-off and installation records (8130-3, Form 1, 337, logbooks). Where verification fails (AOG Technics) and what would fix it.
research.headline: The return-to-service step works like a bearer instrument: a paper 8130-3 or EASA Form 1 makes a part tradeable and installable, and the only check is a receiving inspector comparing paper against a box. AOG Technics showed this. It was an accredited broker that sold over 60,000 CFM56 and CF6 parts on altered certificates (£39.3M fraud), was caught only when a TAP technician noticed a worn damper papered as new, and even the industry coalition's call for a cross-company verification interface has no owner. That gap is an AI verification play with no direct competitor found: a neutral verifier that checks the document fields, the signer and the physical part, and fits naturally with an Approval Factory whose parts ship digitally signed and physically fingerprinted.

findings.finding: AOG Technics sold more than 60,000 parts (Jan 2019 to Jul 2023), worth £6.9M and mostly CFM56. About 90% of £7.7M revenue was fraudulent, and the SFO put the fraud at £39.3M. Zamora pleaded guilty to fraudulent trading in Dec 2025 and was sentenced to 4 years 8 months in Feb 2026.

Method: genuine release certificates (ARCs) altered on a home computer, forged shipment memos implying the parts came direct from Safran, forged signatures of real and former Safran staff, and invented AOG employees with fake LinkedIn profiles. Sales spiked in late 2019 right after the forgery began.

AOG was accredited under the voluntary distributor program (AC 00-56B) by Transonic Aviation Consultants. The FAA removed Transonic as an accepted accreditor in April 2024, after the fraud came out. Accreditation audits procedures, not individual documents.

Detection came by chance. In June 2023 a TAP Air Portugal technician flagged a worn CFM56 damper papered as new, and Safran confirmed the certificate was fake. EASA and the UK CAA issued suspected-unapproved-parts notices on Aug 4 2023, and the FAA followed on Sep 21 2023. GE and Safran had to go to a UK court to get AOG's sales records. Fewer than 1% of CFM engines were affected, but aircraft were grounded worldwide.

The fakes had machine-checkable flaws: accurate-looking signatures, but purchase-order numbers that did not follow the OEM's format and part numbers that did not match the part. Nobody cross-checked the certificates against the issuer's own records.

The FAA has allowed electronic 8130-3 since 2009 (Order 8130.21), but most ARCs are still paper or PDF. The first digitally signed 8130-3 (Boeing, Southwest and Aeroxchange eARC, using X.509 public-key signatures) shipped in Oct 2025. Each of Boeing's 9 repair centers needs its own FAA authorization for electronic records and signatures.

ASCIC issued 13 unanimous voluntary recommendations. Rec 8 calls for industry-wide software and APIs, possibly hosted by a third party, that query OEM, airline and production-approval-holder databases to validate every ARC field in real time, including whether the signatory was authorized. Rec 9 calls for a back-to-birth database of digitized ARCs; Rec 13 calls for unique digital IDs, digital twins and blockchain for non-serialized parts. The regulator section is one sentence, and none of these three has an owner.

GE Aerospace has digitized more than 18M MRO records since 2023, uses AI to check that ARC fields are valid and consistent, and keeps a source-of-truth database of new-make GE/CFM material. This is the closest existing version of the answer, but it covers only GE's own material and is not offered to others.

AI digital-logbook tools such as Bluetail (claims 30M records and $10B in asset value; cites AC 120-78B and SOC 2 Type 1) organize and search records. They do not authenticate documents, signers or physical parts.

Form 337 major repair records go to the FAA Aircraft Registry as paper scans, and lists of who may sign releases sit in each repair station's internal manual. Neither can be checked by machine. (recalled)

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build the third-party, cross-OEM interface that checks every field of every release certificate (Form 1/8130-3) against the issuer's records (ASCIC Rec 8). Where an issuer has no interface, reconstruct its conventions (purchase-order formats, tracking-number sequences, form revisions, signature biometrics) from very large OCR'd archives.

A registry of who was authorized to sign releases, at which repair station, on which date. It does not exist today; rosters sit inside each station's manual. Build it from public FAA repair-station data, other public sources and issuer onboarding, then lobby the FAA to publish it as machine-readable data.

Automate the TAP technician's catch: AI on receiving-inspection photos or 3D scans that compares the part's wear state with its claimed condition (new, overhauled, as-removed) and its geometry with the drawing.
Graph anomaly detection over broker trade flows. AOG's late-2019 sales spike and its invented staff were detectable signals.

Machine-read the FAA Aircraft Registry's Form 337 archive (via FOIA or bulk request) and confirm that each cited approved-data reference (DER approval, STC, PMA) exists and covers that aircraft and serial number.
A platform-level FAA/EASA acceptance for electronic records, so subscribing repair stations inherit it by reference instead of each needing its own authorization (Boeing needed one per center).
A unique ID or surface fingerprint for non-serialized parts (dampers, bushings: the AOG categories), building the back-to-birth graph of ASCIC Rec 9 one verification at a time.
On liability, sell a risk score plus evidence pack, never the release sign-off itself; later, an insurer-backed provenance warranty priced on SUP loss data.
ai_plays: Provenance verifier of record: a neutral SaaS used at receiving inspection by MROs, airlines, lessors and DoD depots. It cross-checks each release certificate, 337 or logbook entry for internal consistency, issuer conventions, signer existence and authority, the part's physical match to its paper, and anomalies in broker trade flows.

Approval Factory parts made verifiable by default: every new PMA, DLA-approved or DER part ships with a born-digital signed release certificate (Spec 2000 Ch 16) plus a surface fingerprint, using the same geometry and material model built during reverse engineering. That model also becomes the physical reference for verifying anyone's copy of that part.
DLA/DoD counterfeit-prevention service under DFARS 252.246-7007/7008, extending the physical-marking idea DLA already mandates for microcircuits to reverse-engineered mechanical parts.
AI audit of the Form 337 archive, plus a check that the approved data each repair cites actually exists, for owners, lessors and the FAA.
Later, insurance-backed provenance guarantees, with the verification data network (back-to-birth graph) as the moat.

surprises: The fraudster was accredited under the FAA-accepted voluntary distributor program; the accreditor (Transonic) was de-listed only in April 2024.
The FAA has allowed electronic 8130-3 since 2009, yet the first digitally signed one shipped only in Oct 2025, and Boeing still needs FAA authorization center by center.

The industry coalition explicitly asked for a third-party verification interface and back-to-birth database (Recs 8 and 9), and as of this research no one owns either. GE has built one only for its own material.
Detection depended on one technician's eye for wear; it is a perception task that AI on images could do at every receiving dock.

A digital signature alone would not have stopped AOG's method: it altered genuine certificates and impersonated real signers. What catches that is checking content against the issuer's records, which existing digitization efforts do not do.

research.q: Step: continued airworthiness and in-service feedback for non-OEM parts (failure reporting, SDRs, PMA part reliability data). Is there any evidence PMA/non-OEM parts fail more or less? Who tracks it?
research.headline: No one can say whether PMA parts fail more or less. The US system collects failure reports but not the installed base or hours behind them, and the SDR does not require a part number or manufacturer (the FAA tried to require them in 2000 and dropped the rule in 2005). What evidence exists is one qualitative FAA review that found no systemic problem, plus individual ADs such as the ECi PMA cylinders, which separated at about 32x the OEM rate. That leaves a reliability ledger tracked by part number and by approval holder, with fleet hours behind it, as the clearest AI play on the verification side.

findings.finding: FAA's Repair, Alteration and Fabrication (RAF) Team found 'no substantial evidence of failures or unsafe conditions arising from non-TC/PC holder developed data that would indicate a systemic lack of compliance'. It noted that SDRs and ADs on PMA parts 'have not increased proportionally' to the PMA population. The review was qualitative and computed no rates. This is the real source of the trade-press claim that 'FAA/TCCA/EASA found no statistical evidence'.
findings.source: FAA AVS RAF Team Study Rev 1, 2009-05-22 (FR notice 2008-09-05, E8-20460), https://www.pmaparts.org/gvt/raftreport.pdf

findings.finding: The same RAF report admits ADs have been issued on PMA parts and that PMA parts were occasionally linked to accidents. It says aftermarket companies' tracking systems are less comprehensive than OEMs', and that 'there is no requirement for manufacturers and fabricators of parts to track them or to have a tracking system'.

Honeywell, commenting on the RAF report: OEMs track reliability only for their own parts, and that data is 'proprietary and cannot be shared with competitor companies'. Aftermarket parties are 'routinely' missing from investigations.
findings.source: RAF Team Study Appendix D comments

findings.finding: ECi/Airmotive PMA cylinder AD: separation rate 'at least 32 times greater than that of OEM cylinder assemblies'. ECi had 8x the OEM separation count with 1/4 the installed base. It affected about 6,200 US engines, cost an estimated $88.6M (industry estimate $169-320M), and cited two fatal accidents. The FAA used warranty reports, SDRs and field reports. It said an hours-based failure rate cannot be computed because hours data 'is not available for general aviation aircraft', and it noted SDR under-reporting.

Other ADs aimed specifically at PMA parts cluster in piston general-aviation engines: Superior Air Parts cylinders (AD 2009-16-03, superseded 2014), SAP crankshaft (2020), SAP intake valves (2023, after 3 failures), AVStar fuel servo (2012). A quick scan found no AD singling out a transport-category PMA part.

Current 14 CFR 121.703(e) SDR contents do not require the part manufacturer or part number, so OEM and PMA failures cannot be separated systematically. The FAA's 2000 final rule would have required 'manufacturer, manufacturer part number, part name, serial number'. It was prompted by an internal FAA review and by industry concern over data quality, delayed five times, and proposed for withdrawal in 2005 over cost.

Under 14 CFR 21.3, PMA holders must report only listed serious failures, within 24 hours. They may skip a report if they judge the cause was improper maintenance. The rule produces no reliability rates.

SAIB NE-08-40 contains no data. It states that the TC/PC holder 'has no knowledge or data about the PMA and STC parts installed', and that each approval holder owns continued operational safety for its own parts. The rules therefore split COS data by design.

IATA recommends that airline reliability programs 'distinguish between OEM parts and related PMA parts', but each airline does this alone. No pooled or published PMA-vs-OEM MTBUR data exists. IATA's 'just as reliable' claim cites only the RAF report.

MARPA's continued operational safety (COS) guidance is voluntary. It recommends per-article trend analysis, and tells PMA applicants to mine SDRs and ADs for OEM field weaknesses before designing. Today SDRs serve as a design input, not as a scoreboard comparing PMA with OEM.

On the military side (recalled), PQDR and JDRS deficiency reports and PDREP/SPRS supplier scores are tagged by supplier CAGE code. That is better source attribution than the FAA SDR has, but it still lacks installed-base and flight-hour denominators per part number. Aviation critical safety items from alternate sources need design-control-activity approval under FY2004 NDAA §802.

players.what: PMA trade association that publishes voluntary COS guidance. No data pool.

players.what: Deficiency and supplier-quality reporting tagged by CAGE code, with no flight-hour denominators.

what_would_need_to_be_done: A cross-operator reliability ledger keyed by part number and approval holder, with denominators (installed base, flight hours, cycles per serial number). Built from ATA Spec 2000 Ch. 11 reliability data, removal records, 8130-3 tags and shop teardown findings. It does not exist today for PMA vs OEM.

Mandatory or de-facto standard capture of part number and manufacturer in SDRs, recovered by AI from free text, logbooks and 8130-3 tags where those fields are missing. The FAA abandoned the rule in 2005 over cost; automation removes that cost argument.

Statistical equivalence monitoring after approval: sequential or Bayesian tests showing a PMA part's failure rate is no worse than the OEM's within a set confidence, published per part number. This replaces opinion ('equal or better') with evidence.

Leading-indicator substitution for the physics clock: teardown wear measurements, borescope images, oil debris and vibration, plus physics-model priors per part, so equivalence can be shown in far fewer fleet hours than waiting for failures.

Use the ledger as a formal COS system (allowed today, voluntary). Then petition FAA AIR and DLA engineering support activities to accept field-equivalence evidence as grounds for lighter re-approvals, part-number family extensions, or faster Source Approval Requests (SARs). This needs an FAA policy statement or issue paper, plus EASA bilateral acceptance.

Military: fuse JDRS/PQDR/SPRS deficiency data with flight-hour data from IMDS/REMIS (recalled) for reverse-engineered and alternate-source parts. Obtain data rights through an OTA or CRADA with the Rapid Sustainment Office or DLA.

Liability and data-access fixes: protected safety-data status for contributed data (as ASIAS has), federated analysis so raw data never leaves the operator, or owning MRO and component shops to get teardown data first-hand.
ai_plays: 'Credit bureau for parts': an AI layer that ingests heterogeneous maintenance records, SDRs, teardown reports and 8130-3 tags, resolves part number and source, and outputs reliability per part number and approval holder with denominators. Customers: airlines (to justify using PMA parts), lessors (to break OEM-only lease clauses), PMA holders (to prove parity), and DLA engineering support activities.

Approval Factory with continuous field evidence: every part the factory approves ships with an automated COS monitor. That builds a compounding evidence base, which supports faster follow-on approvals and a regulator case for reduced-test approval of similar parts.

SDR and AD mining for targets: NLP over the full SDR history and AD dockets to rank OEM parts with chronic field problems (the design-input step in MARPA's COS guidance), and to spot early warning signs like the ECi case in the factory's own parts.

Leading-indicator inspection AI: borescope and teardown image models and wear-measurement analytics at partner shops. They produce equivalence evidence long before field failures would, compressing the physics clock.

Military variant: per-CAGE reliability scoring for alternate-source parts on C-130 and KC-135, combining JDRS/PQDR with flight hours. This is the evidence ESAs lack when they hesitate on Source Approval Requests.
surprises: The only hard comparative PMA failure rate I found is an anti-PMA data point: ECi cylinders at 32x OEM. The pro-PMA 'evidence' is a qualitative FAA statement with no rates.
The FAA itself says hours-based failure rates cannot be computed for general aviation because the hours data does not exist.
The FAA tried to make part number and manufacturer mandatory in SDRs in 2000, delayed the rule five times, and proposed withdrawing it in 2005 over cost. Today's 121.703 still does not require them.
The 'FAA, Transport Canada and EASA found no statistical evidence' claim, repeated widely in trade press, traces back to a single-agency qualitative FAA RAF Team study.
PMA holders mostly use SDRs as a source of design ideas, mining OEM field problems to improve on them, not to track their own parts' performance.
Military deficiency reporting is attributed to suppliers by CAGE code, which commercial SDRs are not. So the C-130/KC-135 entry point may have better feedback data than commercial aviation.

research.q: Step: liability and insurance for approval holders (product liability for PMA/DER, E&O, recalls). How it is priced; would AI-made packages change it?
research.headline: An FAA approval moves no liability. Approval holders stay fully exposed under state product-liability law (Sikkelee, 3d Cir. 2016/2018, recalled), the FAA is immune for certification errors (Varig, 1984, recalled), and the policy is set by the underwriter and the lessor, who price on track record, part criticality and quality system, not on how the engineering was done. AI-made packages are neutral-to-negative under today's wordings (discovery risk, emerging AI exclusions), but if they carry far more physical and conformance evidence than a traditional package, the AI play is an evidence-priced aviation products MGA plus a 'UL for substantiation'. That would make AI packages insurable and lessor-acceptable, which nobody does today.

findings.finding: The majority US rule is that the OEM is not strictly liable for PMA replacement parts it did not make or sell, so liability sits with the PMA holder. Exception: where a licence gave the OEM exclusive design control (Sikkelee, M.D. Pa. 2012). Imposing liability on the OEM 'would effectively transform the OEM into an insurer of the PMA manufacturer'.
findings.source: Beard & Smith, 82 J. Air L. & Com. (2017), https://www.wiggin.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/38726_disassembling-assembler-liability_journal-of-air-law-and-commerce_ksmith-ebeard.pdf

findings.finding: FAA type certification does not field-preempt state design-defect standards, and conflict preemption was later rejected (cert denied 2019). FAA approval is not a liability shield, only evidence.
findings.source: Sikkelee v. Precision Airmotive, 822 F.3d 680 (3d Cir. 2016); 907 F.3d 701 (3d Cir. 2018) (recalled)

findings.finding: The FAA is immune under the FTCA discretionary-function exception for negligent certification. The regulator's sign-off never moves liability onto the regulator. DERs and ODAs carry their own E&O and products exposure.
findings.source: United States v. Varig Airlines, 467 U.S. 797 (1984) (recalled)

findings.finding: HEICO holds about 20,000 PMAs and adds 400-550 a year. It is a named insured for 'product liability, including grounding'. It warns that claims may be 'not fully insured' and cover may not be available 'at commercially reasonable rates', that customers 'typically require us to maintain substantial insurance coverage', and Item 3 discloses no material product-liability litigation.

Aviation gross written premium exceeded US$8B in 2024, a 20-year high. Of US$15B across 32,000 claims in 2019-2024, 85% of value came from collisions/crashes and 'faulty workmanship or defective products'. Aerospace manufacturers saw 'stable premium offers' in Q1 2025, while social inflation and the Swiss Re exit pressure the wider market.

Aviation products limits are offered up to US$100M (BWI), including bodily injury, property damage and grounding. Premiums are priced as a rate on sales, adjusted for criticality, fleet type, US exposure, loss history and AS9100/PMA quality system. Pricing does not depend on the engineering method.
Under GARA's 18-year repose for general aviation, a newly installed replacement part restarts the clock for that part. A PMA maker selling into legacy GA fleets takes on a fresh 18-year tail.

Military-first is liability-friendlier. Feres bars suits against the government, and the Boyle government contractor defense can cover parts built to government-approved precise specifications (an approved DLA TDP is a plausible fit). The bigger DLA exposure is the False Claims Act over nonconforming parts, which is a conformance-evidence problem.
findings.source: Boyle v. United Technologies, 487 U.S. 500 (1988) (recalled); FCA practice (recalled)

findings.finding: Aviation 'recalls' are Airworthiness Directives (14 CFR Part 39). PMA holders must report failures (14 CFR 21.3) and keep a quality system, and the costly claim line is grounding/loss of use.
findings.source: CFR citations in Beard & Smith PDF

findings.finding: AI-liability insurers exist but cover software. AIUC runs the AIUC-1 standard, audits and insurance on the 'insurers funded UL' model, with a $55M Series A. Armilla is a Lloyd's coverholder backed by Chaucer, AXIS and Convex, with limits up to $25M aggregate and $5M per model. Neither covers hardware or aviation parts.

players.name: HEICO (Flight Support Group)
players.what: Largest PMA house. Self-manages liability on a large book with grounding cover and has no disclosed material PMA product-liability litigation.

players.name: Global Aerospace / AIG / Allianz Commercial / Chubb / Starr / Berkley / USAIG / Lloyd's syndicates
players.what: Write aviation products, grounding and completed-operations cover for PMA holders and repair stations, priced conventionally on sales, criticality and track record.

players.name: AIUC
players.what: AI-agent standard (AIUC-1), audits and insurance on the UL model. Software only.
players.step: Verification and insurance of AI outputs

players.name: Armilla AI
players.what: Lloyd's MGA for affirmative AI liability, including model errors and property damage from AI. Software focus.
players.funding_or_scale: Capacity from Chaucer, AXIS, Convex; limits up to $25M aggregate

players.name: Munich Re aiSure
players.what: AI performance guarantee insurance (recalled).

players.name: Brokers (Marsh, Aon, Gallagher, WTW, BWI)
players.what: Place aviation products liability. They would be the channel for an evidence-priced MGA.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build an evidence-priced aviation products MGA (Lloyd's coverholder) for PMA, DER and military reverse-engineered parts. Rates would be set from measured margins, per-serial CT and conformance data, and fleet failure-mode mining rather than track record; the approval factory would be the anchor insured.

Create a 'UL for engineering substantiation': an independent standard and score for AI-generated packages, mapped to FAA Order 8110.42 and DLA SAR/TDP rules, that insurers, lessors and juries accept, with no FAA rule change needed.
Offer a lessor residual-value or 'PMA-neutral lease return' guarantee to remove the lease-condition ban on PMA/DER content, which suppresses demand more than tort risk does.
Ship continuous post-entry-into-service surveillance that automates 14 CFR 21.3 reporting and gives early warning from operator maintenance data, shortening the claim tail and grounding losses.

Produce litigation-grade, Daubert-proof evidence packages with reproducible simulation, physical test anchors and human sign-off logs. For DLA work, build the record that satisfies the Boyle contractor-defense prongs and False Claims Act conformance proof.
Long-shot law changes: statutory indemnity or safe harbor (P.L. 85-804-style) for DLA-approved reverse-engineered parts on obsolete platforms, and a GARA-style repose for PMA parts on legacy fleets.
ai_plays: AI underwriting engine plus MGA that prices failure probability and grounding cost per part, using the package and fleet data as a moat. Revenue comes from commissions and float, and the approval factory feeds it data.
A verification lab that issues an insurable 'evidence grade' on any PMA/DER/TDP package, selling to insurers, lessors, airlines, DLA and incumbents such as HEICO.
Post-certification fleet surveillance SaaS for PMA holders and operators, feeding 21.3 reports, AD avoidance and underwriting.
Bundle every approval-factory part with liability, grounding cover and a lessor value guarantee to neutralize OEM fear, uncertainty and doubt and the trust gap against HEICO.
Automated conformance digital thread for DLA suppliers to cut False Claims Act exposure: per-serial proof that the delivered part matches the approved TDP.
surprises: An FAA approval gives essentially no tort immunity (Sikkelee), and the FAA itself is immune (Varig). The insurer and the lessor are the hidden co-signers of every approval.
GARA's rolling provision means new PMA parts on old GA aircraft create a fresh 18-year liability tail.

HEICO's roughly 20,000-PMA book discloses no material product-liability litigation. Actual PMA risk looks low, and premiums price trust more than measured risk, which leaves room for evidence-based pricing.
On the military side the biggest liability is the False Claims Act over conformance, not tort, which makes it a verification problem by definition.
AI-insurance startups (AIUC, Armilla) are funded and using the UL/insurer model, but only for software agents. Nobody is doing it for physical engineering substantiation.

research.q: Certification by analysis (CbA): NASA/Boeing/Airbus CbA roadmaps, how far simulation can replace physical tests for structures, fatigue and materials by 2030, and what regulators need to accept it.
research.headline: By 2030, simulation will shrink physical test matrices for structures, fatigue and materials, but it will not replace them. The FAA/NASA CM4QC roadmap (March 2026) puts the next 1-5 years at "guide and optimize testing" and calls the eventual test-to-simulation balance "undetermined"; the FAA "approves the data, not the analytical technique." The AI opening on the verification side is the missing evidence regulators say they need: side-by-side predicted-vs-tested track records, quantified uncertainty and credibility dossiers. An Approval Factory produces exactly that as a byproduct of every package it runs.

findings.finding: The FAA/NASA CM4QC strategy document was published March 2026 (Glaessgen of NASA, Gorelik of the FAA, plus Sandia, Lockheed, NIST, Boeing, Honeywell, AFRL, CMU, UTSA). Its phases: near term (1-5 yrs), use existing commercial software to guide conventional qualification and certification (Q&C) by designing experiments and guiding testing; mid term (5-10 yrs), partnerships and incorporation into commercial tools; long term (>10 yrs), new CM techniques.

FAA regulatory view (NIST workshop slides, Apr 2026): 'Future State: Balance between Test Data and CM-informed Q&C is Undetermined'. Also: 'Current approaches for Q&C simply do not have procedures for making use of CM results'. The stated goal is to augment testing, not replace it.

'Model-friendly' domains already accepted: Part 25 damage tolerance (AC 25.571-1D, 'analysis supported by test evidence'); Part 33 damage tolerance (AC 33.70-1, analysis validated against test plus a probabilistic element); AC 20-146 dynamic seats, which the FAA calls 'one of the few examples of certification by analysis'. Baseline rule: test articles should be full-scale and representative of production.

CM4QC gaps: predicting process to microstructure to property to fatigue/damage tolerance (including surface finish and defects), residual stress, build reproducibility, NDE, uncertainty quantification; 'resources to conduct side-by-side CM-related and conventional Q&C activities'; public validation data (AM Bench); non-proprietary formats; maintained commercial codes.

CM maturity scale 1-5. Only level 5, 'widely adopted by industry, predictions directly applicable to Q&C', counts as certification credit. Next steps: a NIST-led pathfinder exercise, best practice guides, outreach to certification authorities.
NASA/Boeing 'A Guide for Aircraft Certification by Analysis' (May 2021; Mauery, Alonso, Mavriplis et al.) is focused on CFD, aero, propulsion and stall, i.e. flight and engine tests, not materials.

In 2018 the FAA accepted RANS CFD in place of flight test for A350-certified antennas/radomes on the A330-200 and 737-800 (a derivative change). Boeing says the FAA accepts CbA for minor changes and that the flight-test matrix could eventually be cut 50%. EASA accepts virtual tests case by case for derivatives with validated models, and wants software vendors to create their own QA standards because it lacks the resources to vet tools.

Alonso: quantifying model-form uncertainty is the 'holy grail' of CbA and not yet practical. The target is 4-5 nines. RANS vs LES CLmax differ 10-15%. Full-aircraft LES needs 10k-100k cores. A ~3000x speedup from GPU/ASIC would make 100k-run ensembles routine in 10-15 yrs. Certification flight tests take 12-18 months.
FAA position (CAASE 2018): 'The FAA approves the data, not the analytical technique'; the burden is on the applicant to validate the FEM.
DLR (Markus Fischer, ILA 2026) expects CbA in the next EU research framework.
Vendor CbA claims are marketing only. Dassault 'Smarter Testing' with an Airbus wing demonstrator names no regulator approval and gives no figures.

(recalled) Metallic allowables (MMPDS A/B-basis) and composite coupon allowables (CMH-17, AC 20-107B building block) still require statistical physical test populations; there is no CbA path for material allowables. The Boeing 777X static test article failed at ~99% of ultimate load in Sept 2019, which is why the full-scale test stays.

(recalled) The FDA's Nov 2023 guidance on credibility of computational modeling in medical device submissions, plus ASME V&V 40, is a formal credibility framework. Aviation has no codified equivalent, so it is a template for an FAA policy.

This is the side-by-side evidence that CM4QC says nobody resources.

Build regulator-side reviewer-assist tooling: independent re-run, sanity checks and automated comparison to the validation corpus. This cuts reviewer hours, the second half of the Approval Factory KPI, and fills EASA's stated tool-vetting capacity gap.
Push the FAA, via the CM4QC/NIST pathfinder, to issue a policy statement and then an AC on simulation credibility. Offer the company's evidence ledger as the pathfinder dataset.
Shrink physics clocks: high-frequency (ultrasonic) fatigue rigs, parallel test cells and automated labs, paired with model credit, so the remaining confirmation tests take days rather than months.
ai_plays: Verification ledger company: an Approval Factory whose real asset is a growing, proprietary predicted-vs-tested dataset per part family and failure mode. Each package lowers the test burden of the next and eventually earns formal test credit. The metric is test hours avoided per approval.

Credibility-as-a-service: AI that writes and defends the V&V/UQ case (CM4QC maturity level, validation metrics, applicability domain) for DERs, PMA holders and DLA source-approval request applicants. A wedge into regulator workflow.

Test-matrix optimizer for allowables and first article testing: Bayesian design of experiments that cuts coupon counts while holding statistical basis. Sellable to test labs and PMA houses, and used internally.

Reviewer copilot for the FAA, EASA and DLA engineering support activities: independent re-analysis and anomaly flagging. It addresses the regulator capacity gap and positions the company as a trusted intermediary, e.g. through ODA/DER-style delegation.

Equivalence engine for reverse engineering: scan-to-allowable inference (chemistry, microstructure, NDE to predicted property envelope) that replaces much of the qualification testing for orphaned legacy parts.
surprises: The FAA's own Chief Scientist for Fatigue co-leads the roadmap, and it explicitly calls direct replacement of testing a 'naive expectation'. Augmenting tests is the sanctioned path to 2030.
CbA precedents are almost all derivatives and minor changes (seats, antennas). That is exactly the repair/PMA/reverse-engineering niche, not new type certificates.
EASA says it lacks the resources to vet simulation tools and wants vendors to self-standardize. A credibility standard is an open lane.
The binding missing input is not model accuracy but a funded side-by-side track record. A company doing hundreds of tested approvals a year generates it for free.
There is no aviation equivalent of the FDA's 2023 computational-model credibility guidance, despite the FDA having one for medical devices.

research.q: Model-assisted probability of detection (MAPOD) and simulated POD for NDT methods: maturity, regulator acceptance, what it would take to qualify AI inspection methods without huge physical specimen sets.
research.headline: Model-assisted POD (MAPOD) is a mature method. Nuclear guidance already allows simulated and augmented flaw data for qualifying ML inspection, under ENIQ RP13 (2021) and EPRI's 2025 frozen-model, human-in-loop concept. Aviation and defense have no accepted credibility standard for simulation, no POD metric built for ML outputs, no standing independent body to qualify AI inspection, and no regulatory precedent. Every acceptance today reads "AI assists, the human signs". The open AI play is a "qualification engine": physics simulation plus virtual flaws plus a small, robotically grown physical anchor set, producing a90/95 POD dossiers at about 10x lower cost. It could run standalone or inside the Approval Factory, plus authorship of the ML-POD and simulation-credibility standards that nobody has written.

findings.finding: EPRI's AI-assisted UT model was exposed to more than 5x the PDI data required for a traditional procedure qualification and flagged all flaw types. EPRI proposes freezing the model and handing it to the qualification body; the human reviews the flags. Its conclusion: 'AI qualifiable when paired with human analyst'. A full reactor vessel head was analysed in under 3 hours.

ENIQ RP13 Issue 1 (June 2021) allows data augmentation and simulated data for ML training and qualification if physical reasoning justifies it. It requires frozen, versioned models and recommends blind-only trials. It concedes that scalar-threshold POD does not map onto ML outputs and that ML-NDT experience is limited.

BINDT 2022 workshop: POD modules are standard in CIVA. DSTL (UK MOD) commissioned a new protocol for model-assisted qualification (MAQ) in the air domain (Wall and Schneider). Experimental trial-based qualification 'not going to be able to meet the time and cost requirements'. Aviation's origin case was a ~6 mm critical defect in the Aging Aircraft programme (1989-93).

Trueflaw's eFlaw method inserts real flaw signals into flawless data, giving 'effectively unlimited' flaws for training and POD. Deep models need hundreds of thousands of samples. Trueflaw sells virtual cracks, real cracked samples, ML automatic defect recognition and POD-as-a-service; logos include Safran, ITP Aero, Blue Origin and DEKRA.
The AFRL/NASA/FAA MAPOD Working Group defined two classes, transfer-function and full MAPOD. MAPOD is included in MIL-HDBK-1823A; there is a USAF transfer-function example.
findings.source: Search result: QNDE 2019 AFRL overview, iastatedigitalpress.com/qnde/article/id/8550 (page blocked by bot wall)

findings.finding: No FAA rule, policy or advisory circular was found that qualifies AI inspection through MAPOD. FAA personnel-qualification guidance mentions AI only as a future trend.
Donecle says its drone inspection is 'approved by aviation authorities and listed in the Boeing and Airbus AMM'. No certification of the AI detection algorithm is named.

Physical POD studies: hit/miss demonstrations at a90/95 need at least 29 of 29 detections or about 60+ flaws; fatigue-cracked specimens cost about $1k-10k+ each; full studies run about $250k to millions and 6-24 months (recalled, order of magnitude).

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: ENIQ allows it if justified, but no standard metric of how representative synthetic data is

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Frozen-model rule means any retrain triggers full requalification; no PCCP-like route as at FDA

research.q: Bayesian and small-sample statistical frameworks for allowables and equivalence (CMH-17 equivalence testing, MMPDS B-basis, ICME). Could equivalence of a replacement part be proven with far fewer tests?
research.headline: Yes, probably by a large factor. The regulations never fix the number of tests: small samples are already allowed but punished with lower allowables, so a prior that regulators accept is what would let a part keep a high allowable with 3-8 confirmatory specimens instead of 18-55 or more. Everyone working on this (Dyndrite/RTX AIM-4AM, Senvol, AlphaSTAR) targets new-material allowables, mostly for additive manufacturing (AM). Nobody applies Bayesian or adaptive equivalence statistics to reverse-engineered replacement parts, which is the opening for the Approval Factory.

findings.finding: CMH-17 minimum sampling: B-basis robust 10 batches/55 specimens, reduced 3 batches/18. A-basis robust 10/75, reduced 5/55. Different B-basis methods give different values.

Industry practice is about 30-80 coupon tests per property for a B-basis value. Bayesian updating from element tests shows element tests matter more than coupon tests, so coupon counts could fall under reliability-based design.

NCAMP runs a shared database plus a small-subset equivalency route, accepted by the FAA (Memo AIR100-2010-120-003) and by EASA. About 22 systems are qualified. Its AGATE predecessor claims 4x less certification time and 10x less cost. This is a de facto institutional prior already accepted by regulators.

AIM-4AM (America Makes/NCDMM, funded by OSW ManTech): $2M to Dyndrite, Mimo Technik and RTX Technology Research Center. ML picks the most informative tests for LPBF 17-4PH H1025, and every test reduction must be tied to a quantified probabilistic risk category. Announced 11 June 2026.

AlphaSTAR combines multiscale progressive failure analysis, probabilistic methods and Bayesian updating to get A/B-basis values with fewer tests. For S2-glass, its B-basis predictions came within 5% of values from full CMH-17 test sets (2011 papers). Its site makes no FAA acceptance claim.

Senvol ML uses ML and transfer learning to predict AM allowables and to size builds and specimens for a target confidence. It has USAF (FlexSpecs, EOS M400-4), Army and Navy ONR work, and claims no regulator acceptance.

Tolerance-factor penalty (recalled): B-basis k is about 2.35 at n=10, 1.78 at n=30, 1.53 at n=100. At 6% CV, going from n=100 to n=10 costs about 5% of the mean. Fewer tests are legal; the cost is a lower allowable.

FAA/CMH-17 equivalency (DOT/FAA/AR-03/19) typically uses 1-2 batches and about 8 specimens per key property, with tests on the mean and on the minimum individual value at alpha about 0.05. MMPDS direct A/B-basis needs about 100 observations from 10 or more heats. Both figures are recalled; the FAA PDF returned a 503 error.

Define part-level equivalence statistics for reverse-engineered parts: fuse CT, dimensional, microstructure, hardness/conductivity and residual-stress evidence with a few fatigue tests into one quantified equivalence posterior
Use Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential (SPRT-style) stopping so specimens run until the decision is made, not to a fixed n
Shorten the physics clock with parallel robotic fatigue cells, ultrasonic (20 kHz) and step-stress testing, and physics-based life models

Prior-bank data network: pool test data from the many small shops and labs doing SARs and PMAs; each new package gets cheaper, and the pooled data is the moat

surprises: The regulations never fix the number of tests. Small n is legal and is penalized through tolerance factors, so the value of a Bayesian method is keeping a high allowable with fewer tests, not getting permission to test less

NCAMP's shared database plus small equivalency subset already works as an institutional prior that the FAA and EASA accept, with claimed 4x time and 10x cost cuts. Only the formal Bayesian method is missing
The newest US program (AIM-4AM, June 2026) and every other effort found target AM or composite material allowables; none target reverse-engineered replacement-part equivalence

Most legacy spare parts use commodity-spec metals already covered by MMPDS, so no new allowables are needed. The real burden is part-level identity and fatigue evidence, which is unstandardized and so more open to a new statistical method

research.q: Process fingerprinting and in-situ monitoring as qualification evidence ("qualify the process, not the part"; ASTM F42, America Makes, FAA AM roadmap). What it would take to make every part born-certified.
research.headline: Many companies monitor AM builds, but nobody sells regulator-accepted certification credit: no FAA, EASA, NASA or DLA framework yet lets an in-situ signature replace CT and witness coupons (SAE ARP7068 is still in draft, and EASA-FAA WG3 is still defining "reliability requirements"). The verification-side AI play is to build the missing probability-of-detection (POD) and signature-basis allowables corpus and accreditation layer. Run it inside the Approval Factory so its own instrumented parts generate the evidence, get military engineering support activities (ESAs) to accept it first, then license the credit outward.

findings.finding: Joint EASA-FAA AM Workshop (held since 2015; 21-23 Oct 2025, Cologne): WG3 on in-situ process monitoring is advancing SAE ARP7068 (building on ARP7065) and working on use cases, data-sharing barriers and reliability requirements. Its roadmap goal is for monitoring to 'replace or supplement conventional inspections for critical AM parts'. No credit approach has been agreed. WG1 is paused until revised EASA CM-S-008 is published.
ASTM AM CoE in-situ Technology Readiness strategic guide (NASA-sponsored with America Makes; workshop June 2022, published July 2023) is a gap roadmap, not a statement that the technology is ready.
NASA: current qualification and certification of metallic materials, AM included, is 'entirely based on test data'.

NASA-STD-6030 baseline 21 Apr 2021, due for 5-year review Apr 2026. (recalled) It uses a frozen Qualified Metallurgical Process / Qualified Part Process model; in-situ monitoring is a process-control aid with no acceptance credit.

Freeform raised a $67M Series B on 19 Feb 2026 (Founders Fund, NVentures, Threshold, Two Sigma Ventures, among others; PitchBook valuation $179M). Its Skyfall platform uses hundreds of lasers with GPU-based real-time sensing, simulation and control, plus an on-site H200 cluster. No certification approach disclosed.
Sigma Additive, the only public pure-play in-situ QA vendor, sold all its software and IP to Divergent in Oct 2023. Monitoring without certification credit did not work as a standalone business.
Additive Assurance (AMiRIS) says conventional NDT and validation take 25-50% of AM part cost, and says its system works on 8+ L-PBF machine brands, so retrofit is feasible (vendor claims).
Senvol received Navy funding in Jan 2026 for AM sensor fusion of in-situ data. It is the closest existing effort to a statistical-equivalence engine.
ICAM 2026 still frames in-situ monitoring as something that 'could' reduce NDE reliance and speed up qualification.

(recalled) Precedents for qualifying the process rather than the part: GE LEAP fuel nozzle and T25 housing (2015-16) and Norsk Titanium RPD 787 structural parts (2017). All relied on frozen processes plus heavy testing, not monitoring credit.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a public-grade POD corpus: millions of layers with seeded defects, each paired voxel by voxel with CT and sectioning ground truth, plus fatigue on stratified samples. Publish MIL-HDBK-1823A-style a90/95 curves per sensor, alloy and machine family. This is the dataset regulators say is missing.
Break the fatigue physics clock: 20 kHz ultrasonic fatigue (10^9 cycles in ~14 hours) plus robotic cells running hundreds of test frames in parallel.

Write and push a 'signature-basis allowables' statistical method (allowables conditioned on the in-situ envelope instead of a frozen recipe) through ASTM F42, SAE AMS-AM and MMPDS. Supply ARP7068 with real data.
Create an assurance-case framework (like DO-330/DO-178) for qualifying AI closed-loop controllers: bounded action envelope plus a runtime monitor that keeps output inside the qualified envelope.
Cross-machine calibration artifacts and a neutral sensor-data schema so fingerprints transfer between serial numbers and OEMs.
A Nadcap-style accreditation body for in-situ monitoring systems, plus DER/DAR-style designees who can sign signature-based acceptance.

Get an explicit policy or acceptance-criteria statement that in-situ evidence counts as 'test and computation' data, first from military ESAs (NAVAIR, AFLCMC, DEVCOM) for DLA SARs, then FAA PMA guidance.

Extend born-certified to conventional processes regulators already accept fingerprints for (AMS2750 heat-treat pyrometry, weld schedules, cure records): instrumented CNC plus heat treat plus NDT cells where sensor logs replace separate CMM first-article inspection.
Liability wrapper: warranty or insurance priced from POD statistics so the signer of signature-based acceptance can carry the residual risk of escapes.
ai_plays: Evidence compiler inside the Approval Factory: every part comes off an instrumented cell, and its sensor log, CT and coupon data compile automatically into the DLA SAR, PMA or first-article package. Cuts the reviewer side of the hours-per-approval KPI.

'UL for in-situ' / POD-as-a-service: a neutral lab producing POD curves and signature-basis allowables, earning per-machine accreditation and per-part credit fees. This is the permission layer nobody holds today, and the most venture-scale option.
Qualified-controller licensing: an AI closed-loop controller plus its regulator-facing assurance case, licensed into EOS, Nikon SLM and Velo3D machines.

Born-certified spares cell: reverse-engineered sole-source parts made on fingerprint-accredited cells (AM or CNC), so per-part acceptance moves from CT plus coupons (25-50% of part cost) to a signature check. Military ESAs are the first approving authority.

Recommended combination: the Approval Factory builds its own POD and signature corpus from the parts it makes, gets military ESAs to accept it first, then licenses certification credit to third parties.
surprises: Sigma Additive, the only public pure-play in-situ QA vendor, failed and sold its IP to Divergent in 2023. Monitoring that earns no certification credit is a cost, not a product.

As of late 2025, the regulators' own working group was still defining 'reliability requirements' and 'data-sharing barriers' for in-situ monitoring. The rules are still open for a newcomer to help write.
The best-funded player with the most process data (Freeform, $67M Feb 2026, H200 cluster) discloses no certification strategy.
Process-fingerprint acceptance already exists for conventional special processes (AMS2750 pyrometry, Nadcap), so born-certified machining or heat treat may get regulator acceptance sooner than AM.
Vendor claim: NDT and validation take 25-50% of AM part cost. That is the prize for whoever wins certification credit.

research.q: Non-destructive "material passport" of an existing part: could CT + XRF + ultrasonic + EBSD-like methods + ML fully determine alloy, temper and microstructure without cutting? State of the art and gaps.
research.headline: No mix of today's non-destructive methods can fully determine a part's alloy, temper and microstructure without cutting it. Ti interstitials (O/N/H), cleanliness and melt route (VAR vs air melt), forging grain flow, and bulk texture and residual stress in thick sections all still need sectioning or a neutron or synchrotron facility. Approvals only need to know which published spec and temper the OEM part matches, not its full microstructure, and that is a classification problem; AMS 2658 (recalled) already accepts eddy-current conductivity plus hardness as proof of aluminum heat treatment. The open play is a calibrated "spec passport" (several NDE methods fused by ML) backed by a paired NDE-plus-destructive dataset that nobody owns, plus writing the missing steel, Ti and Ni standards.

findings.finding: Handheld XRF reliably sorts major-element grades but is weak below Mg (cannot see Li, Be, B, C, O, N, H), so close grades like 2024 vs 2124 and Ti ELI vs standard are hard or impossible to separate; handheld LIBS adds C/Li/B but leaves micro-craters
findings.source: (recalled) instrument vendor specs: Thermo Niton, Evident Vanta, SciAps

findings.finding: Al temper verification by eddy-current conductivity (%IACS) plus hardness is already a standardized, accepted practice (AMS 2658); no equivalent standard exists for steels, Ti or Ni superalloys
The 2024 review of ML-based eddy current testing finds no common datasets, no sample-size guidance and no uncertainty quantification for ML models
An ML (RBF neural net) model with multi-frequency eddy current sorts correctly vs incorrectly tempered 100Cr6 steel cams, a research proof that ML can classify heat-treatment condition
Laser-ultrasonic SAW measures residual stress and grain size together on peened Ti-6Al-4V, about 30 µm resolution, checked against XRD, hole drilling and EBSD
Swerim laser ultrasonics grain size and texture correlate very well with destructive EBSD; used online in hot rolling
Nottingham SRAS maps grain size and orientation on curved, as-made surfaces non-destructively; Rolls-Royce and Renishaw collaborations, licensed to CPI; surface only; throughput not published
Zeiss/Xnovo LabDCT gives true 3D grain maps without sectioning, but only on samples of about 8 mm^3 with grains of 20-40 µm or larger, so it cannot scan whole parts
Industrial CT resolution scales with part size (roughly 1/1000-2000 of field of view), so it sees porosity and geometry but not small inclusions, texture or chemistry
Bulk residual stress and texture in thick parts need neutron diffraction (ORNL VULCAN, NIST, ISIS ENGIN-X); surface XRD stress tools (Proto, Pulstec) need layer removal for depth profiles

Current PMA/DLA reverse engineering typically sections several OEM samples for chemistry, hardness, microstructure and grain flow; for sole-source or orphaned parts the samples themselves are scarce, so destructive analysis is a cost and availability bottleneck

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a Material Fingerprint Atlas: 10k+ scrap aerospace parts of known pedigree (from the AMARG boneyard, teardown firms, MRO scrap, DLA disposal), each scanned with every NDE mode (XRF, LIBS, multi-frequency eddy current, hardness, ultrasonic velocity/attenuation/backscatter, SRAS, Barkhausen, XRD, CT) and then fully sectioned for ground truth (chemistry, EBSD, macroetch grain flow, tensile)
Train a Bayesian fusion model that outputs a posterior over alloy, spec, temper, product form and melt route plus property bounds, and recommends the smallest destructive sample only when needed
Develop physics-based forward models (ultrasonic scattering from simulated microstructure, eddy current response from precipitation state) so the model generalizes beyond the training data
Calibrate LIBS and ultrasonic proxies for Ti interstitials (O/N/H) and define the micro-crater surface damage as non-detrimental in a spec
Build an automated robotic passport cell with model-driven scan planning for whole parts
Write SAE AMS / ASTM E07 standards that extend AMS 2658 to steel, Ti and Ni, with stated false-match rates, and run FAA ACO/DER and DLA engineering pilots on C-130/KC-135 parts

Reframe the approval argument: the passport identifies the OEM spec; the replacement is made to that published spec with its own lot coupons, so rare-defect populations never have to be read from the single OEM part
Package passport output as the materials section of the TDP/PMA submission, plus an insurance-priced liability model based on calibrated error rates
ai_plays: Material passport as a service: NDE-to-spec inference with calibrated uncertainty for PMA houses, DLA reverse-engineering contractors and depots (OC-ALC, WR-ALC); reduces sample destruction and engineer-weeks of materials work
Counterfeit and unapproved-part metal verification at receiving inspection using the same model
Owning the paired NDE-plus-destructive dataset (the Atlas) as a data moat
Standards-setting moat: supplying validation data for new AMS 2658-style standards for steel, Ti and Ni
Active-learning scan planner that chooses the next measurement to maximize information per minute and flags the minimal destructive cut
