research.q: Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) and digital twins of microstructure to predict properties: maturity, cases where it replaced tests (GE, Ford, QuesTek), what is missing.
research.headline: ICME and microstructure digital twins shorten and de-risk qualification today, but nowhere have they legally replaced the statistical test basis. The FAA/NASA CM4QC strategy (March 2026) says current certification "simply do[es] not have procedures for making use of CM results", and the best case, QuesTek M54 (3 heats instead of 10), still had to finish its full MMPDS testing. Nobody uses ICME to win third-party approvals (PMA/DLA SAR) on legacy alloys. An AI "allowables and equivalence engine" that infers processing history from a legacy part, predicts its property distribution with uncertainty, and then runs only the most informative confirmation tests would be new, and so would a side-by-side validation ledger regulators could use to grant test reductions.

findings.finding: FAA/NASA CM4QC strategy (NASA/TM-20260001729, DOT/FAA/TC-26/10, Mar 2026): CM should 'augment rather than replace' testing; 'Current approaches for Q&C simply do not have procedures for making use of CM results'; future split between test data and CM-informed qualification is 'Undetermined'.
findings.number: Near-term 1-5 yr: guide testing only; >10 yr for major change

findings.finding: CM4QC gap list includes prediction of process-microstructure-property-performance (fatigue, defects, surface finish), residual stress, build reproducibility, NDE, UQ, public validation data, non-proprietary I/O, and explicitly 'resources to conduct side-by-side CM-related and conventional Q&C activities'. The next step is a NIST-led pathfinder exercise.
findings.source: CM4QC deck, Glaessgen (NASA) and Gorelik (FAA), NIST workshop Apr 28-May 1 2026

findings.finding: Five-level CM maturity scale (adapted from Cowles, Backman, Dutton 2012). Only level 5 = 'Model predictions are directly applicable to Q&C'. Validation metrics must be quantitative, carry statistical confidence, and be kept separate from acceptance criteria.

FAA-named 'model-friendly' domains: Part 25 DT (AC 25.571-1D, analysis supported by test), Part 33 DT (AC 33.70-1, probabilistic, validated analysis), AC 20-146 seat certification by analysis ('one of the few examples of certification by analysis'). The FAA also requires test articles that are full-scale and representative.

QuesTek Ferrium M54: an AIM analysis of 3 production heats predicted MMPDS A/B-basis minima (normally from 10 heats), first published in MMPDS-09. This let the Navy T-45 program fund hook-shank rig tests before approval. Clean-sheet design to flight qualification took under 6 years versus 15-20. Navy SBIR funded.

QuesTek's own caveat: 'MMPDS A- or B-basis testing allowables are still required to be met before a component can meet certification requirements to fly... despite the need to ultimately complete the full testing dataset'. The gain was parallelization and early failure detection, not test deletion.

Conventional AM fatigue qualification is 500+ fatigue tests, about $1M per alloy or process parameter set. A true 99th-percentile fatigue life needs about 100 tests per condition. AIM plus models can predict 99th-percentile minimum properties from about 15 experiments.

MMPDS defines no A/B/S-basis for fatigue minimum life. Methods for lower-bound life 'must be accepted by the appropriate regulatory agency and may be negotiated by type certificate applicants and the regulators'. That leaves a negotiable opening for model-based minimum-life arguments.

Ford Virtual Aluminum Castings: cast Al blocks and heads 'designed and virtually cast, heat treated and tested for durability, all on a workstation'. Recalled NRC 2008 figures: ~$15M investment, ROI >7:1, 15-25% shorter development time (recalled, not re-verified).
findings.source: JOM 58(11) 2006 Allison et al.; NRC 2008 ICME report NAP 12199 (recalled)

findings.finding: DARPA AIM (~2000-2004), GE Aviation and P&W on Ni disk alloys and Boeing AIM-C on composites, created the method of model-predicted property distributions plus sparse data. GE Rene N515 low-Re alloy was designed computationally (recalled). SwRI DARWIN probabilistic rotor code is recognized in FAA engine ACs, the clearest precedent of a regulator-recognized computational compliance tool (recalled).
findings.source: recalled; AC 33.70-1 cited in CM4QC deck

findings.finding: America Makes AIM-4AM, $2M OSD ManTech funded, led by Dyndrite (June 2026): an AI framework to quantify risk in current allowables for L-PBF 17-4PH H1025 and use ML-chosen tests to 'safely reduce physical testing' tied to probabilistic risk categories.
QuesTek launched ICMD 2.0 on Sept 14 2026 and a Niobium suite with CBMM in Aug 2026. It claims users save 20-80% of time per phase. No VC funding is disclosed.

research.q: Regulator-side AI and capacity: FAA, EASA, NRC, DoD use of AI to review submissions; FAA Reauthorization Act 2024 provisions on delegation/ODA; whether a private party could supply reviewer tooling or become a delegated authority faster.
research.headline: Nuclear is the only domain where AI on the reviewer side is real and funded. The NRC runs SimplifAI and cut one review category from 4 years to 9 months, and DOE/INL modelling says 95% of applicant-regulator exchanges are non-blocking, so AI intermediaries could cut licensing time 65% and labour up to 77%. FAA, DLA and EASA have no public reviewer-side AI, and the FAA Reauthorization Act 2024 tightened ODA oversight rather than widening delegation. The open play is to own delegated signing capacity (buy an ODA/DER/DOA shop, or contract as the ESA's evaluator) and put AI pre-adjudication behind it, measured in reviewer hours per approval.

findings.finding: The NRC says AI helped compress one licensing category from about 4 years to 9 months against an 18-month EO 14300 target. Its internal tool SimplifAI (Azure OpenAI, v2.0) drafts and checks precedent, and the NRC is testing Claude, GPT and Gemini via GSA OneGov. The figure has not been independently audited.

INL/ANL analysed 1,200+ advanced-reactor docket documents: 95% of NRC-applicant interactions (RAIs, audits) had no blocking issue. A proposed Regulatory Communication Protocol with AI agents as intermediaries models $28M and 15 months versus NuScale's roughly $500M and 7 years, a 65% time cut and up to 77% less labour.
Everstar's Gordian converted a 208-page DOE safety analysis into NRC-format sections in 1 day versus the usual 4-6 weeks, in a DOE/INL/ANL/Microsoft test.
The FAA still works in a 'spreadsheet-and-hard-copy era' for certification, and I found no public FAA AI tool for reviewing certification submissions. Its visible AI spend is on air traffic (SMART).
There are 75 current FAA ODA holders. Sec. 304 of the 2024 Act imposes recurrent ethics training on ODA unit members, implemented by Notice N 8100.20. HEICO Aerospace commented on it.

FAA Reauthorization Act 2024 (P.L. 118-63): Sec. 303 (an ODA forum every 2 years), Sec. 304 (ethics training), and Sec. 306 (extends ACSAA ODA unit-member oversight to FY2028) all tighten delegation; none expands it. Sec. 310 orders an FFRDC study of 'digital tools... for efficient and virtual evaluation of an applicant design', report due about Nov 2025. Sec. 348 tells the FAA to prefer 'production-ready configurable' commercial solutions (for safety data). Sec. 349 sets up an ICA rulemaking committee with PMA holders and repair-station DERs on ICA availability and proprietary data.

Xcert AI SA (Geneva) offers an AI certification co-pilot covering requirements, verification and quality, with a product line for authorities and regulators. It won the EASA AI Olympics out of 50 cases, raised CHF 1.1M (Nov 2025), and lists ZeroAvia and ESA as customers. EASA has a concept paper out for comment (Jun 2026) but no internal AI review tool.

I found no public evidence of DLA or service ESAs using AI to evaluate Source Approval Requests. (Recalled:) SAR evaluation queues run 6-18+ months and are limited by government engineer hours, and military airworthiness and ESA authority cannot be delegated to a private party.

DOE/INL issued RFI INL-26-047, 'Reviewing Smarter: AI Tools for Building International Nuclear Regulatory Capacity' (closed Jul 2026). It asks for cited, auditable, source-grounded outputs, which signals procurement of regulator-side tooling.

research.q: A "bioequivalence for parts" rule: has anyone proposed a standardized equivalence pathway for replacement parts (like ANDA)? What law/rule change would it take (FAA rulemaking, DoD 10 USC 3243, NDAA), and who would lobby for or against?
research.headline: I found no explicit proposal for an "ANDA for parts", but search was out this run, so that is weak evidence. What exists is in pieces: FAA PMA identicality and test-and-computation routes, the DoD qualification statute 10 USC 3243 (which requires stated reasons for rejection and test-cost reimbursement but sets no deadline and no evidence standard), nuclear commercial-grade dedication (the closest precedent), FDA 510(k) for devices, and the insurer-funded CAPA certification for car collision parts. The most workable route is an NDAA amendment adding an "abbreviated qualification for replacement items" subsection to 10 USC 3243: a statutory evidence standard, a review deadline with automatic approval if missed, accredited third-party reviewers, a legal safe harbor for reverse engineering, and something for the incumbents (Hatch-Waxman-style) such as excluding new platforms. Expect MARPA, ASA, airlines and the Warren/Sheehy coalition to back it, and AIA, NDIA, GAMA, the big OEMs and TransDigm to oppose it.

findings.finding: 10 USC 3243 already requires the agency to justify any qualification requirement, set standards 'as unrestrictive as possible', estimate offerors' test costs, offer a prompt chance to qualify (for a fee), give specific reasons for rejection, and revalidate every 7 years. Subsection (d): with fewer than 2 sources the agency must seek more and pay small businesses' qualification test costs. Subsection (e) requires expedited qualification of advanced-manufacturing sources in wartime. There is no decision deadline: the agency 'doesn't have to delay a procurement'. There is no equivalence evidence standard.

FAA PMA allows two routes: identicality (licensed or shown) and test reports plus computations with a compliance certification. Identicality without a license is the nearest thing to an ANDA in any industry, but there are no published per-class equivalence criteria and no review deadline.

Hatch-Waxman template: FDA may ask an ANDA filer only about manufacturing, quality and bioequivalence. The act added a research safe harbor, Paragraph IV patent challenges and 180-day exclusivity for the first filer. In exchange, brands got patent-term restoration and 5-year data exclusivity. Generics went from 13% of prescriptions to 84% by 2012.

Closest existing standardized equivalence pathway: nuclear commercial-grade dedication under 10 CFR 21 (identify critical characteristics, verify by EPRI NP-5652 methods; NRC GL 89-02, RG 1.164). The dedicating entity carries the liability.

Private equivalence certifier precedent: CAPA (1987, funded by insurers) certifies aftermarket collision parts. The PARTS Act, which would cut design-patent enforcement on collision parts to 2.5 years, has been introduced repeatedly since about 2011 and has never passed. OEMs (Alliance for Automotive Innovation) oppose it.

Military right to repair: the Warren-Sheehy language was in the Senate FY2026 NDAA (Sec. 836, recalled). Industry backed a House 'data-as-a-service' alternative. My recollection is that the Dec 2025 conference dropped or diluted it. This is about data rights, not an equivalence standard.

Vehicle timing: the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (P.L. 118-63, 16 May 2024) runs to 30 Sep 2028, so the next reauthorization can direct an equivalence standard and a PMA review deadline. The NDAA passes every year, so FY2028 NDAA markup in spring 2027 is the DoD vehicle.

ASA's current advocacy is about Part 145 and EASA guidance (Aug 2026 items). MARPA's public stance is 'uniform standards' and 'without needless resource burdens'. Neither publicly proposes an equivalence pathway.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Draft and lobby for a new 10 USC 3243 subsection on abbreviated qualification for replacement items: a published criticality-class evidence standard, a 90-180 day deadline after which the part is deemed approved unless rejected with specific reasons, accredited third-party equivalence reviewers (building on the existing 3243(b)(5) rule that testing contractors must not benefit from a lack of sources), and an expanded 3243(d) that pays second-source qualification costs whenever there is only one source.

Before any statute, get a USD(A&S) memo or DLA SAR guide revision that publishes class-wide equivalence criteria and a SAR review deadline, piloted on out-of-production platforms (C-130H, KC-135, B-52).

Write an FAA Advisory Circular or Policy Statement defining a standard equivalence evidence package under the existing test-and-computation route (no rulemaking needed), plus delegation of PMA findings to ODAs. Then use the 2028 FAA reauthorization to require it, with a PMA review deadline.

Create an 'Orange Book for parts': a public list of reference NSNs and part numbers with their critical characteristics and accepted test matrices, maintained by DLA or the FAA, with test matrices drafted by SAE or ASTM consensus committees.

Add a reverse-engineering safe harbor like 35 USC 271(e)(1) for measuring and testing government-owned reference hardware, plus a Paragraph-IV-style challenge path for OEM-asserted data-rights legends.
Offer incumbents a Hatch-Waxman bargain: N years of protection for new platforms after IOC, or a data-access royalty schedule.
Allocate liability: extend P.L. 85-804 indemnification or the government-contractor defense to parts approved under the equivalence standard, and build an insurance market to price the residual risk.
Build the side-by-side corpus (equivalence-pathway results against conventional qualification) that regulators need to justify reducing tests.
ai_plays: Write the standard: the Approval Factory drafts the class-by-class equivalence evidence spec (an 'eCTD for parts') and becomes the reference implementation regulators adopt, as generic makers supplied the bioequivalence methods for Hatch-Waxman.
Dossier compiler: automatically assembles each equivalence package in a standard schema, every requirement traced to its CT, CMM, material or test evidence.
Critical-characteristics extractor: automates the EPRI NP-5652 approach, proposing what must be verified from a part's function, failure history and criticality.
Statistical equivalence engine: TOST-style equivalence tests on dimensional and material data against reference lots, with uncertainty quantification.
Reviewer-side tooling sold to DLA ESAs and FAA ODAs: completeness checks, consistency checks, and a precedent engine that answers 'similar to a previously approved part'.
Data-rights challenge assistant: tests OEM restrictive-data legends against 10 USC 3771 and DFARS 252.227-7013 records.
Become an accredited third-party equivalence review organization under a future 3243 amendment or FAA ODA. That accreditation is a permission asset in its own right.
surprises: 10 USC 3243 already has much of the ANDA skeleton (stated reasons for rejection, reimbursed test costs, 7-year revalidation, expedited advanced-manufacturing qualification). It lacks only an evidence standard, a deadline and a safe harbor, so the legislative change needed is small.
The best precedents are outside aviation: nuclear commercial-grade dedication and the insurer-funded CAPA certification of auto parts.
An FAA equivalence pathway may need no rulemaking at all, because test and computation already accepts any compliance showing; an Advisory Circular could standardize it.
HEICO's position is ambiguous: a standard both erodes its moat and cuts its own cost per PMA.

research.q: Proof-carrying parts: digital thread, signed certificates and physical unclonable functions/fingerprints that bind a physical part to its evidence (ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16, DoD digital thread, PUFs for mechanical parts). Gaps.
research.headline: Nothing today physically ties a part to its paperwork. Electronic certificates are legal and Spec 2000 Ch.16 defines signed ones, but neither links the serial number to the actual piece of metal, and no regulator accepts a mechanical fingerprint as evidence. The AI play on the verification side is to ship every Approval Factory part with signed, machine-checkable conformity evidence and a fingerprint, and to run a shared registry of those certificates. That is what would cut reviewer-hours per approval and make forgeries like AOG Technics detectable. (Web search quota was gone and most primary-source fetches failed, so most facts below are recalled from memory.)

findings.finding: Electronic release certificates and signatures are already permitted. Adoption in the used-serviceable-parts trade is low, and paper or PDF scans dominate.
findings.source: FAA Order 8130.21H (2018); FAA AC 120-78A (2016); ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16 (recalled; primary-source fetches failed)

findings.finding: Wikipedia lists 40+ PUF types, including optical PUFs that use random surface particle distributions on physical objects. None of the commercial products it names is aimed at mechanical parts; they are mostly silicon PUFs (Intrinsic ID, eMemory/PUFsecurity, Verayo).
Alitheon sells FeaturePrint, an optical-AI surface fingerprint for physical objects. It is the closest commercial mechanical-part fingerprint, but no aviation regulator recognises it.
AOG Technics sold CFM56/CF6 parts with forged EASA Form 1s that reached major airline fleets, showing that paper certificates cannot be verified at the point of use.

The DoD digital thread is mandated for new programs only. Legacy fleets such as the C-130 and KC-135 still use paper or microfiche technical data packages, and GAO has reported IUID marking as incomplete.
findings.source: DoDI 5000.97 (Dec 2023); MIL-STD-31000B; DFARS 252.211-7003; GAO IUID reports (recalled)

findings.finding: Precedent exists for a mandated physical anti-counterfeit marker: DLA has required DNA marking on FSC 5962 microcircuits since 2012.
findings.source: DLA / Applied DNA Sciences SigNature program (recalled)

findings.finding: The digital thread concept dates to a 2013 USAF Global Horizons report. Federated digital threads link data across lifecycle stages, but the article does not address part provenance.

research.q: Electronics: AI reconstruction of netlists, firmware and behaviour of obsolete boards and chips (from X-ray, delayering, signal capture), and how a re-created part is proven equivalent (FPGA emulation, formal equivalence checking).
research.headline: Many people re-create obsolete electronics: licensed re-manufacturers (Rochester, Lansdale), DLA's GEM emulation line, depots and board-cloning shops. Reverse-engineering imaging also exists (TechInsights, IARPA RAVEN, Lumafield CT). Nobody turns "the physical original" into "a proven-equivalent replacement" with a quantified, regulator-accepted equivalence certificate. That missing verification link is the AI play: active-learning conformance testing of golden parts, plus formal equivalence from the reconstructed model to the new part, plus a reusable corpus of legacy part behaviour, packaged as the dossier a DLA, engineering support activity or DO-254 reviewer can sign quickly.

findings.finding: Rochester Electronics re-manufactures obsolete semiconductors under OCM licence, using OCM-transferred data. This is a permission model, not reverse engineering, and the page does not describe how equivalence is proven.
findings.number: >20,000 device types made; >12B die in stock; can make >70,000 types

findings.finding: TechInsights sells chip reverse engineering as competitive and IP intelligence, not as replacement parts.

IARPA RAVEN showed rapid full-layer imaging of advanced ICs. Performers were Varioscale and MIT, with national-lab T&E. The imaging physics is largely solved, but turning images into a trusted netlist is not.
findings.number: Image all layers of 1 cm2 of a 10/14nm IC in 25 days; BAA Jan 2016

findings.finding: Lumafield sells X-ray CT plus AI software and lists PCB inspection and reverse engineering. It supplies imaging only, with no netlist or equivalence product.
Cybord uses AI to authenticate components and provenance on SMT lines. Its customers include Cisco, NVIDIA, Intel and SpaceX. It is an adjacent verification layer (authenticity, not equivalence).

DARPA TRACTOR (LLM-assisted C-to-Rust) has an independent MIT Lincoln Lab T&E harness with benchmark batteries every 6 months. This is a precedent for government-run evaluation of AI re-creation equivalence, and no hardware analogue exists.

(recalled) DLA GEM has emulated obsolete digital ICs on gate arrays since the late 1980s (Sarnoff, then SRI and BAE), qualified to MIL-PRF-38535/SMD. Equivalence is test-vector-based against the datasheet and a golden part, not formally proven.

(recalled) Commercial logic equivalence checkers (Cadence Conformal, Synopsys Formality, Siemens Questa/SLEC) only prove equivalence between two designs that both exist as models. The link from physical obsolete silicon or a board to a reconstructed model is plain testing, with ad hoc coverage and no quantified residual risk.

(recalled) Innovasic (acquired by Analog Devices around 2019) re-created obsolete MCUs (80C186, Z80, 8051 families) by clean-room black-box characterisation plus new RTL. It is the closest precedent to AI behavioural reconstruction.

(recalled) For aviation, DO-254 treats an FPGA replacement as complex hardware requiring requirements-based verification at the design assurance level. 'Equivalent to the obsolete part' is not an accepted assurance argument by itself. This is a methodology gap the regulator would need to close.

pathway_steps.step: 1. Acquire golden originals (multiple date codes)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Ad hoc, scarce, counterfeit-prone. Nobody builds a specimen bank from depot scrap or DLA returns.

pathway_steps.step: 2. Non-destructive X-ray CT of board or package
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Imaging is fine. Converting CT into a netlist is semi-manual.

pathway_steps.step: 3. Destructive delayering (PCB grind; IC decap, SEM delayer)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Image-to-netlist error rates are not bounded or published, and modalities are not cross-checked.

pathway_steps.step: 4. Electrical characterisation and signal capture
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Done per job with no reusable behavioural fingerprint corpus. Test vectors are chosen by humans rather than by active learning.

pathway_steps.step: 5. Firmware extraction
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Blocked by fuse and protection bits, with DMCA 1201, copyright and ITAR grey zones.

pathway_steps.step: 6. Model reconstruction (netlist to RTL, firmware to behavioural spec)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual, scarce experts, no confidence metrics. This is the main AI acceleration point.
pathway_steps.cost: largest share of the $50k-$500k per card (recalled)

pathway_steps.step: 7. Re-implementation (FPGA, ASIC/gate array, modern-part redesign)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Each part is re-qualified from scratch. There is no pre-qualified universal emulation substrate per package family.

pathway_steps.step: 8. Equivalence demonstration
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: The original-to-model link is test-only with no quantified coverage. Formal LEC is used only from model to new design. Nobody issues a quantified equivalence certificate.

pathway_steps.step: 9. Qualification (MIL-PRF-38535/38534, MIL-STD-883, MIL-STD-810, DO-160, radiation)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Physics clock that cannot be skipped. It could be inherited by similarity if a pre-qualified substrate were reused.

pathway_steps.step: 10. Platform acceptance (ESA / DLA SAR / ECP; FAA DO-254 + DO-178C via DER)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No accepted methodology credits AI reconstruction plus formal/statistical equivalence. The human reviewer is the bottleneck.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Rights and TDPs are often not captured, so the next cycle repeats the reverse engineering.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a hardware-in-the-loop active-learning rig. AI picks the next test vector to maximise disagreement between candidate models of a live golden part (automata/model learning), producing a behavioural model with a measured coverage and residual-difference bound.

Build multi-modal, error-bounded netlist reconstruction: X-ray CT, delayer SEM and electrical probing cross-checked against each other, so each extracted net carries a confidence and conflicts trigger re-imaging automatically.

Create a quantified equivalence certificate: a formal LEC/SEC proof from reconstructed model to replacement, chained with a statistical conformance bound from original to model. The output is a machine-checkable dossier formatted for ESA, DLA SAR or DER review.

Build pre-qualified universal emulation substrates (an FPGA or structured-ASIC carrier per legacy package family, already through MIL-PRF / MIL-STD-883 / radiation) so each new part needs only functional equivalence and the physics-clock qualification is inherited by similarity.
Build a legacy part behaviour corpus: fingerprints, errata and undocumented modes across date codes, accumulated from every part on the bench and from depot scrap and DLA returns.

Set up a public or government independent T&E benchmark for hardware reconstruction (a TRACTOR/Lincoln-Lab analogue): chips and boards with hidden ground truth, to give regulators an error-rate basis for accepting AI reconstruction.

Get a methodology accepted: pilot one NSN with a single ESA (for example, the C-130 or KC-135 program office, or DLA Land and Maritime), then codify it via the SD-22 DMSMS guidebook, SAE G-19/G-12, and an FAA issue paper or DO-254 alternate method.

Secure a legal route: use government purpose rights and DFARS deferred ordering to authorise RE for sustainment, rely on the 10-year Semiconductor Chip Protection Act mask-work term having expired for most legacy parts, and handle DMCA 1201 and ITAR through government-sponsored RE agreements.
Price the residual risk: use the quantified equivalence bound to underwrite a warranty or insurance on replacement parts, so liability becomes a priced product feature.
ai_plays: Equivalence-as-a-service: an AI lab that takes a golden part and returns a reconstructed model, a replacement on a pre-qualified substrate, and a reviewer-ready equivalence dossier. The KPI is reviewer-hours per approval.

Independent verifier: sell the equivalence engine to DLA, depots and primes to certify other vendors' F3 replacements and counterfeits. This is the hardware analogue of Lincoln Lab's TRACTOR T&E, and the verifier role becomes the permission chokepoint.
An AI-native GEM: a universal emulation substrate plus an automated reconstruction pipeline, turning per-part qualification into per-substrate qualification.
Reviewer copilot: auto-generate DO-254/DO-178C compliance artefacts and SAR packages from the reconstruction and equivalence data, which cuts DER and ESA review time.
Corpus moat: a behavioural fingerprint database of legacy chips and boards that doubles as counterfeit detection (Cybord-adjacent) and obsolescence forecasting.
surprises: Web search was unavailable (shared quota exhausted) and most .mil pages returned 403/404/503, so much of the landscape is recalled rather than verified this session.

The software world already has a government-run independent T&E for AI re-creation equivalence (DARPA TRACTOR with MIT Lincoln Lab), but hardware has none, despite IARPA RAVEN having largely solved imaging since 2016.
Commercial formal equivalence tools cannot touch the step that actually matters: the link from physical obsolete silicon to a model. That link is pure ad hoc testing everywhere.
Mask-work protection lasts only 10 years (17 USC 904), so for most legacy ICs the binding legal constraint is data rights, DMCA and ITAR, not IP in the layout (recalled).
The caspiatech.com domain (an AI hardware-security startup) is parked, so that player's status is unclear.

research.q: Automated physical test labs: robotic coupon prep, autonomous fatigue/tensile labs, self-driving labs (A-Lab, Emerald Cloud Lab analogs for mechanical testing). Could test cost and queue time drop 10x? Who is building it?
research.headline: Queue time can drop 10x, and so can the cost of static tests and material identification, if you own captive, lights-out robotic capacity that handles many different parts and specs. Fatigue gets about 3-5x from running many cheap frames in parallel, and reaches 10x only if regulators accept fewer coupons (via model-informed statistics) or ultrasonic fatigue results. Nobody sells robotic, accredited qualification testing: robot test cells serve steel and polymer factory QC, and the more than $800M (partly recalled) in self-driving-lab funding (Periodic, Lila, Radical AI) goes to materials discovery, not approval testing.

findings.finding: ZwickRoell sells robotic test systems (roboTest R up to 400 metal specimens, L 160, P 300) and claims 'Unsupervised 24/7 system operation'. The customers it names are steel and polymer firms (Tata Steel, Baosteel, BASF, Covestro, Henkel), with no aerospace.
Westmoreland Mechanical Testing (WMT&R), a major Nadcap/17025 contract lab, markets quick turnaround and large capacity but describes no robotic automation. It writes its control software in-house.
findings.number: 300,000+ sq ft; frames up to 1,000,000 lb

findings.finding: NCAMP's shared composite allowables, accepted by FAA and EASA, let a user prove equivalency instead of re-qualifying. The AGATE process behind it cut certification time 4x and cost 10x. This is a regulator precedent for a 10x cost cut through statistics and data sharing rather than robots.
Periodic Labs builds AI plus autonomous labs (a16z, Felicis, DST, NVentures, Accel), focused on superconductors and chip thermal problems. Its site mentions no mechanical testing.
Lila Sciences runs 'AI Science Factory' autonomous labs. It lists aerospace and defense and structural materials as targets, but describes no structural or qualification testing.
Radical AI runs a self-driving materials lab with automated sample prep (Makino) and benchmarks against C103 refractory alloy, but does no mechanical qualification testing.
Emerald Cloud Lab offers 200+ remotely operated instrument models 24/7, but only for life sciences and analytical chemistry. It lists no mechanical test methods.

Test economics: a tensile test costs about $150-400 plus $100-500 for machining, and most of that is labor. An HCF coupon costs about $500-2,500, and 10^7 cycles at 20-30 Hz takes 4-6 days of frame time. Contract-lab queues run 3-12 weeks. A B-basis allowable needs about 18+ coupons over 3 batches per condition.
Ultrasonic fatigue at 20 kHz reaches 10^9 cycles in about 14 hours, but regulators do not accept it for design allowables because of frequency effects.
findings.source: recalled; the Shimadzu USF-2000A page returned 404

research.q: Can AI predict which non-OEM parts will be accepted or rejected by reviewers, and pre-empt rework? Data on SAR/PMA rejection reasons and rework cycles.
research.headline: AI could predict reviewer outcomes for non-OEM parts, but no labelled dataset exists anywhere. The FAA publishes approvals only, and DLA publishes only aggregate counts and a five-reason taxonomy, so the corpus has to come from filing many packages yourself plus FOIA requests and bid-protest records. The figures that do exist say most decided SARs get approved (about 91% in the RPPOB data). The loss is in pending loops, "need more data / qualification testing" round trips and packages never filed, so the target is review cycles per approval and the questions each reviewer will ask, not a yes/no call.

findings.finding: DLA SAR responses: data available; data missing; need qualification testing ('good on paper, but need to prove will work in application'); or rejected for one of 5 reasons: business case/not in Government interest, incomplete, weapons criticality, application upgraded/discontinued, 'can't validate part (no government data to compare)'. Four of the five can be predicted or pre-empted before any engineering is done.
findings.source: DLA Land & Maritime 2016 NDIA deck, via sibling g03: https://ndia.dtic.mil/wp-content/uploads/2016/DLA/SourceApprovalRequestsCastingandForging.pdf

findings.finding: FY16 DLA L&M: 211 SAR packages received, 55 approved ($2.35M in annual savings), 184 pending ($28.5M). The VE completeness gate accepted 90%. The value is stuck in pending loops, not in rejections.
RPPOB 2014-16: 742 bailment requests became only 55 SARs, which went 40 approved, 4 rejected, 11 pending, so about 91% of decided cases were approved. Typical time to full approval was 12-18 months.

Rotair (Black Hawk drag brace, a CSI): SAR filed 29 Jan 2014, Army review began only on 28 Apr 2014, and the 5-yr IDIQ went to the incumbent on 2 May 2014. On 15 Aug 2014 the SAR was put on hold, with revisions requested in six areas and 60 days to respond. GAO denied the protest because agencies need not delay award for qualification. One review loop cost a 5-year contract. GAO and COFC protest decisions are the only public, text-rich corpus of agency reasons for refusing source approval.
findings.number: 6 deficiency areas, ~6.5 months to first findings

findings.finding: FAA issued AC 33-13 'Sample Size Considerations for Comparative Test and Analysis' for turbine engine and APU PMA and third-party repair parts on 16 Sep 2026. This suggests sample-size adequacy has been a recurring source of reviewer disagreement and rework, and it is now codified criteria a machine can check.

Eligibility (installation) evidence is a separate PMA hurdle. OEMs threaten carriers over use of ICAs, so carriers supply technical assistance letters instead. A reader comment reports that newer FAA staff read 'product' as the carrier's own fleet. That is reviewer-to-reviewer variance a model would need to capture.
FAA AIR-600 is being realigned into product branches AIR-660/670/680/690 to cut review layers (Oct 2026). Who reviews and who owns policy is changing, so any reviewer model needs retraining.

The only reviewer-side AI found is ELEVAN LLC with UTSA: USAF STTR Phase I FA8649-24-P-0130, $109,997, Feb-May 2024, AI/ML plus computer vision to cut the 'thousands of unbudgeted hours' engineers spend reviewing source-approval requests. No Phase II was found.

Building-permit analogs show a reviewer-comment corpus is a moat: PermitFlow claims 12M+ data points on requirements, comments and decisions ($54M raised); GreenLite claims 0.5 average resubmission cycles ($49.5M Series B); CivCheck is free to cities and applicants pay a prescreen fee. Failure mode: AI over-flags and invents requirements (East Hampton, Jul 2026). All figures are vendor claims.
findings.source: sibling notes c31/c32: https://www.permitflow.com/ , https://www.greenlite.com/ , https://www.civcheck.ai/

findings.finding: FDA analog: structured submission (eSTAR, mandatory for 510(k)s from Oct 2023) and test-plan pre-agreement (Q-Sub) removed more loops than prediction did (recalled).

Most PMA rework drivers here are recalled, not verified: criticality and critical-part disputes, comparative-test sample size, material and process equivalence, eligibility, ICA and design-change tracking, production quality system readiness, ACO sequencing and queue. The FAA publishes no rejection or cycle statistics; DRS lists approvals only.
findings.source: (recalled) FAA Order 8110.42D, 14 CFR 21.303; faa.gov returned 403 here

Mine GAO and Court of Federal Claims bid protests involving SARs, alternate offers, CSIs, AMSC B/C/D and qualification requirements into a taxonomy of rejection reasons. Nobody has done this.
FOIA the SAR disposition letters (10 USC 3243 requires agencies to promptly tell offerors why they failed qualification) and FAA issue papers.

Encode the DLA and service SAR guides, AFMC Form 260 first-article requirements, FAA Order 8110.42D, AC 33-13 sample-size logic and the CSI handbooks as machine-checkable requirement-to-evidence rules, so 'incomplete' and 'data missing' rejects are caught before filing.

Create a test-plan concurrence step with the ESA, a defence version of FDA's Q-Sub, so predicted reviewer questions are settled before physical testing.
Use downstream field data (PQDR, GIDEP, FAA SDR, ADs) as labels for false accepts, so the model becomes a risk model reviewers can trust.
Port the model to the reviewer side as an ESA triage and disposition copilot via an SBIR Phase II or OTA, with an IL4/5 ATO and CUI/ITAR handling.
Use an NSN-level predictor of approval odds, cycles and time from FLIS/DIBBS to file ahead of J&A expiry, since award will not wait for qualification (Rotair).
ai_plays: A reviewer-twin inside the Approval Factory: a per-ESA and per-ACO model of the questions each reviewer will ask, with the KPI driven toward 1.0 review cycles per approval. The moat is the corpus built from the factory's own filings.
'CivCheck for ESAs': a free or SBIR-funded government triage and disposition copilot trained on the same corpus; applicants pay for pre-screened status.
A portfolio selector: predict approval odds, cycles and time for each NSN from public FLIS/DIBBS data plus the reject taxonomy, and pick targets that will clear before the next solicitation or J&A.
A corpus of rejection reasons from bid protests and FOIA: a one-time build that seeds the taxonomy, possibly also a product for protest counsel and SBIR shops.
A false-accept risk model trained on field failures (PQDR, SDR), giving reviewers bounded-risk evidence to approve faster. This is the bridge toward approvals that give credit for modelling.
surprises: Once decided, most SARs are approved (about 91% in RPPOB). Pending loops and packages never filed are the real loss, so the target should be cycle count, not accept/reject.
In FY16 the pending SAR pile held 12x the savings of the approved pile.
In Rotair, the Army took about 3 months just to start reviewing the SAR, and the first deficiency list (six areas) arrived after award. The lost contract was a 5-year IDIQ.
The FAA issued an AC on comparative-test sample size for engine PMA only in September 2026 (AC 33-13): a newly codified, machine-checkable review criterion.

Bid-protest decisions are a public, unmined text corpus of agency reasons for refusing source approval.

research.q: Qualification-by-similarity at scale: using large fleets of approved designs to argue new part equivalence (MIL-STD, NASA similarity rules). Could a massive similarity graph of approved parts become evidence?
research.headline: Regulators already accept similarity as evidence in narrow forms: DLA SAR Category II (the offeror's own similar item), MIL-PRF-38535 QML and AEC-Q family qualification, and the pooled MMPDS and NCAMP databases. No one has been found turning a cross-part, cross-supplier similarity graph into submitted approval evidence, or back-testing such a graph against field failures. That calibrated graph is the open play for verification, but it needs data access (PQDR/GIDEP) and a DLA policy change, not a change in law. (Caveat: web search was unavailable, so this is from fetches plus recalled knowledge.)

findings.finding: 14 CFR 21.303(a)(4) requires test reports and computations showing airworthiness, unless the applicant shows the design is identical to the TC'd article. Comparative analysis against the OAH part is an accepted test-and-computation technique.

DLA SAR categories (recalled): Cat I is the actual item made for the OEM or Government; Cat II is a similar item, credited only on the offeror's own history; Cat III needs a full TDP and first article. Similarity is already a formal but manual, one-to-one category.
findings.source: DLA Aviation SAR guidance (recalled; the page returned 403)

findings.finding: NCAMP (NIAR/Wichita State) is the closest precedent: a material is qualified once into a shared database, and later users run reduced equivalency tests that FAA accepts under AC 20-107B and DOT/FAA/AR-03/19.
findings.number: equivalency is a handful of specimens versus a full program (recalled)

findings.finding: MMPDS (Battelle) and CMH-17 turn pooled multi-source data into FAA-accepted A/B-basis allowables. Pooled evidence is accepted for materials, not parts.
MIL-PRF-38535 QML and AEC-Q100 family/generic-data qualification let thousands of part numbers inherit one process-flow qualification. This is similarity at scale, but inside one supplier.

NASA GSFC-STD-7000 (GEVS) and SMC-S-016 allow qualification by similarity only for the same design, manufacturer and process within the qualified envelope; any difference triggers a delta-qualification.

Physna calls itself the world's leading geometric search engine. CADDi is an AI manufacturing-data platform with drawing search and a Design Reuse Simulator. Neither mentions qualification or approval evidence.
No published validation of any part-similarity metric against field failures (SDR/PQDR/AD/GIDEP) was found.

research.q: Remote/virtual witness testing and digital inspection evidence accepted by regulators (FAA remote inspections post-COVID, DNV remote surveys, NRC remote inspections). What became permanent?
research.headline: Remote review of documents and records became permanent across nearly every regulator. Remote observation (video witness) became mainstream only where the verifier is a private firm competing for business (DNV and the other class societies); at the NRC, FAA and EASA it survives only as a contingency mode or at an official's discretion. No regulator accepts test evidence that verifies itself (cryptographically attested, machine-checkable), and the NRC itself named data access, not video, as what limits remote inspection. That leaves an open verification-side play: an attested-evidence and reviewer-acceleration layer. Search quota was exhausted, so FAA, DNV and EASA specifics are recalled; only the NRC documents were read directly.

findings.finding: The NRC made remote/hybrid inspection permanent as a contingency mode for public health emergencies or any condition that restricts onsite presence, including floods and hurricanes. Options run up to '100 percent Remote Inspection' and 'Remote Inspection with Onsite Follow-Up'; under the latter the inspection stays open until someone can go on site.

For inservice inspections, NRC inspectors 'should maximize the use of record reviews, remote video or recorded inservice inspections where possible'. This is explicit acceptance of licensee-recorded video as evidence, but only in constrained conditions.

The NRC working group concluded that on-site inspection is 'the most effective and preferred' method and that hybrid flexibilities 'have always existed within the ROP', to be used case-by-case. No remote-by-default regime was created.

The NRC found the binding constraint on hybrid inspection is the availability and timeliness of licensee documents, not video. Hybrid inspections overran their 3-5 week windows. It set minimum functions for an inspector-licensee evidence platform (secure two-way upload, logging of questions and responses, open/closed tracking, a reference repository), noted that no rule requires licensees to adopt one, and recommended a voluntary standard plus R&D on virtual-desktop access.

DNV began remote surveys before COVID (around 2017) and now uses them routinely for occasional, damage and condition-of-class surveys, with statutory work only where the flag state agrees. Renewal and close-up surveys still need an attending surveyor. IACS Rec 42 covers remote inspection techniques (drones, ROVs). A later IACS unified requirement on remote surveys is believed to be UR Z29.
findings.number: of the order of 15,000+ remote surveys by 2020 (recalled)

findings.finding: FAA AIR and Flight Standards allowed virtual conformity, test witnessing and audits by video during COVID, at the discretion of FAA staff or designees. Part 21 never required physical presence, so the method is a guidance and discretion question rather than law. It persists as a tool officials may accept, not a right applicants can invoke.

Remote-audit provisions became permanent but conditional elsewhere: EASA AMC remote audits (not normally for initial approvals), IAF MD 4 for ISO/AS9100 certification audits, and FDA Remote Regulatory Assessments as a supplement to inspections.

DLA Source Approval Request evaluation is already a remote paper review: an Engineering Support Activity reviews the technical data package and comparison analysis. The physical gates are First Article Test and production lot testing. For the Approval Factory's first market the bottleneck is reviewer hours and queue, not witness presence.

what_would_need_to_be_done: A consensus standard (SAE/ASTM) for cryptographically attested test and inspection evidence: signed sensor streams, CMM/CT scan provenance, chain of custody. Then an FAA policy statement or advisory circular, and DLA engineering-support-activity acceptance, treating it as equivalent to witnessed data. No law change is needed, because Part 21 and the SAR rules do not require physical presence.

Instrumented 'continuous witness' test cells that a designee or regulator can watch live or replay, with AI flagging deviations from the approved test plan. Officials review flagged segments instead of attending whole tests. The physics clock is unchanged; reviewer hours fall.

Build the inspector-facing evidence portal the NRC has already specified (requests and responses, tracking, reference repository, secure exchange) and generalise it to FAA designee packages and DLA SAR reviews, with AI pre-review against each reviewer's own checklist.

Automated equivalence cases: scan the OEM part and the reverse-engineered part, generate the AS9102 first article report automatically, run statistical material-equivalence analysis, and package the result as a machine-checkable argument the reviewer can audit quickly.
Free reviewer-side tools for the FAA, DLA and NRC (summaries, traceability matrices, diffs against prior approvals) to shrink queues for the founder's own packages.

Pilots with one ODA holder, one DLA engineering support activity (C-130/KC-135) and one class society, to create precedent. Then a published policy memo turning discretionary remote acceptance into a predictable process.

Liability design: give the signing designee more evidence than in-person attendance would (a full sensor record and replay), so accepting remote or attested evidence lowers rather than raises their personal risk.
ai_plays: Attested evidence layer ('C2PA for test rigs'): hardware and software that sign test data at the sensor and produce regulator-ready, tamper-evident packages. Sell it to every applicant, and use it inside the Approval Factory.

An AI pre-reviewer that mirrors the reviewer: trained on DLA SAR checklists, FAA 8110-3 compliance findings and NRC inspection procedures, it pre-answers the reviewer's likely requests for information and cuts review cycles.
AI that monitors recorded or live tests against the approved test plan, so one designee can witness many tests remotely at once.
Scan-to-equivalence automation: CT or optical scans plus AI produce the dimensional and material equivalence argument and the AS9102 report.
A neutral evidence-exchange platform for inspector-licensee information (spec already written by the NRC; no incumbent owns it), extended to aviation and defense.

A private-verifier strategy: copy the class-society model by becoming an accredited third-party verifier or ODA-like body that accepts its own remote evidence. Maritime shows this is where remote acceptance became permanent.
surprises: Neither the FAA rules nor the NRC rules ever required physical presence. Remote acceptance is limited by guidance, discretion and liability, not law.
The NRC's own review found that document and data access, not video, limits remote inspection. It wrote a five-function spec for an evidence platform and left it to industry to build voluntarily.
Remote verification became most permanent in maritime because class societies are private competitors that save money by doing it; public regulators kept it only as contingency.
DLA SAR evaluation is already remote paper review, so 'remote witness' matters little for the first market. Reviewer hours and the quality of evidence are the real levers.

research.q: Cybersecurity and supply chain trust as verification (NIST SP 800-161, CMMC, NERC CIP-013, SBOM/HBOM for hardware): is there a verification layer for hardware provenance that AI can automate?
research.headline: Yes, there is a verification layer AI could automate, and nobody does it today. That layer ties physical evidence about a specific lot, serial number or die (images, X-ray, CT, chemistry and electrical fingerprints) to the legal attestations that new rules require. Those rules are DFARS 252.246-7008 testing, the NDAA s.5949 ban on SMIC, YMTC and CXMT chips (about Dec 2027) and the BIS ban on Chinese connected-vehicle hardware (Jan 2029). Today they are met with supplier paperwork, questionnaires and slow, destructive, sample-based lab tests, and the same CT, decap and characterization lab the Approval Factory needs could sell this as recurring authenticity and origin evidence.

findings.finding: DFARS 252.246-7008 (Jan 2023): if parts don't come from the original manufacturer or an authorized source, or traceability fails, the contractor must inspect, test and authenticate them to industry standards, notify the CO, and carry the authenticity liability. The clause flows down to subcontracts, including commercial items.

The BIS Connected Vehicles rule was issued Jan 14 2025 and took effect Mar 17 2025. Software bans start MY2027 and the hardware import ban starts MY2030 / Jan 1 2029. Importers and OEMs file annual Declarations of Conformity, and BIS names no evidence standard for them.
CISA's HBOM Framework (Sep 25 2023) is voluntary naming and format guidance only. It is not mandatory and contains no verification method.

Cybord does AI visual inspection of every component using the images pick-and-place machines already capture, checking for counterfeits, country of origin and lot genealogy. It announced a $7M extended Series A, and its customer logos include Cisco, NVIDIA, Intel, SpaceX and Siemens. This is the closest existing company to physical provenance work, but it sits on the production line and is sold as quality data.

Fortress Information Security does HBOM/SBOM-based vendor risk, a shared vendor-assessment exchange (A2V) and a component library (NAESAD). It claims 8 of the top 10 US investor-owned utilities and 40% of the North American grid. This is paperwork attestation of the kind CIP-013 requires, with no physical verification.

Exiger (850+ staff, FedRAMP authorized, which calls itself the largest supply-chain tech provider to the US government) and Altana (trade graph, about $1B valuation, recalled) map suppliers and documents. They do not physically verify parts.

Lumafield sells industrial CT scanners plus AI analysis, with aerospace and defense customers including a USMC logo, and does not position itself for counterfeit or origin detection. Caspia does agentic AI security verification of chip designs (RTL), not provenance.

NDAA FY2023 s.5949 bars federal agencies from buying products that contain SMIC, YMTC or CXMT semiconductors from about Dec 23 2027 (recalled). Proving a board contains none of these dies is a die-level problem that paperwork cannot settle.

AS6171 lab authentication (visual, XRF, X-ray, decap, electrical) is destructive and sample-based, costs roughly $500 to $5,000+ per lot and takes 1 to 3 weeks. Every buyer re-tests the same lots, and GIDEP and ERAI record only failures, not passes.
CMMC 2.0 (program rule Dec 2024, acquisition rule Nov 2025) and NERC CIP-013 cover cyber controls and supply-chain plans. Neither requires physical verification of delivered hardware.

research.q: Physics clocks that cannot be compressed (fatigue cycles, creep, thermal aging, radiation): which qualification tests are fundamentally time-bound, and accelerated testing methods with regulator acceptance.
research.headline: For replacement parts (DLA Source Approval Requests on C-130/KC-135 parts, then FAA PMA), physics clocks usually take weeks to a few months per package. Specimens can run in parallel, so the binding limits are reviewer queues and test-frame capacity. Clocks that truly cannot be compressed (creep beyond 10^5 h, low-dose-rate radiation, real-time calendar aging, full-scale airframe fatigue) are mostly avoided by proving equivalence to the OEM part, which already has a service history, rather than proving absolute life. That opens a verification-side AI play: comparative accelerated testing, adaptive statistical test design and autonomous parallel test farms.

findings.finding: FAA engine endurance test is a fixed 150-hour clock: a 6-hour sequence repeated 25 times plus 100 starts. The only flexibility: the FAA sets the run order, accessory loading can be shown on a separate rig with approved analysis, and bleed allowances.

Widespread-fatigue-damage limit of validity must rest on full-scale fatigue test evidence. A type certificate can be issued before the test finishes, but aircraft may fly only up to half the cycles accumulated on the test article. This is an existing precedent for progressive, lead-the-fleet approval.
Engine life-limited parts may be lifed by 'validated analysis, test, or service experience'. The rule prescribes no method, so validation is the gate.
A PMA needs 'test reports and computations' unless the design is identical under licence. There is no fixed test list; sufficiency is decided case by case.

High-cycle fatigue S-N coupons to 10^7 cycles at 20-30 Hz take 4-6 days each. A 15-30 specimen curve takes 2-4 months on one frame or about 1-2 weeks on 10 frames. Ultrasonic 20 kHz fatigue (10^9 cycles in about 14 h) is generally not accepted for certification allowables.
findings.source: (recalled) ASTM E466 practice; gigacycle fatigue literature

findings.finding: Creep is the hardest clock. Extrapolation is accepted only to about 3x the longest test, so a 10^5 h design life needs tests of 10^4 h or more. The ASME Sec III Div 5 Alloy 617 code case (~2019) took more than a decade.

Arrhenius thermal aging is accepted for nuclear environmental qualification (10 CFR 50.49, IEEE 323, Reg Guide 1.89). Its known weak points are choice of activation energy and diffusion-limited oxidation, which under-predict degradation.

Total ionizing dose: high dose rate with anneal is accepted for CMOS (MIL-STD-883 TM1019). Bipolar ELDRS needs about 10 mrad(Si)/s, which takes weeks to months. Cyclotron single-event-effect beam time is a capacity clock with months-long queues. NRC does not accept ion irradiation in place of neutron irradiation.

Composites: FAA AC 20-107B accepts load enhancement and life factors (LEF ~1.15) and the building-block approach. NCAMP/CMH-17 equivalency lets a new user run about 1 batch instead of 3-5. This is the closest existing 'inherit qualification, prove equivalence' mechanism.
Salt fog ASTM B117 runs 500-3,000 h and correlates poorly with field corrosion, yet MIL/DLA drawings still specify it. Changing that is a specification fight, not physics.
DLA Source Approval Request review queues (reported 6-18 months or more) far exceed the physics clocks of typical first article and qualification tests, which take weeks.

QuesTek's ICMD platform has an 'Accelerated Qualification and Certification' toolkit. Ferrium M54 went from concept to Navy aircraft in about 6 years versus 15-20, a NIST figure cited on QuesTek's site.
Senvol sells AM data and ML software and received Navy funding in Jan 2026 for an in-situ sensor-fusion project. Its site makes no claim about FAA qualification.
No WebSearch was available: the shared quota was used up before this agent ran. Most numbers are from memory and marked (recalled) in the notes.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Done ad hoc per package by a DER or the engineering support activity. No formal per-failure-mode framework for proving equivalence to the OEM part.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Fast (days). Mostly solved.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Run serially on scarce lab frames. Not adaptive. Run to fixed counts rather than stopped early on in-situ crack detection.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Legacy specs (B117) correlate poorly with the field. Acceleration models are rarely cross-validated per material.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual. Reviewer queues of 6-18 months or more dominate the physics clocks.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Write comparative accelerated test protocols, per failure mode, that put the OEM part and the copy side by side in the same rig at the same elevated stress, temperature or dose, so errors in the acceleration model cancel. Get DLA/ESA and the FAA to accept them as an equivalence standard, much like NCAMP equivalency.

Build an autonomous 24/7 test farm with hundreds of cheap resonant or electrodynamic frames and robotic specimen handling, so each specimen's fixed clock runs in parallel (~$10-30M capital for ~200 frames, recalled).
Use Bayesian adaptive test design aimed at the regulator's A/B-basis tolerance bounds, to cut specimen counts. Pre-justify the statistics so the regulator accepts the method, not just the count.
Use in-situ damage monitoring (acoustic emission, DIC, potential drop, thermography) to stop tests early, and get crack-initiation criteria agreed in place of run-out.

Assemble public acceleration-validity dossiers by alloy and polymer family: ultrasonic vs conventional fatigue, Arrhenius activation energies, dose-rate effects, cross-checked by fractography. Take them through ASTM/MMPDS/CMH-17 to widen what regulators accept.

Create a part-level progressive approval modelled on 25.571's half-cycles rule. Grant life in blocks as fleet-leader parts or a parallel real-time test accumulate, backed by tail-number usage tracking.
Get access to USAF ASIP and OEM service-history and fatigue data for C-130/KC-135 (via a CRADA, FOIA or an ASIP contract), so copies inherit the long-life evidence instead of re-proving it.

Build reviewer-side tooling: auto-generated requirement-to-test-to-evidence matrices and pre-checks against engineering-support-activity criteria, to cut the 6-18+ month review queue, which is the real clock.
ai_plays: An equivalence-first qualification planner: an AI that writes the minimal test plan per failure mode in the regulator's own vocabulary (MIL-STD-1530, AC 20-107B, MMPDS, CMH-17), sold to DERs and applicants or used internally by the Approval Factory.

Autonomous parallel test lab as a service: robotic, 24/7, with reports auto-generated in DLA/DER format. It turns physics clocks into a capital problem and becomes the Approval Factory's in-house edge.
Adaptive Bayesian test design plus in-situ early stopping, which reaches the same tolerance bounds with fewer specimens and shorter runs.
A cross-validation library of acceleration factors used to lobby standards bodies; it becomes a data moat on which accelerated methods regulators accept.
Progressive-approval packages with fleet-leader digital-twin monitoring, so parts ship now and life unlocks over time.
Reviewer copilot / package pre-check, which attacks the review queue, the binding clock, and directly cuts the Approval Factory's KPI of engineering and reviewer hours per approval.
surprises: For replacement parts, physics clocks are usually much shorter than regulator review queues. The binding limit is permission and reviewer capacity, not physics.
25.571 already lets aircraft operate on incomplete fatigue tests, up to half the cycles on the test article. That is a ready-made precedent for progressive approval.

NCAMP/CMH-17 equivalency already embodies 'inherit qualification, prove equivalence' for composites, but there is no general equivalent for metallic replacement parts under DLA Source Approval Requests.
ASTM B117 salt fog is still specified widely despite poor field correlation, so some time-bound tests exist through specification inertia, not physics.
Comparative testing makes acceleration-model uncertainty largely irrelevant, which removes the main reason regulators distrust accelerated tests.

research.q: DoD demand: data on sole-source price spikes, DLA spend on AMSC C/D/P items, number of sole-source NSNs, DoD IG reports, and budget lines that pay for second sourcing and reverse engineering.
research.headline: The demand is large and documented. In FY2025, DLA awarded about $3.4B non-competitively for aviation hardware alone (60-68% of airframe, component and engine dollars). DoD-wide, roughly $15-20B a year of component and repair spend is non-competed, and DoD's own data call found most sole-source justifications trace to missing technical data or rights, not to an inability to make the part. On the verification side the gaps are rights discovery (DoD canceled its AI data-rights scraper for lack of funding), the lack of any AMSC-weighted demand map, and limited government engineering review capacity for Source Approval Requests (SARs); incumbents (TransDigm, StandardAero) are buying approval capability rather than building it.

findings.finding: DLA FY2025 non-competed obligations total $10.38B (vs $45.56B competed). By supply group: aircraft/airframe $1.24B non-competed vs $0.72B competed (63%), aircraft components $1.10B vs $0.74B (60%), engines $0.87B vs $0.40B (68%), guided missiles $0.94B vs $0.11B (90%). Common hardware and valves are only 19% non-competed, so sole-sourcing is concentrated in engineered aviation parts.
findings.source: Original analysis, USAspending API spending_by_category/psc, FY2025, extent competed B/C/G vs A/D/F (approximate; delivery orders inherit the parent contract's code)

findings.finding: DoD-wide FY2025: aircraft components $6.39B non-competed vs $1.56B competed (80%); engines $8.35B vs $1.19B (87%); engine accessories $1.38B vs $0.31B (82%); equipment maintenance and repair $11.8B vs $10.55B; equipment modification $2.72B vs $0.72B. Total DoD non-competed is $232B.

A DoD data call to more than 200 programs in sustainment found that a majority of sole-source justifications were based on inadequate technical data, software or license rights, and that half of programs hit data deficiencies that blocked competition.

Vendor lock was found on all 5 programs GAO reviewed. On F/A-18, data rights for RF cables went unobtained for over a decade; reverse engineering was judged too costly, so maintainers cannibalize grounded aircraft. On Stryker, a 2024 sole-source support contract cost about $534M over 5 years.

The DoD IP Cadre's AI tool to scrape previously purchased data rights from contract databases was unfunded and canceled. The Air Force DART IPR Module saved about $1.75M in labor on RQ-4 contract review. NAVAIR's DRSAVE part-level data-rights repository is in CH-53K testing, with wider NAVAIR launch planned for summer 2026. The lessons-learned pilot stopped in FY2023.

The DoD IG Dec 2021 TransDigm audit recommended a voluntary refund of at least $21M excess profit on 150 contracts (Jan 2017-Jun 2019); TransDigm disputes it and has booked no contingency. About 90% of TransDigm sales come from proprietary products. Its 10-K says customers have reduced incentive to certify another supplier because of certification cost and time.

(Recalled, unverified) DoD IG 2019 TransDigm audit found excess profit on 46 of 47 parts, about $16.1M, later refunded, with markups up to about 9,400% (a metal pin). DoD IG Oct 2024 found the Air Force overpaid Boeing about $1M on C-17 spares, including a soap dispenser at about 7,943% over a fair price.
findings.source: DODIG-2019-060; DoD IG C-17 audit Oct 2024 (recalled)

findings.finding: TransDigm agreed to buy PMA houses Jet Parts Engineering and Victor Sierra for about $2.2B, about 7.9x their roughly $280M CY2025 revenue (closing announced Apr 2026). The incumbent monopolist is buying the alternative-approval capability.

StandardAero bought Aero Turbine Inc. for $120M upfront plus up to $21M earnout (about $25M expected 2025 EBITDA), citing military Source Approval Request expertise. SAR capability carries an acquisition premium.

AMSC code is not a USAspending field, and no public source publishes spend by AMSC C/D/P or a count of sole-source NSNs. Building either requires joining FLIS/WebFLIS AMSC data to DLA demand and award history. (Recalled) DLA manages about 5M NSNs; DLA Aviation manages about 1.1-1.2M.

Readiness context: only 2 of 49 aircraft met mission-capable goals in FY2021, and maintenance costs rose $1.2B over FY2011-2020. For the F-35, more than 10,000 components were awaiting repair, sustainment is $1.3T of $1.7T life-cycle cost, and the mission-capable rate was about 55%.

(Recalled) Funding for reverse engineering is fragmented across many small pots and has no dedicated production line: the DLA working capital fund (engineering support and source development), DLA R&D manufacturing technology and SBIR, the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office and the OC-ALC REACT reverse-engineering lab, Navy FRC/NAVSUP obsolescence (DMSMS) funds, IBAS/DPA Title III, and many SBIR awards for AI-enabled reverse engineering or technical data package generation.

research.q: Airline and lessor demand for PMA/DER and for verified trace: adoption rates by airline, savings, lessor return-condition restrictions, post-AOG-Technics behaviour.
research.headline: Airlines with their own MROs already pull PMA parts and DER repairs in, because they save 20-50%. Lessors and OEM service contracts still ban both at lease return, and engine leases signed in August 2026, three years after AOG Technics, still carry the ban, so the real demand gate is residual-value and trace permission, not airline willingness. AOG Technics showed that no one can check an 8130-3 or Form 1 release certificate against the shop that supposedly issued it. The verification-side AI play is a trace oracle plus a PMA residual-value underwriter that turns the lessor's "no" into a priced "yes".

findings.finding: A GlobalX engine lease (lessor Gryphon Trading, IAE V2527-A5) says the engine 'shall not have installed any DER-approved repairs or PMA parts', except PMA parts already present at commencement. The lessee must certify that no non-OEM repairs or PMA parts were used, and the lessor disclaims 'the accuracy, validity or traceability of any of the engine documentation'.
A second GlobalX lease (UMB Bank as owner trustee for AvCap 3349, CFM56-5B4/3) carries the same PMA and DER ban and the same no-non-OEM statements, and requires dual FAA 8130-3 / EASA Form 1 release.

Pratt & Whitney's fixed-price overhaul agreement with Willis Lease bills PMA parts not approved by the OEM's contract manager, and DER repairs it does not accept, as Excess Work outside the fixed price. At redelivery it requires 'no PMA parts that have not been approved by the OEM'. The OEM acts as gatekeeper over its competitors' parts.

Counter-example from the airline side: Volaris's MRO contract with Aveos lets Volaris approve PMA parts in writing, says Aveos 'shall not unreasonably refuse' them, and requires Aveos to 'use DERs and Extended DER repairs'.

HEICO has about 20,000 FAA PMAs to date and adds about 400-550 a year. Its Flight Support Group is 70% of $4.485B FY25 sales, the top 5 customers are about 20%, and no customer is 10% or more. The filing names no airlines.
PMA parts are 'often priced 20-50% lower' than OEM parts.

FTAI, a lessor that has turned into a parts and repair company, holds 25% of an Advanced Engine Repair JV aimed at repair cost savings. It names parts recertification required by customers, lessees and regulators as a cost and delay. A lessor embraces PMA when it owns the PMA economics.
AOG Technics: about $52M fraud, more than 60,000 parts sold (worth $9.3M), director sentenced 2026-02-23 to 4 years 8 months.

CFM found 126 suspect engines (less than 1% of 22,600 CFM56s) and 95 falsified documents covering 61 part numbers. Most were non-serialized hardware and none were life-limited parts. 16 engines were in CFM's own OEM shops, so OEM-only sourcing did not protect anyone. The fraud was a forged release certificate that no one could check against its issuer.
Airlines hit: Delta (less than 1% of its 2,100+ engines), American, United, Southwest, TAP, Ryanair, WestJet, Virgin Australia. The FAA issued no AD and found no critical forged parts.

Some OEMs threaten airlines with legal action for using their maintenance instructions (ICAs) to show PMA eligibility. Carriers answer with technical-assistance letters, which FAA engineers generally accept.

ProvenAir uses AI and OCR to build back-to-birth trace for life-limited parts and claims analysis drops from weeks to hours. It reads documents and does not verify them with the issuing shop. flydocs (Lufthansa Technik ecosystem, recalled) does records and lease-return work for 75+ customers.

(recalled) PMA is only about 2-5% of global aftermarket parts spend, concentrated on mature engines (CFM56, V2500, PW4000, CF6). Heavy users: United, American, Delta, Lufthansa Technik (about 20% owner of HEICO Aerospace since 1997-98), AF-KLM E&M, Southwest. No per-airline adoption-rate table could be fetched.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a registry where each issuer signs every 8130-3 and EASA Form 1 it issues, so any buyer can check a certificate against the named Part 145 or 21G shop for that serial or lot. Fingerprint non-serialized hardware physically at incoming inspection (spectroscopy, CT, metrology) and match it to design data, to close the bolts-and-bushings gap AOG Technics used.
Pool airline engineering acceptance of PMA parts across carriers, so each part is not re-reviewed by every airline.
Pre-review PMA/DER and DLA technical-data packages with AI for the FAA, DERs and DLA engineering, cutting the reviewer hours per approval.

research.q: Nuclear utility demand for dedicated and obsolete parts: spend, lead times, EPRI obsolescence data, how much they would pay to cut dedication time.
research.headline: US nuclear utilities spend an estimated $2-4B/yr on materials and parts (recalled). A dedicated safety-related item costs 2-10x its commercial price, a reverse-engineered obsolete part takes 6-18 months, and one day of outage on the critical path costs about $1-2M per unit, so utilities would pay per event, not per hour, to cut dedication time. Nobody yet sells an AI-native Appendix B dedicating entity: Nuclearn (70+ facilities) automates parts search and 10 CFR 50.59 screening but says nothing about commercial grade dedication, so the opening is to own the signature and the evidence, not just the software.

findings.finding: Search was unavailable (shared quota exhausted). Most figures below are recalled from memory; only the Nuclearn and Everstar web pages were verified by fetch.

Nuclearn (Phoenix, founded 2021) serves over 70 facilities in North America and the UK. Parts AI covers part discovery, item sourcing and status dashboards, and claims over 70% less research time. Engineering AI automates 10 CFR 50.59 screenings and evaluations. The site does not mention commercial grade dedication, equivalency or obsolescence.

Everstar's site has the Gordian AI platform and Titan manufacturing. It names a Qualification stage for 'materials, parts, and suppliers' backlogs but gives no mechanism, and is mostly aimed at new builds.

Commercial grade dedication pathway: 10 CFR 50 Appendix B and Part 21; EPRI 3002002982 (2014), endorsed by NRC RG 1.164 (2017); acceptance Methods 1-4; NEI 14-05A for accredited labs; EPRI TR-106439/TR-107330 for digital items; 10 CFR 50.49 and IEEE 344 for environmental and seismic qualification; 10 CFR 50.59 when the replacement is not like-for-like.
US fleet non-fuel O&M is about $15B/yr (O&M about $19-21/MWh x about 780 TWh). Materials and parts are about $2-4B/yr, roughly $20-60M per site per year.
findings.source: (recalled) NEI Nuclear Costs in Context; estimate

findings.finding: Dedication premium: a safety-related item typically costs 2-10x the commercial price, and far more for cheap items (a $50 relay can become $2-5k). One dedication package costs about $5k-$50k; a complex or digital one $100k-$500k or more.

Lead times: a new commercial grade dedication takes 3-9 months; reverse engineering an obsolete part 6-18 months; environmental requalification 12-24 months; large power transformers 2-4 years (2023-25).

Each site carries about 50k-100k+ catalogued items, of which 10-30% have no current OEM source. Thousands of part numbers go obsolete each year, and analog instrumentation and control (Foxboro Spec 200, Westinghouse 7300) is the worst cluster.

A forced outage or outage extension costs about $1-2M per day per 1 GW unit. Power purchase agreements with data-centre buyers (Constellation-Microsoft for Crane, Talen-Amazon, Constellation-Meta) raise the value of each lost day.

Existing obsolescence infrastructure tracks inventory, not engineering evidence: POMS, RAPID (Utilities Service Alliance), PUSH pooled spares, NUOG, and NUPIC joint supplier audits. Each utility and vendor re-dedicates the same items, and the packages are proprietary PDFs.

Willingness to pay has three parts: (1) outage-critical emergent parts, $100k-$1M per event; (2) routine labour savings of $5k-$40k per package, an estimated $50-300M/yr industry-wide; (3) inventory reduction from dedicating on demand, worth hundreds of millions per year fleetwide.

research.q: Power, oil & gas and process industry demand for non-OEM part qualification and inspection sign-off: spend and pain.
research.headline: Of these industries, nuclear has the clearest regulated verification pathway outside aerospace and defense: 10 CFR Part 21 commercial-grade dedication. The NRC itself says reverse engineering is rising because of obsolescence, cost and lead times, and that it fails at recovering requirements (the design basis), not at copying geometry. Appendix B already lets analysis count as design verification, so the barrier is regulator acceptance and liability, not the law. The AI play on the verification side is an AI-native Appendix B / Part 21 dedication house, with a design-basis requirements graph and a cross-owner equivalence registry. Gas turbines and oil & gas are gated by insurers, certifiers and owner engineers rather than a regulator, and the gap there is evidence sharing plus an insurer-backed warranty.

findings.finding: The NRC states licensees and suppliers are 'increasingly using reverse engineering techniques' for safety-related replacements 'including obsolescence, cost, and extended delivery schedules'.

Concrete failures: at Callaway, reverse-engineered controller cards from Nuclear Logistics Inc. failed in service and made auxiliary feedwater valves inoperable. At River Bend, 18 reverse-engineered Tobul accumulators had no verification of flow, leakage, pressure, stroke time or seismic performance. NOVA Machine Products built about 881 reverse-engineered HCU accumulators with no design verification.

The NRC's diagnosis: physical examination alone 'is typically not sufficient to identify all the functional requirements'. The bottleneck is recovering requirements and the design basis, which is information work an AI can do.

Appendix B Criterion III already allows design verification 'by design reviews, ... alternate or simplified calculation methods, or ... a suitable testing program'. The law permits analysis credit; what is missing is acceptance in practice.
findings.source: 10 CFR 50 App B as quoted in IN 2016-09 (fetched)

findings.finding: GL 89-02 endorsed the EPRI NP-5652 dedication methods. A supplier survey (Method 2) or a performance record (Method 4) cannot be the sole basis for acceptance unless the record reflects industry-wide data and change control has been audited. Pooled, fleet-wide performance data is therefore a regulatory lever.
The NRC issued a 2016 notice (IN-16-01) on commercial-grade dedication of Allen Bradley 700-RTC relays: CGD problems recur and are inspected for.

API Monogram, APIQR and Repair/Remanufacture programmes together cover more than 4,300 organizations in 75 countries. In oil & gas, non-OEM part acceptance runs through API Q1 and the API product specs, including API 20S for AM parts (2021, recalled), and through DNV-ST-B203 (recalled).

GE Vernova revenue was US$38.07B in 2025. The heavy-duty gas turbine aftermarket is about $20-25B/yr, OEMs hold about 80%+ through long-term service agreements, and non-OEM share is about 10-20% (recalled). Qualification is gated by owner engineering, insurers (FM Global, HSB) and LTSA terms, with lead-unit field trials of about 8,000-24,000 hours.

Dedication cost per item is often several times the commercial part price. Packages run about $5k-$50k+, and complex reverse-engineered items reach six figures. About 94 US reactors are moving to 60- and 80-year licences, and N-stamp holders fell from about 600 to about 200.

Refineries and offshore assets hold $50-150M of MRO spares per site, mostly slow-moving. Each operator redoes like-for-like equivalency work for the same obsolete parts, and there is no shared registry. Turnaround downtime costs about $1-2M/day, so authorised-inspector sign-off is on the critical path.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a machine-readable design-basis and requirements graph for each plant system by ingesting UFSARs, purchase specs, calcs and OEM manuals. It would generate critical characteristics automatically and close the gap the NRC cites in IN 2016-09.

Create a cross-owner registry of dedications and equivalencies, with in-service performance attached. That would make EPRI Method 4 (supplier performance record) usable on industry-wide data, as GL 89-02 requires, and let one qualification be accepted across 94 reactors or a whole gas turbine frame fleet.

The NRC documented about 881 reverse-engineered safety-related accumulators shipped with no design verification. Demand for reverse engineering is real and the quality is poor.
Gas turbines and oil & gas have no regulator gating non-OEM parts; the gate is insurers, certifiers and OEM service-contract terms. Liability and warranty, not approval, are the moat there.
