research.q: Rail, transit and marine operator demand for qualified obsolete spares (London Underground, DB, Amtrak, US Navy surface fleet).
research.headline: Rail, transit and Navy operators badly need qualified obsolete spares. London Underground already strips 1972 Stock trains for spares and will run them to about twice their design life (late 2030s to 2040s), and the Navy routinely cannibalises parts across surface ships. No company sells a repeatable service that turns an obsolete part into an approved part across many operators. The best verification play is rail-specific: for a like-for-like replacement, the operator or its Entity in Charge of Maintenance approves the part itself, with an independent Assessment Body only for significant changes. An AI-run, accredited Assessment Body or a dossier factory sold to operators could make the buyer's own yes 10x cheaper; a Navy technical-data-package and warrant-holder workbench is the high-value-per-part version.

findings.finding: London Underground's 1972 Stock (Bakerloo line, built 1972-74) is the oldest UK fleet in regular service. Its replacement may slip to the late 2030s or early 2040s, about double its design life, and a set was stripped for spares at Ruislip in 2022.
London Underground's 1973 Stock (Piccadilly line) is replaced by 94 Siemens 2024 Stock trains from Dec 2026 to Jun 2027, and all units retire by 2030. Its demand tail is short.

Amtrak had 447 Amfleet I and 136 Amfleet II cars (built 1975-83) in service in Oct 2025. Airo deliveries start in 2026, Amfleet I retires 2027-2030, and Amtrak issued an RFI in Oct 2025 for firms to scrap the fleet.

Deutsche Bahn has 3D-printed more than 100k spare parts since 2015-16 and co-founded the Mobility goes Additive network in 2016. Most parts are non-safety-critical interiors and housings that DB approves itself as maintenance entity; very few are safety-critical.
findings.source: recalled; sibling note l02; DB pages fetched without content

findings.finding: Under EU rules (Regulation 2019/779 on maintenance entities and the CSM-RA risk method, 402/2013), approval of a like-for-like spare rests with the operator's maintenance entity. Only a 'significant' change needs an independent Assessment Body. The US FRA likewise does not approve individual parts; the railroad self-certifies compliance with 49 CFR 238 and 231. The buyer is the approver.

The Navy surface-fleet route runs through NAVSEA Technical Warrant Holders and the NAVSUP WSS / DLA Land and Maritime source-approval path. Ships may print only low-criticality parts, with commanding-officer approval. BlueForge paid AML3D US$1.84M for 5 non-critical obsolete submarine parts (Mar 2026), and the Danville AM Center of Excellence has delivered more than 300 parts. No public money goes to AI for reverse engineering or approval.

Physics-clock tests in rail are EN 45545-2 fire, smoke and toxicity (weeks, a few k€ to 20k€ per material or part, recalled), EN 61373 shock and vibration, EN 50155 electronics, and EN 15085 welding. Navy equivalents are first article testing, MIL-S-901 shock and MIL-STD-167 vibration. Fire data is not pooled between operators.

research.q: Insurers and lenders as payers for verification (aviation insurers, engineering insurers, lessors' residual value): what they would pay for verified evidence.
research.headline: Insurers and lenders would not pay for FAA or DLA approvals themselves. On the military first wedge they are absent: the government self-insures and contractors who build to government specs are largely shielded by the Boyle defense. On the commercial side, lessors (about 40% or more of the fleet) are effectively a second regulator who often block PMA parts and DER repairs at lease return. What they would pay for, and what nobody provides, is a neutral, data-driven rating backed by an insurance carrier that certifies non-OEM content as value- and risk-neutral, with machine-verified provenance. Call it a CAPA or HSB for aviation PMA/DER, built on the Approval Factory's evidence and wrapped in a Munich Re or Lloyd's value warranty.

findings.finding: Lloyd's Register was formed in 1760 by marine underwriters to grade the ships they insured. Class status still determines whether a ship can be insured. Insurers have historically built the verification bodies they need.

Hartford Steam Boiler combined inspection and insurance from 1866 and imposed design rules (the Hartford Loop) on insured boilers. It has 1,200+ engineers and inspectors, about half its staff, and Munich Re acquired it in April 2009.

Munich Re aiSure (in AI insurance since 2018) backs AI performance and value warranties, including Barkr's AI luxury-asset valuation value warranty, the MKIII credit model and SeismicAI. This is the template for a value warranty on non-OEM parts.

Armilla, a Lloyd's coverholder backed by Chaucer, AXIS and Convex, prices AI liability from a technical review of each system. Limits go up to $25M aggregate and $5M per model. Carriers will underwrite based on third-party technical verification.

flydocs digitizes records back to an aircraft's birth, handles back-to-birth gaps for life-limited parts, and runs AI component inspection with AMOS, for 75+ partners including easyJet, Qantas, Airbus and Northrop Grumman. It stores and organizes evidence but neither rates non-OEM equivalence nor takes risk.

Lessors hold a large share of the fleet: AerCap 1,734 aircraft, SMBC 783, Avolon 685, DAE 622, ALC 592 (2026), with about 40% of jets leased (2017). Lease return conditions commonly bar PMA/DER content or require lessor consent (recalled industry practice), so lessors gate commercial market access for PMA.

AOG Technics (2023) supplied CFM56 parts with forged EASA Form 1 certificates. Initial reports put the affected engines at 100+, across several major airlines. Release-certificate verification is still visual and trust-based, and lessors and insurers bore the cost.

CAPA was founded in 1987 with auto-insurer backing to certify non-OEM collision parts so insurers could specify them. It is the direct precedent for insurer-driven certification of non-OEM parts. Avery v. State Farm (about $1.2B verdict in 1999, reversed in 2005) shows the liability risk.

Order-of-magnitude economics (recalled): engine shop visits cost roughly $4-8M for CFM56/V2500 and more for LEAP. PMA/DER can cut them by about 15-40%. Lease transitions cost $1-5M per aircraft including downtime. Aerospace insurance premiums total about $8-10bn a year.

research.q: Size the total market for "verification and approval" itself: TIC, certification consulting, DER/ODA services, qualification testing labs, CGD services; growth and margins.
research.headline: Testing, inspection and certification (TIC) is a market of about $263B (2025), growing about 4.6% a year; roughly $197B of that is outsourced. Big incumbents earn 14-18% operating margins on labor-heavy delivery at about €80k revenue per employee. The slice the Approval Factory can reach directly (aerospace and defense qualification testing, FAA DER/ODA engineering, PMA and DLA Source Approval Request (SAR) packages, nuclear commercial-grade dedication, defense certification consulting) is about $5-10B a year. That is an estimate built from parts, and the value is captured best by owning the approvals, not by selling hours.

findings.finding: Global TIC market was $263.4B in 2025, forecast at $345.4B by 2031 (4.62% CAGR). Outsourced work is 74.65% of it (about $197B).
Bureau Veritas: €6.47B revenue, €992M operating income (about 15.3%), 82,000 employees in 2025. That is about €79k revenue per employee.
Intertek: £3.43B revenue and £619.6M operating income (about 18%) in 2025, with 45,000 employees.
SGS: CHF 6.6B revenue in 2023, 99,600 employees. Adjusted EBIT is about 14-15% (recalled).
Eurofins: €6.95B revenue in 2024, about 63,000 employees.

Temasek bought Element Materials Technology (aerospace and defense qualification labs) from Bridgepoint in Jan 2022 at a $7B valuation. Element's 2021 revenue was £913M, so that is very roughly 25-30x EBITDA. Element owns NTS (recalled).

Rough sizes for the Approval Factory slices, all estimated or recalled: aerospace and defense TIC about $8-12B; US aerospace and defense qualification labs about $2-4B; US FAA designee services about $1-2B; PMA/SAR approval engineering about $0.3-1B; US nuclear commercial-grade dedication about $0.3-0.7B; security certification (FedRAMP, CMMC, Common Criteria, SOC 2) about $5-10B.

Margins by layer (opinion). Signed attestation by designees is the highest margin per hour. Physical test labs run about 18-25% adjusted EBITDA because test capacity is scarce. Assembling documents and evidence is about 50-70% of hours, has a low moat, and is where AI cuts cost.
Market values attached to approvals: HEICO (about $35-40B market cap, built on PMAs, recalled), Element at $7B, and Vanta/Drata in AI-native compliance software (recalled).

research.q: Pricing power cases: what DERs, ODA holders, CGD vendors, NRTLs and TIC firms charge per approval or test; margins of certification businesses (UL Solutions, Element, NTS, Applus).
research.headline: Margins in certification rise with how mandatory and how scarce the sign-off is, not with how much engineering goes into it. Mistras sells certified NDT labor at 12.6% adj. EBITDA and is being sold for about 9.5x. UL Solutions owns a mandated mark and earns 25.9%, with its Industrial segment at 34.9%. HEICO owns PMA approvals and its Flight Support Group earns 24.1% operating margin. So the Approval Factory should own the approvals it produces and the recurring revenue for keeping them valid, not sell DER-style approval hours. Note: no web searches were possible (shared quota exhausted). Filing figures were fetched from EDGAR and eCFR mirrors. Per-approval prices are recalled and marked as such.

findings.finding: UL Solutions FY2025: revenue $3,053M, adj. EBITDA $792M at 25.9% (+300bp), FCF $403M. Industrial segment $1,341M at 34.9% adj. EBITDA, Consumer 18.9%, Software & Advisory 19.1%. FY2026 guide is about 27%.

About 33% of UL revenue is Ongoing Certification Services: follow-up factory inspections and label fees that keep a past approval valid. Certification testing itself is only ~28%. 80,000+ customers, 14,587 employees (~9,900 technical).
UL Q2 2026: revenue $816M, adj. EBITDA margin 26.8%, Industrial 32.3%, Consumer 21.3%.

Mistras (NDT technician services) FY2025: revenue $724.0M, gross margin 28.2%, adj. EBITDA $91.1M at 12.6%. H.I.G. Capital agreed to take it private on 2026-09-18 at $20.35/share, EV about $866M, roughly 9.5x EBITDA (my calculation). This is the low end of the margin ladder: labor that is certified but commoditized.
HEICO FY2025: net sales $4,485M. Flight Support Group (PMA parts plus DER repairs) $3,117M at 24.1% operating margin, up from 22.5%. Consolidated operating margin 22.7%.

Element Materials Technology: 2021 revenue £913M, EBIT £43.4M (depressed by amortization). Temasek took control in Jan 2022 at a $7bn valuation. Exova was bought for £620M in 2017. Underlying EBITDA in the mid-20s% is recalled.

The NRC bills $337 per professional staff-hour. Advanced-reactor applicants and pre-applicants pay a reduced $154/hr under the ADVANCE Act. Every hour of reviewer confusion is billed to the applicant, which makes it measurable per docket.

The FAA charges no user fees for TC, STC, PMA or repair approvals. The price of an approval is therefore paid entirely in private DER/ODA labor and FAA queue time. EASA does charge fees under Reg. (EU) 2019/2153: flat fees by aircraft class plus an hourly rate, recalled at about EUR 250-300.

Consultant DERs charge about $150-350/hr. A simple 8110-3 repair approval costs about $2-10k. A substantiated major repair costs about $10-75k. PMA test-and-computation substantiation costs $50-500k. Transport-category STCs through an ODA cost $250k-$2M+.

In nuclear commercial-grade dedication, dedicated items sell at about 3-20x the commercial price (a $100 relay becomes a $1,500-3,000 dedicated relay). Dedication plans cost $5-50k per item. EQ or seismic qualification costs $50-500k. The premium pays for acceptance of 10 CFR Part 21 liability and an Appendix B QA program.

NRTL listing costs about $5-25k for simple products and $25-150k+ for complex industrial or hazardous-location equipment. Annual follow-up runs about $2-10k per factory plus label fees. UL 9540A large-scale fire testing runs $100-500k+. There are about 19 OSHA-recognized NRTLs.

Applus+ was taken private in 2024 through a delisting bid by Amber EquityCo (Apollo/TDR). Recalled: about EUR 12.78/share, EV about EUR 2.6-2.8bn, adj. operating margin about 11-12%, with statutory vehicle-inspection concessions at about 25%+.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build an AI-native ODA or DER-holding unit. Human unit members sign, and software produces the substantiation. This is already legal under 14 CFR 183 Subpart D. The missing piece is FAA acceptance of the software as a qualified engineering tool, in the spirit of DO-330 tool qualification.

Capture the keep-valid annuity, the analog of UL's ~33% follow-up revenue. Offer continuous compliance on approvals already granted: ICA upkeep, PMA quality-system audits, CGD re-dedication when a supplier changes, Part 21 evaluations.

Become a commercial-grade dedicator that accepts Part 21 liability under its own Appendix B program. AI would generate critical-characteristic plans and acceptance dossiers, pushing the cost per dedicated item toward zero while the 3-20x price premium remains.

Build a public dataset of reviewer hours per review type from NRC fee-recovery billing ($337/hr) and FAA application-to-approval times. Use it to prove that machine-checkable packages cut RAIs and issue papers.
Run simulation-minimized physical testing (fewer specimens, tests that validate a model) in owned lab capacity. Lab hours sell for $150-400, and that capacity is the physics clock.
Use the public FAA PMA and DRS databases plus DLA sole-source lists to price-target parts where the OEM aftermarket margin (~50%) leaves the most room for an owned approval.
ai_plays: Approval owner, not approval labor: own the PMA, SAR or TDP outcome (HEICO-like 24%+ margins) instead of selling DER hours (Mistras-like ~12%).
AI-native ODA or DER house: automated substantiation plus human delegated signers. Sells speed in a market where the FAA charges nothing and the queue is the price.
AI commercial-grade dedication house for nuclear: dossier generation plus assumed Part 21 liability. Captures the 3-20x markup.
Continuous compliance annuity: monitor and re-verify approved parts, suppliers and repairs, the analog of UL's Ongoing Certification Services (~33% of revenue).
Reviewer-side tooling for regulators and NRTLs: machine-checkable submissions that cut NRC billed hours ($337/hr) and FAA issue papers.
Simulation-first qualification lab: cut physical test campaigns (fatigue, EQ, 9540A fire) to the minimum validating set.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Manual and bespoke. No reuse across similar parts, no machine-checkable format.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Too many specimens and little test-to-validate-model approach. Lab capacity is scarce.

pathway_steps.who_does_it: FAA (no fee) or ODA/DER; NRC ($337/hr); EASA (fees); DLA ESA for SARs
pathway_steps.cost: FAA $0 fee, paid in time; NRC hourly billing
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Reviewer capacity is the bottleneck. RAIs and issue papers loop repeatedly.

pathway_steps.who_does_it: NRTL follow-up services, QA auditors, NUPIC
pathway_steps.cost: $2-10k per factory per year for NRTL (recalled)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Periodic sampling instead of continuous verification. This is a large annuity (~33% of UL revenue).

surprises: UL's Industrial segment earns 34.9% adj. EBITDA versus 18.9% in Consumer. The same lab work earns double margin where the mark is mandated.
A third of UL's revenue is paid for staying certified, not for getting certified.
Mistras, deep in the inspection and verification chain, is selling for only about $866M EV (about 9.5x EBITDA). Proximity to verification without owning the sign-off earns little.

The NRC already prices reviewer time at $337/hr, so any AI that reduces reviewer hours has a directly measurable dollar value per docket. The FAA charges nothing, so there its value shows up only as time saved.

research.q: Vanta/Drata: how SOC 2 compliance automation became a multi-billion business; what was automated, why auditors accepted it, and how the model maps to hardware certification.
research.headline: Vanta did not automate the audit. It cut most of the applicant's prep hours with API evidence collection and continuous monitoring, gave the licensed CPA a read-only portal, and brought auditors deal flow. The signature stayed human and the hours collapsed, which reached about $300M ARR, 16k customers and a $4.15B valuation. The hardware equivalent (signed physical-test evidence, a machine-readable compliance case, a DER/ESA reviewer portal and a DER marketplace) appears nobody has built for PMA/SAR; Ketryx (FDA software) and Istari (Air Force digital engineering) are the nearest.

findings.finding: Vanta: founded 2018 (YC W18). Series A $50M (2021); Series B $1.6B (2022); Series C $2.45B (Jul 2024); Series D $150M at $4.15B (Jul 2025). ARR about $10M in 2021 and $300M in Apr 2026. More than 16,000 customers (about $19k ARR each).
Drata: founded 2020. Series C $200M at $2B (Dec 2022). Acquired oak9 and SafeBase (about $250M). About $100M+ ARR. All figures from memory, not checked this session.

What was automated: read-only API evidence pulls from cloud, identity, HR and code systems; daily control tests across the Type II window; templated policies mapped across frameworks; workflows; an auditor portal; trust centers and AI questionnaires. Not automated: the CPA attestation opinion under SSAE 18.
findings.source: Wikipedia product history plus recalled product knowledge

findings.finding: Why auditors accepted it: no regulator rule change was needed, because SOC 2 is set by the market and the AICPA and companies design their own controls. Evidence pulled by API is more reliable than screenshots. The platforms sent auditors deal flow through partner networks. Liability stayed with the CPA. Cost per audit fell but volume rose.

Delve (YC W24) uses AI agents to collect evidence (including screenshots), write reports and autofill questionnaires. Industry criticism of cheap 'audit mill' firms shows the quality failure mode to avoid in safety-critical work.

Istari Digital pitches 'validate and certify system integrity in real time' and auditable engineering workflows. It works with the Department of the Air Force and announced 'Industry Øne' on May 20 2026.
ConsuNova offers DO-178C/DO-254 consulting plus traceGEAR and reviewGEAR tools. It is services-led and covers software and avionics, not PMA hardware parts.

Mapping: the DER/ODA is a close analog of the CPA (private, paid by the applicant, licensed through delegation). The DLA ESA is not: it is a capacity-limited government engineer. The largest gap is that hardware evidence (CMM, NDT, coupon and fatigue tests, conformity inspections) is physical, not natively digital or tamper-evident.

A machine-readable compliance-case graph (requirement to analysis to test to conformity) that outputs FAA 8110-3, PMA and MIL-STD-31000 TDP formats
A pre-review agent trained on DER/ESA rejection reasons that flags gaps before submission (needs data from SAR disapprovals and DER comments)

A reviewer copilot for DLA ESAs and FAA ACO/DERs that structures packages and checks completeness, the highest-leverage point because reviewer capacity is the bottleneck
A trusted evidence-integrity layer (signed test-equipment data) as the moat that LLM drafting cannot copy
A DER network marketplace as the distribution and approval channel
surprises: Vanta's moat was never the AI or the integrations alone. It was the auditor channel plus the fact that SOC 2 needed no regulator rule change.
SOC 2's Type II observation window is a 'clock' Vanta couldn't shorten, only make painless: the same posture applies to physics test clocks
The DER system is structurally closer to the CPA model than DLA's government ESA is, so the FAA PMA side may suit the Vanta playbook better than DLA SAR
Revenue per SOC 2 customer is only about $19k. A hardware approval is worth $100k+ but there are far fewer of them, which favors owning approvals over selling seats.

research.q: UL's history (1894-today): how a private lab became the de facto gate for electrical safety, its business model, and lessons for a private hardware verification authority.
research.headline: UL became the electrical-safety gate by being paid by the party carrying the risk (fire insurers, 1894), writing its own standards and getting them into model codes that states turned into law (NEC, enforced by local inspectors (AHJs)), and selling a mark that saved inspectors work. Recurring factory checks on certified products (33% of revenue) made it a $3.05B, 25.9% adjusted-EBITDA business (FY2025). The lesson for an Approval Factory: own the evidence standard and the surveillance layer, stay neutral and recognized by category rather than by name, and sell reviewer-hour savings to whoever is short of reviewers. A verification authority that also makes parts conflicts with the neutrality the gate depends on.

findings.finding: Founded 1894 by W.H. Merrill after insurers hired him to inspect wiring at the 1893 Columbian Exposition. Funded by the Chicago Fire Underwriters' Association and the Western Insurance Union. First test report 24 Mar 1894, using $350 of equipment.

First standard 1903 (tin-clad fire doors). Label Service 1906, which became the UL Mark plus factory follow-up. Merrill was NFPA Secretary 1903-09 and NFPA President 1910-12, so the gatekeeper also sat on the code body.
FY2025 revenue $3,053M (2024: $2,870M). Net income $345M. Adjusted EBITDA $792M (25.9% margin, up from 21.0% in 2023). Operating cash flow $600M.

Revenue by service type: Certification Testing about 28%, Ongoing Certification Services about 33% (mandatory inspection and monitoring to keep the right to use the mark, plus label sales), Non-certification Testing about 30%, Software about 9%.
Industrial segment (code-driven) $1,341M at 28.8% segment operating margin, against Consumer $1,319M at about 9% and Software and Advisory $393M at 3.6%. Code-mandated gates earn the margin.
The 10-K says demand is 'driven primarily by state and local governments as enforced through the use of model codes', and that large retailers and AHJs also demand third-party certification.

Scale: more than 80,000 customers, over 110 countries, 14,587 full-time employees (about 9,900 technical), more than 650 accreditations, more than 1,200 standards panels, certifies against more than 4,000 standards.

Structure: nonprofit until 2012 (for-profit UL LLC from 1 Jan 2012). Three-way split on 26 Jun 2022. IPO April 2024 raised about $950M at about $6.8-7B. ULSE (nonprofit) still holds 61.6% of the equity and 94.1% of the votes.

OSHA now recognizes 21 NRTLs (UL LLC, CSA, Intertek, TUV SUD, TUV Rheinland, SGS, DEKRA, FM Approvals, Nemko, NSF, Eurofins, SolarPTL, SwRI and others). The original OSHA rules named UL and FM. The open NRTL rule (29 CFR 1910.7, 1988) came after a MET Labs challenge (recalled), and UL still dominates.

UL's own risk factors name AI tools that replicate its services, rules requiring it to 'accept third-party test results ... in lieu of collecting its own data and conducting its own tests', and self-declaration of conformity (post-Chevron) as threats that would commoditize it.

Courts have mostly not held certifiers liable as insurers of the products they certify. Hempstead v. General Fire Extinguisher (D. Del. 1967) is an early case that allowed a negligence claim (recalled).

players.funding_or_scale: HEICO adds about 400-550 PMAs a year (from prior review)

what_would_need_to_be_done: Write and publish a consensus 'evidence standard for reverse-engineered part equivalence' (scan, material and test requirements for each criticality class) via SAE or a DoD handbook annex, so that DLA/ESA SAR guidance and FAA DER practice reference it. That would be the ULSE-style asset.

Get recognized by category, not by name: FAA ODA for PMA, accredited ISO/IEC 17065/17025 conformity body status, EASA 21J/21G equivalents, so the authority survives the same opening-up that turned UL's named status into 21 NRTLs.

Build ongoing surveillance of approved alternate parts (lot verification, field-return monitoring, re-validation when a supplier changes a process). This is UL's 33% recurring line, and almost nobody does it for alternate parts after first-article approval.
Publish a simulation-credibility standard (modeled on ASME V&V 40) so regulators accept analysis plus a reduced physical test matrix, shortening the physics clock.
Separate governance of verification from part manufacture (UL's 2022 three-entity split as the template), or commit to selling only tools to reviewers, to keep the neutrality the gate depends on.
Pool field-failure and approval data (DLA quality records, operator data) into a precedent database as a substitute for withheld OEM technical data packages.
Find a party that bears the risk and will pay for the gate, the way insurers funded UL: aviation insurers, fleet sustainment commands, or operators facing obsolescence.
ai_plays: A reviewer copilot sold to the gatekeepers (DLA and service ESAs, FAA ACOs, DER firms). It checks SAR/PMA packages against requirements and cites precedent approvals. KPI: reviewer hours per approval.
An AI-first private equivalence verification body: write the standard, get accredited or become an ODA, and charge for first approval plus recurring lot surveillance (UL model).

Continuous conformity from production telemetry: in-process CT, metrology and sensor streams with AI anomaly detection replacing periodic factory audits. This attacks TIC's most recurring revenue line, which UL itself names as an AI risk.
A test-matrix minimizer: simulation and digital twins plus uncertainty quantification to cut physical tests to the minimum the evidence standard requires.

Certification for new hardware where no standard exists yet (humanoid and mobile robots, BESS retrofits, AI data-center power gear, eVTOL and defense drone parts), UL-1894 style: write the standard, then sell the mark.
surprises: The Industrial (code-mandated) segment earns about 3x the margin of Consumer on similar revenue: about 29% against 9%.
UL's 10-K explicitly names AI tools that replicate its services, and any rule forcing it to accept third-party test data, as threats that would make its services obsolete or commoditized.
Physical UL Mark labels, ordered through a single US supplier, are 'material' to the certification business.
Losing its named OSHA status in 1988 did not dent UL's dominance. Brand, installed base and standards ownership mattered more than exclusive recognition.
UL ran as a nonprofit for 118 years before going for-profit, and the nonprofit still holds 94.1% of the votes after the IPO.

research.q: Automotive virtual crash testing and Euro NCAP / UNECE virtual testing acceptance: how simulation entered homologation and how long it took.
research.headline: Simulation was never accepted as a replacement for crash tests. It got in as "the applicant predicts everything, the assessor physically spot-checks a sample of its own choosing, and misses are penalized", one act at a time from a regulator-approved list, and that took 24 to 40 years: the first full-car simulation was in 1986, EU law allowed virtual testing only for simple geometric acts from 2010, Euro NCAP used OEM predictions for pedestrian tests around 2013, and human-body-model and occupant-diversity virtual assessments came in 2023 to 2026, while the regulatory full-scale crash test is still physical in 2026. For an Approval Factory, the lesson is that the scale-up comes from a codified, statistical verification protocol plus an accredited third party, and that protocol, along with tools that produce simulation-credibility evidence, does not exist today for DLA source approvals or FAA PMA.

findings.finding: First successful full frontal car crash simulation: ESI's VW Polo at 50 km/h into a rigid barrier. ESI had shown a jet-into-nuclear-plant impact simulation on 30 May 1978. The German FAT consortium of 7 OEMs then got runs down to overnight (under one day).

EU Reg. 2018/858, Art. 30(7): virtual testing can replace physical tests only at the manufacturer's request and with the approval authority's agreement, in line with Annex VIII (general conditions, specific conditions, validation process). Art. 30(8) lets the Commission extend the list of eligible acts by delegated act. Art. 3(54) defines a virtual testing method as computer simulation, including calculation.

Directive 2007/46/EC Annex XVI, with Commission Reg. 371/2010, first listed the acts eligible for virtual testing. All were geometric or quasi-static (external projections, underrun protection, field of vision, plate space, towing devices). Frontal and side crash acts (UN R94/R95) were not eligible and remain physical.

Euro NCAP's pedestrian grid: the OEM predicts the head-impact result at every grid point, Euro NCAP physically tests a subset, and a correction factor applies if the tests deviate from the predictions. Active bonnets must be shown by human-body-model simulation to deploy before head contact. This is the template for 'predict, spot-check, penalize'.

Euro NCAP added the far-side sled test and the MPDB test in 2020. A far-side virtual assessment using human body models, verified by a physical sled test and objective curve correlation (ISO/TS 18571), followed around 2023.

Euro NCAP 2026 ratings explicitly credit simulation. The ZEEKR 7GT result cites 'Virtual modelling and sled testing across the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles' as part of the occupant-diversity assessment.

UNECE's NATM for automated driving (master document 2021) makes simulation one of five validation pillars, alongside audit, track, real-world and in-service monitoring, and adds a credibility assessment framework for virtual toolchains. EU Reg. 2022/1426 (ADS type-approval) requires a credibility assessment of the toolchain. UN R157 ALKS was adopted in June 2020.

Elapsed time: about 24 years from feasibility to the first legal permission (trivial acts only), about 27 years to first use in a consumer rating, and about 37-40 years to human-body-model crash assessment. The rating body (Euro NCAP, voluntary) moved faster than law, and the physical full-scale test was kept as the anchor rather than replaced.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Write a ready-to-adopt 'virtual equivalence' protocol for spare-part approval (DLA SAR/TDP, FAA PMA), modelled on Euro NCAP pedestrian: the applicant predicts every TDP requirement, the government picks k random physical verification tests, and misses trigger a correction or rejection. Include the statistics (sampling plan, consumer's risk) and ship it as a draft SAE ARP, MIL-HDBK or FAA advisory circular.

Get a positive list of low-criticality part classes where analysis plus spot checks is presumptively acceptable, the aero/defense version of EU Reg. 371/2010's list of eligible acts. Then expand it class by class, as the Commission can by delegated act under Art. 30(8).

Build per-part credibility dossiers automatically, aligned to ASME V&V 40, NASA-STD-7009 and the UNECE NATM credibility framework: objective correlation metrics (ISO/TS 18571 style), uncertainty quantification, and an explicit domain of validity.

Create open, regulator-certified reference models for common legacy sole-source part classes (the equivalent of THUMS/GHBMC), so each application reuses an already-accepted model instead of re-validating from scratch.

Stand up an accredited, AI-native independent verification body for aero and defense, playing the role DEKRA or TUV play in EU type-approval, possibly as an FAA ODA or DER house that witnesses virtual verification and spot checks.

Close the loop with in-service data (DLA quality deficiency reports, FAA service difficulty reports), the in-service monitoring pillar of NATM, so approvals carry ongoing evidence and can be granted with less up-front testing.

Use the faster, voluntary route: Euro NCAP accepted simulation 10+ years before law did. Find the aero/defense equivalent (SAE G-34/G-35, ASTM F42, MMPDS/CMH-17, prime-contractor supplier qualification) to set the precedent before DLA and the FAA.
ai_plays: Credibility-as-a-Service: AI that generates and audits the verification and validation evidence for simulation-based approvals (correlation, uncertainty quantification, coverage, domain of validity), sold to regulators, technical services, ODAs and DERs. Automotive has the demand but no dedicated vendor, and aero/defense has neither the protocol nor the vendor.

A reviewer copilot for DLA engineering support activities, FAA certification offices and DERs: it checks SAR or PMA packages against requirements, flags gaps and proposes the minimum spot-check tests, cutting reviewer hours, which is the real bottleneck.
Statistical spot-check design: pick the fewest physical tests that bound the risk of a wrong approval, Euro NCAP's grid-sampling and correction-factor logic generalized to spare parts.
Regulator-grade surrogate models: AI surrogates like Neural Concept's or PhysicsX's, packaged with an acceptable domain-of-validity and uncertainty argument rather than sold for design speed.
An AI-native accredited verification house, the TUV/DEKRA role for legacy aero/defense parts, that owns the protocol and the reference models and acts as the permission layer itself.
surprises: Simulation never replaced the regulatory full-scale crash test. Even in 2026, UN R94/R95 and FMVSS frontal and side tests are physical. Simulation got in by covering the cases nobody physically tests (more occupant sizes, grid points, load cases), with one physical test kept as the anchor.

A voluntary consumer-rating body, Euro NCAP, accepted OEM predictions plus spot checks about 10+ years before the EU allowed virtual testing for crash-relevant acts. Voluntary standards bodies are the faster route.
The first legal permission (2010) was for trivial geometric acts only. Acceptance grew from low-consequence items outward, through an explicit list the regulator can extend.
What made trust work was a correction factor penalizing wrong predictions, not proof that the models were correct. Euro NCAP did not have to trust OEM models; it made dishonest predictions costly.
Free shared reference models (THUMS became free in 2021) were a key enabler of human-body-model virtual assessment. Aero/defense has no equivalent for legacy parts.

research.q: Semiconductor formal verification and EDA sign-off (Synopsys, Cadence, Mentor): how verification became the most valuable layer of chip design and what the analog is for physical parts.
research.headline: Chip verification became the most valuable layer of design for three reasons. Errors that escape are very expensive (a $10M+ mask set, a respin, or the $475M FDIV recall). The spec is fully digital and executable. And the gatekeeper (the foundry) certifies specific tools as "golden sign-off", so permission flows through the tool rather than through a person's signature. Physical replacement parts lack an executable spec, an equivalence checker, and any regulator acceptance of tool output (the FAA and DLA delegate to people: DERs, ODA units and ESA reviewers). The AI play on the verification side is to build that sign-off layer and get a DLA ESA or FAA ACO to accept it.

findings.finding: Synopsys completed its acquisition of Ansys on 2025-07-17. It says this gives it an expanded $31B TAM and plans multiphysics capabilities across the EDA stack in 1H 2026, aimed at chips, automotive and aerospace. EDA is absorbing simulation, but not regulatory sign-off for physical parts.

The FDIV recall cost Intel a $475M pretax charge, about $891M in 2024 dollars. Formal verification for floating point became standard afterwards, and Nehalem (2008) was the first Intel design with formal as its primary validation method. Verification spend scales with the cost of an escape.

Per the Wilson Research Group / Siemens studies, verification takes about 50 to 60%+ of ASIC project time and verification headcount at least matches design headcount. First-silicon success was about 14% in 2024.
findings.source: Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA 2024 functional verification study (recalled; fetch of blog URL failed)

findings.finding: The moat in chip sign-off is foundry certification of tools (Calibre DRC/LVS, PrimeTime/Tempus STA, RedHawk IR/EM) plus models correlated against measured silicon. A clean report from a certified tool counts as permission to tape out. The physical-part analog is missing: the FAA delegates findings to DERs and ODAs, not to qualified analysis tools, and DO-330 tool qualification covers only software and electronics development tools.

Precedent exists in another regulator. The FDA finalized guidance in Nov 2023 on assessing the credibility of computational modeling in device submissions, built on ASME V&V 40-2018. A safety regulator has written down how a model's output can replace physical testing. The FAA and DLA have no equivalent for compliance-by-analysis of replacement parts.
findings.source: FDA CM&S credibility guidance (fetch returned 401; recalled)

findings.finding: NASA CR-20210015404 (2021; Boeing, Pratt & Whitney, Stanford, U. Wyoming) sets out a vision and research roadmap for Certification by Analysis. It covers airplane and engine compliance, not spare-part equivalence.

AI chip-verification startups such as ChipAgents (backed by B Capital, Bessemer, Micron, MediaTek, Samsung and Ericsson; claims a 50% design-cycle reduction and autonomous regression root-cause analysis) show that the pattern is being funded in chips. Nobody is applying it to physical-part sign-off.

Mapping of chip sign-off elements to physical parts. PDK/DRC deck maps to the cert basis, which exists only as prose (missing). Liberty files map to MMPDS, CMH-17 and NCAMP allowables (partial). The equivalence checker maps to PMA identicality and test-and-computation (done by hand). Coverage closure maps to the compliance matrix (manual). The silicon correlation loop maps to test and service data (siloed).

research.q: FDA in-silico evidence and the ASME V&V 40 / FDA credibility framework; MDDT program; cases where simulation replaced bench or clinical tests.
research.headline: FDA has a working template for letting simulation stand in for physical evidence: ASME V&V 40-2018 sets how much credibility a model needs by weighing how much the decision relies on it against the harm of a wrong decision; the 2023 FDA credibility guidance builds on it; and the MDDT program lets a model be qualified once and cited by any sponsor. Simulation has actually replaced a test only where the regulator co-built or qualified the model (diabetes simulator, MRI implant heating, PBPK drug-interaction waivers), and aviation and DLA have no equivalent, so the verification-side AI play is a credibility-dossier engine plus regulator-qualified computational tools for part classes.

findings.finding: ASME V&V 40-2018 sets required model credibility by model influence (how much the decision relies on the model) times decision consequence (the harm of a wrong decision). It uses engineering judgment, not a formula, builds on V&V 10 and V&V 20, and is still in effect on stabilized maintenance.

The FDA final guidance 'Assessing the Credibility of Computational Modeling and Simulation in Medical Device Submissions' (draft Dec 2021) runs: question of interest -> context of use -> model risk -> credibility goals -> 8 categories of credibility evidence -> adequacy assessment.
findings.source: fda.gov returned 401 and could not be fetched (recalled)

findings.finding: The VICTRE in silico imaging trial used 2,986 virtual patients, Monte Carlo imaging and a computational reader. It reproduced the clinical-trial finding that tomosynthesis beats digital mammography (larger gain for masses than calcifications). FDA authors called in silico trials a viable source of regulatory evidence.
findings.source: Badano et al. JAMA Netw Open 2018;1(7):e185474, doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.5474 (fetched via Europe PMC)

findings.finding: The MDDT program qualifies a tool for a specific context of use, after which any sponsor can cite it. Its categories are clinical outcome assessment, biomarker test and nonclinical assessment model. Few tools have been qualified and very few are computational; the main in silico one is IMAnalytics (ZMT/IT'IS), which assesses MRI RF heating of implants using Virtual Population models.
findings.number: About 15-20 tools qualified since 2017; IMAnalytics about 2021 (recalled)
findings.source: fda.gov MDDT page returned 401 (recalled); Hart 2023 J Pathol PMID 37794720 shows sponsors still at the initial-interaction stage

findings.finding: FDA accepted the UVA/Padova Type 1 Diabetes Simulator as a substitute for preclinical animal testing of closed-loop insulin control algorithms. It is the clearest precedent of simulation replacing a test outright.
For active implants, MR-Conditional labeling relies on ISO/TS 10974 tiered simulation across virtual human models plus bench transfer-function measurement, instead of in vivo heating measurement.
An FDA/Medtronic study (Haddad et al. 2017) used virtual-patient lead-fracture simulations as an informative Bayesian prior to reduce the number of patients a device trial had to enroll.
findings.source: Haddad et al. 2017, J Biopharm Stat (recalled)

findings.finding: On the drug side, Certara's Simcyp PBPK models routinely waive dedicated clinical drug-interaction and pediatric dosing studies. Unlearn.AI's PROCOVA digital-twin method received an EMA qualification opinion that shrinks trial control arms.
Dassault's Living Heart Project and FDA signed a 5-year research agreement on an in silico trial for mitral valve repair devices. No approval wholly based on it is publicly known.

The general pattern: simulation first selects which worst cases get physically tested (common, e.g. stent and orthopedic FEA), then augments physical data as a prior (growing), and only rarely replaces a test. Replacement happens where the physics is bounded, a validation comparator exists, and the regulator co-built or qualified the model.

Aviation has no MDDT-like qualify-once, cite-many program for computational tools. The closest analogs are shared materials-allowables datasets (MMPDS, CMH-17, NCAMP). NASA's 'Certification by Analysis 2040' study names model credibility, uncertainty quantification and an agreed process as gaps.
InSilicoTrials offers pharma trial simulation with an 'IRIS' multi-agent layer and claims co-authorship of 'Toward Good Simulation Practice' with FDA, but its site shows no regulatory acceptances.

research.q: Performance-based building codes and fire engineering: how alternative-means-of-compliance pathways work and who profits.
research.headline: Building codes already have a legal path for doing things the code doesn't prescribe (IBC 104.11, IFC 104.10, NFPA 101 Ch. 5, NCC Performance Solutions, UK Building Safety Act Gateway 2). The money goes to whoever holds a seat that grants approval: fire engineers on both the design and peer-review side, scarce furnace labs, and ICC-ES with its acceptance criteria. AI plan-review startups (Archistar, CodeComply, UpCodes) only automate the prescriptive checks. Nobody is doing AI-native performance-based peer review, evaluation-report production, cross-jurisdiction precedent tracking, or checks on whether a building still meets its approved design years later, and laws such as Florida 553.791 already let a licensed private firm hold the sign-off.

findings.finding: IBC 104.11 lets a building official approve alternatives that are at least equivalent in quality, strength, effectiveness, fire resistance, durability and safety. 104.11.1 accepts research reports from approved sources, which in practice means ICC-ES ESRs. 104.11.2 lets the official demand tests at the applicant's expense. Each approval is decided by one of roughly 20,000 US authorities and is not published as precedent.

Under IFC 104.7.2 the fire official can require a technical opinion and report at the applicant's expense. This is the legal basis for third-party peer review of performance-based fire designs, paid for by the applicant.

ICC-ES evaluates products against Acceptance Criteria that an Evaluation Committee approves in public hearings, and publishes 'thousands of reports'. Each report states conditions of use, and state supplements such as Florida's are available.

Archistar AI PreCheck automates code and zoning checks for 30-plus governments, including LA County, Austin, Cape Coral and Yonkers, and claims up to a 55% cut in permit review cycles. It checks prescriptive rules only.

CodeComply does AI checks against ICC, NFPA, ADA, FHA and local amendments, with separate products for designers, pre-check and reviewers. CivicPlus names it its official plan review tool. Customers include Marriott, Mortenson, Suffolk and Princeton.

Florida Stat. 553.791 lets an owner hire a licensed private provider to do plan review and inspections in place of the city or county, which must accept the work within statutory deadlines. Texas allows third-party review when a city misses its deadlines. This is the building-code equivalent of FAA delegated sign-off (DER/ODA).

Under the UK Building Safety Act 2022, higher-risk buildings need Building Safety Regulator approval before construction (Gateway 2), and a digital 'golden thread' of building information is mandatory. Gateway 2 decisions ran far past the 12-week target, at 40+ weeks median in 2024-25, and the regulator was restructured in 2025.

The incumbents who profit: fire engineering firms (Jensen Hughes, Arup, WSP, Holmes, Code Consultants, Olsson), labs (UL Solutions, NYSE: ULS, about $2.9B revenue in 2024; Intertek; SGS; FM Approvals; SwRI), and evaluation services (ICC-ES, IAPMO UES). A performance-based design costs about $20k-$300k, a peer review $10k-$100k, a full-scale fire test $10k-$200k+, and a new ESR takes 6-18 months.

Mass timber, and battery storage before NFPA 855 and UL 9540A, had to get approval building by building through the alternatives route. Every new technology class goes through the same bottleneck until the code catches up.

research.q: Financial audit and rating agencies (Big Four, Moody's/S&P): the economics of being a paid verifier, independence problems, and AI disruption of audit.
research.headline: In audit and ratings the margin goes to whoever holds the regulator-recognised signature (PCAOB-registered firm, NRSRO): rating agencies run about 60% margins and the Big Four hold about 99% of large-cap audits despite about 31% of inspected audits being deficient. AI has so far automated the labour (Fieldguide, DataSnipper, Vanta) without dislodging the signer. The verification-side play for the Approval Factory is therefore to own or partner with the signer (captive DER/ODA, the Thoropass pattern), or to become a government-paid independent evaluator of approval packages (the Kroll pattern), with machine-checkable evidence anyone can re-run that removes the independence conflict.

findings.finding: Big Four FY2025 revenue was $219.0bn, of which $66.5bn (~30%) is audit and assurance and $107.1bn (48.6%) is consulting. Deloitte gets only about 21% of its revenue from audit, so the signature is the door-opener for consulting.

PCAOB inspectors found about 31% of Big Four audits deficient (808 cases), but only about 6.6% of those led to enforcement, and there were just 18 cases against the Big Four in 16 years. The signature keeps its value even when quality is poor.
Big Four audited 99% of the FTSE 100 (2011) and about 95% of the FTSE 250 (2019).
Global rating share: S&P 50.0%, Moody's 31.7%, Fitch 12.5% (about 94% combined). Eight of nine NRSROs use issuer-pays; Egan-Jones is the subscriber-pays exception.

Agencies moved to issuer-pays around 1970, partly because photocopiers let investors share reports for free. In 2005 Moody's put issuer fees at about 90% of rating-agency revenue. Structured finance rose from 28% of Moody's revenue in 1998 to about 50% in 2007.

Moody's revenue was $5.9bn in 2023. It settled for about $864m in January 2017 and paid an EU fine of €3.7m for conflicts of interest in 2021. 73% of its 2006 AAA mortgage-backed securities were junk within two years.

Dodd-Frank made ratings subject to expert liability, but the agencies refused consent to be named in ABS filings, and the SEC issued a no-action letter. Verifiers in a statutorily required slot can resist accountability. (Mechanism recalled.)

Fieldguide sells agentic AI ('Field Agents') to audit firms for testing, evidence verification, review and drafting. It claims more than half of the top 100 firms as customers, 55% fewer engagement hours and 50%+ better realization. The signer stays the CPA firm.

The PCAOB amended AS 1105 and AS 2301 for technology-assisted analysis (adopted June 2024, effective for fiscal years from 15 December 2025). This is precedent for a regulator codifying machine-performed testing of whole populations. (recalled)

Compliance automation (Vanta at about a $4bn valuation in 2025, Drata, Secureframe, Delve YC, Thoropass) has software generate the evidence while a licensed CPA firm signs. Thoropass bundles its own affiliated audit firm, the closest analogue to an AI-native verifier. (valuations recalled)
Kroll Bond Rating Agency, founded in 2010, took real share in CMBS, ABS and private credit. A new designated verifier can win a niche where incumbents are slow. (recalled)

Avoid being only a tool vendor to DERs (the Fieldguide/DataSnipper position): real business, but a thin slice while the signer keeps the margin
surprises: Regulators find many audit failures (about 31% of inspected Big Four audits) but punish about 6.6%; the signature keeps its price regardless of quality
Rating agencies defeated Dodd-Frank liability by refusing consent and freezing the ABS market, so designated verifiers can face down regulators
The photocopier pushed ratings to issuer-pays; cheap copying of verification output changes who pays
Even with AI cutting engagement hours by about 55% (Fieldguide claim), audit fees have not collapsed; the firms keep the gains as margin
Cheap SOC 2 'report mills' have hurt the credential, a warning that lowering verification cost without reproducibility brings regulator backlash (NAIC is doing the same to private letter ratings)

research.q: Credit bureaus and Carfax: how a records/provenance layer captures value in a fragmented market; lessons for parts provenance.
research.headline: Carfax and the credit bureaus won by starting from public records and by having fragmented contributors hand over data for free in exchange for marketing or relief from a chore. They charge whoever verifies, per report, at the moment of a decision, and the most money goes to the score that rules name (FICO) rather than to the database. Parts are ripe for the same play, because airworthiness already consists of paperwork, the AOG Technics forgeries showed that the OEM's serial registry went unchecked at purchase, and no one yet owns a per-serial provenance score that buyers, insurers or DLA rely on.

findings.finding: Carfax was founded in 1984 and sold a fax dealer report in 1986. It claims more than 151,000 data sources and over 35B records (30B in Dec 2022). Owners: Polk (1999), IHS (2013), IHS Markit (2016), S&P Global (2022, inside a ~$44B deal). Mobility Global Inc became public on Jul 1, 2026.

The Carfax model has three parts. It seeded from state DMV title data, so no one had to join. Service shops and dealers contribute records for free marketing. Consumers pay per report (~$45, recalled) and dealers pay subscriptions so they can show reports as a sales tool.

US credit reporting started after 1837 and had more than 1,000 bureaus by the 1930s. Computerization from 1965 drove consolidation to 3. FCRA (1970) set accuracy and dispute duties, which legitimized and entrenched the bureaus. Furnishing is voluntary but rewarded through reciprocity, and furnishers include creditors, utilities, collectors and courts.

FICO owns no consumer data. It owns the score that lenders and the GSEs name in their rules: 2025 revenue ~$1.99B, operating income ~$925M (~46% margin), more than 10B scores bought by lenders in 2013. Antitrust suits (2020-23) allege inflated prices, which points to pricing power from being named in regulation.

Equifax (2024 revenue $5.68B) runs The Work Number. Employers and payroll firms contribute payroll data because it removes their verification chore, and lenders pay per check. Workforce Solutions is ~40% of revenue at ~50% margins (recalled). A May 2024 class action alleges an income-verification monopoly. This is the closest template for parts provenance.

AOG Technics (London, 2023) forged EASA Form 1 release certificates for CFM56 parts that ended up on more than 100 engines across TAP, Southwest, United, Delta and Virgin Australia, and the UK SFO prosecuted. The fraud was found because records were cross-checked against OEM serial and certificate data that nobody queried at purchase. It is the parts equivalent of odometer rollback.

Many parts-provenance attempts exist: SkyThread blockchain, Aerotrax, Moog VeriPart, GE blockchain pilots, Honeywell GoDirect Trade, ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16 e-certificates. None has become the standard lookup. They resemble TradeLens (IBM/Maersk, shut 2023): the technology worked but contributors had no reason to join.
findings.source: https://www.skythread.aero/ (fetched; no customers or funding listed); others recalled

findings.finding: Defense counterfeit-parts infrastructure (NDAA FY2012 Sec. 818, DFARS 252.246-7007/7008, GIDEP, ERAI, DLA DNA marking of FSC 5962 microcircuits) is reactive and runs on voluntary reports. No body assigns a proactive per-serial trust score.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build a per-serial life graph. Ingest and OCR every obtainable 8130-3, Form 1, teardown report, broker listing, FAA SDR, AD, PMA database entry, DLA FLIS/DIBBS award history and GIDEP alert, then resolve P/N + S/N across them to reconstruct back-to-birth chains automatically.
Detect forgery in release certificates: check signatories, repair-station certificate numbers, form versions and dates against FAA/EASA registries, and look for PDF or image tampering.

Sign API or data-sharing deals with OEM serial registries (CFM, GE, P&W, Honeywell) so the AOG Technics failure (registry never queried) cannot recur. This is the data-access constraint, and AOG-type liability fear is the lever for getting the deals.
Become the validation lookup for ATA Spec 2000 Ch.16 electronic certificates as FAA and EASA move to e-8130-3 / e-Form 1, the parts equivalent of NMVTIS.
Copy the Work Number model: take over the records-reconciliation chore for brokers, MROs and lessors so they contribute trace packages for free, then charge buyers, insurers and lessors per pull.
Get the provenance score written into procedures: AS9120 distributor QMS, airline receiving inspection, aviation insurers' underwriting, DLA/DCMA source approval, and the FAA SUP program.
Adopt FCRA-like disciplines voluntarily (accuracy duty, dispute process, E&O cover) so relying on the score is defensible for whoever uses it.
Build a proactive GIDEP-plus for defense that scans DIBBS awardees and broker inventory for counterfeit risk instead of waiting for voluntary reports.
ai_plays: A parts credit bureau: an AI-built back-to-birth reconstruction plus a provenance confidence score per serial, sold per check at purchase, receiving inspection, lease return or install.

A thin-file credit history for new sources: give every reverse-engineered part from the Approval Factory full digital provenance and field-failure tracking, so the accumulated service record lowers regulator and insurer resistance to the next DLA SAR or PMA.

A single evidence engine with two outputs: the conformity and equivalence package for a new approval, and the provenance score for an existing part. Both are built from the same serial-level evidence (material certs, CT/CMM scans, test data, field history).
OEM field reliability data mined from SDRs and operator removal records, used as similarity and equivalence evidence in PMA test-and-computation and DLA SAR submissions.
An e-certificate validation and forgery-detection API: the low-cost entry wedge that later becomes the regulator-recognized lookup.
surprises: The score layer (FICO, ~46% operating margin) earns more than the data holders, so the prize is the number that procedures name, not the database.

Most aviation blockchain provenance efforts stalled because contributors had no reason to join, not because of the technology. Carfax succeeded with no cryptography, only public-record seeding and give-to-get.
In AOG Technics the authoritative data already existed at the OEM. The gap was that no lookup happened at the moment of purchase.
Law (FCRA, NMVTIS) came after market adoption and then locked in the incumbents. Regulation is the moat once the product is the de facto standard, not the way to start.

research.q: Hatch-Waxman deep dive on the verification side: the bioequivalence standard, CROs that run BE studies, first-filer exclusivity, and who earned most (CROs, first filers, payers).
research.headline: This agent got no web searches (shared quota exhausted, FDA.gov returned 401), so only three Wikipedia pages were checked; every other figure is from memory, marked (recalled), and must be verified. Hatch-Waxman shows that once a regulator accepts a cheap, standard proof that a copy is the same (bioequivalence: the 90% CI of AUC and Cmax within 80–125%), most of the value goes to payers and to holders of scarce first-filer slots, while the labs that run the tests (BE CROs) end up a small, fraud-prone commodity; so the Approval Factory should hold the approvals and change what counts as proof, not sell testing.

findings.finding: Generics went from 13% of US prescriptions in 1983 to 84% in 2012 after Hatch-Waxman replaced re-proving safety and efficacy with an ANDA plus a bioequivalence study.

The bioequivalence standard: the 90% confidence interval of the test/reference ratio for Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-inf must sit within 80-125%, usually in a crossover study of healthy volunteers; fed studies are generally required too. Highly variable drugs get wider limits (WHO/EMA allow Cmax 69.84-143.19%); narrow-therapeutic-index drugs get tighter limits.

Approval of a copy hinges on one simple statistical number, and FDA publishes about 2,000+ Product-Specific Guidances setting out the accepted evidence per drug. Aviation PMA and DLA source approval have neither; every package is negotiated case by case.

BCS Class I/III biowaivers (ICH M9, 2019) let a lab dissolution test replace a human BE study. This is the precedent for a regulator accepting a bench test or model in place of a physical in-body test.
A simple oral BE study costs about $0.3-1.5M and takes 3-6 months; clinical-endpoint BE (topicals, inhalers) costs $5-30M+. The ANDA user fee is about $0.32M (FY25).
findings.source: recalled industry figures; GDUFA fee notice (recalled)

findings.finding: BE CROs are a commodity: Lambda, Veeda, Raptim, Synchron, Semler and MTRL in India; Celerion, BioPharma Services, Pharma Medica, Altasciences and Frontage in North America. Even the largest specialists earn about $50-150M a year.

Fake test data is the chronic failure of this system, and it is found late: Cetero Research (2011, bankrupt 2012), Semler (2016, substituted samples), MTRL (EMA suspensions, 2017), Synchron and Panexcell (2021-22), Ranbaxy ($500M fine).
The first filer with a Paragraph IV certification gets 180 days of exclusivity, shared by same-day filers since 2003. MMA 2003 added forfeiture rules to stop first filers parking on it.

The 180-day window is worth hundreds of millions per blockbuster: Barr on Prozac (2001) about $360M+; Ranbaxy on Lipitor (2011) about $600M. Prices fall more than 95% once 6+ generics enter. A brand's own authorized generic cuts first-filer revenue by 40-52%.
findings.source: recalled; FTC 2011 Authorized Generics report; FDA 2019 generic price competition analysis (recalled)

findings.finding: First-filer exclusivity made pay-for-delay settlements valuable. The FTC estimated they cost consumers about $3.5B a year. FTC v. Actavis (June 17, 2013, 5-3) put these deals under antitrust (rule-of-reason) review.

The Competitive Generic Therapy pathway (FDARA 2017) gives 180-day exclusivity to the first approved generic of a drug with inadequate competition, with no patent challenge needed. Congress created a first-mover monopoly to draw copiers into orphaned markets. Aviation and DLA spares have no equivalent.

Who earned most: payers, PBMs and patients by far (about $408-445B a year in generic savings, roughly $3T over a decade). Then first filers on blockbusters, then patent litigators, then brands that settled. BE CROs earned least.

pathway_steps.step: Target selection: Orange Book patents/exclusivities and the Product-Specific Guidance
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Knowledge only, already cheap. The aviation analogue (which parts are orphaned or sole-source) has no public Orange Book or guidance.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Stability testing is a physics clock (6 months accelerated, 12+ months real time).

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Commodity and fraud-prone (Cetero, Semler, Synchron); fraud is found after the fact by inspection or tips.

pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Solved. The point is that aviation has no equivalent single acceptance number.

what_would_need_to_be_done: Write 'Product-Specific Guidance' equivalents for aviation and defence part families (bushings, seals, brackets, castings): pre-agreed per-family evidence recipes, adopted through FAA advisory circulars, DLA engineering support activities or SAE/ASTM.

Define a 'BE number' for parts: a statistical equivalence acceptance criterion (like the 90% CI within 80-125%) on measured properties, with variability-scaled limits (like RSABE for highly variable drugs) and sample sizes set by scatter.
Create a biowaiver analogue: class-based waivers that let low-criticality part classes qualify by bench test plus model, with no full physical test series.

Generate the calibration datasets (run many physical tests once) that would get model-integrated evidence (physics plus ML surrogates) accepted in place of some tests, as PBPK virtual BE was in pharma.

Build continuous data-integrity verification: cryptographically signed test-rig data and statistical forensics at submission, catching Semler-style sample swaps or AOG Technics-style forged certificates before approval rather than after.
Lobby for a CGT-style exclusivity in the NDAA or DLA acquisition policy: a protected window for the first approved source on an orphaned or sole-source spare.

Train an AI on deficiency letters (FDA complete response letters, DLA source-approval rejections) that predicts reviewer objections and guarantees a first-cycle-complete package, possibly as an accepted third-party review like FAA ODA delegation.
Fund regulatory science for parts (FAA and DoD have nothing like GDUFA research money) so regulators can validate new evidence methods quickly.
ai_plays: Be the applicant that holds the approvals, not the CRO: AI cuts cost per package so the company files on far more orphaned parts than incumbents and keeps the permission. Hatch-Waxman shows the money sits with the slot holder.
Model-integrated evidence for parts (the Certara analogue): physics plus ML surrogates accepted in place of some physical qualification tests; the moat is regulator acceptance of the method.
Data-integrity and provenance verification layer that regulators and primes rely on, working across pharma BE, aerospace PMA and DLA source approval; currently unowned.
Write the accepted evidence recipes and equivalence statistics for part families: whoever authors the accepted method gets a structural cost lead.
Deficiency-prediction pre-review sold per package, aimed at first-cycle approval.
Policy play: pair the factory with a lobbying push for CGT-style first-source exclusivity on orphaned DoD spares.
surprises: The verification providers (BE CROs) captured the least value of anyone in Hatch-Waxman; a pure 'AI DER/CRO service' risks the same fate.
Competitive Generic Therapy (2017) is a direct legislative template for paying copiers to enter orphaned markets; nothing similar exists for spare parts.
Data fraud at test labs, not test difficulty, has been the recurring verification failure (Cetero, Semler, MTRL, Synchron, Ranbaxy), and regulators detect it mostly after approval.
Even a fixed, well-defined test can miss real differences: FDA reversed its own equivalence finding for Budeprion XL 300 in 2012.
Most of a generic's lifetime profit can come from 180 days; after that, prices fall more than 95% with 6+ entrants, which later fed into generic-drug shortages.

research.q: Open-source hardware and standards bodies (SAE, ASTM, IEC) as verification authorities: how a standard becomes mandatory and who earns from it.
research.headline: Standards bodies (SAE, ASTM, IEC) only write documents. A standard becomes binding when someone with authority points at it: a regulation that incorporates it by reference, an FAA-accepted means of compliance, an EU harmonised-standard citation, a prime contractor's purchase order, or an insurer's requirement. The money goes to the pointer-holders and to conformity assessors such as UL Solutions ($2.68B revenue in 2023), not to the standards bodies. The verification-side AI play with the most room is an approach regulators already accept for composites (NCAMP's pooled qualification data, accepted by the FAA and EASA, with claimed 10x lower cost and 4x faster certification), applied to reverse-engineered legacy metal parts, sold through an accredited AI-native lab that also writes the consensus standard it will be judged by.

findings.finding: NCAMP qualifies material systems and publishes the data in a shared database. Aircraft makers show their use is equivalent instead of requalifying. The FAA (memo AIR100-2010-120-003) and EASA (CM-S-004) accept the values. NCAMP claims 4x faster and 10x cheaper certification under AGATE. It lists about 22 qualified systems, including AM materials.

Nadcap is an industry-run accreditation for special processes, founded in 1990 and run by PRI, an SAE affiliate. It covers 24 critical processes, has 4,500+ accredited suppliers and 60+ subscribing OEMs, and is governed by subscriber votes. It becomes mandatory through contract flowdown, not regulation.

UL Solutions had 2023 revenue of $2.68B and net income of $276M. It went public in April 2024 at about $7B and is still controlled by UL's nonprofit parent. It is an OSHA-recognized NRTL. Conformity assessment, not standards writing, is where the money is.

ASTM v. Public.Resource.Org: in 2022 the district court allowed free reproduction of 184 incorporated standards as fair use, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed in 2023. Georgia v. PRO (2020) held annotated law cannot be copyrighted. The paywalls on mandatory standards are eroding.

The NTTAA (PL 104-113, signed Mar 7 1996) requires federal agencies to use voluntary consensus standards. OMB A-119 (revised 2016, recalled) puts this into practice. DoD adopts non-government standards such as SAE AMS through ASSIST (recalled).

The Part 23 rewrite (Amendment 64, effective Aug 30 2017) made rules performance-based and let industry-written ASTM F44 standards serve as FAA-accepted means of compliance. This is the precedent for a company writing the method it will be judged by.
findings.source: (recalled) Federal Register 2017-12350; the fetch was blocked

findings.finding: EU: harmonised standards cited in the OJEU give a presumption of conformity. CJEU C-588/21 P (Mar 2024) held they must be freely accessible. The Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 (applies Jan 2027) and the Cyber Resilience Act (Dec 2027) create new mandatory conformity assessment.

Any AI tool that produces certification evidence must be qualified under DO-330 or have its outputs independently verified. SAE G-34 / EUROCAE WG-114 (AS6983) and the FAA's 2024 AI Safety Assurance Roadmap are setting the rules for ML.

Open-source hardware bodies certify openness, not safety. OSHWA certification covers licensing and documentation, and DIN SPEC 3105 covers documentation peer review. No open-hardware body is a safety verification authority. The working form of 'open verification' is pooled regulator-accepted data (NCAMP, MMPDS, CMH-17).

Nominal sells a hardware test-data platform to Anduril, Regent, Hermeus and Scout AI. It reports cutting Anduril's test-review time from 5+ hours to near real time. It is infrastructure, not an approval authority.

pathway_steps.step: A. Pull the governing spec tree off the drawing (AMS/MIL/AS/process specs)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Specs are PDF prose that machines cannot read. Mapping superseded MIL specs to AMS is done by hand

pathway_steps.step: B. Show material equivalence against the AMS spec and MMPDS/CMH-17 allowables
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No pooled equivalence database for legacy metals. Every applicant reruns coupons. There is no NCAMP for metals in reverse engineering

pathway_steps.step: C. Show process equivalence (heat treat, NDT, plating)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Evidence is periodic and checklist-based. Continuous process data is not accepted

pathway_steps.step: D. Show dimensional and functional equivalence (Y14.5, test plan)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No consensus standard for statistical reverse-engineering equivalence. Each test plan is written from scratch

pathway_steps.step: E. Software / tool evidence (DO-178C, DO-254, DO-330)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: No qualified AI tool for generating evidence

pathway_steps.step: F. Compliance finding and sign-off (14 CFR 21.303 PMA, DLA SAR)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Reviewer capacity is scarce and packages are unstructured. Reviewers have no pre-check tooling

pathway_steps.step: G. Surveillance (AS9100, Nadcap, MIDO)
pathway_steps.undone_or_broken: Surveillance is sampled and periodic, not continuous

what_would_need_to_be_done: Build an 'NCAMP for reverse engineering': a pooled equivalence and allowables database for legacy alloys, forgings and processes on C-130, KC-135 and B-52 parts. Win an FAA memo plus DLA and Air Force engineering-authority acceptance so applicants cite pooled data instead of rerunning coupons. Coupons are still tested, but once for the whole industry.

Write a consensus standard (ASTM E08/F42 or SAE AMS/AS) for statistical equivalence of reverse-engineered parts from digital inspection, then get it accepted as an FAA means of compliance and as DLA SAR guidance, following the Part 23 / ASTM F44 precedent.

Compile AMS, MIL, Nadcap AC7xxx and ASTM documents into machine-readable requirement graphs (requirement, test, acceptance criterion), which would make test plans and compliance reports executable. Free-access rulings on mandatory standards reduce the licensing barrier.
Qualify an AI checker under DO-330, starting at a low tool-qualification level, and work through SAE G-34 / AS6983 so AI-generated evidence becomes admissible.
Replace annual Nadcap audits with continuous streamed process evidence (pyrometry, NDT, CMM), which needs a Nadcap Management Council vote.
Become an accredited conformity-assessment body: ISO/IEC 17025 lab, then 17065 certifier, then DER/ODA staff, with Notified Body status for the EU Machinery Regulation and CRA in adjacent sectors.
Arrange insurance priced on the AI verification track record, making insurers another gatekeeper that rewards the method.
ai_plays: An AI-native 17025-accredited lab plus the pooled equivalence database for legacy military parts: a UL/Element-scale business built for the reverse-engineering era, earning per approval and from data subscriptions
A standards-to-test-plan compiler: drawing and spec tree in, a DER/DLA-ready test plan and draft compliance report out
A reviewer-side pre-check copilot sold to FAA ACOs, DLA ESAs and Nadcap auditors to cut reviewer hours per approval
Authoring the consensus standard for AI-assisted equivalence, so the company's method becomes the accepted means of compliance
Continuous-evidence certification of special processes to replace periodic Nadcap audits
surprises: Regulators already accept pooled, non-applicant-specific qualification data (NCAMP, through FAA and EASA memos). Nobody has applied this to reverse engineering of legacy metal parts.

Binding power sits with the pointer (CFR incorporation by reference, an FAA Notice of Availability, an OJEU citation, a prime's PO), not with the standards body. Standards-body revenue is small and its paywalls are legally eroding.
Consensus rules require balanced committees, so a startup can win a seat and write the means of compliance it will be judged by.
Open-source hardware has no safety-verification authority. Pooled evidence works where shared designs do not.
A verification authority can be venture-scale: UL is about $7B and public, and Element sold for about $7B (recalled).

**Threat key.** **Direct** means it competes for the same outcome: approved sources, approvals or signed packages for replacement parts. **Adjacent** means it owns a neighbouring layer and could move into ours, or would be a partner, supplier or acquirer. **None** means it is relevant context but no threat.
