NUPIC and utility QA must accept tool-generated evaluations, and NRC inspection is the backstop. WHAT IT OWNS: the dedication signature and Part 21 obligation, a cross-utility library of critical characteristics and equivalency evaluations across about 90+ US units and new SMR fleets (no manual dedicator reuses these), and scarce EQ and seismic throughput. WHO PAYS: utilities (Constellation, Duke, Southern, TVA, Vistra, Dominion) per item and through outage retainers, priced against outage days at about $1-2M each; restarts (Palisades, Duane Arnold, Crane); SMR and advanced-reactor developers (TerraPower, X-energy, Kairos, NuScale); DOE and naval-reactor suppliers; later hydro, gas-plant and grid users. WEDGE: acquire or partner with a small NUPIC-accepted dedicator and take one restart or life-extension utility's obsolescence backlog of mild-environment, non-EQ Class 1E commodity items (relays, breakers, transmitters, fasteners, valve internals). Target cycle time under 2 weeks, 10x fewer engineering hours, zero vendor-inspection findings, then a guarantee to dedicate emergent outage parts within 72 hours. MARKET: Westinghouse dedicates about 50k parts/yr and Mirion paid about $585M for manual Paragon. US nuclear O&M supply spend is $5-8B/yr, the dedication, reverse-engineering and obsolescence share is $1.5-2.5B, and 80-year licences, restarts and the SMR build-out are adding to it. Korea and CANDU fleets follow. COMPETITORS: Paragon (Mirion), Curtiss-Wright, Westinghouse, Framatome, UCI, Park Nuclear and utility central labs (all manual); Everstar/Gordian (claims qualification 'at scale' with no published evidence, the startup to watch); Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, 70+ facilities, procurement and 50.59 but no CGD, likely fast follower or partner); MIRAE-EN REDiX (Korean academic pilot); Wyle/NTS and Element EQ labs (capacity-limited).
finalist.why: It is the one regime where the permission sits with a private dedicator, not a regulator queue, so the AI-collapsible labour is the bottleneck and no rule needs to change. Outage-day economics let it charge for speed in a way DLA cannot match. Demand tailwinds are strong (AI data-centre PPAs, 80-year licences, restarts, SMR build-out). It fits the founder's energy focus best. The only AI-native claimant (Everstar) has published nothing. It holds verification and signature in one entity, the margin-capturing position in every analogue.

competitors_found.name: Paragon Energy Solutions (Mirion, about $585M acquisition)
competitors_found.overlap: The largest independent US dedicator. It does CGD, reverse engineering, obsolescence work, EQ and seismic. It is manual and labour-heavy and holds NUPIC-audited Appendix B status. It is the direct incumbent and also the natural acquirer or blocker. I could not see any public AI product (my fetch of its page returned 403).

competitors_found.name: Curtiss-Wright Nuclear (including Scientech, and NLI-style dedication lines)
competitors_found.overlap: Dedication, replacement parts, an EQ test lab and obsolescence engineering in a single house. It owns test capacity and holds Part 21 obligations. Its process is manual.

competitors_found.name: Westinghouse / Framatome OEM parts groups
competitors_found.overlap: Dedicate tens of thousands of parts a year for their own fleets and hold OEM design data. They are the strongest position on data rights. They are adding additive-manufacturing replacement-part qualification, but have no AI-native dedication offer.

competitors_found.name: UCI (United Controls International), Park Nuclear, AZZ/NLI, Zachry, ENERCON, Sargent & Lundy
competitors_found.overlap: Mid-size and small NUPIC-accepted dedicators and engineering firms that do technical evaluations, equivalency and reverse engineering. These are the acquisition targets for the wedge. All manual.

competitors_found.name: Everstar (Gordian: Charter, Axiom, Anvil, Manifest)
competitors_found.overlap: Its site has a 'Qualification' phase (materials, parts, suppliers), Anvil (NQA-1 autonomous manufacturing) and Manifest (supply chain). It names DOE, INL, Argonne, NuScale, Southern and Evergy as partners. Its main evidence is a case study of 1 day instead of 200 person-days. The site does not mention commercial-grade dedication or EQ. It is the most likely startup to move into this space, but it sells software and holds no dedication signature.

competitors_found.name: Nuclearn
competitors_found.overlap: Sells Parts AI, Engineering AI and Equipment AI to 70+ facilities in North America and the UK. It is already inside utility procurement and engineering workflows. Its site makes no CGD or tech-eval claim, but Parts AI is the obvious step toward drafting technical evaluations as a tool sold to utilities. It is a fast follower or a partner, not a dedicator.

competitors_found.name: Atomic Canyon (Neutron)
competitors_found.overlap: AI search and retrieval over plant licensing and engineering documents (Diablo Canyon, ORNL). This is the FSAR and design-basis retrieval layer the tech-eval engine needs. It is a tool, not an entity that signs.

competitors_found.name: EPRI (NP-5652, 3002002982, Plant Engineering and JUTG programs)
competitors_found.overlap: Owns the methodology and the guidance documents that utilities accept. Utility-funded work on digital tools and standards for this space could commoditise a cross-utility library or set the format for it. A partner or standards channel.

competitors_found.name: Utility central labs and supply-chain groups (e.g. TVA, Duke, Southern, Constellation)
competitors_found.overlap: Dedicate internally under their own Appendix B programs. They compete for the same work and are also the customers.

competitors_found.name: EQ and seismic labs: Wyle/NTS, Element, Kinectrics, Curtiss-Wright EQ, National Technical Systems
competitors_found.overlap: Own the scarce LOCA, radiation-ageing and shake-table capacity. That capacity is booked months ahead and is the physical bottleneck the robotic EQ step targets.

competitors_found.name: MIRAE-EN REDiX and KHNP/KAERI academic pilots
competitors_found.overlap: Korean research into AI-assisted dedication and reverse engineering. It shows the idea is being looked at, but it is not commercial in the US.

killers.killer: Utility QA and NUPIC refuse to accept machine-generated technical evaluations, or require full human re-derivation, which wipes out the 10x hours saving
killers.answer: Position the engine as drafting plus a deterministic traceability checker. A qualified engineer signs, which Appendix B already allows. Get pre-acceptance by inviting a NUPIC joint audit and one utility's QA to audit the tool's software QA (NQA-1 Subpart 2.7) before scale. Publish a validation set: blind re-dedication of past items with discrepancy rates. The change needed is cultural and evidential, not legal.

killers.killer: Paragon, Curtiss-Wright or Westinghouse buy or build the same tooling and use their existing NUPIC status and relationships to block a newcomer
killers.answer: Incumbents' margins come from billable engineering hours, so a 10x hours cut cannibalises them. Win on guaranteed cycle time (72 hours for emergent outage parts) priced against outage days, a deal they are structurally slow to offer. Buying a small dedicator gets the permission straight away.

killers.killer: NRC vendor-inspection finding or Part 21 event on an AI-assisted dedication early on
killers.answer: Start with mild-environment, non-EQ commodity items where failure consequences are bounded. Use conservative critical-characteristic selection and a NEIL/ANI liability tower. One finding early on could be fatal to reputation, so zero findings is the gating KPI.

killers.killer: Design-basis and EQ file access: FSARs are partly public, but design-basis documents, EQ binders and vendor data sit in utility systems and under OEM proprietary rights
killers.answer: Utilities hand over their own design-basis data under contract for the specific items. A cross-utility library has to be built from the dedicator's own evaluations, with derived critical characteristics rather than copied OEM data. Contract terms must grant the right to reuse.

killers.killer: Physics clocks: EQ thermal and radiation ageing and LOCA tests take weeks to months and cannot be compressed by software
killers.answer: The wedge avoids EQ items completely. Later, owned parallel capacity plus qualification by similarity (IEEE 323/344 permit analysis and similarity) cuts how many tests are needed. Early stopping from condition monitoring would need IEEE and NRC endorsement (via RG 1.89 updates), a multi-year standards effort.

killers.killer: Market size: dedication and obsolescence share may be closer to $1-2B, fragmented across about 94 units; SMR demand slips
killers.answer: Restarts, 80-year licence renewals and the DOE/naval market add volume. Expansion goes to the international CANDU and Korean fleets, then to the adjacent non-nuclear safety-critical market (hydro, grid, defense) using the same engine.

attacks.surviving_version: Nobody I could find holds the dedication signature and is AI-native. The incumbents (Paragon/Mirion, Curtiss-Wright, Westinghouse, Framatome, UCI, Park, NLI) all work manually. The AI startups (Nuclearn Parts AI and Engineering AI, Everstar Gordian, Atomic Canyon) sell tools to utilities and do not sign or carry Part 21. The surviving version is an entity, not software. Buy a small NUPIC-accepted dedicator to get the Appendix B program and audit status on day 1. Run one restart or life-extension utility's obsolescence backlog of mild-environment, non-EQ commodity items through an AI tech-eval and equivalency engine, with a deterministic traceability checker built under NQA-1 software QA. Then sell a 72-hour emergent-outage dedication guarantee priced against outage days. On the verification side, the AI play has three parts. (1) A traceability checker that QA and NRC inspectors can audit: the thing that turns 'AI drafted it' into 'reviewers can check it in minutes', so reviewer hours per item are the real KPI. (2) A cross-utility library of critical characteristics and equivalency evaluations that compounds with each item, because nobody pools these today. (3) A robotic acceptance cell that signs evidence at capture, so Method 1 testing and remote source verification stop needing travel. Owned EQ and seismic capacity and the similarity libraries come after the wedge works. Optionally, Nuclearn or Atomic Canyon could be partners for document retrieval rather than built in-house. Note: the web search budget ran out before my searches ran. This rests on direct fetches of the Everstar and Nuclearn sites plus prior knowledge, so Everstar's qualification roadmap and any recent EPRI digital-CGD effort should be checked in a follow-up search.
attacks.first_test: Sign a letter of intent with one small NUPIC-accepted dedicator, such as a UCI- or Park-scale firm. Get 50 closed, already-dedicated commodity items from a utility's obsolescence backlog. Generate technical evaluations, critical characteristics and acceptance plans blind with the engine. Have the dedicator's qualified engineers and one utility QA auditor score them against the signed originals, measuring discrepancies, missed critical characteristics and reviewer minutes per item. Pass means 80% or more accepted with only minor edits, zero missed safety-significant characteristics, and reviewer time under 20% of the original engineering hours. Ask the auditor directly whether they would accept the tool under NQA-1 software QA.

competitors_found.name: Paragon Energy Solutions (Mirion)
competitors_found.overlap: The largest independent NUPIC-audited dedicator and reverse-engineering house, with EQ and seismic capability. Its work is manual. It is the main acquirer and price-setter, and it could adopt AI tooling itself.

competitors_found.name: Everstar / Gordian
competitors_found.overlap: The site describes Gordian as an 'AI backbone for nuclear work' and lists a qualification phase in which materials, parts and suppliers are 'cleared at scale'. It never mentions CGD, NUPIC or Appendix B, and names no customers. It is a direct software threat but has not shown that it holds a signature.

competitors_found.name: Nuclearn
competitors_found.overlap: Sells Parts AI, Engineering AI and Equipment AI to more than 70 facilities. It already sits inside utility procurement and engineering workflows, so it is the most likely fast follower, or a channel that captures the software layer while utilities keep the signature in-house.

competitors_found.name: Curtiss-Wright Nuclear, Westinghouse, Framatome
competitors_found.overlap: OEM and large-vendor dedication programs. Westinghouse dedicates about 50k parts a year. They own the OEM design data and the EQ reports.

competitors_found.name: UCI, Park Nuclear and other small dedicators; utility central labs (e.g. Duke, TVA)
competitors_found.overlap: Manual CGD. These are the acquisition targets. In-house labs are the real substitute for buying from an outside dedicator.

competitors_found.name: Wyle/NTS, Element, Kinectrics
competitors_found.overlap: EQ, LOCA, radiation and seismic test capacity. They are capacity-limited, which is why owned throughput could become a moat.

competitors_found.name: MIRAE-EN REDiX (Korea)
competitors_found.overlap: An academic pilot of digitalized dedication. It shows the idea is being explored but is not commercial.

killers.killer: Liability and Part 21 make the AI-built evaluation socially unacceptable. Utility QA and the NUPIC auditors who sign off are rewarded for zero findings, not for speed. One miss on a critical characteristic means a Part 21 report, an NRC vendor-inspection Notice of Nonconformance, and possibly loss of NUPIC acceptance, which ends the business.
killers.answer: Partly. The machine should never be the claimant. Its job is to produce a deterministic, auditable trace from each critical characteristic back to a safety function, a failure mode and a design-basis citation, and a qualified human signs it. Run shadow dedications in parallel with a manual dedicator at zero findings for 12-18 months. Then invite NUPIC and an NRC vendor inspection early, because a clean inspection is the acceptance event. Buy an existing acceptance rather than building one. Adoption pace is set by the auditors, not by technology.

killers.killer: Access to design-basis data. The technical evaluation needs the FSAR, design-basis documents, EQ files and OEM drawings. Utilities hold these and are protective of them, OEMs hold the proprietary data, and some of it is export-controlled under Part 810. A cross-utility library also collides with each utility's ownership of its own evaluations.
killers.answer: Yes, but it is contractual work, not technical. Deploy per utility inside its own environment (on-prem or FedRAMP-style) so the data never pools. The cross-utility library would hold only de-identified characteristic-to-item mappings and test methods, which are the dedicator's own work product. Commodity items (relays, fasteners, breakers) need little proprietary data. The cross-utility moat is weaker than the pitch claims until contracts explicitly grant the right to reuse work product.

killers.killer: Unit economics and TAM. Per-item dedication fees are small, and much of the cost sits in testing, source verification and paperwork that AI does not remove. The $1.5-2.5B figure blends parts resale with services. Pure dedication engineering is probably a few hundred million dollars, spread across about 94 reactors whose operators already have in-house programs.
killers.answer: Price against outage-day risk, through retainers and a 72-hour emergent-part guarantee, rather than per evaluation. Capture the margin on the dedicated part itself: buy the commercial item, dedicate it, and resell it at nuclear-grade markups of 3-10x. Pre-dedicated shelf stock turns this into a distribution business. EQ throughput and SMR supply chains extend the TAM. Venture scale probably needs parts margin and EQ capacity, not software fees alone.

killers.killer: Physics clocks. EQ (IEEE 323/344, thermal and radiation ageing, LOCA) and seismic testing take months, so AI cannot cut harsh-environment items to days.
killers.answer: The wedge deliberately avoids EQ, and mild-environment commodity items are physics-light. For EQ, use similarity and analysis under IEEE 323 and 344 with a qualified analogue to avoid re-testing. Use parallel owned ovens, Co-60 cells and shake tables to remove queue time, which is the real delay, rather than test time. Use condition monitoring (indenter modulus, OIT) to support early stopping. Whether reviewers accept early-stop ageing is uncertain, but similarity arguments are already standard practice.

killers.killer: Incumbent response and the sales cycle. Utility supply chains run 12-24-month vendor qualifications, and Paragon (Mirion), Curtiss-Wright and Westinghouse can bolt AI tooling onto their existing programs, signatures and OEM data. Nuclearn already has 70 or more sites and could ship a CGD module that utilities run in-house, removing the need for an outside dedicator.
killers.answer: Partly. Speed and the 72-hour guarantee are what differentiate, and incumbents resist them because of headcount-based billing. Restarts (Palisades, Duane Arnold, Crane) and SMR builders have acute, greenfield needs and shorter decision paths. Acquiring a NUPIC-accepted dedicator brings existing approved-supplier-list status and skips qualification. Still, an incumbent or Nuclearn copy is a real risk to the software margin. The defensible pieces are the signature, the inventory and EQ capacity.

killers.killer: Regulator posture. NRC does not approve dedication plans, but its vendor inspections and RIS/IN guidance on CGD (e.g. 10 CFR 21.3 definitions, EPRI 3002002982 endorsement) could treat AI-generated evaluations skeptically, and a single public finding would be lethal reputationally.
killers.answer: Yes. No rule change is needed. Engage NRC's vendor inspection branch proactively, publish the methodology, and keep the human engineer as the documented technical-evaluation author. The current NRC posture toward digital tools under the ADVANCE Act and the recent executive orders is permissive.

killers.killer: Starting the Appendix B and NUPIC program from scratch is slow, so a YC-stage team cannot ship within 24 months.
killers.answer: Acquire a small dedicator or lab (UCI-scale, low tens of millions of dollars, or an earn-out partner). Until then, run as an engineering-services subcontractor under someone else's Appendix B program, which is a legitimate structure.

attacks.surviving_version: This survives as a full-stack parts company, not as a pure AI dedication service. Acquire or partner with a NUPIC-accepted dedicator and sell dedicated parts, not evaluations: buy commercial items, dedicate them with a machine-drafted, human-signed technical evaluation, and resell at nuclear-grade margin. Hold pre-dedicated stock on outage calendars and sell a 72-hour emergent-part guarantee as a retainer. Start with mild-environment Class 1E commodity items for restarts and SMR builders, where obsolescence backlogs are acute and decisions are fast. The AI value is the auditable traceability engine (safety function to failure mode to critical characteristic to acceptance method to evidence) together with the robotic acceptance cell. The KPI is engineering hours and calendar days per dedicated item, at zero inspection findings. Owned EQ and seismic capacity (parallel ageing, Co-60, LOCA, shake tables) is phase 2 and the real long-term moat, because test throughput is what is scarce. Expand next into DOE, naval and SMR supply chains, then hydro and gas plants. The cross-utility library is real only if contracts grant reuse rights to the work product.
attacks.first_test: Within 60 days, get one restart or life-extension utility (Palisades/Holtec, or Duane Arnold/NextEra) to hand over 25-50 closed, already-dedicated commodity items from its obsolescence backlog. Generate the technical evaluations, critical characteristics and acceptance plans with the engine, blind. Have the utility's own CGD engineers and a retired NUPIC lead auditor grade them against the signed originals for missed critical characteristics, traceability defects and hours saved. The pass bar is zero missed safety-relevant characteristics, at least 5x fewer engineer hours, and a written statement from the utility that it would buy from an Appendix B dedicator using this method. In parallel, get an LOI or price from one small NUPIC-accepted dedicator for acquisition or a subcontract.

competitors_found.name: Everstar (Gordian AI backbone + Titan manufacturing)
competitors_found.overlap: Its site lists a 'Qualification' phase described as 'clearing materials, parts, and suppliers at scale'. It does not mention commercial-grade dedication (CGD), names no customers and shows no evidence of signed dedications. It is the closest software threat, but it is not a dedicating entity carrying Part 21 obligations. It could become a partner, an acquirer or a fast follower.

competitors_found.name: Nuclearn
competitors_found.overlap: Sells Parts AI, Engineering AI, CM Predictor and AtomAssist to 70+ facilities. Its site shows no CGD, technical-evaluation or Part 21 role. It already sits inside utility procurement and engineering workflows, so it is the natural way in or a feature competitor. It holds no signature.

competitors_found.name: Paragon Energy Solutions (Mirion)
competitors_found.overlap: A manual dedicator and reverse-engineering house (roughly $585M acquisition). It is the incumbent and the obvious buyer. It holds the NUPIC standing and the obsolescence relationships.

competitors_found.name: Westinghouse / Framatome / Curtiss-Wright (NQA-1 dedication and EQ labs)
competitors_found.overlap: OEM-level dedication of about 50k parts/yr at Westinghouse. They own EQ files and design-basis data, and they could add AI internally.

competitors_found.name: UCI, Park Nuclear, NLI and other small dedicators
competitors_found.overlap: Manual Appendix B dedicators. These are acquisition targets for getting NUPIC acceptance on day one.

competitors_found.name: Wyle/NTS, Element, Kinectrics (EQ/seismic labs)
competitors_found.overlap: Thermal ageing, radiation ageing, LOCA and shake-table capacity. This is the scarce throughput Dedicate plans to own later. Lead times are months.

competitors_found.name: Utility central labs and procurement engineering (e.g., Constellation PowerLabs, TVA, Duke)
competitors_found.overlap: In-house dedication. They are both the customer and the 'build it ourselves' substitute.

competitors_found.name: MIRAE-EN REDiX (Korea)
competitors_found.overlap: An academic/industry pilot for AI-assisted reverse engineering and dedication. It is evidence the idea works but has no US standing.

killers.killer: Permission sits with utility QA and NUPIC, not the NRC. Utilities are extremely conservative and may refuse AI-generated technical evaluations, or audit them so heavily that the time savings disappear.
killers.answer: Don't sell 'AI'. Sell a dedicator with Appendix B standing whose tools are controlled, verified and validated software under NQA-1 Subpart 2.7. The model drafts. A deterministic traceability checker links every critical characteristic to an FSAR or design-basis clause, a failure mode and an acceptance method. A qualified human signs. Get standing by acquiring a NUPIC-accepted dedicator, so the next joint audit tests an existing program rather than a new one. Shape the norm too: fund an EPRI or NEI guidance update covering software-assisted technical evaluations, much as EPRI 3002002982 updated NP-5652. Then publish blind A/B results: the same items dedicated manually and by machine, with QA findings compared.

killers.killer: The real bottleneck is physical (receipt, testing, source verification, EQ ageing), not paperwork. Faster technical evaluations alone do not get 3-9 months down to days.
killers.answer: Order the work so the wedge avoids the physics clock. Start with mild-environment, non-EQ commodity items, where acceptance means Method 1 testing (PMI, hardness, dimensional, functional) that a robotic cell can finish in hours. Pre-dedicated shelf stock, placed against outage calendars, turns lead time into an inventory problem. EQ items come later: owned parallel ageing capacity, early stopping driven by condition monitoring (indenter modulus, OIT), and above all similarity libraries, so most replacements cite an already-qualified analogue under IEEE 323/344 and IEC/IEEE 60780-323 similarity provisions instead of re-ageing. Arrhenius-time ageing physics does not move. You get around it by owning more chambers and by needing fewer runs.

killers.killer: Data access: FSARs, design-basis documents, EQ files and OEM drawings belong to utilities or OEMs and are restricted (proprietary, some SUNSI/ECI). Without them the engine has nothing to reason over.
killers.answer: Make data access part of the contract. An outage retainer gives on-prem or enclave access to the utility's EQ master list, design basis, work orders and past dedication packages. Public FSAR/UFSAR text, NRC ADAMS, Part 21 reports and the EPRI guidance seed general knowledge. The cross-utility library is built from Dedicate's own outputs (critical characteristics, test results, equivalency evaluations), which Dedicate owns as the dedicator. No utility's design data is pooled. Reverse engineering in the robotic cell (CT, PMI) produces first-party characterisation data that does not depend on OEM drawings.

killers.killer: Part 21 liability and reputational tail: one escaped counterfeit or mis-dedicated part found in a safety system could end the company.
killers.answer: The machine helps the safety case more than it hurts it. It applies critical characteristics consistently, captures evidence and signs it at the point of capture, catches counterfeit/fraudulent/suspect items (CFSI) through PMI on every item rather than sampling, and can query the whole fleet at once when a Part 21 notice lands. Start with the lowest-consequence Class 1E commodities. Build an insurance tower (nuclear liability through ANI/NEIL plus professional liability), with pricing tied to a published escape rate. Contractually cap per-item liability at industry norms. Report every outcome openly to build a track record that underwriters can price.

killers.killer: Incumbents (Mirion/Paragon, Westinghouse, Curtiss-Wright) add AI and win on relationships and NUPIC history. Nuclearn or Everstar layers software on top of them.
killers.answer: Incumbents bill engineering hours, so cutting hours tenfold eats their revenue. They will adopt slowly, and Dedicate can price per item or per outage day saved. Software-only players hold no signature, so partner with Nuclearn or Everstar as the front end and stay the signing entity that owns the cross-utility library. A credible exit is also a moat: being acquired by Mirion or Curtiss-Wright is a good outcome.

killers.killer: Market size: dedication is a services line ($1.5-2.5B), and services multiples could cap it below venture scale.
killers.answer: Venture scale comes from (a) owning scarce EQ and seismic throughput, which is a capacity monopoly, (b) the SMR and advanced-reactor build-out, where every developer needs a qualified commercial-grade supply chain and Dedicate becomes their outsourced qualification department, and (c) extending the same permission engine to DOE/naval, hydro and gas Class-1E-like users, then Korea and CANDU fleets. Gross margin rises as library reuse lifts the share of items citing an existing analogue.

killers.killer: NUPIC timing: the audit cycle is roughly 33 months, and building a program from scratch takes 12-24 months, so it doesn't fit a YC timeline.
killers.answer: Buy, don't build: acquire or JV with a small NUPIC-accepted dedicator, keep its program, and introduce tools through controlled procedure revisions. Before acquiring, run as an engineering contractor that drafts technical evaluations under the client's or partner dedicator's Appendix B program. That earns revenue within months while standing transfers.

attacks.surviving_version:
The version that lives is a software-first dedicating entity, in three stages. The verification step that nobody does well is a machine-checkable, auditable traceability chain from design basis to safety function to failure mode to critical characteristic to acceptance method to signed evidence. That chain is the actual product and the main AI play.

Stage 0 (months 0-6): act as an engineering contractor under a partner dedicator's or utility's Appendix B program. Draft technical evaluations, equivalency evaluations and 50.59 screens for one restart or life-extension utility's backlog of mild-environment obsolete commodity items, using a deterministic checker that QA can audit. KPI: engineering hours per technical evaluation and QA findings, in blind A/B against manual work.

Stage 1: acquire a small NUPIC-accepted dedicator to own the signature and Part 21 obligation. Add a robotic Method 1 acceptance cell (XRF/LIBS PMI, hardness, CT, functional) with evidence signed at capture, plus shelf stock pre-dedicated against outage calendars. Offer the 72-hour emergent-outage guarantee priced against roughly $1-2M per outage day.

Stage 2: become the outsourced qualification department for SMR and advanced-reactor developers, and build owned parallel EQ and seismic capacity plus similarity libraries, so that most EQ replacements cite a qualified analogue.

Rule and norm change to pursue: an EPRI/NEI guidance revision recognising software-assisted technical evaluations under NQA-1 Subpart 2.7, and NRC vendor-inspection acceptance of remote or asynchronous source verification. Everstar and Nuclearn are partners or front ends, not signers. Mirion and Curtiss-Wright are the exit. Evidence limits: two web fetches only. Everstar's site claims qualification 'at scale' but shows no CGD or customers, and Nuclearn's site shows no CGD feature. The search budget ran out, so further competitor validation is still to do.
attacks.first_test: In 6 weeks, get 25-50 already-closed CGD packages (technical evaluations plus acceptance test plans) for mild-environment Class 1E commodity items from one restart or life-extension utility (Palisades, Crane, or a Constellation or TVA site), or from a small dedicator. Have the engine regenerate each technical evaluation and test plan from the FSAR, design basis and procurement specs alone. Then have the utility's procurement-engineering supervisor and a former NUPIC lead auditor score the machine outputs blind against the originals, on completeness of critical characteristics, traceability and findings. Pass means at least 90% parity or better, zero missed safety-related critical characteristics, under 20% of the manual engineering hours, and a signed letter of intent for a paid backlog pilot under a partner dedicator's Appendix B program.

finalist.name: Twin Silicon: a behavioural-equivalence foundry for obsolete defence electronics
merged_from: Twin Silicon (a behavioural-equivalence re-creation house for obsolete defence electronics)
Behavioural Equivalence Foundry for Legacy Electronics
finalist.description: WHAT IT DOES: Turns obsolete chips and circuit cards into certified drop-in replacements with measured behavioural coverage, and holds the SMD/QML listings, SARs and platform ECP approvals. Golden parts (often only 1-3 units) go through active-learning conformance testing on a robotic ATE farm across voltage, temperature, timing and corner states, which yields an executable behavioural model with auditable state and timing coverage. Formal equivalence then runs from the extracted model to new RTL, with AI-assisted netlist and firmware lifting from CT, delayering and binaries (V-SPELLS-style). Replacements are built on a family of pre-qualified emulation substrates (FPGA, structured-ASIC or chiplet carriers in each legacy package outline). Each substrate is qualified once for radiation, temperature and life, so burn-in, roughly 1,000 h of HTOL and ELDRS are paid per substrate rather than per part, and system re-qualification drops from Class I to Class II. Massively parallel burn-in and HTOL racks and owned Co-60 low-dose-rate cells absorb the clocks that remain. WHAT MUST BE BUILT: coverage-guided black-box exploration with metrics a reviewer can audit; checking from measured silicon to new design (an extension of Cadence/Synopsys equivalence); methods that are non-destructive first to protect golden samples; hundreds of DUT sockets per rack; a certificate format accepted by program offices; US-only ITAR facilities and DMEA trusted accreditation. ACCEPTANCE: DLA Land and Maritime grants an 'approve once, use everywhere' SMD-level designation citing the substrate (SRI GEM shows DLA already accepts emulated parts); program offices classify swaps as Class II under MIL-PRF-38535 and DO-254 similarity and test-deletion provisions. WHAT IT OWNS: equivalence certificates and approved-source listings per part, the qualified substrate library, and the largest library of measured legacy-part behaviour, with each part making the next cheaper. WHO PAYS: DLA (GEM/AME-type contracts), depots (WR-ALC REARM, OC-ALC REACT, Tobyhanna, FRCs), primes' sustainment programmes (a single $46.7M F-16 sole-source board buy drew zero RFI responses), space programmes (radiation qualification by similarity), nuclear I&C and grid-protection relay owners, and commercial avionics MROs. WEDGE: obsolete 5V TTL/CMOS logic, memory, interface and simple ASICs on C-130/KC-135/F-16 cards already flagged by REARM and REACT. Under a depot CRADA, deliver 20 behavioural-equivalence packages in 6 months against GEM's 48-week baseline on one ceramic-DIP/LCC substrate family, and secure a DLA SMD that cites the substrate. MARKET: DoD DMSMS and microelectronics sustainment runs to $1B+/yr (SRI GEM $73.7M contract, DMEA multi-billion IDIQ ceiling, Rochester about $275-500M revenue unverified), expanding to nuclear I&C, rail signalling and avionics. COMPETITORS: SRI GEM/AME (48 weeks per part), Rochester (licensed continuation, about 18 months for SRP), DMEA, Lansdale, Innovasic/ADI, Micross, Teledyne e2v, Tekmos, KaiSemi, Global Circuit Innovations ($7.2M), Chip Scan, Mobilio (schematic checks only), radiation labs (RTS, VPT, Alter, TRAD), board-test makers (Seica, Huntron, Diagnosys). AI verification start-ups (ChipAgents, Axiomise) target new designs only.
finalist.why: The economics are already proven (SRI and Rochester), so demand risk is low. The bottleneck is throughput (48 weeks to 18 months per part), because each part and platform is qualified from scratch, and AI-driven coverage exploration plus formal methods plus qualify-once substrates attack exactly that. Physics clocks (life tests, ELDRS) are paid once per substrate rather than per part, which is the 'change the constraint' move. The founder's defence and security-tech focus fits directly, and the overlap with hardware assurance (counterfeit and trust) widens the market. ITAR, trusted-foundry status, the substrate library and the certificate corpus give defensibility.

competitors_found.name: SRI International GEM / AME (DLA Land and Maritime)
competitors_found.overlap: Most direct incumbent. Emulates obsolete microcircuits using a gate-array/standard-cell library in the original package and footprint, and DLA accepts and stocks the parts. That acceptance is the precedent Twin Silicon needs. It is slow (about 48 weeks per part), artisanal, uses no active-learning coverage metric, and has no substrate-level 'approve once' designation. Strong customer lock-in through a long-running DLA contract.

competitors_found.name: Rochester Electronics
competitors_found.overlap: Licensed continuation: OEM die banks, wafer and IP transfer, and re-fabbed parts sold under original part numbers. Its moat is OEM data rights rather than verification. It competes for the same DLA and prime sustainment dollars, but only where an OEM licence exists. Orphaned parts with no licensor are outside its reach.

competitors_found.name: Global Circuit Innovations (GCI)
competitors_found.overlap: Form-fit-function drop-in replacements and die extraction/repackaging for DoD (Black Hawk, Maverick test box, USAF avionics). AS9100D. Small company with the same customer set and no visible formal-equivalence or coverage methodology.

competitors_found.name: Innovasic (now Analog Devices)
competitors_found.overlap: Historically made form-fit-function re-creations of obsolete microprocessors and peripherals (80C186, 8051 family, etc.) using in-house verification and extensive ATE comparison. This is the closest earlier version of 'behavioural equivalence' as a product line. Now a niche inside ADI.

competitors_found.name: Lansdale Semiconductor
competitors_found.overlap: Licensed continuation manufacturing of obsolete Intel, Motorola and AMD parts, a smaller Rochester-type model.

competitors_found.name: Tekmos
competitors_found.overlap: Re-designs obsolete microcontrollers and logic as pin-compatible replacements and converts FPGAs to ASICs. Direct overlap with the 5V logic, MCU and simple-ASIC wedge.

competitors_found.name: KaiSemi
competitors_found.overlap: Converts obsolete FPGAs and ASICs to new ASIC or FPGA in compatible packages for aerospace and defence. Direct overlap on the substrate idea, without a certification or listing play.

competitors_found.name: DMEA (Defense Microelectronics Activity) and ATSP IDIQ primes
competitors_found.overlap: Government emulation and re-design capability with a trusted foundry and multi-billion-dollar IDIQ ceilings. It is a customer, a channel and a competitor at once. DMEA Trusted accreditation is a gate Twin Silicon must pass.

competitors_found.name: Micross, Teledyne e2v, VPT, Alter, TRAD, Radiation Test Solutions
competitors_found.overlap: Hi-rel packaging, die processing, screening and radiation qualification. They own the physical-clock capacity (burn-in, HTOL, Co-60/ELDRS) that Twin Silicon proposes to build in-house. They could be partners or acquirers.

competitors_found.name: TechInsights, Battelle, Sandia, Chip Scan
competitors_found.overlap: Commercial and government delayering, imaging and netlist extraction, plus hardware assurance and Trojan detection. They have the 'measured silicon to netlist' capability but do not turn it into certified replacements.

competitors_found.name: IARPA RAVEN; DARPA IRIS, TRUST and V-SPELLS
competitors_found.overlap: Government R&D on rapid IC imaging and layout extraction (RAVEN), non-destructive netlist and function recovery of unknown ICs (IRIS), and lifting legacy software into maintainable models (V-SPELLS). The underlying research exists, but no team has turned it into products or certifications.

competitors_found.name: Open-source die RE community (Visual6502, siliconpr0n/John McMaster, MAME decap, Ken Shirriff)
competitors_found.overlap: Transistor-accurate netlists recovered from die photos of legacy chips. This shows that non-destructive-to-netlist lifting of 5V-era parts is tractable. It is a free dataset and benchmark source, and a talent pool.

competitors_found.name: AI chip-verification start-ups (ChipAgents, Axiomise, Cognichip, Bronco, Normal Computing) and Cadence Conformal / Synopsys Formality
competitors_found.overlap: They build formal and AI-assisted verification for new RTL. None works from measured silicon or legacy parts or holds a certification. They could add a 'silicon-to-RTL' mode, but the market is too small for them to care.

competitors_found.name: Board-level obsolescence and test (Seica, Huntron, Diagnosys, Mobilio, primes' DMSMS shops)
competitors_found.overlap: Card-level test and schematic checks used in depot workflows. They are adjacent, not equivalent.

killers.killer: Black-box behavioural equivalence cannot prove the absence of unobserved state. Hidden modes, test modes, undocumented opcodes and analog edge behaviour mean 'coverage' is never 'equivalence', and a program office may reject a certificate built on it.
killers.answer: Combine three evidence streams so the certificate is not black-box. (1) Non-destructive CT and IR imaging, plus delayering of a sacrificial or lower-grade lot-mate, to recover the netlist. Formal equivalence then runs netlist-to-RTL, which Conformal and Formality can already do. (2) Active-learning ATE across PVT and timing corners, used to validate the extracted netlist against the golden part. (3) Mutation-score metrics a reviewer can audit (seeded divergences the test campaign must catch). For 5V TTL/CMOS, memory and simple ASICs the gate counts are small enough that full netlist recovery is realistic, as Visual6502 shows. Hard analog, mixed-signal and high-speed parts stay out of scope.

killers.killer: Regulator and program-office acceptance. 'Approve once, use everywhere' at substrate level does not exist in MIL-PRF-38535 or DLA practice today. Each SMD, SAR or ECP is approved part by part and platform by platform, and Class I versus Class II calls belong to each program office's engineering authority.
killers.answer: There is precedent: DLA already stocks GEM emulations under SMDs, and QML certification already qualifies a manufacturer's process or technology flow once, with parts listed under it. Pitch the substrate as a QML technology flow (a QML-style baseline with a 'qualification family' and similarity rules), not as a new regime. Get one DLA Land and Maritime VA letter and one depot (WR-ALC REARM) Class II determination as proof points. Expect 18-36 months to standardise. Meanwhile, revenue comes part by part through the depots, as SRI's does.

killers.killer: Incumbent lock-in and procurement friction. SRI holds GEM and AME through long DLA contracts. DMEA has an in-house mandate. DoD sustainment buys move through IDIQs, CRADAs and sole-source justifications with 12-24 month cycles.
killers.answer: Enter as a subcontractor or tool vendor to SRI, DMEA or depots: sell the equivalence-certificate engine and ATE throughput to cut their 48 weeks. Run in parallel through SBIR/STRATFI (AFRL, OSD ManTech, DMSMS office) and depot CRADAs. The $46.7M F-16 board buy with zero RFI responses shows demand going unserved.

killers.killer: Small, fragmented unit volumes (tens to thousands of parts per number), so revenue per certificate may not cover qualification and listing costs; TAM is maybe low single-digit billions even with nuclear, rail and avionics.
killers.answer: The economics depend on cost per package falling as the substrate library and behaviour corpus grow. Price on avoided system redesign (often $10M+ per LRU redesign), not per chip. Expand to nuclear I&C (10 CFR 50.59, EPRI dedication of commercial-grade items), grid relays and space, where the same certificate format carries over.

killers.killer: Legal and IP: reproducing a proprietary OEM ASIC or microcontroller by reverse engineering can draw OEM IP claims (mask work rights, copyright on firmware), and ITAR, export control and trusted-source rules constrain where parts are made.
killers.answer: The Semiconductor Chip Protection Act explicitly allows reverse engineering for analysis and new designs, and many 1980s-90s mask works have already expired (10-year term). Government-purpose rights, or 28 USC 1498 for the government as buyer, cover much of the risk. Firmware lifting needs per-part legal review. Build US-only, ITAR-registered facilities and pursue DMEA Trusted accreditation (about 12-18 months) from day one.

killers.killer: Golden-sample scarcity and destruction risk: with 1-3 units, any destructive step can end the programme.
killers.answer: Use non-destructive methods first: CT, lock-in thermography, ATE characterisation. Source lot-mates from DLA stock, GIDEP, broker inventory and scrapped cards to use as sacrificial units. Rochester and DLA hold lot inventory that could be bought for teardown.

killers.killer: Physics clocks: radiation (ELDRS low-dose-rate testing takes months), HTOL (about 1,000 h) and burn-in cannot be compressed per test.
killers.answer: Qualifying substrate families amortises these clocks across many parts. Parallel racks and owned Co-60 cells remove queueing at outside labs. ELDRS mostly matters for bipolar linear parts, which are outside the digital wedge.

attacks.surviving_version: A white-box-assisted equivalence certificate house for obsolete digital microcircuits, rather than pure black-box behavioural cloning. It recovers the netlist non-destructively or from a sacrificial unit (CT, imaging, delayering; AI-assisted netlist extraction in the RAVEN/Visual6502 style). It proves formal equivalence from recovered netlist to new RTL using existing Conformal/Formality engines. It validates against golden parts with active-learning ATE across PVT and timing corners, and reports an auditable mutation-kill coverage score. The output is a standard evidence package: VHDL model, coverage report, equivalence proof, and test vectors on the original program's test equipment. The 'approve once' piece is framed as a QML-style qualified technology flow with similarity rules, not a new regime. Go-to-market starts as a throughput supplier and subcontractor to the existing acceptance pathways (SRI GEM/AME, DMEA, WR-ALC REARM, OC-ALC REACT) and does not attack them, so its certificates ride on accepted vehicles. Over time it becomes the default evidence standard for DMSMS microcircuit replacement and carries over to nuclear I&C commercial-grade dedication and space radiation-by-similarity. The verification-side AI play is the certificate engine (coverage-guided silicon exploration plus silicon-to-RTL equivalence plus an evidence format reviewers accept), which nobody currently sells. The moat is the measured-behaviour and netlist corpus plus the qualified substrate library. Scope is limited to digital parts below roughly 100k gates; analog, mixed-signal and high-speed parts stay out.
attacks.first_test: A blind-equivalence bake-off with a reviewer in the loop, run within 90 days. (1) Pick 5 obsolete 5V parts from REARM/REACT flags or the DLA DMSMS list, such as 82C54/82C55-class peripherals, a 54LS/54HC MSI part, a small SRAM and a simple ASIC or PAL. Include at least 2 whose original RTL or netlist is known to a referee but hidden from the team; Visual6502-recovered parts and opencores-equivalent parts work for this. (2) Have the referee seed 10-20 behavioural divergences (corner timing, undocumented modes) into an FPGA 'impostor' in the same package. (3) Run the active-learning ATE plus netlist recovery pipeline, then measure what fraction of divergences it catches, golden-unit hours used, and calendar time against GEM's 48 weeks. (4) Put the resulting evidence package in front of a DLA Land and Maritime engineer and a WR-ALC REARM engineering authority. The pass condition is a written statement that the package would support an SMD or a Class II determination, plus a CRADA or SBIR for 20 parts. If they say coverage evidence cannot replace their existing qualification test flow, pivot to selling the engine to SRI, DMEA and GCI as a tool.
attacks.competitors_found_note_ignored: Search budget was exhausted (shared turn limit), so only 2 successful WebFetches were possible: GCI's site, which confirmed form-fit-function drop-in replacements for DoD. The rest of the competitor map comes from prior knowledge as of mid-2026 and should be re-verified with follow-up searches.

competitors_found.name: SRI International GEM / AME (DLA programme)
competitors_found.overlap: Direct. This is DLA's standing emulation source and the reason DLA already accepts emulated drop-in parts. It covers the same part classes (digital logic, memory, simple ASICs). Its weaknesses are a weeks-to-a-year turnaround (48 weeks is the figure in the brief, not checked here) and a cell-library, gate-array style method with no behavioural-coverage certificate. Evidence pages could not be fetched (404).

competitors_found.name: DMEA (Defense Microelectronics Activity) and the ATSP IDIQ primes
competitors_found.overlap: Direct. The government's own in-house emulation and re-engineering foundry, plus a multi-billion-dollar contract vehicle. It holds the Trusted accreditation authority the company would need, so it is a channel and a competitor at once.

competitors_found.name: Rochester Electronics
competitors_found.overlap: Licensed continuation and re-creation from the original maker's die, masks and data. Wins whenever the original maker's IP still exists, because no equivalence argument is needed. The site returned no content when fetched.

competitors_found.name: Lansdale Semiconductor
competitors_found.overlap: Makes more than 3,000 classic ICs, from AMD, Fairchild, Intel, Motorola and others, 'exactly like they used to' in their original packages. Takes the easy 5V TTL/CMOS share of the wedge with no qualification question (confirmed from its site).

competitors_found.name: Innovasic (now ADI)
competitors_found.overlap: Fidelity re-creation of obsolete microcontrollers and peripherals, checked against original silicon. It is the closest existing behavioural-equivalence business (site unavailable when fetched).

competitors_found.name: Tekmos, KaiSemi, Micross, Teledyne e2v
competitors_found.overlap: Redesigns or remanufactures obsolete ICs as FFF replacements, and in Micross and e2v's case holds QML and space flows.

competitors_found.name: Global Circuit Innovations
competitors_found.overlap: Obsolescence fixes for legacy aircraft, hermetic re-packaging and circuit-card solutions such as the DSM-157 for Maverick. Its site does not claim DLA qualification or IC emulation.

competitors_found.name: Galois and others in DARPA V-SPELLS / binary-lifting research
competitors_found.overlap: The firmware and binary lifting part of the stack. Research teams, not a sustainment supplier.

competitors_found.name: Chip Scan, Battelle Barricade, Sandia and other hardware-assurance and RE labs
competitors_found.overlap: CT, delayering and netlist extraction services, which are the white-box half of the pipeline.

competitors_found.name: ChipAgents, Axiomise, Cadence JasperGold / Synopsys Formality
competitors_found.overlap: Formal and AI verification of RTL against RTL. Nobody offers equivalence from measured silicon to new RTL, which is the open gap.

killers.killer: Black-box behavioural learning cannot prove equivalence. Hidden states, test modes, power-up behaviour, metastability and analog parametrics such as drive strength, edge rates, input thresholds, ground bounce and ICC can stay unobserved, and old boards often depend on undocumented timing slack. One missed corner case on a flight-critical card is a field failure that ends the company's credibility.
killers.answer: Partly answered, and it depends on part class. For the wedge (SSI/MSI TTL/CMOS logic, small FSMs, memories, interface parts) the state spaces are small enough that L*-style automata learning plus exhaustive pattern and parametric sweeps gives near-complete coverage. For anything with possible hidden state, make the white-box path mandatory (CT or delayering, then netlist extraction, then formal equivalence against the black-box model as a cross-check), and spend golden parts only after non-destructive work. Add in-situ checks on the host card, by characterising the card's timing margins on the depot's board tester, so the certificate states equivalence within the board's actual operating envelope rather than claiming universal equivalence. Complex ASICs and mixed-signal parts stay out of scope until the method has a track record.

killers.killer: Program offices and the platform engineering authority, not DLA, decide whether a swap is Class I or Class II. Risk-averse authorities (for example the C-130 SPO or KC-135 engineering) may treat any FPGA or structured-ASIC substitute as a new design. That brings back full system re-qualification and erases the cost advantage.
killers.answer: Answers exist. Precedent: DLA already stocks GEM emulations under the original NSN or part number as form-fit-function (FFF) substitutes, a model the brief cites and that could not be re-verified here. The approach is to enter through the depots' own engineering authority, since REARM and REACT already flagged these parts, publish the certificate format jointly with DLA Land and Maritime and the depot, and ask for a written Class II determination on the first 5 parts before scaling. For DO-254 avionics, FPGA content becomes complex electronic hardware (DAL A-C), which pulls the other way. Stay military-first, where MIL-PRF-38535 QML technology flows apply.

killers.killer: Incumbent lock-in: SRI holds the GEM/AME vehicle and DMEA is the government's in-house emulator and Trusted accreditor. DLA can reach either without competition, and a startup offering faster delivery still has to get onto a contract vehicle.
killers.answer: Partly answered. Option 1: sell the verification layer (active-learning ATE and the measured-silicon-to-RTL equivalence certificate) to SRI, DMEA and the ATSP primes as a tool or subcontract. That opens revenue in months and builds the measured-behaviour library. Option 2: go direct to depots on CRADAs, SBIR Phase III or OTAs, using the publicly documented F-16 board buy that drew zero RFI responses as proof of unmet demand. Expect a channel conflict between those two options.

killers.killer: Unit economics. Obsolete-part demand is tiny, often tens to a few hundred units per NSN, so revenue is mostly NRE per package. Rochester's revenue comes mainly from stocked inventory and licensed continuation, not emulation. The pure emulation NRE pool may be only about $100-300M/yr, below venture scale.
killers.answer: Answered only if the library compounds. Price per package, in the $150-500k range typical of DMSMS resolutions, because the alternative is a board redesign or a sole-source buy costing $1-50M. Keep life-of-type buy and stocking revenue on every certified part, as Rochester does. Grow into adjacent buyers who have the same problem: board- and LRU-level equivalence, space radiation-by-similarity, nuclear I&C and grid relays. Venture scale depends on certificates becoming the standard evidence DLA requires of anyone, including SRI, which turns the business into infrastructure.

killers.killer: Physics clocks that cannot be amortised. Per-unit screening (burn-in of 160 h or more), periodic QCI Group C and D life testing, temperature cycling, and ELDRS for any linear bipolar parts still run on every lot. Space programmes may refuse radiation-by-similarity across substrates.
killers.answer: Yes. QML-38535 is a technology and line qualification, so qualifying the substrate once and adding new device types via SMD is how the system is meant to work. Per-unit burn-in runs in parallel racks, so its clock is roughly fixed and short. The wedge is digital CMOS on a modern substrate, which needs no ELDRS. Space radiation-by-similarity is a later expansion that needs separate acceptance.

killers.killer: 5V TTL/CMOS drop-in electrical fidelity on modern substrates (FPGAs and modern ASICs run at 1.8 V or less). That requires level translation, input threshold matching, output drive and slew emulation, power-sequencing tolerance and matching quiescent current, all inside a legacy ceramic DIP or LCC outline with matching thermal and hermetic behaviour.
killers.answer: Yes. SRI GEM and Innovasic already ship this way. The answer is a family of carrier substrates with programmable I/O cells tuned to the measured parametrics of the golden part. That is engineering work, not a scientific barrier.

killers.killer: Access to golden parts and data. There may be only 1-3 golden units, original documentation is missing, ITAR and export rules apply, and DMEA Trusted accreditation plus a US-only facility take 12-24 months. Destroying a golden part to delayer it can end the programme.
killers.answer: Yes. Depots and DLA supply golden parts and failed field units under CRADA. Field returns and scrap boards are often plentiful even when new stock is not. The order of work is CT first and delayering last. Apply for Trusted accreditation from day one, which DMEA grants to small firms.

killers.killer: Liability and sales cycle. A flight-safety failure traced to a substitute part brings litigation, debarment risk and reputational damage. DoD procurement takes 18-36 months, longer than a YC runway.
killers.answer: Partly answered. When the government accepts the part under its own engineering authority, liability largely moves to that approval (the government contractor defense), so liability is manageable. The sales cycle is the real constraint. A CRADA plus SBIR, AFWERX or OTA path can fund the first 20 packages in 6-12 months. Selling the verification layer to SRI, DMEA and the primes earns revenue sooner than holding SMDs directly.

attacks.surviving_version: Start on the verification side, not as a foundry. Build the missing layer that nobody does: active-learning conformance testing on robotic ATE, plus formal checking from measured silicon to new RTL. Each run produces a behavioural-equivalence certificate with auditable state, timing and parametric coverage, cross-checked against a netlist extracted non-destructively from CT. Phase 1, months 0-9: sell certificates and the measured-behaviour library to whoever already makes replacements (SRI GEM, DMEA, the ATSP primes, Rochester, Tekmos, Micross) and to depot engineering authorities as the evidence that backs a Class II determination. Co-author the certificate format with DLA Land and Maritime so it becomes the required evidence for any emulated SMD part. Phase 2: once the certificate is accepted, build parts directly on one qualified ceramic-DIP/LCC CMOS substrate family under QML technology qualification, for the simple digital parts REARM and REACT have flagged. Phase 3: expand to board-level and LRU equivalence (zero-response sole-source buys like the F-16 board), space radiation-by-similarity, nuclear I&C and grid relays. The moat is the certificate standard plus the measured-behaviour library, not the substrate.
attacks.first_test: Get 5-10 parts flagged by REARM or REACT that already have a GEM emulation or a Rochester or Lansdale replacement, so the right answer is known, plus golden originals from a depot under a CRADA or a no-cost loan. In 6-8 weeks, run the active-learning ATE and the formal pipeline on both the original and the existing replacement. Pass criteria: (a) produce a coverage-backed equivalence certificate per part in under 2 weeks each; (b) find at least one real behavioural or parametric discrepancy the incumbent's validation missed, or prove there is none, with an auditable coverage number. Then take the evidence packages to DLA Land and Maritime's microcircuit engineering group and one depot's engineering authority. Ask two questions: would this certificate support an SMD listing, and would it support a written Class II determination? A yes, or a documented list of what is missing, decides whether the company exists. Note: evidence gathering for this review was limited. The web-search budget was exhausted and the SRI, DLA, Rochester and Innovasic pages could not be fetched. Only the Lansdale and GCI sites were confirmed, so GEM's turnaround and its DLA acceptance practice should be re-verified before the YC application.

competitors_found.name: SRI International, Microcircuit Emulation Center (GEM/AME for DLA)
competitors_found.overlap: Direct incumbent. It holds DLA's long-running emulation contract and its emulated parts are already issued under DLA drawings, so the precedent exists. Its weak point is about 48 weeks per part, done by hand-crafted re-design, with no auditable behavioural-coverage metric. SRI's site search confirmed only that the Center and its staff exist; GEM contract details are from prior research.

competitors_found.name: Rochester Electronics
competitors_found.overlap: Licensed continuation and re-creation of OEM die using OEM data and masks, DLA-authorized. Covers the share of parts where the OEM transferred its IP. It does not cover orphaned parts, and its Semiconductor Replication Program (SRP) takes about 18 months. Fetch of rocelec.com returned an empty page.

competitors_found.name: Tekmos / Lansdale / Innovasic (ADI) MILES / KaiSemi / Teledyne e2v / Micross
competitors_found.overlap: Form-fit-function re-designs of obsolete MCUs, peripherals and logic, one at a time with conventional test benches. Their output is a part, not an equivalence certificate. They could become customers of a coverage engine or be displaced by one.

competitors_found.name: Global Circuit Innovations
competitors_found.overlap: Extracts and repackages die (die harvest) to restore obsolete parts. It keeps the original silicon, so it competes only where viable die exist. Its domain did not resolve when fetched.

competitors_found.name: DMEA (ATSP/foundry) and DMEA-accredited trusted suppliers
competitors_found.overlap: Government-owned capability for re-creating obsolete microelectronics, plus the trust accreditation gate. It is both a competitor and the required accreditor or partner.

competitors_found.name: Board-level reverse engineering and test (Seica, Huntron, Diagnosys, Mobilio, depot REARM/REACT cells)
competitors_found.overlap: Card-level schematic recovery and fault test only, with no chip-level behavioural equivalence. They are natural channel partners and the source of the target lists.

competitors_found.name: AI and formal verification start-ups (ChipAgents, Axiomise, Cycuity) and EDA equivalence tools (Cadence Conformal, Synopsys Formality)
competitors_found.overlap: They prove RTL-to-netlist equivalence for new designs. None goes from measured silicon to a new design, the gap Twin Silicon would fill.

competitors_found.name: DARPA V-SPELLS and related binary-lifting research
competitors_found.overlap: Research on lifting legacy software and firmware. It is a source of methods, not a competitor. The DARPA program page returned 404 when fetched.

killers.killer: Black-box testing of 1-3 golden parts cannot prove equivalence. Hidden states, undocumented modes, test modes, metastability, and analog I/O behaviour (TTL drive, edge rates, ground bounce, power-up states) can all escape active learning. Reviewers will treat a certificate of coverage as different from proof of equivalence.
killers.answer: Change the claim from global equivalence to equivalence within the envelope the part is actually used in, and prove that envelope. (1) Instrument the host cards in situ: interposer loggers on depot test stands and the platform's own tests record every stimulus the part actually sees, which defines the envelope to cover. (2) Fuse black-box learning with a white-box netlist. On 5V-era geometries (1-3um), non-destructive X-ray ptychography (IARPA RAVEN-type) or one sacrificial delayered sample gives a full transistor netlist that AI converts to gates. Formal equivalence then runs netlist to new RTL, and the measured silicon only cross-validates the extracted netlist. (3) Characterize the electrical I/O and replay it on a substrate with programmable drive strength and slew. (4) Calibrate the method blind on parts with known ground truth (6502/Z80 transistor netlists, seeded faults) and publish the escape rate, so 'coverage' becomes a measured, auditable number.

killers.killer: Regulators and program offices will not accept 'approve once, use everywhere'. Each platform's engineering authority may classify an FPGA or emulated swap as Class I or a major change, and an FPGA brings DO-254 DAL A scrutiny and, in nuclear, digital common-cause-failure concerns.
killers.answer: Use the precedent that already exists. MIL-PRF-38535 QML certifies a manufacturing and technology flow, not each part. Qualify the emulation flow plus the substrate as a QML-style technology, and issue each part as a DLA drawing under it, which is how GEM parts already exist. Avoid the word 'programmable': make the substrate a metal-programmable sea-of-gates base wafer (one or two masks at a trusted foundry such as SkyWater), so each part is a fixed-function ASIC, not an FPGA. That keeps DO-254 and nuclear digital reviews closer to 'COTS part replacement'. Start with an ALC depot whose engineering authority signs Class II for its own cards, and get a written acceptance criterion before building. Data from 20 packages becomes the case for DLA to adopt it.

killers.killer: Incumbency and contract lock: SRI holds the DLA emulation vehicle, DMEA holds the trust gate, and a start-up cannot bid on most of this budget.
killers.answer: Enter through vehicles that bypass the GEM contract. Options: SBIR/STTR with DMEA, AFRL or AFLCMC, leading to Phase III sole source; a depot CRADA; an OTA via DIU or ALC innovation cells (REARM/REACT); and direct buys by primes' sustainment groups (zero-response sole-source RFIs like the $46.7M F-16 board show unserved demand). Alternatively, sell the verification engine and certificate format to SRI, Rochester and Tekmos as a speed-up tool first, then integrate forward. Partner with or license from DMEA rather than racing it.

killers.killer: Market size and lumpiness. Thousands of part numbers but tiny volumes (tens to hundreds of units each), budget-driven buying and long cycles. This caps a pure parts foundry at a few hundred million dollars.
killers.answer: Charge for the evidence, not the units: NRE per certificate ($150k-$1M) plus long-term supply and lifetime-buy guarantees, and price against the cost of not replacing (platform downtime, board redesigns that cost $5-50M). The behavioural library compounds: each new part reuses cells, so marginal cost falls toward compute plus tester time. Expand to sectors with the same problem and a regulator: nuclear I&C (NRC and EPRI equivalency-evaluation regime), rail signalling (EN 50129), grid protection relays, commercial avionics MRO (PMA/DER), industrial control, and space.

killers.killer: Radiation and life qualification by similarity will not carry over. A modern CMOS substrate replacing bipolar or older CMOS changes total-dose, ELDRS and single-event behaviour, so space and strategic programs will demand part-specific testing.
killers.answer: Qualify the substrate per process lot (TID, SEE, ELDRS, HTOL) in the company's own Co-60 low-dose-rate cells and in partner heavy-ion time. Each part then inherits a lot-level radiation report plus a short per-part confirmation test. Start in non-space depot avionics, where radiation does not gate approval, and add space after the lot data builds up.

killers.killer: Lifting firmware and netlists may infringe IP: mask-work rights, copyright in firmware or microcode, and ITAR or export-controlled technical data.
killers.answer: The Semiconductor Chip Protection Act explicitly allows reverse engineering to analyze and build an original design, and mask-work protection lasts 10 years, so it has long expired on these parts. Firmware gets government-purpose rights or depot licence under DFARS, or is re-implemented clean-room from the behavioural spec, or the OEM is defunct. Run the work in a US-only ITAR facility and hold DMEA trusted accreditation (12-18 months; start on day 1 or partner with an accredited supplier).

killers.killer: Golden parts are scarce. Destructive methods can consume the only reference sample.
killers.answer: Work non-destructive first (ATE learning, X-ray ptychography, IR emission). Sweep GIDEP, DLA disposition, depot scrap and broker stock for extra units, using authenticated suspect-counterfeit lots as sacrificial samples. Once one die is extracted, the netlist removes any further dependence on scarce units.

attacks.surviving_version: Start on the verification side and grow into a foundry, not the reverse. Phase 1 product: a 'Silicon-to-Spec Equivalence Engine'. It fuses three inputs: (a) in-situ capture of each part's real use envelope on host cards and depot test stands; (b) active-learning conformance testing on a robotic ATE farm across voltage, temperature and timing; (c) AI-reconstructed netlists from non-destructive X-ray or one sacrificial die. It outputs an executable model and a formal-equivalence certificate with an escape rate calibrated blind on parts with known ground truth. The certificate format would be co-written with one ALC depot engineering authority (WR-ALC or OC-ALC) as the evidence for a Class II classification. It is sold first as a speed-up service to depots and to existing re-creators (Tekmos, Rochester, SRI and others), cutting about 48 weeks to a few. Phase 2: own the replacement. A metal-programmable trusted sea-of-gates substrate in DIP, LCC and flatpack carriers is qualified once as a QML-style technology flow (radiation, HTOL, ELDRS per lot in owned cells), and each part is issued as a DLA drawing under it. What it owns: the certificate standard, the calibrated escape-rate data, the substrate qualification, and the largest library of measured legacy-part behaviour. Then expand the same engine into nuclear I&C equivalency, rail signalling, grid relays, PMA/DER avionics and space. The defensible asset is the regulator-accepted verification standard plus the library. The fab work is commoditized execution.
attacks.first_test: Blind calibration plus a depot letter, in 8-10 weeks. (1) Pick 5 legacy parts with public transistor-level ground truth (MOS 6502 and Z80 from visual6502-style netlists, an 8255, two 74-series/PAL parts), including ones with known undocumented behaviour, such as 6502 illegal opcodes. Have a third party seed hidden behaviours into FPGA stand-ins. (2) Run the active-learning ATE loop black-box and report how many hidden behaviours are found against test hours, giving a measured escape rate. (3) Take that result to a WR-ALC REARM or OC-ALC REACT engineer and ask for a written statement of what coverage evidence would let them classify a drop-in as Class II for one named obsolete part on a C-130 or KC-135 card. Kill criterion: escape rate above 0 on seeded behaviours within the part's use envelope after bounded test time, or no engineering authority willing to define acceptance criteria. Caveat: evidence gathering this session was thin. The web-search budget was exhausted and fetches of the SRI GEM page, DLA, DARPA V-SPELLS, GCI, Rochester and Innovasic failed. Competitor details (GEM at about 48 weeks, Rochester SRP at about 18 months, revenue figures) rest on prior research and need checking.
